# TriTrack — Security Model

**Status:** Design complete for Phase 10 (task 10.0), 2026-08-01.
No server code has been written. This document precedes it deliberately.

**Standing:** this is the authority for security decisions in Phase 10 and
Phase 11. Where it disagrees with `DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md`, this document wins and
the plan gets corrected (per task 10.0's acceptance criteria). Where a later
task wants to do something this document forbids, that is a conversation to
have explicitly, not a judgment call to make in a pull request.

**How to use it.** Every decision in section 4 records its *reasoning*, and each
one ends with a line naming what would violate it. That line is the point. A
future task will propose something reasonable-sounding — stateless JWTs, a
faster hash, a config default, a helpful log line — and the reasoning is what
tells you whether the proposal is a refinement or a regression. If you are about
to change something here, read why it is the way it is first.

## Where the derivation stops *(task 11.123, 2026-09-06)*

**One derived section in a hand-kept document is more dangerous than none**,
because it teaches a reader to trust the rest. This document is 300-odd
headings of argument and one of them is now checked by a test, so it has to say
which.

**Every section of this document is hand-kept — no test reads its words —
except the ones listed here.** That is the statement, and it is deliberately
made once rather than repeated under 300 headings, where it would be 600 lines
of noise that nobody reads and everybody stops updating. **The two lists are
kept honest against each other by a check**:
`test/documentation/permissions_matrix_membership_test.dart` requires that the
sections named below are exactly the sections carrying a `***Derived***` marker
in the body, so neither list can grow or shrink alone.

| Section | Derived by | What is derived, and what is not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| §4.21.2 Cross-project isolation — a verdict per endpoint | `test/documentation/permissions_matrix_membership_test.dart` | **That a row exists for every route the server declares, and that every route the table cites is one the server declares** — both directions, from every file under `server/lib/` that mounts a route. And, since task 11.302, **that the row for `POST /projects/<projectId>/deletion` names every action the shared `ProjectDeletionAction` enum declares** — a new action adds no route, so the route-level check cannot see one. **Otherwise the verdict text is prose and no test reads it**: the check sees that an action is named, not that what the row says about it is true. |
| §4.28 What a row of `GET /projects/mine` may carry | `test/documentation/project_directory_field_set_test.dart` | That the field table here and the fields the route actually returns are the same set. |
| §4.28.1 The second route: what a row of `GET /projects/deleted/mine` may carry | `test/documentation/project_directory_field_set_test.dart` | The same check on the second table, and that the line above each of the two tables names the route it belongs to, so they cannot be swapped without the test noticing. |
| Appendix — decision index (no section number, so the pairing check below skips it) | `test/documentation/security_model_decision_index_test.dart` | **The first column only.** That every top-level `### 4.N` decision has a row and every row names a heading that exists. **The Decision, Implemented by, Gate and verdict columns are hand-kept prose and no test reads them** — a row can point at the right section and be years out of date. |

**Hand-kept does not mean unenforced.** Most of section 4's decisions are
enforced by named tests and by gate instruments; what is hand-kept is *this
document's account of them*. Those tests do not open this file, so the code and
the sentence describing it can drift apart, and the only thing that catches it
is a person re-reading. **That is exactly what happened to §4.21.2**, which sat
wrong in both directions at once for a week.

---


## 0. Why this app is not a generic CRUD app

TriTrack stores precise, timestamped locations of collared animals, at full
float64 precision, in four tables (`Observations`, `Non_Detections`,
`Estimated_Positions`, `Actual_Tag_Locations`), plus a project bounding box on
`Projects`. For endangered or commercially trafficked species, that dataset is
directly and immediately useful to poachers. Targeting researchers' telemetry
data is a documented pattern in conservation technology, not a hypothetical.

The consequence is that this system has a **physical-world failure mode**. A
leaked project database is not an embarrassment or a compliance event; it is
potentially a dead animal. Nothing about the data is legally regulated — there
is no HIPAA, no FERPA, no GDPR obligation forcing the issue — and that is
exactly why the bar has to be set deliberately here rather than inherited from a
regulator.

**The bar: treat this data as you would medical records.** That is the
calibration to use whenever a decision in this document seems stricter than a
project of this size would normally warrant.

---

## 1. Assets, ranked

Ranked, because ranking is what makes tradeoffs decidable. When two controls
conflict, the one protecting the higher-ranked asset wins.

### 1. Precise animal locations

**What:** latitude/longitude at full float64 precision, bearings and bearing
uncertainty, signal strength, and the timestamps that turn a location into a
pattern of movement. Held in `Observations`, `Non_Detections`,
`Estimated_Positions` (including its error ellipse), `Actual_Tag_Locations`, and
in aggregate as `Projects.bbox_*`. Also present in every exported backup zip,
every CSV export, and every `TT1:` share payload.

**Cost of loss:** physical harm to animals, potentially to researchers in
enforcement contexts. A single `Actual_Tag_Locations` row for a nest or den site
is more damaging than a hundred bearings, because it needs no interpretation.

**Ranked first because this is the only asset whose compromise cannot be
undone.** A token can be rotated. An account can be recovered. A corrupted row
can be corrected from a backup. A disclosed nest location stays disclosed
forever, and no subsequent action by anyone recovers it.

### 2. Integrity and availability of the field record

**What:** that a bearing in the database is the bearing that was recorded in the
field, by the person it says recorded it, at the time it says. And that it is
still there next year.

**Cost of loss:** a falsified or silently corrupted bearing propagates through
`observationIdsUsed` into a saved position estimate, and from there into a
publication, a permit application, or an enforcement action. Nobody knows to go
looking. On the availability side: a lost season of observations is
unrecoverable in a way that lost documents are not — you cannot re-observe last
Tuesday.

**Ranked second, above account access, because integrity failures are silent.**
A confidentiality breach eventually surfaces. A wrong number does not.

### 3. Account access

**What:** magic-link tokens, session tokens, and the server-side rows behind
them.

**Cost of loss:** whatever assets 1 and 2 are worth, because account access is
the key to both.

**Deliberately ranked below the assets it protects.** This matters for real
decisions. Long-lived sessions are a convenience for field devices; if
convenience of account access ever competes with protection of locations,
locations win. See §4.3, where a long session lifetime is accepted *only*
because immediate revocation is built alongside it.

### 4. Researcher identity and contact information

**What:** `Users.first_name`, `last_name`, `email`, plus `User_Emails` — which is
a permanent, never-pruned historical log of every address a user has ever used.
Also, implicitly, the observer's own whereabouts and working hours: an
observation carries `timestamp_local` and `timezone_offset` alongside the
position, so the dataset describes where the *researcher* was as precisely as it
describes the animal.

**Cost of loss:** targeted phishing and social engineering of team members,
which is the realistic first move against this system (§2.1). In enforcement
contexts, personal risk to the researcher.

**Ranked fourth** because the volume is small and academic contact information
is often already public — not because the harm is small. The social-engineering
path runs through this asset, so it is not ignorable.

### 5. Server availability

**Ranked last, deliberately.** TriTrack is offline-first by design and Phase 10
does not change that: the app is fully functional with no server configured, and
with a configured server permanently unreachable. A server outage costs delay,
nothing else.

**This ranking is load-bearing: it is why we always fail closed.** Refusing a
request that should have succeeded costs a retry. Serving a request that should
have been refused costs asset 1. Any time a control's failure mode is ambiguous,
resolve it toward refusal.

---

## 2. Threat actors

For each: what they can realistically do, what they would actually try *here*,
and what stops them.

### 2.1 Poachers and wildlife traffickers

**Capability:** motivated, funded well enough to matter, specifically interested
in this exact data class. Not necessarily technical.

**What they would actually do.** Not write an exploit. The efficient path to a
project's locations is a person: a graduate student who will forward a
spreadsheet to someone claiming to be a collaborator, a field tech who will
click a link that looks like a TriTrack sign-in email, an inherited laptop, a
public conference poster with a map on it. Assume social engineering comes
first, and assume the attacker knows who is on the project because the grant is
public.

**Controls that actually help:**

- Magic-link authentication means there is **no password to phish**. This is the
  single largest structural win in the auth design and a large part of why it
  was chosen (§4.2). The phishing payload becomes "get the victim to forward you
  a live one-time link within 15 minutes," which is a much harder ask than "get
  them to type a password into a lookalike page."
- Rate limits on link requests (§4.4) bound how much lookalike email an attacker
  can get TriTrack itself to send.
- Immediate all-devices and per-device revocation (§4.3) so that a suspected
  compromise has a response that takes effect in seconds.
- Never logging coordinates (§4.7) so that the number of places a copy of asset 1
  exists stays small and enumerable.
- Encrypted server backups (§4.9), because a backup on a departing student's
  external drive is a realistic acquisition path that involves no attack at all.

**Residual, stated plainly:** a team member who is deceived into sending data
they are authorized to see is not defended against by this system. See §5.

### 2.2 Opportunistic internet scanners

**Capability:** automated, indiscriminate, fast. An exposed Postgres port, an
unauthenticated endpoint, or a default credential is found within hours of
becoming publicly routable — not days.

**What they would actually do here:** find the Postgres port because
`docker-compose.yml` published 5432 to the host and the host is on a routable
network; find the diagnostics console because it bound `0.0.0.0`; find a
`/health` endpoint that helpfully returns the schema version and the framework
version.

**Controls:**

- Postgres is **never published to a host interface**. It is reachable only on
  the Docker Compose internal network, by the server container. This is a 10.3
  requirement, not a deployment preference.
- The diagnostics console is **off by default and localhost-only when on**
  (§4.10) — and off is the default even in development, because the default is
  what gets deployed.
- No unauthenticated endpoint except `/health` and `/ready`, and between them
  they reveal two bits: this process is alive, and its database is or is not
  reachable. No version, no schema number, no dependency list. Version
  information is available on the authenticated diagnostics console, where it is
  useful, not on an open endpoint where it is reconnaissance.
  - **`/ready` is task 11.128's amendment to this bullet, and it was measured
    rather than argued.** On a server started with no database,
    `POST /auth/magic-link` answers `404 Route not found` — the auth router is
    not mounted — while a healthy server answers `202`. Both measured on
    2026-09-02. **So one unauthenticated request already distinguished the two
    states before `/ready` existed**, and `/ready` adds no fact a scanner could
    not already have; it makes an existing disclosure legible to the operator
    who needs it. The word `database` is the only word it can print, fixed by
    an enum in `server/lib/src/readiness.dart`, so this bullet cannot be widened
    by accident — adding a subsystem is an edit to that enum, which is where the
    next person is required to re-ask this question.
- TLS everywhere non-loopback (§4.1), so a scanner's traffic capture yields
  nothing.
- The localhost-only restriction stays in force until task 10.16 passes, which is
  what keeps this actor out of scope for the entire build.

### 2.3 Removed team members

**Capability:** a valid session token on one or more devices, complete knowledge
of the project, and a full local copy of everything they ever synced.

**What they would actually do:** keep syncing, because nothing told their app to
stop. Or, less charitably, pull once more after being removed.

**Controls:**

- Sessions are **opaque server-side rows checked on every request** (§4.3). The
  moment `end_date` is set, the next request from any of their devices fails.
  There is no window during which a revoked member's device continues to work,
  and specifically **no grandfathering of an in-progress chunked sync** — a long
  first-sync does not get to finish on a revoked session.
  **One stated exemption since task 11.60 (2026-08-29), written here rather than
  only in the section that made it, per §4.24:** a `pull` from a device whose
  stint has ended is answered with that person's **own closed membership rows and
  nothing else**, so their app can say *you were removed from this project* rather
  than *the server is refusing access* — and so they can delete their local copy
  through the path that already exists. No project data crosses, push and ack are
  refused exactly as before, and §4.27 states what it may return and what it must
  be indistinguishable from.
- Revocation is **all-devices** (§4.3). Revoking the session that happened to
  make the last request, while their other phone keeps syncing, is the same as
  not revoking.
- Their observations are retained and their authorship is preserved — this is a
  data-integrity requirement (asset 2), not a leniency. Deleting a departed
  member's bearings would corrupt every position estimate that cites them.

**Residual:** their local copy is permanent and unrecoverable. This is inherent
to offline-first. See §5.1.

### 2.4 Curious insiders

**Capability:** a fully valid session, legitimate access to project A, and an
HTTP client.

**What they would actually do:** change a project id in a request and see what
comes back. Not maliciously, usually — a grad student wondering whether their
advisor's other study is visible.

**This is the most likely real breach in the entire system, and the least
dramatic.** It is not an exploit; it is an endpoint that checked
"authenticated?" and forgot to check "authorized *for this project*?" That
mistake is one missing line, it produces no error, and it is invisible in
testing unless the test is specifically written to look for it.

**Controls:**

- Every endpoint touching project data verifies membership in **that specific
  project**. Being a valid user of the system grants access to nothing by
  itself.
- Project scope is derived from the **session**, joined against membership —
  never taken from a client-supplied field and trusted (§4.11).
- Cross-project isolation is testable in Phase 10 with no teams at all: one user
  owning two of their own projects. That test exists in 10.15 and Gate B gates
  on it.
- The server's authorization implementation **fails closed where the client's
  fails open** (§4.12). This is the specific trap in porting Phase 8's rules to
  the server.

### 2.5 Network eavesdroppers

**Capability:** passive capture on a shared network. Acutely relevant during the
LAN prototype stage, where cleartext HTTP is temporarily in play — a university
campus Wi-Fi network, a field station's shared router, a motel network the night
before a survey.

**What they would get from cleartext:** the session token (→ full project
access), the magic-link token if a sign-in happens on that network (→ account
takeover), and the entire sync payload (→ asset 1, directly, in bulk).

**Controls:**

- TLS on every non-loopback listener in production, with the dev cleartext
  exemption made structurally unable to ship (§4.1).
- The cleartext window is confined to development, on a network the developer
  controls, before any real project data exists on the server.
- Session tokens are bearer tokens and are therefore worth exactly as much as
  the transport protecting them. That is the reason §4.1 is non-negotiable
  rather than a best practice.

---

## 3. Attack surface inventory

For each surface: what an attacker gains, and what prevents it.

### 3.1 The HTTP API

**Gain:** everything. This is the front door to assets 1 and 2.

**Prevented by:** authentication on every route but `/health` and `/ready`
(§2.2); per-project
authorization on every route touching project data (§4.11, §4.12); parameterized
queries without exception; server-side row validation using the shared
`RowValidator` so a hand-crafted request cannot insert what the client's forms
would reject; uniform error responses that reveal neither existence nor
structure (§4.13); rate limits on the unauthenticated routes (§4.4); request
body size limits and bounded batch sizes (10.7's chunking is a security control
as well as a reliability one — an unbounded push is a memory exhaustion
primitive); an explicit length bound on every caller-supplied identifier
field, not just the request body as a whole (task 10.56) — `device_id` and
`project_id` both land in a Postgres btree index, and an oversized value there
does not draw a typed refusal, it throws mid-`INSERT` (§11.8's I-4, `500` on
`/sync/push`).

**The specific thing to get right:** the sync endpoint is the highest-risk route
in the system, because it is the one that legitimately reads and writes many
rows across many tables in one call. Every other endpoint touches one row and is
easy to reason about. The sync endpoint must filter by project on both
directions and must re-derive the project from the session rather than from the
payload.

### 3.2 Magic-link tokens

**Gain:** a session, and therefore everything. A live unconsumed magic link is
an account takeover waiting to be clicked.

**Prevented by:** 256 bits of CSPRNG entropy; SHA-256 hashed at rest so a
database read does not yield usable tokens; single-use enforced by an atomic
conditional UPDATE rather than a check-then-set; 15-minute expiry; at most one
live link per address; **redemption requires a POST** so that mail-scanner link
prefetching cannot consume it (§4.2); never logged, and the redemption route's
URL is excluded from request logging entirely.

**Delivery is out of our control.** The token travels through email, which means
mailbox compromise equals account compromise. Stated as a non-goal in §5.3
rather than pretended away.

### 3.3 Session tokens

**Gain:** everything the user can reach, for as long as the session lives.

**Prevented by:** 256 bits of entropy, hashed at rest, transmitted only over TLS
(§4.1); stored on the device in the platform keychain/keystore and **never** in
SharedPreferences or the SQLite database (§4.8); looked up by hash so there is
no plaintext copy anywhere on the server; revocable per-device and all-devices
with effect on the next request (§4.3); never logged, never included in an error
response, never rendered by the diagnostics console (§4.10).

### 3.4 The transport

**Gain:** see §2.5 — tokens and bulk asset 1.

**Prevented by:** §4.1, and by the fact that the cleartext exemption is scoped
to private-network hosts in debug builds only and is enforced by a test, not a
comment.

### 3.5 The diagnostics console (task 10.13)

**Gain:** a read-only web view over the whole server — every project, recent
rows of every table, the sync log, the identity mapping, the device registry.
That is asset 1 in a browser, with no authentication if it is misconfigured.

**Prevented by:** off by default, and disabling it **removes the routes** rather
than hiding links; localhost binding unless an explicit opt-in flag is passed;
never enabled in a production deployment; strictly read-only with no mutation
route of any kind; and it never renders session tokens or unconsumed magic-link
tokens — a console that displays a live magic link is an account-takeover page
(§4.10).

**Note the tension and accept it:** the console's most valuable view (which rows
lost last-write-wins) inherently displays coordinates. That is why the console
is off by default and localhost-only rather than merely authenticated.

### 3.6 The database at rest, and its backups

**Gain:** everything, in bulk, all projects at once. The highest-value single
target in the system.

**Prevented by:** Postgres never reachable off the Docker network; credentials
from environment only (§4.6); disk-level encryption on the host as a deployment
requirement; token values stored only as hashes so a dump does not yield working
credentials; and **backups encrypted with a public key whose private half is not
on the server** (§4.9).

**Backups are the weak half of this surface, not the database.** The live
database is behind a running system with access controls. A backup is a file,
and files get copied to laptops, cloud drives, and departing students' external
disks. That is why §4.9 is unconditional.

### 3.7 Device-local SQLite (and everything beside it)

**Gain:** one project's full history, as synced to that device — plus, if
carelessly stored, a live session token granting continued server access, which
is strictly worse.

**Current state:** `tri_track.db` is a plain unencrypted SQLite file in the app
documents directory. `device_id` is a plaintext value in SharedPreferences.
Neither is a defect on its own; both are inputs to §4.8.

**Three adjacent exposures that are not the database and are easy to overlook:**

1. **The auto cloud backup path.** `CloudBackupService` writes an unencrypted zip
   containing every table for a project — all users' names and emails, every
   full-precision coordinate — into a user-linked third-party cloud folder
   (iCloud, Drive, Dropbox) on a schedule. This is the largest existing
   disclosure surface in the app, it exists today with no server involved, and
   it is outside every control in this document. See §6 (discovered scope).
2. **The `TT1:` share payload.** `ObservationShare.encode` is base64 — encoding,
   not encryption — and carries the observer's email, name, user id,
   `origin_device_id`, `revision`, and full-precision position. `decode` accepts
   any well-formed payload with **no signature or MAC**, so a pasted payload's
   claimed author, device, and revision are entirely attacker-controlled and
   feed directly into merge ordering. This is an integrity hole in asset 2 that
   predates the server and gets worse once those rows sync onward. See §4.12 and
   §6.
3. **`device_id` is forgeable** — a `Uuid().v4()` in SharedPreferences — and it
   is the final tiebreaker in last-write-wins. A chosen `device_id` can win ties
   deterministically. See §4.12.

**Prevented by:** §4.8 (token in keychain, passcode expectation, per-device
revocation as the real mitigation) and the OS sandbox plus platform full-disk
encryption, which is where the actual confidentiality guarantee lives.

### 3.8 The dependency supply chain

**Gain:** arbitrary code execution inside the server process, or inside the app,
depending on which side the compromised package is on. The most complete
compromise available and the one requiring the least skill against *us*
specifically.

**Prevented by:** pinned exact versions in `pubspec.yaml` for the server, with
`pubspec.lock` committed; a documented `dart pub outdated` /advisory audit
command run at each review gate; and a hard rule that **every new dependency is
justified in its task's summary by name, reason, and what it is trusted with**
(the standing criterion, and it exists precisely because trust is what a
dependency actually costs).

**Two dependencies get scrutiny beyond the rest**, because they sit directly on
assets 1–3: whatever sends email (it handles magic-link tokens) and whatever
talks to Postgres (it handles everything). Prefer the most widely used, most
boring option for both. Novelty is not a virtue here.

**The backup image's two tools are pinned by their Alpine release, not by a
version (task 11.327, replacing task 11.175's reasoning).** `age` (which
encrypts every backup, §4.9) and `minisign` (which signs it, §4.9.2) come from
Alpine's package index, which `apk` reads over the network when
`server/backup/Dockerfile` is built. **No Alpine index keeps a package's old
versions, including a stable release's:** Alpine 3.24-stable rebuilt `age` on
2026-09-04 and upgraded it from 1.3.1 to 1.3.2 on 2026-10-04. So both pins this
file has had broke on Alpine's schedule rather than ours: an exact packaging
revision (`age=1.3.1-r5`) on 2026-09-06, and an exact upstream version
(`age=~1.3.1`) on 2026-10-04. Each time the image could not be built from
scratch and the gate's restore drill went red with it. The first was caught within
two days by GitHub's runners, which start with no build cache; the second was
hidden by the VM's cache until somebody cleared it, because GitHub's checks are
paused. **A new deployment has no cache, so it would have been the first to
find out.**

- **The pin is the release in `FROM` (`postgres:16-alpine3.24`).** A stable
  release changes packages only for fixes, its index stays on the mirrors after
  it retires, and old image tags stay on Docker Hub, so the image builds on any
  date. Moving to a new release, and to whatever `age` and `minisign` it
  carries, is a deliberate edit. The `apk add` line carries **floors** at the
  versions last reviewed (`age>=1.3.2`, `minisign>=0.12`), so an edit to an
  *older* release is refused at build time rather than quietly downgrading.
- **What it gives up.** A fix release Alpine ships *inside* 3.24 is taken
  without an edit here; 1.3.2 was one, and it changed nothing §4.9 relies on.
  `scripts/nightly_check.sh` builds the image with no cache every night and
  prints the versions it installed, so such a change shows up the next morning.
  **And the release stops receiving fixes for these two when Alpine retires its
  community repository, which happens when the next release ships** (2026-11-01
  for 3.24; Alpine publishes the date in `releases.json`). From then on the image
  goes stale rather than broken. The night's preflight reads that date and warns
  from a month before it.
- **Refused alternatives.** An exact or minor-version pin makes every upgrade a
  deliberate edit, but only by turning every fix release into an outage.
  Pinning `FROM` by digest freezes the base image but not the index `apk`
  reads. Vendoring the binaries with checksums pins the bytes, but it costs a
  hand-tracked download and two checksums per tool (arm64 and amd64), and
  nothing announces a security fix. The full reasoning is beside the line in
  the Dockerfile.

**Violated by:** an exact package version, revision or minor-version window on
that `apk add` line; a `FROM` without an Alpine release in its tag; removing the
nightly no-cache build or the preflight's release-date warning.

**The shared package's first dependency, and the app's first bundled map data
(task 11.331, 2026-10-10; for the planning session's review).** A deployment
day is now the field site's day, read in the project's time zone (`CLAUDE.md`
standing decision 4). That needs two things from outside, and both are named
here as this section requires.

- **`timezone` 0.11.1, pinned exactly in `packages/tritrack_sync/pubspec.yaml`**
  (and therefore resolved into the app and the server through that path
  dependency; both lockfiles carry it). Published by the Dart team
  (`labs.dart.dev`), the long-standing Dart implementation of the IANA tz
  database, BSD-licensed; it carries tz database **2025c** as generated Dart
  source (`latest_all.dart`, about 450 KB of data, compiled in, no file or
  network read at run time). **Trusted with one thing:** turning an instant into
  a wall-clock date in a named zone and back. It never sees a row, an id, a
  name or a token. It is in the server process because the server's interlock
  must read a row's bare day in the row's zone (§4.13's "one function, two
  enforcers"); there it holds no credential and makes no network call (its
  `browser.dart` HTTP loader, which pulls in `http`, is not imported anywhere).
  **This ends "the shared package has zero runtime dependencies"**, which the
  §11/§13 scorecards recorded as a strength; it is now one, pinned, and
  reviewed here. Updating the tz rules means moving this pin.
- **The time-zone boundaries: timezone-boundary-builder release 2026d**
  (`timezones-with-oceans.geojson.zip`, SHA-256 `e391c92c…1034`, OpenStreetMap
  data under the ODbL), simplified to 100 m with mapshaper 0.6.102 and encoded
  into `assets/time_zones/boundaries.bin` by `scripts/time_zone_boundaries/build.sh`,
  which pins the release, the checksum and the tool version and refuses a
  download that does not match. **Data, not code:** read by TriTrack's own
  parser (`lib/core/time/time_zone_boundaries.dart`, which refuses a file
  without its magic and version), used only to suggest a new project's zone,
  which the creator sees and confirms. **Measured size: 3,984,822 bytes (about
  4.0 MB)** in the app, against the task's 15 MB ceiling; the unsimplified
  release is 56 MB zipped and 184 MB unpacked. The worst a corrupted file can
  do is suggest a wrong zone on a screen that shows it in words. The variant
  matters and was measured: the "-1970" and "-now" variants merge zones that
  keep the same clock, which labels the open Pacific `Pacific/Honolulu` and the
  mid-Atlantic `America/Cayenne`, so the unmerged variant is the one shipped.
- **Alternatives considered.** (1) *Writing the zone rules ourselves* from the
  IANA source: a parser and a rule engine for a data format with decades of
  special cases, to avoid a Dart-team package that already does it; rejected.
  (2) *A device time-zone plugin* (`flutter_timezone`, to read the phone's IANA
  name): native code on three platforms for a value only needed when a new
  project has no area yet, and its latest release was a week old; instead the
  phone's zone is worked out in Dart from its clock over the year (`TZ` first,
  where a process has one), and the creator confirms it
  (`lib/core/time/device_time_zone.dart`). (3) *A boundary-lookup package*:
  none on pub.dev is maintained for current data (the one candidate,
  `lat_lng_to_timezone`, was last published in 2021); the plan's own
  alternative, "writing the lookup from the published boundary data", is what
  was built, in about 200 lines that read a format we wrote. (4) *Shipping the
  unsimplified boundaries*: over the ceiling. (5) *A coarser grid lookup*
  (the approach of `tz-lookup`): smaller, but wrong for kilometers near a
  border, which is exactly where the Navajo Nation's line inside Arizona is.

**Violated by:** a caret or open range on `timezone`; importing
`package:timezone/browser.dart` or anything that makes the package fetch data;
replacing `boundaries.bin` other than through `build.sh` with its pinned
checksum; a reader that trusts a zone name it does not know instead of falling
back as `FieldTimeZone` does.

---

## 4. Decisions

Each decision records what was decided, why, which task implements it, and what
would violate it.

### 4.1 TLS everywhere, and keeping the dev exemption from shipping

**Decision.** Every listener on any interface other than loopback serves TLS.
Cleartext HTTP is permitted only when *both* of the following hold: the client
build is a debug build, and the target host is loopback or a private-range
address. Never in a release or profile build. Never to a public address.

**Corrected by task 10.57 (2026-08-15), finding I-7.** This paragraph
previously read "the client build is debug or profile," which never matched
either the client's own §3.4 summary ("debug builds only") or the shipped
Android implementation below (`network_security_config.xml` scoped to the
debug variant, never profile) — only the Dart validator agreed with the
wrong text, because it was gated on `kReleaseMode`, which is `false` in a
profile build too. Three of four artifacts already said "debug only"; this
sentence was the one that disagreed, so it is the one that moved, not the
code or the Android config.

**Reasoning.** Session tokens are bearer tokens; they are worth exactly what the
transport is worth (§2.5). And the LAN prototype stage puts real cleartext on a
real shared network, which is not a theoretical exposure — it is a
several-week-long window on a campus Wi-Fi network.

**Implementation, on both sides:**

- **Server (10.3, hardened in 10.14, second condition added in 10.22):** refuses
  to bind a non-loopback interface unless TLS is configured *or*
  `TRITRACK_ALLOW_CLEARTEXT_LAN=1` is explicitly set. That flag logs a prominent
  warning on every startup, is rejected outright when `TRITRACK_ENV=production`,
  and **is rejected when this machine holds a publicly routable address** —
  `TransportSecurityConfig.assertExposureIsPrivate` enumerates the host's
  interfaces before anything binds. Default with no configuration at all is
  loopback-only.
- **Client (10.2 seam, 10.4 platform config, 10.14 enforcement, 10.22 second
  condition, 10.57 third):** the server-URL validator rejects `http://` in
  release **and profile** builds, gated on `!kDebugMode` (not `kReleaseMode`
  — task 10.57, finding I-7: `kReleaseMode` is `false` in a profile build
  too, so an internal-distribution build silently kept the LAN-cleartext
  exemption meant only for a developer's own machine) so it is a
  compile-time constant the tree-shaker can see — **and rejects `http://` to
  a non-private target in every build**, because the debug exemption is for
  a LAN server, not for cleartext generally.
- **One definition of "private", shared:** `isPrivateNetworkAddress` in
  `packages/tritrack_sync`, called by both of the above. Two enforcement points
  with two hand-rolled range lists is one refactor away from disagreeing, and
  the disagreement would be silent.
- **The shipped defaults are part of the control (10.22).** `docker-compose.yml`
  publishes the server on `127.0.0.1`; `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` in
  `.env` is what opens it to the LAN. This is §4.10's reasoning applied here:
  the default is what gets deployed, so the default is the safe one and the
  exposure is the typed decision.
- **iOS/macOS:** `NSAllowsLocalNetworking`, which relaxes App Transport Security
  only for local hostnames and private addresses. This is safe to ship as-is and
  is the reason not to reach for `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads`, which is not.
- **Android:** a `network_security_config.xml` scoped to the **debug variant
  only**. A blanket `usesCleartextTraffic="true"` in the main manifest is
  forbidden.

**Structural enforcement, not a comment asking nicely (10.14):** a test that
inspects the merged release manifest and the release `Info.plist` and fails if
either permits cleartext beyond local networking, plus a test asserting the
non-debug (release or profile) URL validator rejects `http://`. A control with
no failing-path test is decoration.

**Known blind spot, recorded rather than implied (10.22).** The server's
private-range refusal reads *its own* interfaces, and inside a container those
are always the Docker bridge — private by construction. So the refusal cannot
fire for a compose deployment on a publicly-addressed host; what confines that
case is the `127.0.0.1` publish default, which is a default, not a control. A
deployment on a public host must configure TLS. This is written here, in
`.env.example` where the override is typed, and in `server/README.md`, because
a control's blind spot belongs next to the control and not in a commit message.

**Violated by:** any code path that constructs an HTTP client for a
non-private-range host; a blanket Android cleartext flag; `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads`;
a runtime configuration flag that could enable cleartext in a release build;
**a shipped default — compose file, Dockerfile, or script — that serves
cleartext off-host without someone typing something**; removing either
enforcement test.

### 4.2 Token design

**Decision.** Two token types, both built the same way.

| | Magic-link token | Session token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entropy | 256 bits, `Random.secure()` | 256 bits, `Random.secure()` |
| Encoding | base64url, unpadded (43 chars) | base64url, unpadded |
| At rest | SHA-256 hash only | SHA-256 hash only |
| Lifetime | 15 minutes | see §4.3 |
| Single-use | yes, atomically | no (it is the session) |
| Comparison | by hash lookup; constant-time where compared in code | same |

**Reasoning on entropy:** 256 bits from the platform CSPRNG makes guessing
irrelevant as an attack, which removes an entire class of problem for the cost
of a longer string. There is no reason to be economical here.

**Reasoning on SHA-256 rather than bcrypt/argon2 — record this, it looks
wrong at a glance.** These are high-entropy random secrets, not user-chosen
passwords. There is no dictionary and no plausible brute force, so a slow KDF
buys nothing while costing latency on the hot path of every authenticated
request. Password hashing is slow to defend weak inputs; the input here is
strong by construction. **If a password ever enters this system, that reasoning
inverts and argon2id becomes mandatory** — but there is no password, by design
(§2.1).

**Reasoning on no pepper:** hashing protects against "attacker reads the
database, obtains working tokens." A pepper stored on the same host that the
database credentials are on adds nothing against that attacker. Skipped
deliberately; not an omission.

**Single-use, done correctly:** consumption is one atomic statement —

```
UPDATE magic_links SET consumed_at = now()
 WHERE token_hash = $1 AND consumed_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now()
 RETURNING user_id
```

— returning zero rows on any failure. A `SELECT` followed by an `UPDATE` is a
race in which two concurrent redemptions both succeed. Do not write that
version.

**15-minute expiry, reasoned against the actual use case:** long enough for
email delivery plus walking to a laptop; short enough that a mailbox skimmed
tomorrow yields nothing. Requesting a new link invalidates any prior unconsumed
one for that address, so a user who clicks "resend" three times has one live
token, not three.

**Redemption is a POST, not a GET.** The emailed URL leads to a minimal page
with a "Sign in on this device" button that POSTs the token. **Reasoning:**
corporate mail scanners and messaging-app link previewers prefetch URLs. A
GET-consumes design means a scanner silently burns the single-use token and the
user's link is dead on arrival — an availability bug that reads as a broken
sign-in and invites someone to "fix" it by making tokens reusable. It also means
any intermediary that logs URLs has logged a working credential. POST-to-consume
removes both.

**The session belongs to the redeeming device, never the requesting one.** A
link requested on the laptop and opened on the phone signs in *the phone*.
10.6 decides how the laptop is told; the security constraint is only that it
must never be possible for one device's redemption to mint a session on a
different device.

**Violated by:** storing any token in plaintext; a `SELECT`-then-`UPDATE`
consumption path; a GET route that consumes; reusable tokens; expiry longer than
an hour; a token in a log, an error body, a test fixture, or a diagnostics
response; introducing a password.

#### 4.2.1 The one named exception: a project join code is stored readably (task 11.81, 2026-08-31)

**This is an exception to "storing any token in plaintext", it is deliberate, and
Michael made the call in writing on 2026-08-31.** It is written here rather than
left in a commit message because an unexplained departure from this section is
exactly the drift this project keeps finding, and a future reader who meets
`project_join_settings.code` and cannot find this paragraph will either "fix" it
or copy it.

**What is stored readably.** One value: `project_join_settings.code`, the
8-character Crockford Base32 join code an owner hands out for a project. Nothing
else changes. Magic-link tokens and session tokens are unaffected and stay
SHA-256-only — the rule above is intact for everything the word *token* covers.

**Why this is not a violation of what §4.2 is for.** §4.2 forbids plaintext
storage so that **a database read does not yield working credentials.** A join
code stopped being a credential when task 11.81 shipped. Before it, holding an
invite code *was* membership: you typed it in, the server wrote your membership
row, and you were on the project reading collar locations. Under the join-code
design, holding the code buys **only the right to ask**, and an owner decides.
The role is chosen at approval and is never in the code, so there is no such
thing as a leaked owner code. So the thing a database read yields is the ability
to appear in an owner's pending list, which is a nuisance rather than an access.

**And the marginal harm against this specific attacker is close to zero.**
Somebody holding a dump of this database already holds the field data — every
observation, every bearing, every collar location — which is the asset §1 ranks
first. That they could additionally ask to join a project they can already read
is not a meaningful increment.

**What is bought with it, which is the reason it was asked for.** An owner can
re-read the code after closing the screen. Under a per-person invite code,
losing one cost a re-issue to one person. Under a **shared** code, the only
recovery is rotation — which kills the copy on the field-site whiteboard, in the
WhatsApp thread, and in everyone's notes, and forces the owner to re-broadcast
to the whole crew. "The code on the whiteboard went dead because the owner lost
their phone" is an operational failure that will happen; the exposure traded for
it is one Michael has already accepted by design.

**What this exception does NOT license, stated so it cannot be cited wider than
it is:**

- It covers `project_join_settings.code` and nothing else. It is not a
  precedent for any other value, and a second use of it needs its own paragraph
  here.
- It does not make the code public. `GET /projects/<id>/join-settings` returns
  it **to a project owner only**, through the same `_requireOwner` gate as every
  other owner route, and never to a member, a requester, or an unauthenticated
  caller.
- It does not survive a change of design. **If a join code is ever again made
  sufficient to grant membership without an owner's decision, this exception
  lapses immediately and the code goes back to a hash** — because the sentence
  it rests on ("a join code is no longer a credential") would have become false.

**Reopen condition, so this is a check rather than a promise:** any change that
lets a join code produce a membership row without a distinct owner action must
either restore hash-only storage or replace this paragraph. `join_service.dart`
carries a comment pointing here.

**Implemented by:** 10.6, hardened in 10.14, gated at Gate A. Exception 4.2.1 by
task 11.81.

### 4.3 Session lifetime, rotation, and revocation

**Decision: opaque, database-backed sessions. Not JWTs.**

A session is a row: `(session_id, user_id, device_id, token_hash, created_at,
last_seen_at, expires_at, revoked_at, revoked_reason)`. Every authenticated
request looks it up by token hash and checks `revoked_at IS NULL` and not
expired.

**Reasoning, and this is the decision a future task is most likely to
challenge.** JWTs are attractive because they avoid a database read per request.
But a JWT is valid until it expires, by construction — revoking one requires a
server-side blocklist, which is a database read per request, which is the thing
JWTs were chosen to avoid. Since **immediate revocation is a hard requirement**
here (§2.3, and task 11.2's member removal is cosmetic without it), the stateless
option collapses into the stateful one with extra steps and a footgun. Choose the
boring version. A single indexed primary-key lookup is not the bottleneck in a
system whose hot path is bulk row merging.

**Lifetime: 90 days absolute, 30 days idle.** Reasoning: field devices go
offline for weeks at a stretch, and a session that expires mid-season forces a
sign-in exactly when there is no connectivity to receive the email — the app
would appear broken at the worst possible moment. That is a long time for a
bearer token, and it is only acceptable **because** revocation is immediate and
server-side. The two decisions are a package; do not shorten the revocation
guarantee while keeping the long lifetime, and note that a session outliving the
tombstone retention window (§4.5-adjacent, decided in 10.11) is a case 10.11
must handle explicitly.

**Rotation: on sign-in only, not per request.** Reasoning: per-request rotation
detects token theft by making the old token fail, but on a marginal field
connection a rotation whose response is lost locks the device out of a sync it
was midway through. Availability of the field sync path (asset 2) outranks a
detection mechanism that the device registry's `last_seen_at` already partly
provides. Revisit if session theft ever becomes an observed problem rather than
a hypothetical one.

**Revocation, two granularities, both built in 10.14:**

- **All-devices**, keyed on `user_id`: every session row for that user. This is
  the user's own "sign out everywhere" — self-service only (§4.11's rule that
  authorization inputs never come from client-supplied values, applied to a
  route that destroys credentials). Revoking only the most recent session
  while the same person's other phone keeps syncing is the same as not
  revoking. **Reachable from the app since task 11.28 (2026-08-23)**, on the
  Server Connection screen. Until then this section described a control nobody
  could invoke: the route was built and correct and no screen called it, so the
  documented answer to "I think somebody has my token" was, in practice, that
  the person could do nothing. The control confirms first (it signs this device
  out too), reports how many sign-ins ended, and — unlike ordinary sign-out,
  which proceeds against an unreachable server on purpose — **refuses to clear
  the local session unless the server confirmed**, because somebody reaching for
  this believes their credentials are compromised and a false confirmation is
  the worst thing it could do.
- **Per-device**, keyed on `(user_id, device_id)`: sign out one lost or stolen
  device without signing the user out everywhere. This is the practical
  mitigation for §4.8's device-loss scenario and depends on the device registry.
  **The obstacle was a missing read rather than a missing button** (task
  11.28): the route needs the lost device's id, and nothing listed a caller's
  own sessions, so nothing could offer a picker. **Task 11.35 (2026-08-23)
  built the read** — `GET /auth/sessions`, an authenticated list of the
  caller's own devices, resolved from the session and never from the request,
  bounded and rate-limited per user (10.56). Three things about its shape are
  decisions, not details:

  - **One row per device, not per session.** Revocation is keyed on
    `(user_id, device_id)` and ends every session on that device together, so a
    list showing two rows for one phone would offer a control that silently
    also closed the row next to it.
  - **No source address on any row.** A device id and a last-used time are
    enough to pick a lost phone out of a list; an address would put a record of
    where each of a person's devices last was onto a new read surface, for a
    convenience. Where a device signed in from remains a diagnostics question
    with its own authorization (§4.7).
  - **No device label, because the server stores none.** `device_id` is the
    client's install id and the only thing naming a device anywhere in the
    schema. Inventing a friendly name from a user agent would be a guess
    presented as a fact.

  **No screen calls it yet**, so what the app offers today is still
  sign-out-everywhere, which reaches the same end state — the lost device is
  locked out from that moment — at the cost of one sign-in on each device still
  held, and the screen says so rather than implying a finer control exists. The
  route is trust-boundary inventory entry 27, verdict **Open**: correctly built
  and not yet attacked by a gate. Note what neither granularity reaches: a
  revoked device keeps the project data already downloaded onto it (§2.3,
  §5.1).

**This section used to say member removal calls the all-devices revocation
above. It does not, and it must not — corrected by task 11.27 (2026-08-22).**
Sessions belong to a person, not a project; calling it here would sign a field
tech out of every other study they are on because one of them ended, which is
exactly the assumption Phase 11 forbids (the planning session proposed this
once and task 11.2 corrected it). What actually makes removal immediate is
that project access is resolved from membership **on every request**, with no
cached decision — the mechanism this section's opening paragraph is for. A
removed member's session is untouched and keeps working for everything they
are still entitled to; their very next request to the project they left is
refused regardless, on that same unexpired session. Pinned by
`server/test/integration/membership_and_joining_test.dart`, group "removal,
and what it does not reach". See §4.24 for the general shape this correction
is one instance of.

**Revocation takes effect on the next request, with no exceptions for work in
progress.** A chunked first sync that is 80% done and gets revoked mid-transfer
stops. It does not finish "since it already started." Fail closed (§1.5).

**Concurrent sessions per user are normal, not an edge case.** One row per
`(user, device)`; signing in on the phone must not touch the laptop's row.

**Violated by:** JWTs or any self-validating token; a session cache that serves
a revoked session; checking revocation once per sync rather than per request;
"finishing" an in-flight operation on a revoked session; a single session row
per user; unbounded lifetime.

### 4.4 Rate limiting

**Decision.** Limits on every unauthenticated route, keyed two ways where an
email is in play and per-source alone where it is not.

| Route | Per normalized email | Per source address |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Magic-link request | 3 / 15 min, 10 / day | 10 / 15 min, 60 / hour |
| Magic-link redemption | — | 20 / min |
| Link-status poll | — | 30 / min |

**Link-status added by task 10.56 (§11.8's I-5).** `/auth/link-status/<id>` was
unauthenticated and rate-limited by nothing until then — 60 requests, 60 ×
`200`, no `429`, no audit row, contradicting this section's own claim below
§3.1. No per-email rule: the request carries a request id, not an address (see
`auth_schema.dart`'s comment on `auth_link_requests`), so there is no third
party's fact a 429 here could disclose — the same reasoning that makes
redemption's limit per-source-only.

**Reasoning on keying both ways:** per-email alone lets one attacker bomb a
thousand different colleagues. Per-source alone lets a botnet bomb one
colleague. Neither is sufficient; both together bound the two attacks that
actually matter — email bombing a team member, and enumeration by volume.

**Reasoning on the response when limited — this is subtle.** For the **per-email**
limit, return the same generic 202 as a successful request and silently do not
send. A 429 keyed on an email address tells the caller that somebody recently
requested links for that address, which is a weak but real oracle about a third
party. For the **per-source** limit, return 429 honestly: that fact is about the
caller, not about anyone else, and telling them is useful.

**Storage: in-process counters for the single-instance prototype, and this is
explicitly a prototype-only shortcut.** Before any second instance or any
load-balanced deployment, limits move to Postgres or Redis — per-instance
counters silently multiply the effective limit by the instance count, which is
the kind of failure that looks like the control is working. Documented as a
deployment precondition in 10.14 and re-checked at 10.16.

**Violated by:** a limit on only one key; per-email 429s; relying on in-process
counters in a multi-instance deployment; limits configurable to zero or absent;
no test that exceeds them; **a per-source key that does not identify a source**
(see below).

#### 4.4.1 What "per source" means behind a reverse proxy (task 10.52, 2026-08-15)

**The decision: an explicit trusted-proxy scheme, keyed on an allowlist of peer
addresses. The merged bucket is rejected, not accepted.**

Task 10.14 filed this question in its 2026-08-07 Discovered Scope — whoever put
a proxy in front "must either refuse `/diagnostics/*` at the proxy and accept
the rate-limit merge, or introduce a trusted-proxy header with all the care that
needs." Task 10.49 shipped the proxy and did neither. §11.3 is the result,
reproduced live in both the shipped compose and the Caddy deployment: every
request's TCP peer is the proxy, so the per-source bucket is one bucket, and ten
unauthenticated requests deny magic-link sign-in to **every user of the
deployment** for fifteen minutes. This section is the answer that was owed.

**Why the merged bucket is not acceptable, stated plainly.** §5.6 declines to
defend availability against hostile load, and it would be easy to file this
there. That reading is wrong, for three reasons:

1. This is not a control failing to help — it is a control **inverted**. The
   rule written to stop a botnet bombing one colleague becomes a lever any
   stranger can pull on everyone, at a cost of ten HTTP requests. §5.6 accepts
   that TriTrack cannot survive a flood; it does not accept shipping the flood
   as a feature.
2. §4.1 mandates a reverse proxy for any real deployment. So the merged bucket
   is not an edge case — it is the *only* configuration that ever ships, which
   means accepting it is accepting that §4.4 is decoration everywhere it counts.
3. It voids §4.7 and finding C-5's entire contribution. Attribution is what an
   audit log is for; 158 events with one distinct `source_address` between them
   is a timestamp list. "Was my account compromised in March?" cannot be
   answered by rows that all name the same machine.

And the merge is not forced by the trust boundary. The proxy is *already*
completely trusted — same host, same compose file, same operator, and it
terminates the TLS every request arrives on. There is no integrity question
about what it reports; the historical catastrophe with forwarding headers is
always the same one, a header read from a peer that was not the proxy.

**The mechanism, and the invariant that survives from before.** The server's
refusal to read `X-Forwarded-For` from an arbitrary peer is unchanged and
unconditional. What was added is an allowlist of **peer addresses**
(`TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES`, `trusted_proxies.dart`), and the order is the whole
design: *the socket decides whether a header is read at all*. A caller who is
not on the allowlist cannot make their own header mean anything by sending it,
so there is no configuration in which a header grants a caller their choice of
rate-limit bucket. The allowlist is empty by default — including in every test
and every directly-bound server — which is byte-for-byte the behavior that
shipped through task 10.51.

Three supporting requirements, each of which the scheme is worthless without:

- **The proxy must overwrite the header, not append to it.** `proxy/Caddyfile`
  uses `header_up X-Forwarded-For {remote_host}`, so a caller's own value is
  discarded at the first trusted hop. The origin parses a multi-hop chain
  correctly anyway (right to left, skipping trusted hops), but a boundary worth
  getting right is worth making unambiguous rather than merely parsing
  carefully.
- **Production must declare its posture, or the server refuses to start.**
  `TRITRACK_ENV=production` with no `TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES` is a refusal
  (exit 78), with a message naming the denial of service. This is the structural
  half, and it is the part aimed at the actual failure: the requirement was not
  missing on 2026-08-14, it was unread. A comment asking the next person to
  remember would have failed the same way. The process now asks the question by
  refusing to run until it is answered.
- **A degenerate key must refuse nobody.** If a declared proxy sends no usable
  forwarding header, every caller behind it resolves to the same value. The
  per-source rule is then **suspended**, and the per-email rule alone governs
  the request (`RequestSource.isDistinguishing`). A key that cannot tell two
  callers apart cannot refuse one of them — it can only refuse all of them, and
  that is finding I-1 restated. What this costs is the volume bound on
  enumeration; what it buys is that a misconfiguration cannot become a global
  outage. The attack the per-source rule names is defined by its *victim's*
  address, so the per-email rule still bounds it unchanged, and §4.5 already
  treats the enumeration residue as bounded by the per-email daily cap and by
  the email carrying no attacker-controlled content. Suspension is loud: a
  warning on a repeating interval, and `proxy-unattributed` in the audit column
  rather than the proxy's address — a row naming the wrong machine is worse than
  one admitting it does not know.

**What this is explicitly not.** The resolved source address is for
**rate-limit keying and audit attribution only. It is never an authorization
input.** In particular the diagnostics console's loopback gate (§4.10) reads the
raw TCP peer directly and must keep doing so: routing it through this resolver
would let anyone who can reach the proxy claim `127.0.0.1`. Behind Caddy the
console therefore fails closed, which §11.3 verified rather than assumed, and
`scripts/verify_i1_source_identity.sh` step 4 is the regression guard on it.

**Verified, in the configuration that ships.** The reason this survived four
gates is that every per-source test built its source address in-process, and the
one live stack the gate attacks disables the limiter outright
(`docker-compose.e2e.yml`, finding I-3). `scripts/verify_i1_source_identity.sh`
brings up the TLS overlay with the limiter enabled and attacks it from two
client containers at distinct addresses: the flooder gets its 429, an unrelated
client still gets its 202, and the audit rows name both clients and neither
names the proxy. It carries a **negative control** — the same attack with the
allowlist pointed at the wrong address, where the merged bucket must return —
and reports FAIL if it does not, because an instrument that cannot fail is not
measuring anything. That control earned its keep during authoring: the first
draft of the drill passed a value compose was ignoring, and the "negative
control" silently ran the correct configuration.

**Violated by:** reading a forwarding header from any peer not on the allowlist;
an allowlist that defaults to anything but empty; a proxy that appends rather
than overwrites; a production deployment with no declared posture; a per-source
refusal issued on a key that cannot distinguish callers; using the resolved
address for any authorization decision.

#### 4.4.2 Which deployments have a per-source limit at all (task 10.62, 2026-08-16)

§4.4.1 answers "who is the caller" **given a source address that distinguishes
callers**. Finding J-2 is that nothing had ever established the premise, and
that in the deployment this project documented it was false.

**The premise is a property of the host's publish path, not of this server.**
Between a caller and a containerised process sits whatever forwards the host's
published port. On Linux with `iptables` DNAT the caller's address normally
survives. On Docker Desktop it does not: the VM boundary rewrites every inbound
connection's source to one gateway address before any container sees it. The
server has no way to tell which case it is in — inside a container every
interface is the Docker bridge, which is the same blind spot §4.1's
`assertExposureIsPrivate` already records.

Measured on the shipped harness (macOS, Docker Desktop 29.6.2), two distinct
off-host callers plus the host itself:

```
direct        (base compose, published port)     remote=192.168.65.1  x3
proxied       (TLS overlay, published port)      xff=192.168.65.1     x3
proxied-onnet (caller on the compose network)    xff=172.31.246.60 / .61
```

**The second line is the part that was not known before this task.** Caddy
forwards the address it sees, and the address it sees is already collapsed — so
`docker-compose.tls.yml` inherits the same defect for every caller arriving over
a published host port, and the only path that preserves identity is the one
`verify_i1_source_identity.sh` happens to test: a client already on the compose
network. 10.52 is correct and its drill is correct; between them they cover a
narrower set of callers than either claims.

**So the question is now asked, and answering it wrong is refused.**

- The trigger is **reachability**, not `TRITRACK_ENV=production`. The README's
  walkthrough was not production, declared nothing, and got the default. The
  compose files now pass `TRITRACK_PUBLISH_ADDRESS` into the container —
  verbatim from `ports:` — because it is the one fact the server was missing,
  and it is the fact that distinguishes the loopback default (one possible
  caller, so a single bucket **is** the per-source bucket) from an exposed
  deployment (many callers, and on some hosts one address).
- `TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES=none` is **no longer an acceptable answer** for a
  reachable deployment. It is a claim about the network path, the server cannot
  check it, and this project shipped it as a default while it was false. The
  replacement, `peer-verified`, means the same thing about headers and adds that
  somebody measured it.
- The measurement is `scripts/verify_source_identity.sh`, which reports
  `PRESERVED`/`COLLAPSED`/`NO VERDICT` per shape. **Corrected by task 10.110 —
  the sentence this bullet used to carry was wrong in both halves.** It did not
  measure "two genuinely distinct off-host callers": it measured two containers
  on a second Docker network, which is not an off-host caller and on Linux
  measured the host's own hairpin NAT. And the negative control it advertised
  could only ever fail if the log, the proxy header or the parser broke — it
  exercised the on-network path and said nothing about the off-host path the
  verdicts described. See §4.4.3 for what replaced both.

**Supported deployments, with a verdict each.** No third option, per this
task's acceptance:

| Shape | Per-source limit | How it is known |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loopback (the default, `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS` unset) | **Yes** | Exactly one caller can connect, so the bucket is per-source by construction. Asserted in `trusted_proxies_test.dart`. |
| Behind a proxy callers reach without crossing a rewriting publish path | **Yes** | `verify_i1_source_identity.sh`, live, both arms plus a negative control. |
| Proxy-less, exposed, on a host where the probe reports `PRESERVED` | **Yes** | `verify_source_identity.sh --assisted` against that host, from two real off-host devices (§4.4.4 — the automatic mode cannot return `PRESERVED` and never had the standing to); `peer-verified` is what the operator writes afterwards. |
| Proxy-less, exposed, publish path rewrites (all Docker Desktop) | **Removed and refused** | Server exits 78 with `REFUSING TO START — source identity`. Withdrawn from `README.md`. |
| Behind the TLS overlay, callers crossing a rewriting publish path | **Removed and refused** (task 10.74) | Server exits 78 unless `TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY` declares a measured `proxied: PRESERVED`. See §4.4.3. |

**Violated by:** a documented deployment whose source key has not been measured;
accepting an unverifiable claim as a declaration; inferring reachability from
anything the container can see; a probe without a negative control.

#### 4.4.3 The exposable deployment is qualified by a probe run, not by a host (task 10.74, 2026-08-16)

§4.4.2 closed the proxy-*less* exposed deployment and left one row open: the
TLS overlay, reached from a real network. Finding K-2 is that this row is not a
footnote — it is **the only deployment §4.1 permits to be exposed at all**, and
in it §4.4's limits do not function. `verify_source_identity.sh`, run as a gate
on this host with its negative control passing in the same run:

```
direct   (base compose, published port):      COLLAPSED
proxied  (TLS overlay, off-host caller):      COLLAPSED
negative control (proxied, on-network):       distinct callers stayed distinct
```

**The mechanism, because it is the part that is easy to get wrong.** The
allowlist in `docker-compose.tls.yml` is correct. Caddy's `header_up
X-Forwarded-For {remote_host}` is correct. The origin's parse of that header is
correct. Every control is working, and the caller's address was destroyed one
hop *upstream of all of them*, at the host publish path in front of the proxy,
which no participant can see. Correctness of the allowlist was never evidence
about source identity, and §4.4.1's premise is no more established behind a
proxy than it was in front of one.

**Decision — option 1 of the three, and the reason the other two were not
taken.**

- *Option 2, find a publish path that preserves addresses on this host*: there
  is none. On Docker Desktop the rewrite happens at the VM boundary before any
  container exists to be configured. This was not accepted on the probe's
  say-so — it is what `direct` and `proxied` both measure. *(The corroboration
  originally cited here was "while the on-network control passes", which §4.4.4
  shows proves nothing about this path. The conclusion survives on better
  evidence: task 10.110 re-measured it in `--assisted` mode from two genuinely
  off-host LAN callers, and both arrived as `192.168.65.1`.)*
- *Option 3, accept the collapse with the per-email limit carrying the load*:
  refused. The per-email limit bounds what one *address* can be sent; it does
  nothing about the unauthenticated per-source limit, which is the one an
  attacker pulls. Accepting the collapse means accepting that **ten
  unauthenticated requests from one stranger deny magic-link sign-in to every
  member of the deployment for fifteen minutes, repeatable indefinitely, from
  anywhere that can reach the host** — a remote denial of service on
  authentication for the whole team, by design rather than by defect — and that
  `auth_audit_log.source_address` names a gateway in every row, so the incident
  cannot afterwards be attributed to anyone. For a field application whose
  users sign in from a truck at a trailhead, that is not a residual risk; it is
  the failure the control was written to prevent, generalised from one victim
  to everybody.
- *Option 1, taken*: **the exposable deployment is qualified by a passing
  probe run on the host it will run on.** Not by operating system. Nobody has
  measured a Linux host for this project, so "Linux is probably fine" is not
  what is written down anywhere in it; `iptables` DNAT normally preserving
  source addresses is a reason to *run the probe expecting a pass*, not a
  substitute for running it.

**The qualification is enforced by the server, not by this document.** An
allowlist in `TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES` now additionally requires
`TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY`, and the process exits 78 naming the collapse
until it reads one of exactly two values:

| Value | Asserts | Exposable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `probe-verified` | `verify_source_identity.sh --assisted` was run **on this host**, from two real off-host devices, and its `proxied` shape reported `PRESERVED` (§4.4.4) | Yes — this is the qualification |
| `on-network-only` | nothing off this host reaches the proxy; every caller is on the compose network, crossing no publish path | No — the drills and a single-host stack |

There is no third spelling and no "unknown", for the same reason `none` stopped
being an answer in §4.4.2: the value of asking is entirely in refusing the
answer that means *nobody looked*.

**Why a startup refusal rather than a README line.** The requirement to run the
probe against the TLS overlay already existed in prose — in `README.md`, in
`server/README.md`, and in `docker-compose.tls.yml`'s own comment, written by
the task that discovered the mechanism. The deployment shipped anyway and a
gate found it. That is the third instance of this project's characteristic
failure (10.14's requirement unread by 10.49; §4.4.2's own note unread by the
overlay it was written into), and prose has now lost that argument three times.

**`docker-compose.tls.yml` does not answer this variable and must not.** Every
other value that file needs it hardcodes, because those are facts about the
file. This one is a fact about the host, and a shipped default would be this
repository vouching for a machine it has never seen — which is the assumption
K-2 is made of. `shipped_defaults_test.dart` asserts the pass-through has no
default, over every compose file rather than the one where it mattered.

**Consequence accepted, stated plainly:** on Docker Desktop — the platform this
project is developed on — **there is now no deployment that can be exposed at
all.** The server will not start in the only configuration §4.1 permits to be
reachable, and the correct response is not an override but a different host, or
loopback. TriTrack's exposable deployment therefore exists as a *procedure* —
run the probe, read `proxied`, declare what it said — and not as a machine
anybody has yet stood up. Phase 11 must not assume one exists.

**Violated by:** any deployment exposed on an unmeasured host; a default,
inferred or hardcoded value for `TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY`; qualifying a
deployment by operating system rather than by a probe run; an allowlist treated
as evidence that callers arrive distinguishable.

**Gate C's seventh re-run (2026-08-16) found this enforcement incomplete —
finding L-1, blocking, §14.2.** The refusal above is real and was measured
firing three ways. It does not fire when `TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES` holds a
value that is non-empty and parses to *zero* entries (`,`): the allowlist branch
is taken, `_assertProxySourceIdentityDeclared` is skipped by the
`!allowlist.isEmpty` guard, and the function returns before §4.4.2's own refusal
can ask its question either. A reachable deployment then starts, silently, with
neither question answered — which is I-1 in the shape this section exists to
make impossible. Until task 10.92 lands, **this section describes the intended
control and not the whole of the shipped one.**

#### 4.4.4 The instrument that enforced §4.4.3 could not say yes (task 10.110, 2026-08-19)

§4.4.3 made the exposable deployment conditional on a passing probe run. **The
probe could not produce one.** As shipped it returned `COLLAPSED` for both the
`direct` and `proxied` shapes on *every* Linux host, so no host could ever be
licensed, no deployment could ever be exposed, and the March beta had nowhere to
run. The refusal §4.4.3 built was correct; the instrument implementing it was
not.

**Measured 2026-08-17 on Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 under Parallels Desktop (bridged
networking), Docker installed natively — and contradicted by hand on the same
host in the same session:**

```
verify_source_identity.sh (as shipped)     direct: COLLAPSED   proxied: COLLAPSED
                                           negative control:   PASSED

traefik/whoami published on 18099, two genuinely off-host callers
  phone :  RemoteAddr = 192.168.0.153:62516
  Mac   :  RemoteAddr = 192.168.0.88:61861
```

Distinct real LAN addresses, preserved. **That named configuration does not
collapse source identity, and the probe's verdict was an artefact of its own
method.** Recorded here as evidence about *that configuration* and nothing
wider: `iptables` DNAT normally preserving addresses remains a reason to run the
probe expecting a pass, never a substitute for running it, and "Linux is fine"
is the generalisation §4.4.3 deliberately refused to write.

**The mechanism.** The probe had no off-host caller. It created a second Docker
network and had containers there dial the host's LAN address, so the traffic
left one bridge, touched the host, and was DNAT'd back into another — and Linux
masqueraded that hairpin to the destination bridge's gateway, `172.31.246.1`,
**which is the probe's own gateway and was visible in its own output.** On
Docker Desktop the distinction does not exist, because the whole stack lives in
one VM and the collapse is real and total. The method was authored and validated
where it happened to be sound, and it is not sound on the platform this project
has to deploy on.

**The second defect, which nobody had reported: the same method could have
produced a FALSE PASS.** The hairpin is masqueraded on the Linux configurations
tested, but that is a property of the daemon's iptables rules, not a law. On a
Linux host that does not masquerade it, the two containers keep their own
addresses, and the shipped probe would have printed `PRESERVED` and licensed
`peer-verified` on a host **nobody had measured with any off-host caller at
all**. A false negative blocks a deployment; that one would have opened one.
Both arms are closed by the same change: **Stage A has no PASS branch.**

**The design constraint, stated because it is what makes the fix look the way it
does.** The question needs two real network endpoints, and a probe holding only
containers cannot manufacture one. **A fully automatic verdict is not available
on Linux**, and pretending otherwise is exactly how the defect above happened.

**The shape taken: operator-assisted, and the operator supplies packets rather
than conclusions.**

| Stage | Callers | Can say |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A — automatic screen (default) | containers on a second Docker network | `COLLAPSED` (only when the collapse address is one the host's container substrate cannot explain) or `NO VERDICT`. **Never `PRESERVED`.** |
| B — `--assisted` | two real off-host devices, driven by a human | `PRESERVED`, `COLLAPSED`, or `NO VERDICT` |

Stage B prints one URL per device, waits, reads its own access log and **issues
the verdict itself**. There is no flag, no prompt and no environment variable by
which an operator can assert `PRESERVED`. Every address that arrives is
classified first, against a set of addresses the host is **measured** — not
assumed, not sniffed from `docker info` — to be able to produce on its own:

| Class | Meaning | Can license |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `off-host` | none of the below | **yes, and only this** |
| `loopback` | 127.0.0.0/8 | no |
| `host-interface` | configured on one of this host's interfaces | no |
| `container-subnet` | inside a Docker network on this host — either a container called in, or a real caller was rewritten to a bridge gateway, and the probe cannot tell those apart | no |
| `rewrite-artifact` | what this host is observed to arrive as when it calls its own published port (Docker Desktop: `192.168.65.1`) — a real caller arriving as this has had its address destroyed | no, and it is **positive evidence of collapse** |

Stage A's confound test falls straight out of that table: if the two containers
collapse onto a `container-subnet` address, that is the hairpin and the stage
reports `NO VERDICT`; if they collapse onto anything else, no innocent
explanation exists and the collapse is real.

**The negative control was re-examined, because it passed beside two wrong
verdicts and §12.11 exists for exactly that.** The old control proved the probe
could tell preservation from collapse *on the on-network path* — a path that
crosses no publish path at all — while the verdicts beside it were about the
off-host path. It is kept, demoted to control 3, and now prints its own limit
instead of the sentence it used to print about the verdicts meaning something.
Two controls were added that can fail for the off-host path:

- **Control 1 — attribution.** Every address produced by the probe's own
  containers, which are provably on this host and are *exactly the callers the
  old method mistook for off-host*, must classify as not-`off-host`. If one of
  them is ever called `off-host`, the machinery that gates every PASS is broken
  and the probe refuses to report anything. This is the regression control for
  this finding.
- **Control 2 — falsifiability.** The verdict engine is run over synthetic
  observations and must return `PRESERVED` for a distinct off-host pair,
  `COLLAPSED` for an identical one, and `NO VERDICT` for a pair containing a
  local address. **This is what would have caught the original defect as a
  regression: it asserts the PASS branch exists and is reachable**, which is the
  property the shipped probe had silently lost.

All three controls were demonstrated failing, not asserted:
`TRITRACK_PROBE_SELFTEST=blind-filter` disables the classifier and control 1
fires (`a container ON THIS HOST … arrived as 192.168.65.1 and the classifier
called it off-host`, exit 1); `TRITRACK_PROBE_SELFTEST=break-machinery` gives
the two on-network clients one address and control 3 fires (exit 1). Both modes
exit non-zero whatever they find and license nothing.

**Measured after the rebuild, 2026-08-19:**

| Run | Result |
| --- | --- |
| macOS 26.6, Docker Desktop 29.6.2, Stage A | `direct` **COLLAPSED**, `proxied` **COLLAPSED**, all three controls pass, exit 1 — the §4.4.3 verdict is unchanged and the macOS diagnosis is not regressed |
| macOS, Stage B, **two genuinely off-host LAN callers** (`192.168.0.136` and `192.168.0.211`, a separate bridged machine with its own MAC) | both arrived as `192.168.65.1` → **COLLAPSED**, decisive. The macOS collapse is now measured with real off-host traffic rather than inferred from containers |
| Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 / Parallels bridged / native Docker, Stage A | `direct` **NO VERDICT**, `proxied` **NO VERDICT** — both containers arrived as `172.31.246.1`, named as the hairpin confound. **The false `COLLAPSED` is gone** |
| Same host, Stage B, one real off-host caller (`192.168.0.88`) | `direct-a` and `proxied-a` both recorded `192.168.0.88`, classified `off-host` — **that host's publish path preserves a real off-host address on both shapes**. Device 2 was left unfilled, so the probe reported **NO VERDICT** and licensed nothing |
