| Same host, Stage B, deliberately manufactured traffic into device 2 — from the host itself, from a container on the host, and from loopback | every one rejected (`192.168.0.136 — an address configured on this host`), the slot stayed unfilled, and the run ended `NO VERDICT`. **Traffic a host manufactures for itself cannot fill a device slot** |

**What is still owed, stated rather than left to be discovered.** The final
two-device `PRESERVED` run on the candidate host is **task 10.88's**, and it
needs a human with two devices — that is the shape of the instrument, not an
omission in it. Until 10.88 records that run, no host is licensed, and the
consequence §4.4.3 stated plainly still holds: TriTrack's exposable deployment
exists as a *procedure*, not as a machine anybody has stood up.

**Violated by:** an instrument that can only return the refusing verdict; a
probe that treats a container on the host as an off-host caller; a control whose
only failure mode is on a path other than the one the verdicts describe; an
operator-assertable PASS; recording a probe run as evidence for anything wider
than the named configuration it was run on.

### 4.5 Account enumeration

**Decision.** `POST /auth/magic-link` returns an identical response — same
status (202), same body, same headers — for a registered address, an
unregistered address, and a rate-limited address.

**Timing is part of the response.** The registered path does database work and
sends an email; a naive unregistered path does neither and returns measurably
faster. Mitigations, both required: **enqueue the email asynchronously** so the
response returns before delivery either way, and **perform the same database
lookup in both paths**.

**Decision on unregistered addresses: send the link anyway; create the user row
on successful redemption, never on request.**

Reasoning, because this decision has two failure modes and both are worse:

- *Reject unregistered addresses* → the response necessarily differs, and the
  enumeration oracle is back. Every mitigation above becomes theater.
- *Create a user row on request* → an unauthenticated endpoint that writes rows
  is a database-pollution vector and a second enumeration oracle (row exists ⇒
  address was requested).

Creating on redemption keeps responses identical, keeps the write path behind
proof of mailbox control, and composes with Phase 11: somebody admitted to a
project gets their placeholder user row from the **approving owner's**
authenticated, rate-limited action, without opening the unauthenticated write
path. (Until task 11.81 that action was an invitation; it is now an approval,
and the composition is unchanged — see §4.17.)

**Residual risk, accepted and bounded:** TriTrack can be induced to send a small
number of emails to an arbitrary address. Bounded by the per-email daily cap
(§4.4) and by the email body containing **no attacker-controlled content** — no
"requested by" field, no free text, no referring URL — so it cannot be used as a
message-delivery channel. Record this in 10.16's residual-risk summary.

**Also enumeration surfaces, easy to forget:** sign-in error messages and
project-join responses. "That user is not registered" is the same leak in a
different costume.

**Task 11.81 removed one of these surfaces and added a different one, and both
belong here.** The invite-by-email flow is gone, so there is no longer any route
that takes a third party's address at all — nothing left to distinguish a
registered invitee from an unregistered one. What replaced it discloses
something else: **a correct guess of a project's join code confirms that the
project exists**, because you cannot tell somebody their request to join was
sent without confirming there is something to join. That is inherent to the
design rather than a defect, it is bounded by the per-user rate limit and by the
fact that a *code* is being guessed rather than a project id enumerated, and it
is written into security inventory entry 24 rather than left to be found.

**What this section does not forbid, settled by task 11.298 (2026-09-21): a
`400` keyed on the syntax of the address the caller supplied.** The boundary
has always answered `400 invalid_email` to a string with no `@` in it, and
nobody read that as enumeration, because it is not: the verdict is a function
of the caller's own input, computed by a fixed rule that is the same on every
deployment and readable in this repository, and the caller can reach the same
verdict without asking the server. What §4.5 protects is a fact about *server
state* — whether an account exists — and a syntax refusal reads none. Task
11.298 made the rule the boundary applies the same rule the SMTP sender
applies (`isAcceptableSignInAddress` is defined as the sender's
`isDeliverableAddress` on the normalized string, and a corpus test holds them
equal in both directions), so an address the mail path will not carry — a
non-ASCII local part, a quoted or bracketed form — is refused with a `400`
the app renders as a sentence about the address, instead of the `202` and
silence it got before. **Three of the four addresses the plan named were in
that gap — `üser@example.com` reproduced on a live relay, the other two against
the route in a test — and the person got "sent" and nothing arrived.** The
identity of the `202` between registered and unregistered addresses is
untouched, and the same test that held it before (`auth_route_security_test`)
still does.

**Reopen trigger, and it is specific.** This argument rests on the rule being
a *constant*. The day the sender's rule becomes a property of the relay it is
pointed at — the obvious shape being SMTPUTF8 detected from the relay's `EHLO`
at startup, so that a non-ASCII address is refused on one deployment and
carried on another — a `400` starts to disclose which relay a deployment uses,
which is reconnaissance in §4.13's sense even though it is still nothing about
accounts. That change re-reads this paragraph before it ships; the honest
options then are a rule fixed at build time regardless of relay, or a `202`
for the relay-dependent cases with the refusal moved back behind the boundary
where an operator can see it.

**The finding beside it, recorded so nobody inflates it later.** The sender's
address refusal used to fire its delivery-outcome callback *synchronously*,
inside the request, on the one path that never opens a socket — and the
`undelivered` audit row landed 2 ms *before* the `sent` row on a live server.
**That was not a §4.5 oracle**: the timing keyed on the syntax the caller
chose, not on whether an account exists, and the boundary now refuses that
syntax before the sender sees it. It was a false invariant — task 11.293's
tests asserted the callback fires only after the sender returns and exercised
the two paths that reach an `await`, not the one that did not. Both halves are
fixed: the sender starts every delivery in a microtask, and the route orders
the two rows itself rather than trusting the sender's speed, which a relay
with its port closed would also have beaten.

**Violated by:** any response difference between registered and unregistered;
a synchronous email send; an unauthenticated route that creates rows; a
project-join refusal that distinguishes a wrong code from a real project whose
owner has switched joining off.

### 4.6 Secrets management

**Decision.**

- **Environment variables only.** No secret in a source file, a default value, a
  test fixture, a comment, or a committed config file.
- **`.env` for local development, gitignored.** Add `.env` and `.env.*` to
  `.gitignore` with a `!.env.example` exception. The current `.gitignore` has no
  such pattern — see §6.
- **`.env.example` is committed**, with every required key present and every
  value empty. The required set must be discoverable without possessing a
  secret.
- **The server refuses to start** if a required secret is missing, empty, or
  matches a known placeholder. **No dev fallback defaults, ever.** Reasoning: a
  default that works is the mechanism by which prototypes reach production with
  a known credential. Failing to start is loud, immediate, and harmless. Fail
  closed (§1.5).
- **Committed-secret check** in CI or a pre-commit hook. 10.16 verifies the
  full git history, not just the working tree — a secret removed in a later
  commit is still published.

**Phase 10 secret inventory:** the Postgres password, and the SMTP credentials.
That is the whole list, deliberately: no signing key (no JWTs, §4.3), no pepper
(§4.2). Keeping the list this short is itself a control.

**The SMTP credential became real on 2026-09-20 (task 11.287)** and is
`TRITRACK_SMTP_PASSWORD`: checked against the placeholder list at startup, never
printed on any path including the failure line, and already inside the
committed-secrets test's `SMTP_PASSWORD` pattern — **which is worth stating
plainly, because a pattern that happens to match is not the same as a pattern
written for this and the next credential may not be so lucky.** It is optional:
a relay that trusts the host's address needs no password, and the sender refuses
credentials on an unencrypted connection anywhere.

**Rotation procedure, documented per secret in the server README (10.14):**

1. Create the new credential alongside the old one.
2. Update the environment.
3. Restart.
4. Revoke the old credential.

Non-breaking for both Postgres and SMTP. For a **suspected database dump**,
additionally: rotate the Postgres password, and revoke all sessions. Note the
reasoning on what is *not* needed — token hashes in a dump are not usable
tokens, so magic links do not require mass invalidation on hash exposure alone.
Revoke sessions anyway; it is cheap and the blast radius if wrong is a round of
sign-ins.

**Violated by:** a secret with a working default; a secret in the repo at any
point in history; a `.env` that is committed; a server that starts with a
missing secret; a secret passed as a command-line argument (visible in the
process table).

### 4.7 Audit logging, and what must never be logged

**Decision: two logs, separated because their retention differs and their
sensitivity differs.**

**Authentication audit log — retained 1 year.** Events: magic link requested,
redeemed, redemption failed, session created, session revoked (with actor and
reason), rate limit tripped, authorization denied. Fields: timestamp, event,
`user_id` if known, normalized email, `device_id`, source address, outcome.
One year, because "was my account compromised in March?" is a question that gets
asked in September.

**Data-access log — retained 180 days.** Per sync request: `user_id`,
`device_id`, `project_id`, cursor in and out, rows pushed, pulled, rejected by
validation, rejected by authorization, and **rows that lost last-write-wins**,
plus errors. 180 days because it must outlive a field season — the question
this log answers ("where did my observation go?") arrives when someone sits
down with the data at the end of the season, not the next day.

**Deliberately not logged: individual row reads.** A sync request legitimately
reads thousands of rows; per-row read logging would be enormous, useless, and —
critically — would put coordinates in the log. Log counts and cursor positions.

Both logs are the same store the diagnostics console (10.13) reads. One
recording mechanism, two consumers.

**Retention is a mechanism, as of task 11.79 (2026-09-01).** It was a policy
for six consecutive gates — named at every one and rated blocking by none — and
this paragraph used to say so. `docker compose up` now starts an
`audit-retention` service that sweeps whenever a row passes its window, and its
healthcheck reports **the age of the oldest surviving row**, never whether the
sweep is running: a wedged loop, a stopped container and a database it cannot
write to all go red, because to a person they are one fact. Watched going red on
a real stack. Two further defects surfaced while closing it, and both were
invisible for the same reason — **nothing ran the thing, so nothing could report
that it did not work**: the documented command needed a Dart SDK the shipped
image does not contain, and the sweep ran as the role task 10.83 had revoked
`DELETE` on both audit tables from.

**A third class joined the two above: decided join requests, 30 days** (task
11.79, widening task 11.85's finding R-2). A person who asked to join a project
and was turned down has no reason to be a row on this server a year later, or a
rejection on their screen for ever. **Undecided requests are never swept** — a
pending request is somebody waiting for an answer, and deleting it would answer
them by silence.

**The audit tables cannot erase their own record of a compromise** (task
10.83). The role every persistent server connection runs as (task 10.63) is
granted `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE` on every table `ON ALL TABLES` — a
snapshot that, left unnarrowed, includes `DELETE`/`TRUNCATE` on
`auth_audit_log` and `sync_traffic_log` themselves. Demonstrated live: 310
rows removed through that exact connection. `DELETE` and `TRUNCATE` on both
tables are now revoked from that role on every start (`ensureServerAppRole`),
narrower than the broad grant it follows. This is post-compromise forensic
integrity, not a route to B1–B3 on its own — an attacker must already hold the
server process to reach it — which is why it was scheduled rather than
blocking (§15.6). If the retention purge above is ever implemented, it must
run under its own, narrower-scoped credential rather than reopening this
grant.

> **Which sweep runs as which role, stated 2026-09-21 (task 11.291) because the
> sentence above reads as though it covers all of them and it does not.** The
> *audit* purge (task 11.79) is the one that got its own narrower credential, and
> it needed one because its target is the forensic tables this grant was narrowed
> to protect. **The tombstone purge runs as `tritrack_app`**, on task 11.290's
> reasoning: its targets are ordinary project rows that the application role
> already deletes on every soft delete, so a separate credential would name a
> narrower set of tables than the role already touches for the same rows — an
> assurance with nothing behind it. **The distinction is what the sweep deletes,
> not that it is a sweep**, and a future sweep is asked the same question rather
> than inheriting either answer.

**That sentence was load-bearing and nobody had read it back** (task 11.79).
The purge entrypoint demoted itself to exactly this role, with a comment saying
that role's DML already covered its deletes — true when written, false from the
moment 10.83 landed. It went unnoticed because nothing ran it. The sweep now
runs as `tritrack_retention`: `NOLOGIN`, assumed with `SET ROLE` on an
already-authenticated admin connection like `tritrack_app` and
`tritrack_restore`, holding `SELECT, DELETE` on the three retention tables and
nothing else — no read of field data, no write anywhere. **10.83's property is
intact**: the long-lived server connection still cannot erase the record of
itself, and `server/test/security/retention_role_test.dart` asserts both halves
together, so a "fix" that re-granted `DELETE` to `tritrack_app` fails.

**Never logged, at any level, in any environment, client or server:**

1. Magic-link tokens or any prefix of one.
2. Session tokens or any prefix of one. Log the `session_id`, never the token.
3. The `Authorization` header. Redact it in every request-logging middleware.
4. Full URLs for the magic-link redemption route — strip query strings for that
   path entirely.
5. Database connection strings and SMTP credentials.
6. **Observation coordinates.** Latitude, longitude, and bearing values do not
   appear in any log line, exception message, crash report, or console output.
7. Full row bodies on validation failure. Log the table, the row id, and the
   *name* of the failing field — never its value.

**Rule 6 is the app-specific one and it is the one that will get broken by
accident.** A log line with a lat/lon in it turns every log file, log
aggregator, crash reporter, CI artifact, and terminal scrollback into an
uncontrolled copy of asset 1 — sitting entirely outside every access control
built for the database. Debugging a merge disagreement needs the row id, the
`revision`, and the `updated_at`; it does not need the coordinate. Applies to
the Flutter client's `debugPrint` too, not only the server.

**Violated by:** any of the seven above appearing anywhere; a request-logging
middleware without header redaction; per-row read logging; retention that
quietly grows without bound.

**Denial-audit volume, re-derived at task 10.34 against 10.29's fallout.**
`maxAuditFieldLength` (10.30, §7 D-2) bounds every free-text field
`AuthAuditLog.record` writes, sized against the write it was built to stop: a
caller-controlled `project_id` landing in `outcome` for a **project-level**
`403`, from `refusePush`/the pull `403`/the ack `403`
(`sync_routes.dart:199, 487, 551`) — the only three call sites `auditDenial`
has. Task 10.29 moved the per-row `unauthorized` outcome from corner case to
common case, which raised the question of whether that made these writes
common too. **It did not, and that is D-4's whole point stated the other way
round:** a row-level refusal answers inside a `200`, `auditDenial` is never on
that path, and the only server-side trace is the fixed-width `rows_rejected`
integer on `sync_traffic_log` (180-day log, §4.7 above) — one bounded column
per push, regardless of how many rows it refuses. So the volume the
one-year authentication log actually carries is unchanged by 10.29: a
project-level `403` still requires a caller with no relationship to the
project at all, which importing an unlinked colleague's observation does not
produce (the caller *is* a project member; only the row's *named* person or
tag is outside it). **The existing bound holds and does not need widening or
narrowing.** The volume question that does follow from this — what a *future*
fix for D-4 must budget for before it writes anything — is recorded against
D-4 itself in §8.4, not here, since it is a decision for whoever picks that
task up, not a change to a decision already shipped.

### 4.8 Device-local encryption at rest — decided: no SQLCipher

**Decision: TriTrack does not adopt SQLCipher in Phase 10.** Instead, three
cheaper controls that address the same scenario more effectively. This is a
decision, not a deferral.

**The scenario to reason about, as the plan frames it:** a stolen field phone
holding a season of nest locations.

**What SQLCipher would actually defend:** offline extraction of the SQLite file
from a device the attacker has but has *not* unlocked.

**Why that is nearly empty in practice.** On iOS and Android with a passcode
set, the app sandbox is already covered by file-based/full-disk encryption keyed
to that passcode. SQLCipher adds a second layer over the same threat with the
same dependency — the key has to live in the keychain or keystore, which is
itself gated on the same passcode and the same hardware. It duplicates the
control rather than adding one.

**What it does not defend, which is the realistic loss:** a device that is
*unlocked* when it is lost or handed to someone. A phone in use in the field is
unlocked most of the time it is out of a pocket. SQLCipher is transparently
open in that state.

**The cost side, and this is what settles it.** Swapping to
`sqflite_sqlcipher`, a key ceremony at every launch, and a measurable write
penalty on the write-heavy field capture path — but the real cost is a new
catastrophic failure mode. **A lost key means the season's data is gone.** This
app's users are field biologists and graduate students, not people with a
key-escrow procedure. Against asset 2 (integrity *and availability* of an
unrepeatable field record), that risk is larger than the narrow confidentiality
gain, which the OS already largely provides.

**What we do instead:**

1. **Session tokens live in the platform keychain/keystore** —
   `flutter_secure_storage` or equivalent — and **never** in SharedPreferences
   and never in the SQLite database. This is the highest-value part of this
   decision and it is not optional. A plaintext token on a lost device grants
   *live, ongoing* access to everything the project will ever contain, which is
   strictly worse than the static local copy SQLCipher would have protected.
   New dependency; justified here; adopted by 10.6 (see §6 — 10.6's spec does
   not currently name it).
2. **Expect a device passcode, and say so.** Detect via platform API whether a
   passcode/biometric is set. If not, warn — clearly, once, non-blockingly.
   Do not block: locking a field tech out of a capture tool mid-survey is a
   worse outcome than the risk. For projects handling poaching-target species,
   "devices must have a passcode" is a stated deployment requirement rather than
   a software control.
3. **Per-device revocation (§4.3) is the actual mitigation.** A lost device is
   cut off from anything new within seconds, and the device registry shows
   precisely which cursor it had reached — so the exposure is a known, bounded
   set of rows rather than an unknown one. That answer ("here is exactly what
   that phone had") is more useful to a project lead than encryption would have
   been.

**Revisit triggers, recorded so this is not silently permanent.** Adopt
SQLCipher if any of: (a) a supported platform lacks OS-level full-disk
encryption (a Windows or Linux desktop target); (b) an institutional
data-management plan or IRB condition requires encryption at rest independently
of OS FDE; (c) a real device-loss incident occurs and the retrospective says
otherwise. Any of those is a new task, not a quiet swap.

**Violated by:** a session token in SharedPreferences or the app database; a
token in a plaintext file; adopting SQLCipher without a key-recovery story;
blocking app use on passcode presence.

> **Status note (task 10.79, 2026-09-09).** Control 2 (detect the device's
> lock state, warn once, never block) is now built —
> `lib/core/providers/device_lock_provider.dart`, using
> `LocalAuthentication.isDeviceSupported()` to ask the platform whether a
> passcode/PIN/pattern or biometric-with-fallback is configured, surfaced as a
> dismissible tile on the More screen. First flagged at task 10.40's audit
> (2026-08-13); unbuilt and unrecorded for three gates until now.
>
> **L-10, the platform's own backup channel, is an accepted risk on both
> Android and iOS — not open, and not closed.** §3.7's device-local storage
> finding always assumed the OS sandbox holds; on Android, Auto Backup
> silently copies that sandbox — including `tri_track.db` — to the user's
> Google account regardless, and iOS/iCloud backup does the same via
> `getApplicationSupportDirectory()`. Task 10.79 closed the Android channel
> with `android:allowBackup="false"`. **Task 11.215 (2026-09-10, Michael's
> decision) reopened it deliberately**, after weighing the trade Task 10.79
> made without asking: a phone lost in a canyon is far likelier than a stolen
> cloud account, and the records at risk are the same set either way — the
> ones not yet on the server. For a field app used for days at a time with no
> signal, that redundancy is worth more than the exposure, for essentially
> every project this app serves. **The remedy for the rare project that
> cannot accept the exposure** — working with a species whose location cannot
> afford to leak — **is a user-side control, not an app setting**: a person
> can turn backup off for this app alone in the phone's own settings. iOS has
> always had this; Android gained it in the June 2026 per-app backup control
> rollout. A user guide page (task `/w-17`) documents this for that reader.
> **macOS is a different threat model** (Time Machine requires the user's own
> attached destination) and is not carried as an open or accepted item.

### 4.9 Backup encryption (server database)

> **Note for anyone reading the gate findings below or in §18–§22, added 2026-09-01.** Until
> that date this repository asserted in several places — `docker-compose.yml` among them — that
> `backups/` was *"the directory you sync to encrypted-at-rest storage."* **Nothing synced it,
> and no off-site copy has ever existed.** This section is corrected. **The historical finding
> rows are deliberately not corrected**: they are the record of what was believed when each
> round ran, and rewriting them would destroy the ability to see how the belief formed. **Read
> any pre-2026-09-01 reference to "the off-site copy" as an assumption, not a fact.**

> **Status note (task 10.14, 2026-08-07): NOT implemented, and deliberately so.**
> The Appendix assigns this section to 10.14, but the plan's 10.14 task entry
> does not list it among its nine bullets — a genuine doc/plan disagreement,
> resolved here rather than silently one way or the other.
>
> **It stays open, because its own stated precondition is unmet.** §6 item 8
> requires a custody arrangement for the backup private key — an offline copy and
> a second holder — "before the first backup that matters", and no such
> arrangement exists. Writing the `pg_dump | age` pipeline now would produce
> archives encrypted to a key with no custody story, which satisfies the letter
> of this section while leaving the actual recovery risk (lost key ⇒ lost
> backups) worse than having no backup automation at all. There is also no
> deployed server to back up: this is an operational task for whoever stands one
> up, not client or server code.
>
> Filed under Phase 10's Discovered Scope with its precondition named. Task
> 10.16's audit should treat §4.9 as **open**, not as satisfied by 10.14.

> **Superseded by task 10.24 (2026-08-09), which closed Gate C finding C-4.**
> The precondition above is what 10.24 addressed first: §4.9.1 below is the
> custody arrangement, decided before any code was written, and the pipeline
> exists only because it does. The status note stays visible rather than being
> deleted, because "we deferred this deliberately and here is the condition"
> is the part of the record worth keeping.

**Decision.** Server database backups are **always** encrypted, using
public-key encryption (`age` or GPG) whose **private key is not on the server**.
`pg_dump` output is piped directly into the encryptor and plaintext never lands
on disk, not even in a temp directory.

**Reasoning.** A backup is a complete copy of the highest-ranked asset in the
system, and it is the artifact most likely to end up somewhere unmanaged — a
laptop, a cloud drive, a departing student's external disk. Public-key
encryption specifically, so that the backup job needs no decryption secret on
the box: a host compromise already yields the live database, and it must not
*also* yield every historical snapshot in plaintext.

**Two operational requirements that are part of the decision, not extras:**

- **A backup that has never been restored is not a backup.** Restore-test on a
  documented cadence. An encrypted backup nobody can decrypt is a data-loss
  event wearing a control's clothing — which is the same failure mode §4.8
  refused to accept on devices, so it must not be accepted here either. The
  private key needs a real custody arrangement (offline copy, second holder)
  before the first backup that matters.
- **Retention is bounded and old backups are deleted on schedule.** Every
  retained backup is another full copy of asset 1. Keeping them forever
  increases exposure monotonically for decreasing value.

**Violated by:** an unencrypted dump anywhere, including transiently on disk;
the private key stored on the server or in the repo; a backup path nobody has
restored from; unbounded retention.

**Every archive is on the same machine as the database it protects, and nothing
carries it anywhere else** (task 11.80, recorded 2026-09-01). This section, and
§4.9.2, and the gate findings below, all reason about "the off-site copy" — the
public-key choice exists precisely **so that the machine taking the backup and
the destination holding it cannot read the contents.** That argument presumes a
destination. **There is none.** No script, no step, no instruction anywhere in
the repository moves an archive off the host, and the restore drill has never
restored from a copy that is not on it.

**What that costs, counted:** ten tables live nowhere else — `auth_accounts`,
`auth_sessions`, `auth_magic_links`, `auth_link_requests`, `auth_audit_log`,
`project_invites`, `sync_cursors`, `sync_seq_counter`, `sync_traffic_log`,
`tombstone_purge_floor`. **Losing the machine does not lose field data**; every
device holds its own. It loses every account, every session, the sign-in audit
trail, outstanding invitations, and the numbered line every device's sync
bookmark points into — task 11.58's failure by another road.

**Not the app's cloud backup returning.** That was removed on 2026-08-30 (task
11.30) and it was **unencrypted project data, on by default, to a third party.**
This is an archive encrypted to a key the destination does not hold, signed
against forgery, moved deliberately to a destination the operator chose. Neither
decision bears on the other, and this paragraph exists so nobody reads one as
undoing the other.

**The destination is an unmade decision, not an unimplemented one.** Michael was
asked on 2026-09-01 and chose to wait: part of the answer belongs to NAU — where
an encrypted off-host copy may live, and whether they would prefer a location
they provide — and that question sits in the unsent hosting letter. **Until it is
answered, the gap is stated where an operator will meet it** rather than left
implied: `scripts/backup_status.sh` prints it on every run, the restore drill
ends by saying it has never exercised an off-machine copy, and `server/README.md`
carries the reasoning under "Where the archive is not". When a destination
exists, whatever carries the archive is to be measured the way task 11.78
measures the schedule — **check that a recent archive is present at the
destination**, with fresh, stale, absent and unreachable as four distinguishable
sentences — and the drill must restore from that copy or say plainly that it has
not.

### 4.9.1 Key custody — who holds it, where, what if it is lost, who can decrypt

**Authored by task 10.24 (2026-08-09), before the pipeline was written**, because
§6 item 8 made it a precondition and because this is the one decision in Phase 10
with no undo: an archive's recipients are fixed at the moment it is written, so
a custody mistake is only discovered during a recovery, when it is too late to
fix. Four questions, answered concretely.

**Who holds the key.** Two holders, each with their **own** `age` identity. Every
archive is encrypted to both recipients (`age -r A -r B`), so either can restore
alone and **no private key is ever copied from one person to the other**.

| | Who | Constraint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Holder 1 | The person who runs the server — currently the PI, Michael Shafer | — |
| Holder 2 | A second person, named at deployment | **Must not be the server administrator**, and must not be a student or field assistant on the project |

Holder 2's name is blank in this document on purpose: there is no deployed
server yet, and inventing a name here would be the same kind of paper control
this section exists to refuse. **It must be filled in before the first backup of
real data** — that is the trigger, not a date. Until then the single-recipient
path is what runs, and the backup job prints a warning on every single run
saying so.

*Why two recipients rather than one key with two copies.* Copying a private key
multiplies the places it can leak, and the second copy is invariably the one
nobody tracks — an old laptop, a shared drive, an email to oneself. Two
recipients gives the same redundancy with holder 2's key never leaving holder 2.

**Where the keys live.** Each holder's private key exists in exactly two places:

- On that holder's own machine, at `~/.config/tritrack/backup-identity.txt`,
  mode `0600`. Not on the server. Not in the repository. Not in the cloud
  storage the archives are copied to — a key stored beside its ciphertext is a
  decorative key, and that destination is precisely the "somewhere unmanaged"
  this section is about.
- One offline copy. An `age` identity is a single line of text, so the offline
  copy is that line **written on paper, sealed, and stored somewhere physically
  separate from the machine** — a locked office drawer, a home safe. Paper does
  not have a firmware bug and does not silently fail after four years in a
  drawer, which is more than can be said for the USB stick it is replacing.

The **public** recipient strings are not secret. They live in `.env` as
`TRITRACK_BACKUP_RECIPIENTS`, and it is fine for them to appear in
documentation, tickets, or a commit. That asymmetry is the entire reason §4.9
chose public-key encryption: the machine taking the backups cannot read one.

**What happens if a key is lost.** Stated as blast radius, because this is what
someone will need at the worst possible moment:

- **One holder's key lost, the other intact:** *nothing is lost.* The surviving
  holder decrypts. Recovery is a rotation: the affected holder generates a new
  identity, `TRITRACK_BACKUP_RECIPIENTS` gains it, and archives written from
  that point are readable by both again. Older archives are readable by the
  survivor and simply age out under retention.
- **Every holder's key lost:** **every existing archive is permanently
  unreadable. There is no escrow, no recovery service, and no vendor to call.**
  What is *not* lost is the live database — this key protects backups, not the
  running system. So total key loss is the loss of *history and
  disaster-recovery capability*, not of current data, and the correct response
  is: generate new identities that day, rotate the recipients, take a fresh
  backup immediately, and **delete the old archives**. They are worth nothing to
  the project and remain a full copy of asset 1 to anyone who ever recovers a
  key.
- There is deliberately **no break-glass copy on the server.** Adding one would
  restore exactly the property this section exists to prevent — a host
  compromise yielding every historical snapshot as well as the live database —
  and it would do so silently, since a break-glass key looks like prudence right
  up until it is used by someone else.

**Who can decrypt.** Only the two holders of the private keys. Explicitly *not*:
the server, the backup job, the container, anyone holding the Postgres password,
anyone with read access to the archive directory or the cloud storage it is
synced to, and no student or field assistant at any point. Changing that set is
an edit to `TRITRACK_BACKUP_RECIPIENTS`, and it applies **only to archives
written afterwards** — recipients cannot be added to an archive retroactively,
which is why the second holder has to be arranged before the backups matter
rather than after.

**Three obligations that are part of the arrangement, not extras:**

1. **Restore drill quarterly**, and after any change to the schema, the backup
   image, or the pinned `age` or `minisign` version (§4.9.2).
   `scripts/backup_restore_drill.sh` runs it
   unattended against a throwaway stack; the log lives in `server/README.md`.
2. **Retention stays bounded** — 30 archives by default, pruned newest-first on
   every run, because every retained archive is another full copy of asset 1.
3. **A holder leaving is a key-rotation event**, and it is the §2.1 case in
   miniature. The departing holder's key still decrypts every archive written
   while they held it, so rotating the recipients is not sufficient on its own:
   the archives from their tenure must be deleted, or re-encrypted to the new
   recipient set, and the retention window is the honest upper bound on how long
   that exposure lasts.

> **Amended by task 10.43 (2026-08-14), which closed Gate C finding H-6.**
> Everything above answers *who may **read*** an archive, and it answers it
> well. It does not say who may **write** one that the restore path will
> trust, and the third Gate C re-run reproduced that live: an archive forged
> with nothing but the public recipient string this section publishes was
> promoted over the live database and executed as a Postgres superuser.
> §4.9.2 below is the missing half — the custody arrangement for the key that
> answers the *other* question. Read the two together; neither is complete
> alone.

**Implemented by task 10.24 as:** `server/backup/` (image, `backup.sh`,
`restore.sh`), `scripts/backup_db.sh`, `scripts/restore_db.sh`, and
`scripts/backup_restore_drill.sh`; the `backup` profile in `docker-compose.yml`.
The pipeline runs wholly inside one container so plaintext never crosses a
filesystem, refuses to run with no recipients configured rather than falling
back to anything, and builds each archive under a `.part` name that is only
renamed after `pg_dump` *and* `age` have both succeeded — without that,
`pipefail` off, a dump that dies halfway produces a well-formed archive of a
truncated database, which is the failure this whole section is trying to avoid
wearing a control's clothing.

### 4.9.2 Archive origin — who may *write* a backup the restore path trusts

**Authored by task 10.43 (2026-08-14), after Gate C finding H-6 reproduced
live.** §4.9.1 is a custody arrangement for the key that decides who may
**read** an archive. This is the custody arrangement for the key that decides
who may **write** one, and it exists because for three tasks nothing did.

**The finding, in one sentence.** An archive forged with nothing but the
public recipient string — which §4.9.1 says out loud may appear "in
documentation, tickets, or a commit" — passed every check `restore.sh` made,
had its SQL piped into `psql` as a Postgres **superuser**, and was renamed into
the live database name. Reproduced at `scripts/verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh`.

**Why every check passed.** `restore.sh` gated a restore on a checksum file, a
schema-marker file, and a successful `age` decrypt. The first two sit in the
archive directory, so whoever can write one can write all three. The third is
the one that looks like cryptography and is not: **`age` proves the bytes were
not altered after encryption, and says nothing about who encrypted them.**
Anyone holding the public half can produce a file that decrypts perfectly under
the operator's private half. That is not a flaw in `age`; it is what public-key
encryption is. The flaw was reading it as authentication.

#### The decision

**Every archive is signed on the machine that produced it, and the restore path
verifies that signature against a key configured with the restore procedure —
never one found beside the archive.**

`age` has no signing mode, so this is a separate primitive: **`minisign`**
(Ed25519), pinned in `server/backup/Dockerfile` alongside `age`.

**What is signed, and why it is not just the archive.** The signature covers the
archive bytes, and `minisign`'s *trusted comment* — which is itself signed —
carries the archive's SHA-256, its `schema_major` and its `schema_version`. One
signature therefore binds **all three** of the things `restore.sh` checks. The
`.sha256` and `.schema` sidecars stay, because reading them needs no tooling and
no key, but they stop being what the script decides on: where a sidecar and the
signature disagree, the signature wins and the disagreement is reported as *"a
file in the archive directory was written by something other than the backup
job"*, which is what it is.

#### Where the keys live, and why the answer is the opposite of §4.9.1's

| | §4.9.1's `age` identities | This signing key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answers | who may **read** an archive | who may **write** one that is trusted |
| Private half lives | on the two holders' own machines, **never on the server** | **on the machine that takes backups**, and nowhere else |
| Public half | `TRITRACK_BACKUP_RECIPIENTS`, needs only to be *correct* | `TRITRACK_BACKUP_VERIFY_KEY`, needs to be **authentic** |
| Holders | two people, deliberately | none — it belongs to the machine |
| Losing it costs | every historical archive, permanently | nothing but future verifiability |

The reversal is not an inconsistency, it is the point. A backup job runs
unattended at 3am and must sign without a human, so the signing key has to be
where the job is. §4.9 keeps the *decryption* keys off that machine because a
host compromise already yields the live database and must not also yield every
historical snapshot. A host compromise yielding the *signing* key adds nothing:
whoever holds it already owns the database it signs backups of. **The signing
key defends against exactly the party §4.9 deliberately trusts with ciphertext
and had never thought about as an author** — the off-site copy, the cloud
drive, the sync target, and the incident-time invitation in `restore.sh`'s own
error text to *"fetch another copy"*.

**The verifying key is public but must be authentic**, and that is a different
property from secret. It lives in `.env` as `TRITRACK_BACKUP_VERIFY_KEY`, with
the restore procedure, and is written into `server/README.md`'s drill log at the
moment it is generated. It is **never** read from the archive directory: *an
archive directory that supplies its own verifying key verifies nothing*, which
is H-6 with one extra step. `TRITRACK_BACKUP_VERIFY_KEY` accepts a list, so a
signing-key rotation does not strand the archives written before it.

#### Loss and rotation, stated as blast radius

- **Signing key lost or destroyed:** no data is lost and no archive becomes
  unreadable. Generate a new pair, publish the new verifying key with the
  restore procedure, take a fresh signed backup. Archives signed by the old key
  stay decryptable; they simply become unattributable and fall under the
  never-in-place rule below until they age out under retention. Keep the old
  verifying key in the list until then.
- **Signing key compromised:** the holder can forge archives — and already owns
  the server, so they can also write the live database directly. Rotate, and
  treat every archive written after the compromise as unattributable. This is
  strictly less bad than the §4.9.1 case, which is why the key is allowed to
  live where it does.
- **A holder leaving is not a signing-key event.** This key belongs to the
  machine, not to a person; §4.9.1's rotation obligation is unchanged and
  separate. A *server* rebuild is the event that rotates this one.

#### The two enforcement points, and why they are asymmetric

**Taking a backup with no signing key WARNS. Restoring one REFUSES.** That
asymmetry is deliberate and is the opposite of §4.9's recipients rule, so it is
worth being explicit about why:

- An **unencrypted** archive is a disclosure that cannot be undone, so §4.9
  refuses to write one. There is no unencrypted path.
- An **unsigned** archive is a complete, encrypted, perfectly restorable
  backup that merely cannot prove where it came from. Refusing to *take* one
  would trade a real data-loss risk for a paper control — the same reasoning
  §4.9 already applies when it says an encrypted backup nobody can decrypt is a
  data-loss event wearing a control's clothing.

So the enforcement lives where the trust decision actually is — the restore —
and it is one rule:

> **An archive whose origin cannot be established is never promoted over an
> existing database.**

It may be restored into a name of its own, where an operator can look at it
before believing it, once they type
`TRITRACK_RESTORE_UNSIGNED=I_ACCEPT_UNVERIFIED_ORIGIN`. It may never take over
the name the server reads. No combination of flags permits that, including
`TRITRACK_RESTORE_REPLACE=I_UNDERSTAND` — that flag says the operator accepts
losing what is in the target, not that they have established where the
replacement came from. **A signature that is present and does not verify is
fatal unconditionally**, with no override at all: a missing signature is a
legacy archive, an invalid one is a file claiming an origin it does not have.

This is what keeps the fix from stranding history. Every archive written before
task 10.43 is unsigned, and all of them still restore.

#### What this does not defend

- **A compromised backup host.** It signs whatever it dumps. See above: that
  party already holds the live database.
- **Confidentiality.** Signing is orthogonal to §4.9's encryption and replaces
  none of it.
- **Deletion.** An entity with write access to the archive directory can still
  destroy the history through retention — that is finding H-7, and it is task
  10.44's, not this one's. Signing gives 10.44 the predicate it needs: *an
  archive this backup line can account for* is now a one-line check rather than
  a guess about filenames.

**Violated by:** a restore path that treats decryption as authentication; a
verifying key read from the archive directory, the archive itself, or any
sidecar beside it; any flag combination that promotes an unattributable archive
over a live database; a signature checked over the ciphertext but not over the
sidecars the restore path also believes.

#### The lesson worth carrying out of H-6

**A control designed against accident is not a control against an adversary,
and the two get written down in the same sentence.** `restore.sh:98` said the
decrypt "authenticates the bytes regardless" and `:200-202` said the `pg_dump`
header "proves this is a database dump at all, and not some other file that
happens to be encrypted to the same key". Both are true of a corrupted file and
false of a forged one. Three tasks read that file reasoning carefully about
corruption and truncation — 10.24 wrote it, 10.36 added a marker to it, 10.37
rebuilt its ordering after G-3 — and **nobody asked what someone who can write
a file into that directory can do.** The drill had the same shape: four
destructive cases, every one of them an accident.

The general form, which is what §10.9 should be read against: when a control's
justification names a *failure*, ask what the same sentence claims about an
*actor*. If the answer is "nothing", say so in the comment — because the next
person to read it will otherwise credit the check with the stronger property,
and that is not a hypothetical, it is what happened here three times.

### 4.10 The diagnostics console

**Decision.** Restating 10.13's constraints here because this document is what
10.16 audits against, and strengthening one of them.

- **Off by default — including in development.** The default is what gets
  deployed. Enabling it is an explicit flag.
- **Disabling it removes the routes**, rather than hiding links or returning
  403. An unreachable route cannot be misconfigured into reachability.
- **Localhost binding when enabled.** Reaching it from another machine requires
  an explicit second opt-in or an SSH tunnel — never a config value someone
  forgets to change back.
- **Never enabled in a production deployment.**
- **Strictly read-only.** No mutation route, no "fix this row" button. A console
  that can write is a second, untested, unauthorized mutation path straight past
  task 10.10's authorization boundary. Use `psql`.
- **No token values in any response.** Not session tokens, not unconsumed
  magic-link tokens, not prefixes. A console displaying a live magic link is an
  account-takeover page.

**Reasoning for going beyond 10.13's "localhost by default" to "off by
default":** the console's most valuable view — rows that lost last-write-wins —
inherently renders coordinates for every project on the server. That is asset 1
in a browser with no authentication. Binding is one misconfiguration away from
wrong; not existing is not.

**Enforced since task 10.80 (2026-09-06), not merely written.** Every rule above
that could be violated by configuration now **refuses the server at startup**
(exit 78, `EX_CONFIG`), by name, with a message saying what to fix — and each
refusal was watched refusing a real compiled server:

- **`TRITRACK_DIAGNOSTICS_ENABLED=true` with `TRITRACK_ENV=production`** — the
  "never enabled in a production deployment" rule, which was prose enforced
  nowhere until this task.
- **A token that is a known placeholder, or shorter than 32 characters** — the
  token was exempt from §4.6's placeholder rule and had no length floor, so
  `changeme` started cleanly as the console's entire authentication.
- **`allowRemote` without TLS** — the off-host allowance is now coupled to the
  transport guarantee §4.1 requires everywhere else.

**A refusal, not a degrade, and that was a deliberate reversal.** `bin/server.dart`
previously degraded a misconfigured console to *off* and started anyway. That
produced a server answering 404 on every diagnostics route — **D-5's exact
shape**. Every one of these refusals fires only on a deployment that asked for
the console, so nobody who did not enable it can be stopped by one. **Ratified by
the planning session, 2026-09-06.**

**What the console still does not have, stated rather than assumed.** **There is
no per-user session.** The operator token is its whole authentication: anyone
holding it reads every project on the server — every member, every device, every
sign-in, and every recorded location, including other people's. This is
deliberate (§14.10's route table has always said so) and it is why the console is
off by default, off the network, and refused in production. **The day it grows a
per-user session, §4.11's project-scope rule becomes live for these routes and
this sentence must be rewritten, not deleted.**

**Violated by:** a default-on config; a mutation route; a 403 instead of route
removal; any token value in a response; binding off-host without explicit
opt-in; **starting with the console enabled under `TRITRACK_ENV=production`**;
**a placeholder or under-length operator token**; **an off-host allowance
without TLS**.

### 4.11 Project scope comes from the session, never from the request

**Decision.** On every endpoint touching project data, the set of projects the
request may read or write is derived from the session's `user_id` joined against
membership. A `project_id` in the request body or path is treated as a *filter
within that set*, never as the grant.

**Reasoning.** This is the exact shape of the §2.4 breach — the most likely real
one. An endpoint that reads `project_id` from the payload and queries on it is
correct for every honest client and wide open to a one-line edit in curl. The
sync endpoint is the dangerous one because it legitimately touches many rows in
many tables at once, in both directions: a project filter missing from the
*pull* side leaks, and missing from the *push* side lets a caller write into
someone else's project.

**Corollary — the server does not trust client-asserted identity fields.**
`origin_device_id` and `last_modified_by` arrive in every synced row and must be
stored **verbatim**, because merge correctness and the field record depend on
them (asset 2, and peer-to-peer convergence with devices that never saw the
server). But they are never used for authorization or to identify the calling
device. The calling device is the one bound to the session. Both facts hold at
once: the row's claimed provenance is data, and the session's identity is
authority.

**Violated by:** any query whose project scope comes from request input alone;
authorization keyed on a client-supplied `device_id` or `user_id`; a sync
response assembled before project filtering.

**Implemented by:** 10.7 and 10.10; gated at Gate B; tested in 10.15's
single-user two-project isolation test.

### 4.12 The server's authorization fails closed where the client's fails open

**Decision.** The Phase 8 rule *table* (`author`, `owner`, `projectOwner`,
`anyUser`) is shared. The Phase 8 *implementation* is not ported literally,
because two of its behaviors are correct for an advisory client-side check and
wrong for a security boundary:

1. **`MutationRule.permits` returns true when the governing value is NULL.**
   Client-side this is harmless — there is nothing to compare and the mutation
   affects zero rows. Server-side it is a fail-open: a row with a NULL
   `user_id`, arriving from anywhere, becomes writable by anyone.
   **Server-side, a NULL governing value is a rejection.**
2. **A missing row passes authorization.** Client-side, fine — zero rows
   affected. Server-side, an upsert against a row the server does not have is
   an *insert*, and it must be authorized as one (does the caller belong to the
   project, does the asserted author match the caller or a legitimate
   replication) rather than waved through.

**Amended by task 11.1 (2026-08-20), for the ownership rules.** `owner` and
`projectOwner` no longer resolve to a single `owner_user_id`; they resolve to
the project's open `role='owner'` memberships, via the shared
`resolveProjectOwners`. That keeps this section's fail-closed requirement by
making the two "nothing to compare" cases distinguishable, where the
single-value API could not tell them apart:

- **`null` owners — no such project resolvable.** Permits, on exactly the
  contract clause 1 describes for a null governing value. It is not a
  fail-open here because the *project*-level checks (§4.13, `ProjectAuthorizer`)
  have already decided whether this caller may touch this project at all; the
  reachable instance is a first publish, where the server authorizes every row
  of a batch before writing any of them, so the batch's own `Projects` row is
  not yet stored when its `Project_Memberships` row is judged.
- **Empty owners — the project resolved and named nobody.** Denies. This is
  the case clause 1 is about, and it is now a distinct value rather than
  collapsing into the same `null`.

The last-owner guard belongs to the same section for the same reason: a push
that would leave a project with zero open owner memberships is refused
(`DenialReason.lastOwnerRemoval`), because the alternative is a project no
caller can ever manage again and no operator can repair — a laptop server has
no privileged account to appeal to. The server catches the case no client can:
two devices each ending a *different* owner membership offline, each
legitimate alone.

**Reasoning.** Porting the client's logic verbatim is the natural thing to do
and it silently inverts the failure mode. Recording this here is the point of
this document: `mutation_authorization.dart` says of itself that it is
"advisory controls, not security," and that is accurate. 10.10 is where they
become security, and the two behaviors above are what has to change in the
translation.

**Related integrity gap, same root cause — unauthenticated provenance.** The
`TT1:` share payload has no signature, so a pasted payload's claimed
`user_id`, `origin_device_id`, and `revision` are attacker-controlled and feed
straight into last-write-wins ordering (§3.7). And `device_id` is a forgeable
value in plaintext SharedPreferences that serves as the **final LWW tiebreaker**
— a chosen `device_id` wins ties deterministically. Neither is exploitable at
scale, both are real, and both predate the server. The server-side consequence
is bounded by §4.11 (a pushed row is only accepted into a project the session
already has, and only where its authorization rule permits), which is why this
is a §6 item rather than a Phase 10 blocker. But do not let a future task treat
a client-supplied provenance field as trustworthy on the strength of it having
been signed by nothing.

**Violated by:** sharing `permits()` as-is into the server's enforcement path; a
NULL governing value permitting a server-side write; an upsert of an unknown row
skipping authorization; trusting a payload-supplied author or device.

### 4.13 Uniform error responses

**Decision.** Client-facing errors say what to do without revealing what exists.
A request for a row the caller may not see and a request for a row that does not
exist return the **same** response. Wrong project, wrong user, and nonexistent
are indistinguishable from outside.

**"Indistinguishable from outside" means the answer *and the work done to
produce it*, and saying only the first was this section's third correction of
the same kind (task 11.72, 2026-08-30).** For a year this sentence was read as
a claim about status codes and response bodies. It is not: a caller can see how
long an answer took, and a branch that does more work is slower. That was
measured on a real refusal in August 2026 and is written up at the end of this
section under **"The clock is a channel too."** The rule, stated once so the
next control does not have to rediscover it: **two answers that must be
indistinguishable must also cost the same, and "the same number of queries" is
not "the same amount of work."**

**Reasoning.** A 404-versus-403 distinction is a working oracle for existence,
and existence is itself sensitive here: confirming that a project id or a tag
name exists on this server is reconnaissance for §2.1 and §2.4. Internal detail
— table names, SQL fragments, stack traces, framework versions — is never in a
response body. Correlate with a server-side request id included in the response
so a real support conversation is still possible without leaking anything.

**Version-mismatch refusals are the deliberate exception (10.11):** "your app is
too old to sync, update to continue" is specific and actionable, and reveals
nothing beyond the server's schema version, which an authorized client needs
anyway. Explicit and actionable beats vague, and a client that silently syncs a
subset of columns is data loss.

**How publish survives this, decided by task 10.21 (2026-08-09).** Gate C found
the project-level version of exactly this failure (§7.3 B2), and the reason it
was there is worth recording, because the obvious fix is wrong. Publishing a
project (task 10.9) is by definition a request about a project the server does
not hold, so `ProjectAccess.absent` permitted sync — and that permission is what
made a fabricated id answer `200` where a forbidden one answered `403`. The fix
is **not** to refuse `absent`, which would refuse publish with it. It is to
notice that `absent` was standing in for two different requests, and to permit
the two that say nothing:

1. **A push carrying no rows of that project.** Global rows — `Users` and
   `User_Emails` (~~and `Tags`~~ — **`Tags` left this list on 2026-09-10, task
   11.219**) — belong to no project, and the publisher uploads a
   project's people before the project row exists. The id in the envelope
   selects nothing and authorizes nothing, so the answer cannot depend on
   whether it names anything. For that to be true, a project the caller has no
   relationship to must also **vouch for nothing** in row authorization: it
   contributes no reachability (§4.17 clause 2) and cannot legitimize a tag.
   Without that, the outcome map answered the question the status code no
   longer did — and, worse, naming a stranger's project would have granted
   write access to its tags.
2. **The push that establishes the project**, carrying a valid `Projects` row
   for that id naming the caller as owner. This is publish, and it is the one
   request that genuinely concerns a project that does not exist.

Everything else — pull, ack, and any push of a project's own rows — is refused
identically whether the project is forbidden or fictional.

> **The one written exception, added by task 11.290 (2026-09-20): a
> *destroyed* project is refused by name.** An owner can now schedule a
> project's destruction and the server carries it out (§4.28's fifth field,
> `PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md` M11). Once its rows are gone the project reads as
> `absent` to `ProjectAuthorizer` — **which is exactly the case 2 above lets a
> publish establish.** An owner's device that was offline across the deletion
> and holds a pending change to its `Projects` row would re-create the project
> on its next round, as a publish, with nobody deciding to. So the server
> keeps one row per destroyed id (`project_destruction.executed_at`) and
> `/sync/push`, `/sync/pull` and `/sync/ack` answer it `403
> {"error":"project_destroyed"}` — asked on every request, unconditionally,
> so the work done does not depend on the id. **What this discloses:** that an
> identifier once named a project on this server and no longer does, to a
> signed-in caller who already holds that identifier. It does not disclose a
> live project, a member, or a row. **Why it is named rather than a bare
> `forbidden`:** the refusal has to exist either way to stop the resurrection,
> and a bare one would have the device tell its owner *"an owner may have
> removed you"* (`SyncFailureCause.accessRefused`) — the wrong-cause class —
> where the true cause is one the person is entitled to hear. A global-only
> push (case 1) is still accepted against a destroyed id, because it says
> nothing about the project. **Reopen trigger:** if a route is ever added
> that answers a destroyed id differently from a fictional one *without* the
> caller holding the id already — a listing, a search — this exception does
> not cover it and §4.13 applies in full.

> **Where the tag-only push went, measured 2026-09-10 (task 11.220).** A push
> carrying nothing but `Tags` rows used to be a case 1 push — global rows,
> belonging to no project, permitted through to a per-row decision. `Tags` has a
> `project_id` now, so `sync_routes.dart`'s `_touchesProject` says such a push
> **is** a request about the project it names, and the route refuses it with
> `403 forbidden` when the caller has no relationship to that project. **This
> section's guarantee is unaffected and was re-measured, not assumed**: a real
> foreign project and a fabricated one both answer `403 {"error":"forbidden"}`
> with no detail, and `publish_and_join_test.dart` now asserts the whole
> response body rather than a subset of it. **The refusal moved from row level
> to route level; what a caller can learn did not move.** That predicate's own
> doc comment listed `Tags` among "the tables with no `project_id`" until 11.220
> corrected it — a production comment falsified by a schema change, found by
> measuring rather than by reading.

**The status code is not the only channel, decided by task 10.29 (2026-08-13).**
Gate C's re-run confirmed 10.21's fix holds — pull, push and ack answer a real
foreign project and a fabricated one identically, **including by timing (that
last clause was false; see "The clock is a channel too" at the end of this
section)** — and
then found the *same question* being answered one level down, inside the `200`,
by the push response's per-row `outcomes` map (§8.4, finding D-1). Three arms:
a stranger's registration status, a tag id's existence, a row key's existence.
Two of the three predated 10.21 and had been missed by two gates.

The lesson is in this section's own history. 10.21 recorded above that "the
outcome map answered the question the status code no longer did" — a correct
sentence, applied to the one instance in front of it rather than stated as a
rule. It is now the rule:

> **No per-row outcome may depend on server state the caller has no other way
> to observe.** Where authorization must consult such state, both branches
> answer the same, and the answer is the refusal — because the permissive
> branch performs a write, and a write cannot be concealed by what is reported
> back.

Enforced in `RowAuthorizer` at the point each answer is decided, not at the
point it is reported:

1. **Naming a user** no longer asks whether the server holds that identity. See
   §4.17, where the clause that did was removed.
2. **A no-op is not a free pass.** "The server already holds a copy of that" is
   a statement about the stored row, so a caller who may not be shown that row
   is not told it exists either. The bar is reachability — a row an ordinary
   pull would deliver anyway — so a routine re-offer is unaffected.
3. **A tag may be referenced only where pull would already deliver it.**
   ~~The one exception is the `Project_Tags` row that claims a tag for a
   project, which is the only operation that legitimately widens a project's
   reach; a tag id that names nothing and one another project holds are one
   refusal there too.~~ **The exception is gone with the table, 2026-09-10
   (task 11.219).** There is no operation that widens a project's reach for a
   tag any more: adding a collar to a project **copies** it, creating a row
   *inside* a project the caller is already in. `_authorizeTagReferences` — 161
   lines, and the whole of the old rule — is deleted, and the ordinary project
   scope check does the work. **The clause above still holds; what changed is
   that it now has no exception to carve out.**

**The residual, stated plainly, and it is general.** A *successful* first
publish is still distinguishable from a refusal: push a valid establishing row
and a free id accepts it while a taken one does not. D-1's third arm is the
same signal on `Observations`, and it is the same on every table — this is the
collision inherent to **client-chosen primary keys**, which any create-if-absent
operation has, and it cannot be removed without removing the ability to create
a row. It was recorded here for `Projects` alone until task 10.29; recording it
per-table was itself the mistake pattern this section keeps hitting.

It is bounded to be worth nothing cheaper than itself: the probe must be
authenticated, must carry a well-formed row of a real table, and on a miss
leaves the prober owning a row rather than merely informed. **Existence is all
that escapes** — verified, not assumed: the victim's row is untouched, still in
their project, still attributed to them, and no content comes back (the losing
copy in a conflict report passes its own disclosure check). Every cheaper
variant is closed, including the one where a *deliberately malformed* publish
answered `500` for a free id and `403` for a taken one — the first-publish
attempt runs in a savepoint precisely so that a failed publish and a refusal are
the same answer — and, since 10.29, the one where a dangling reference answered
`500` for an id the server did not hold while a held one answered `200`.

**Decision (task 10.35, 2026-08-13): closed, not bounded — primary keys are
now project-scoped.** The paragraphs above are retained as the record of what
the residual was and how it was reasoned about while it stood; they no longer
describe the shipped system. Rows on the six project-scoped data tables are
keyed `(project_id, <id>)`, so "create a row under this id" is answered against
the caller's own project only. A key another project holds does not collide,
there is no `existing` row to authorize against, and the two branches D-1 arm
(c) distinguished are now literally the same code path.

**Corrected at task 10.25's second gate re-run (2026-08-13, §9.5 G-4).** The
sentence that stood here — that the `Projects` publish-collision was "the sole
remaining member of what used to be a per-table property" — was wrong, and
wrong in the direction this section keeps being wrong in. Project-scoping
reached the six project-scoped data tables. **`Users`, `User_Emails` and `Tags`
are still keyed globally**, and the collision is still observable on them.

**One** of those three is covered anyway, by a rule that does not depend on how
the row is keyed: `Users`, by §4.17's naming invariant, re-verified
indistinguishable live at three gates (`Cc`). The other two are not.

- **`User_Emails` is covered by nothing.** A caller naming *themselves*
  satisfies the naming invariant, there is no tag or membership edge to
  consult, and the key collision is then the whole of the answer. Reproduced
  live: a `user_email_id` another user holds answers `unauthorized`, a free one
  answers `inserted` (G-4, §9.5).
- ~~**`Tags` is covered by nothing either — corrected at the third re-run
  (§10.7, H-3).** This paragraph previously named rule 3 above as covering it,
  and that was written by reading the rule rather than probing the table. Rule 3
  governs whether a caller may *reference* a tag they cannot reach; it says
  nothing about what the conflict resolver answers when they *claim its primary
  key*. Reproduced live: a `tag_id` another project holds answers
  `lost_to_server`, a free one answers `inserted`. The victim's row is
  untouched; the disclosure is the answer, not the write.~~
  **CLOSED 2026-09-10 (task 11.219, measured by task 11.220). Struck through and
  dated rather than deleted, per this document's convention.** Task 11.219 made
  tags project-scoped for a product reason — a project gets its own copy of a
  collar rather than a link to a shared one — and the key became
  `(tag_id, project_id)`, with `Tag_Versions` keyed `(tag_version_id,
  project_id)` alongside it. **That is exactly how task 10.35 closed this oracle
  on the six project-scoped data tables**: a stranger claiming the victim's
  `tag_id` inside their own project names a *different row*, so there is no
  collision left for the server to answer differently about. **Measured, not
  reasoned:** on 2026-09-10 `verify_h3_existence_oracle_sweep.py` reported both
  tables `held='inserted' free='inserted'`, and task 11.220 removed both from
  that script's `RECORDED_FINDINGS`. **Removing them is the load-bearing half.**
  While a table sits on that list a distinguishable result prints `FINDING` and
  the run still exits 0; off it, the same result prints `***NEW***` and fails the
  run — so if a future schema change ever un-scopes either key, the instrument
  says so loudly instead of quietly re-accepting a finding closed years earlier.

So the accurate statement, **as of 2026-09-10**, is: **closed for every
project-scoped table — now nine of them, because `Tags` and `Tag_Versions`
joined the six that task 10.35 scoped and `Project_Memberships` — plus `Users`,
which §4.17's naming invariant covers by a different route. `Projects` survives
because a project's own id *is* its scope. `User_Emails` is the one gap left,
and it is a gap rather than a definition.**

~~The last two are gaps rather than definitions, and both are left standing
deliberately rather than spent on a second major bump — a `user_email_id` and a
`tag_id` are both client-generated UUIDv4s that appear in no share payload, so
probing either means guessing 122 bits for one bit of answer about a key nobody
can predict. If that judgement is ever revisited, the shapes are
`(user_email_id, user_id)` and `(tag_id, <owning scope>)`.~~ **Superseded
2026-09-10.** The second major bump was spent — task 11.219 spent it on
copy-on-add — and it closed the `Tags` half as a side effect rather than as the
design call this sentence deferred. **What is left of that deferred call is
`User_Emails` alone**, on the same reasoning as before: a client-generated
UUIDv4 that appears in no share payload, so probing it means guessing 122 bits
for one bit of answer. If that judgement is ever revisited, the shape is
`(user_email_id, user_id)`.

**Read the provenance of this paragraph before trusting the next one like it.**
It has now been corrected three times, each time by a live probe of a table
whose coverage had been asserted from a rule: C-2 → D-1, D-1 arm (c) → G-4, and
G-4's `Tags` carve-out → H-3. Every table named as covered here should be
assumed uncovered until a probe exists for it.

**What the clean sweep result actually rests on, measured by task 11.127,
2026-09-05 — and it is not a refusal.** **Eight of the nine tables that sweep
calls indistinguishable are indistinguishable *by construction*.**
*(**Nine of ten as of 2026-09-10** — the arithmetic below is unchanged, and
`Tags` and `Tag_Versions` joined the by-construction side while `Project_Tags`
left the list with the table. `Users` is still the one table on the other side
of that split, and still the one the opaque-outcome control is load-bearing
for.)* A
project-scoped table's primary key has included `project_id` since task 10.35,
**so a stranger's claimed key is simply a different key** — there is no
comparison for the server to answer differently about. **Measured rather than
reasoned: with only the opaque-outcome control deleted, one of nine flipped.**
**This does not weaken the sweep's result and it changes what the result is
evidence *for*.** A clean sweep here is evidence that the schema's key shape
holds, and evidence about the opaque-outcome control on **one** table. **Anybody
citing this paragraph as "nine tables' worth of refusal" is citing eight tables'
worth of arithmetic.** The distinction matters the day somebody proposes a
project-scoped table whose key does not carry `project_id` — **that is the
reopen trigger, and it lives in the schema rather than here.**

**Task 10.45 closed that gap the only way it stays closed: it stopped naming
individual tables.** `scripts/verify_h3_existence_oracle_sweep.py` probes
every table in `sync_tables.dart` — mechanically, not the one or two that had a
reproduction — with the same question: does claiming a primary-key value another
caller already used answer differently than claiming a free one? Run live, it
confirms the statement above is now evidence rather than argument.

**The result as of 2026-09-10 (task 11.220): twelve tables, ten
indistinguishable, two recorded findings.** Indistinguishable: `Users`,
`Project_Memberships`, `Tags`, `Tag_Versions`, `Triangulation_Sessions`,
`Observations`, `Observation_Exclusions`, `Non_Detections`,
`Estimated_Positions` and `Actual_Tag_Locations`. Distinguishable and recorded:
`Projects` (this section's stated residual) and `User_Emails` (G-4, §9.5).

~~`Users`, `Project_Memberships`, `Project_Tags`, `Triangulation_Sessions`,
`Observations`, `Observation_Exclusions`, `Non_Detections`,
`Estimated_Positions` and `Actual_Tag_Locations` are all indistinguishable;
`Projects`, `User_Emails` and `Tags` are all distinguishable, and are exactly the
three this section already named and reasoned about — no fourth carve-out turned

`Tag_Versions` moved to the indistinguishable side; the findings list went from
four tables to two. **The count moved for a reason recorded in the schema, not
in this sentence** — which is the point of the next paragraph. The script's own
`RECORDED_FINDINGS` table is the list that would need a new probe result to

**The two paragraphs above have been stale since 2026-09-13, by two tables.** The
sweep's table list is derived from `sync_tables.dart`, so the number is not
restated here; recompute it with `python3 -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,
'scripts'); from gate_wire import PRIMARY_KEYS; print(len(PRIMARY_KEYS))"`. The
two tables that arrived since are decided in the next paragraph, and neither has
a measured result yet.

**`Individuals` and `Deployments`, decided before either was measured (task
11.311, 2026-09-23).** Both joined `syncTables` on 2026-09-13. `Individuals`
(task 11.240, the animal) got a probe the day it landed; `Deployments` (task
11.243, which collar was on which animal between which dates) landed the same
day without one, and from then on the sweep **aborted before probing anything**
— *"1 synced table(s) have no probe: Deployments"*. CI had been off since
2026-09-10. **So no run of the sweep has ever reported a verdict for either
table**, and the instrument refused to let a list edit silence it, which is its
job. The decision, written before the probe that tests it:

- **`Deployments` — an outsider cannot learn that a deployment id exists by
  trying to claim it. Indistinguishable by construction, and the construction
  was checked in the code, not read off the key.** Three things hold it, each
  located:
  1. **The key.** The table is keyed `(deployment_id, project_id)` — in
     `sync_tables.dart` and in the `PRIMARY KEY` of the v17 migration in
     `postgres_schema.dart`. `SyncService._findRow` builds its lookup from the
     whole key, so a stranger claiming the victim's `deployment_id` inside their
     own project looks up a row that does not exist and inserts a new one: the
     same code path, and the same answer, as a fresh id.
  2. **A row that names the victim's project instead.** `_findRow` runs
     *before* authorization, so a stranger's row carrying the victim's
     `project_id` does find the victim's row. It cannot leak: the first
     statement of `RowAuthorizer._decide` refuses any row whose `project_id` is
     not the push's own (`crossProjectClaim`) without looking at the stored row,
     so the answer is `unauthorized` whether the row exists or not. A push
     scoped to the victim's project is refused earlier still, at the route, the
     same way for a real project and a fictional one (case 2 above).
  3. **The one rule this table has that no other table does — the collar
     interlock**, which refuses a deployment that would put one collar on two
     animals, or two collars on one animal, at the same moment. It is the only
     check on this table that reads *other* rows, so it is the one place an
     oracle peculiar to `Deployments` could live. It runs only after the row is
     authorized (`SyncService.applyPush`), and its query reads `WHERE project_id
     = $1` bound to **the push's own project** (`_overlapsAStoredDeployment`),
     so it cannot consult anything in anybody else's project.

  **Expected sweep result:** `held='inserted' free='inserted'`. **What reopens
  it:** a `Deployments` key without `project_id`, or an interlock query that
  drops its project predicate. The first makes a claimed id collide; the second
  makes a refusal depend on a row the caller cannot see. The broken-control
  drill for this sweep (`verify_11_127_broken_control.py`, variant `oracle`)
  already removes the first of those from the server and requires every table
  the sweep calls indistinguishable to flip, and it derives that set from its
  own healthy run — so both new tables are required to flip without anybody
  editing a list.

  **The probe carries one design constraint no other table's does, and it
  exists because of point 3.** Both arms are inserts in the stranger's own
  project. Had they named the same collar and animal over the same dates, the
  second arm would be refused by the interlock *because of the first arm*, and
  the sweep would report a collision the prober made themselves as an oracle on
  the victim. So the two arms name different collars and different animals, and
  the probe declares that its free arm **must** answer `inserted`: if it does
  not, both arms may have been refused for one shared reason, the comparison
  measured nothing, and the run aborts rather than printing `COVERED` (defect
  vocabulary entry 65).
- **`Individuals` — the same verdict, on point 1 alone**: keyed
  `(individual_id, project_id)`, with no rule that reads other rows. Its probe
  existed from 2026-09-13 and produced no result until 2026-09-24, because the
sweep aborted on `Deployments` before probing anything.

**Both verdicts held live on 2026-09-24, and the probe was watched to fail.**
The full gate at commit `fe9cfbbe` passed 25 of 25 on the gate VM, the sweep
among them, with both tables probed and neither distinguishable. The 11.127
drill's `oracle` variant, which removes the control this paragraph relies on,
then flipped `Deployments` (one of the 12 tables it flipped) to distinguishable.
**Provenance:** task 11.311's report in `TASK_COMMS.md` (commits `17d6fde`,
`9489d0e`); that run's per-table lines were not saved, so this records the
verdict, not the printout.

**"All twelve" was "all eleven" for four months, and the count is the finding
(task 11.21, 2026-08-21).** Task 11.7 added `Observation_Exclusions` — the
supersede/exclude marks — and the sweep was never told. So this paragraph went
