   property — a correct-looking message that hides harm — reproduced inside
   J-1's own remediation. Neither column is cosmetic: `origin_device_id` is the
   documented final last-write-wins tiebreaker (`postgres_schema.dart:21`), so
   a lexically-high forged value wins *every future tie* against the holder's
   genuine edits, and `created_at` is falsified provenance.
   `last_modified_by` stays exempt and is the case that shows the criterion is
   the right one rather than a convenient one: it genuinely does move when a
   different person edits, *and* rule 2 already forbids it from carrying the
   payload's claim, so what it changes to is never an attacker's choice.

   **And an exemption has a size as well as a subject — finding M-17**
   (task 10.109). The criterion above asks *which* columns the diff may leave
   out. It cannot ask *how far* one of them may move, and the merge clock is a
   quantity: a payload advancing `revision` by 1000 beside one filled column
   applied with no dialog and left the row a thousand versions ahead of every
   teammate's copy, so their next genuine correction was reported as skipped.
   The answer is not to list the column — that is the dialog on every honest
   import, which is the failure this clause is built around. Consent turns on
   the advance being **unexplained relative to the changes being shown**
   (`explainedRevisionAdvance`), with the old flat bound kept as its cap. The
   same question asked of every other exemption is §4.19.3's second half.

   **The message the user is shown must read the outcome, not assume it.** The
   other half of K-8: `replicaUpdated` had one sentence, written for the
   confirmed-overwrite case and emitted for all of them. An update that
   destroyed nothing now says so — and does not claim a consent nobody was
   asked for.

   **And "destructive" is not "the value was non-null".** A tombstone landing
   on a live row has `was == null`, so the obvious test reads it as an
   addition, while what it does is remove the whole record from every screen
   the holder looks at. The share format never reaches that branch — it carries
   `deleted_at` as a fixed `null`, an exemption the *format* creates, not the
   rule — which is exactly why the predicate is defined on the rule
   (`UntrustedImportRules.isDestructiveChange`) rather than on the one path
   that happens not to need it. K-1's reproduction tombstoned an observation
   this way, counted as nothing changed.

5. **`RowValidator` runs.** This was the only write path in the app that
   skipped it, which meant a payload could plant a row the server will later
   refuse and wedge the project's sync through the very machinery 10.28 built
   for refusals.

6. **An import is a write, and the person doing it must be allowed to write
   here** (task 11.19). The §4.21 role gradient applies to an import exactly as
   it applies to every other write the app makes: a `viewer` may not save a
   pasted payload into a project, and is refused **on the device** rather than
   only when the row reaches the server.
   `UntrustedImportRules.receiverMayImport` is the predicate; a role this
   device cannot resolve permits, identically to
   `BaseRepository.assertRoleMayWrite`, because the two are the same question
   and a second answer to it is the defect this clause exists to avoid.

   **This clause exists because the control was asymmetric, not because it was
   missing.** A row a viewer had no right to create is refused at the server
   today, so nothing hostile survives into a colleague's copy — but every other
   write in this app has *two* independent layers, a screen that does not offer
   the control and a repository that refuses it anyway, and this path had only
   the first. Task 11.14 added the screen gate and correctly declined to patch
   the write path inside a UI sweep. What clause 6 buys is that a bypassed or
   raced screen no longer reaches an unguarded write.

   **Who the actor is — the part that had to be decided before any code, and
   the reason this got its own task.** An import has two people in it and they
   are governed by different rules:

   - **The receiver**, whoever is holding the device. They are performing a
     write into a project, so the gradient governs them. That is this clause.
   - **The payload's claimed author** — a share payload's observer, an archived
     row's `user_id`. They are *not acting*; their name is being transcribed
     onto a record made somewhere else. What governs a name is §4.17's
     row-naming invariant, which on this path is clause 2, and **the gradient
     must not be applied to them.** Requiring a shared observation's observer
     to hold a role in the receiving project would refuse every genuine share
     from a colleague who has not been invited yet — the ordinary case sharing
     exists for — and §4.17 already decided that such a row may legitimately be
     *held* here and simply will not *replicate* until its author is a member.
     Reading the gradient onto the author would convert that documented,
     recorded replication delay into local data loss.

   So the two compose in one order: rights over the receiver first, naming over
   the payload second. A receiver who fails clause 6 is turned away before the
   payload's observer is resolved, so a refused import deposits no `Users` row
   either — the same property the consequence below gives the other refusals.

   **Enforced once per path, not once per branch.** On the share path the check
   is the first statement of `SharedObservationImporter._save`, above all three
   of its write branches (fresh replica insert, `_upsertReplica` update, v1
   receiver-owned copy). One guard per branch would be clause 1's two-lists
   defect in a new place: a fourth branch would inherit nothing.

   **The archive-restore path, and why abstaining is the design rather than a
   loophole in it** (task 11.20). Task 11.19 asked this clause of every row in
   §4.19.1's table and found the picked-`.zip` restore open: `ProjectMerger`
   reaches every column of every synced table (`sync_tables.dart`) and asked nobody whether the
   person restoring could write in the project being restored into, so a
   **viewer** could restore an archive over a project they may only read. As on
   the share path this was an *asymmetry, not a hole* — the server refuses every
   one of those rows on the next sync, so no teammate's field record was ever
   reachable. What the viewer got was their own device showing them a project
   the project does not agree with, until the day they found out.

   **The obvious fix is wrong, and this paragraph exists so the next reader does
   not make it.** *Refuse unless the user is a contributor or owner* breaks the
   feature's most important use. Membership is **server-derived**: a reinstalled
   phone, or a replacement one recovering last season's archive, holds no
   `Project_Memberships` rows for the project and no `Projects` row either. That
   is precisely the case restore exists for, and refusing it would violate
   Phase 10's first invariant — the app works fully with no server. So the
   answer this task had to give was not *what check* but **what a restore does
   when the device has no membership answer at all**, and it is: *nothing
   different*. The clause honours a rung the device has been told and abstains
   when it has not been told one — which is the null-permits reading above,
   reused rather than re-derived. Two states produce that null and no local
   evidence separates them: the project is not on this device (no answer is
   *possible* — the restore is what creates it), or it is here and the user
   holds no open membership row and is not its creator (created offline, shared,
   or not yet synced). What remains is the case where the device *does* have an
   answer and it says `viewer`, and that is now refused.

   **Two candidates were weighed and rejected; the rejections carry more than
   the choice does.** *Allow, and treat the restored project as local until sync
   confirms membership* is today's behavior with a name on it — it leaves the
   viewer case exactly where it was. *Allow, but tell the user their records may
   be refused when they sync* cannot be aimed: the only signal available is the
   same null, so the warning fires on **every** fresh-device restore, including
   the project owner's, where nothing will be refused at all. A warning that is
   usually wrong and always shown is the dialog clause 4 is built to avoid — one
   more thing to dismiss on the day someone is rebuilding a device after losing
   one.

   **Where the check sits is load-bearing three times, and the third was
   measured.** It is the first statement inside `ProjectMerger.merge`'s
   transaction. *Against the manifest's project*, because the merge is already
   scoped there — resolving the role in whatever project happens to be open
   would let an owner of project A restore an archive of project B they may only
   read. *Inside the transaction*, so the answer cannot change between deciding
   and writing. And *before any row is applied*, because *the archive carries
   the project's own `Project_Memberships` rows*: moving the check below
   `_apply` was tried, and the file's row naming the importer as `owner` had
   made them one by the time the question was asked, so it **permitted**. That
   is the class task 11.3's Gate B run named — a permission read from state a
   permissive branch wrote — and here it is a working attack one line of
   reordering away, not a hypothetical.

   **And on this path the clause is not the second layer; it is the only one.**
   The share screen can withhold its own control because it knows which project
   the paste lands in before the user acts. The import screen cannot: which
   project an archive is for is unknown until the file has been picked and
   decoded, so there is no button to gate. That is why task 11.14's control
   sweep did not and could not cover this path, and why whatever is enforced
   here has to be enforced in the merger.

   **What abstaining leaves open, stated rather than implied.** A viewer who
   reinstalls the app and restores the archive onto a device with no membership
   rows passes this check. Their rows are refused at the server on the next
   sync, and what they hold is a private, divergent copy of a project they were
   already entitled to read. That is the residual; it is bounded to their own
   device; it is the price of restore working at all, and it is recorded in
   §5.10 rather than left as a gap for a later gate to rediscover.

**A further consequence, from J-1's transcript:** a refused import writes
*nothing at all*, including no `Users` row for the claimed observer. The old
code created that row during observer resolution, so a payload that was about
to be refused still deposited an identity anchor a later file import could
match on — an import that "failed" leaving a foothold behind.

#### What this rule does not claim

Share payloads are **unauthenticated**. Nothing signs them, and clause 2's
author check resolves the observer by email — so a forger who knows the
victim's address and an `observation_id` can still present as the author. What
clauses 1, 4 and 5 then guarantee is the whole of the defense, and it is
deliberately a *visibility and recoverability* guarantee rather than a
prevention one: the bearing audit trail cannot be erased at all, the ~20
carried fields cannot change without the user reading a field-by-field diff and
accepting it, and the prior version is retained either way.

Signing payloads would close the residual and is **not** in scope here — it
needs a key the sender holds and the receiver trusts, which is Phase 11
identity work. Recorded as Discovered Scope rather than left implicit.

**Enforced by** `SharedObservationImporter` and `ObservationShare.decode`.
Clause 6 additionally by `UntrustedImportRules.receiverMayImport` and
`readProjectRole`, the query hoisted out of `BaseRepository.projectRoleFor` so
the importer, the repository layer and the screens resolve a role from the same
rows by the same rule — **and, since task 11.20, `ProjectMerger` through the
same two** (§4.19.2). Four askers, one implementation; a fifth answer to this
question is the defect the clause exists to avoid.
**Guarded by** `test/security/share_import_authorization_test.dart` (16 tests)
for clause 6 — both write branches plus the v1 fallback, the permitted roles,
the defer-to-the-server case, and a group that pins the actor question in both
directions. Neutralizing the predicate turns the seven refusal tests red and
leaves the nine permitting tests green; substituting the payload's observer for
the receiver turns a different seven red, including the two written for exactly
that mutation.
**Guarded by** `test/security/share_payload_overwrite_test.dart` (21 tests):
the J-1 reproduction, one group per clause, and a `genuine share` group that
exists so the fix cannot quietly become "refuse everything" — a colleague's
observation still imports, and a re-share after the author corrected it still
updates. Each clause was neutralized in turn and the corresponding tests went
red; no clause is guarded only by tests that another clause also satisfies.

**Violated by:** a write set derived from anything other than the declared
carried-column list; any path taking `user_id`, `last_modified_by` or an
authorization decision from payload content; an import path that writes without
asking whether the person performing it may write in that project, or that asks
it of the identity the payload claims instead; a second notion, anywhere, of
what an import may do; clamping a bad clock instead of refusing it; a confirmation prompt that fires on non-destructive changes (it
trains the dismissal); an overwrite that lands before the prior version is
recorded; and any *new* import path that does not answer these five questions
explicitly — see §4.19.1.

#### 4.19.2 The same rule on the archive path (task 10.73, finding K-1)

§4.19 was written against one pasted string reaching one `Observations` row.
**Finding K-1 is the same defect on the picked-`.zip` restore**, which reaches
every column of every synced table (`sync_tables.dart`) — §13.2 reproduced the whole of J-1's
damage profile through it under the *default* strategy with validation on, over
an empty `Sync_Conflicts` table. The clauses were not re-derived for this path;
they were moved to where both paths can reach them
(`UntrustedImportRules`, in the shared `tritrack_sync` package) and applied.
**A rule only one path can reach is a rule the next path re-derives wrongly,
which is how K-1 happened.**

How each clause lands on an archive:

0. **The person restoring must be allowed to write in the project the archive
   is for** (clause 6; added here by task 11.20). Numbered zero because it is
   first in the code — the archive carries the project's own
   `Project_Memberships` rows, so a check made any later can be answered with
   rights the file itself just granted, which was **reproduced** by moving the
   check below `_apply`. Resolved in the project the *manifest* names, not
   whatever project is open. A role this device cannot resolve **permits**, and
   on this path that is the design rather than a caveat: a reinstalled phone has
   no membership rows for the project it is restoring, and that is the case
   restore exists for. Clause 6 carries the reasoning and the rejected
   alternatives.

1. **Write only what the payload expresses.** An archive is a full column dump,
   so there is no narrower carried set to intersect with. What the clause
   forbids here is the *widening*: a column absent from an incoming row is left
   alone rather than written as `NULL`, and columns this build does not
   recognize are held verbatim (`UnknownColumnStore`) rather than dropped.
2. **Authorship never comes from the file.** On a row that already exists, the
   identity columns are **not written at all**, and `last_modified_by` is
   restated as the person performing the import. The enforcement iterates
   `SyncTable.identityUserColumns` — the declared complete set of the ways a
   row can name a person, the same list the server's row-naming invariant
   walks (task 10.20) — so a table that gains a user column inherits the clause
   rather than needing someone to remember it. The fidelity cost is the one
   rule 2 already named and accepted: a file's genuine third-party
   `last_modified_by` does not survive the import.
3. **The clock is bounded on every table, including `deleted_at`,** and
   out-of-range is refused rather than clamped.
4. **Consent is all-or-nothing across the archive.** A per-row prompt over
   every table is a prompt the user clicks through, so one destructive row
   holds the entire import and the screen renders the `was → becomes` list.
   Every accepted overwrite writes the prior row to `Sync_Conflicts` first —
   on the *backup restore* path, "you should have taken a backup" is circular
   reasoning, so recoverability has to be a property of the write.
5. **`RowValidator` runs as an invariant, not an option.** It was already
   running here — but a default is not an invariant, and §4.19.1's own note on
   this path was *"validation is an opt-out parameter."* On this origin the
   value is forced, not merely asserted, because an assert is stripped exactly
   where it would matter.

**Plus one clause §4.19 did not need and this path does: the merge is scoped to
the manifest's project.** A file whose manifest named project A rewrote the
owner of an unrelated local project B, because `manifest.projectId` was read
only for the *"Switch to this project"* button. Applied on both origins — a
page pulled for one project has no business carrying another's rows either, and
a check that runs only where it has already been exploited is how this class
recurs.

**One input, not five.** Every clause above keys on a single `MergeOrigin`
parameter. Until 10.73 the merger took an `IdentityTrust` and nothing else, and
each remaining trust decision was either absent or a separate argument a caller
could set independently — so the file-import call site got the loosest setting
of each, on the path that reaches every table. Clause 1's original lesson was
*two lists that were never the same list and had no reason to stay in step*;
two parameters that must always agree are that defect with a different shape.

**Named residual, not a gap.** Archives are unauthenticated, exactly like share
payloads, so the guarantee here is *visibility and recoverability* rather than
prevention. A file can still create records, and the email dedup — which is
load-bearing on this path and stays, since it is the only thing between "merged
my own phone's export" and two of me — can attribute those created records to a
person the device knows (§13.2's fact (d)). What the dedup owes is a count, and
`MergeReport.rowsReattributed` is it. Signing archives would close the residual
and needs a key the sender holds and the receiver trusts: Phase 11 identity
work, recorded as Discovered Scope.

**Enforced by** `ProjectMerger` and `UntrustedImportRules`. Clause 6
additionally by `readProjectRole`, the same query the share importer, the
repository layer and the screens resolve a role through.
**Guarded by** `test/security/backup_restore_authorization_test.dart` (17
tests) for clause 6: the viewer refusal and that it writes nothing at all, the
five-test `no membership answer` group that guards the *opposite* direction —
the reinstalled phone, the project held with no membership row, the ended
membership, the device with no identity — the permitted rungs, both directions
of "which project is being asked about", the self-authorizing archive, and that
the sync path is not gated. Three mutations were applied and the suite re-run
rather than reasoned about: neutralizing the check turns 7 red and leaves the
`no membership answer` group green (it guards the other direction and must);
making a null role refuse — the obvious fix — turns exactly those 5 red and
closes nothing; and moving the check below `_apply` turns 5 red including both
self-authorization tests, because the archive's own membership row had by then
made the importer an owner and the check **permitted**.
**Guarded by** `test/security/backup_restore_overwrite_test.dart` (29 tests):
§13.2's reproduction transcript line by line, one group per clause, a group for
**the four wrong fixes the gate measured** — each of which would pass a suite
that only ran the reproduction — and `a genuine restore`, which exists because a
fix that quietly became "refuse everything" would be its own data-loss finding
on the feature whose entire job is getting a field season back. Each clause was
neutralized in turn (clause 2, clause 3, clause 4's gate, clause 4's
prior-version capture, the project scope, and clause 5's forcing) and the
corresponding tests went red; no clause is guarded only by tests another clause
also satisfies.

**Violated by:** any path taking `user_id`/`owner_user_id`/`last_modified_by`
from an archive for a row that already exists; naming those columns at a call
site instead of iterating `identityUserColumns`; clamping a bad clock instead of
refusing it; a `validate: false` that a caller can actually reach on this
origin; an overwrite that lands before the prior version is recorded; reading
`manifest.projectId` for display but not for scope; adding a *sixth* trust
parameter beside `MergeOrigin` rather than deriving from it; resolving the
restorer's role anywhere but the manifest's project, or at any point after the
first row of the archive has been applied; and **making a role this device
cannot resolve refuse** — that is not a tightening, it is the reinstalled phone
losing its field season.

#### 4.19.1 The same question asked of every other import path

Per task 10.66's rule, J-1 is a class, not an instance. Every path in the app
where untrusted or external data is parsed into a row was enumerated and asked
the five questions. Verdicts as of 2026-08-16:

| Path | Can it modify an existing row? | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pasted `TT1:` → `Observations` (`SharedObservationImporter`) | yes | **J-1. Closed by this section.** |
| Pasted `TT1:` → `Tags`/`Project_Tags` (`_createTag`, same screen) | insert only | **Was unbounded** — the same pasted string reached a `Tag` write with no `RowValidator`, while CSV import (strictly less exposed) has had one since Phase 4. Fixed by this task. |
| Tag CSV import | insert only | **Safe.** `RowValidator` runs; `tag_id` is freshly minted and the sync clock re-stamped locally, so the file cannot choose identity or the merge clock. |
| Client backup/restore (`ProjectMerger` ← picked `.zip`) | **yes, every table** | **Was finding K-1 — the widest instance of this class. Closed by task 10.73** (§4.19.2). All five clauses now apply, plus project scoping, all keyed on one `MergeOrigin` parameter. **The verdict that stood here was wrong in its exposure reasoning, and that is the part worth keeping on the page:** it read *"a restore is a deliberate whole-project act on a file the user chose, not a casual paste"* — while `data_export_screen.dart:70-72`, on the screen hosting the Import button, tells the user the same archive "can be shared via WhatsApp, email, or cloud storage." **Choosing a file says where the bytes came from, not who wrote them.** **And since task 11.237 that tension is stated behavior rather than a note:** an import by somebody the archive's own `Project_Memberships` rows do not name — a colleague's archive, shared exactly the way that screen suggests — lands as a **read-only snapshot**: the projects list says so, every write into it is refused with the join-code directions, and the push offers the server nothing for it. **Derived on every read from the device's membership rows, never stored**, so the day their real membership arrives by sync the snapshot is a live project with no re-import. None of §4.19.2's clauses is weakened by it: read-only is about what leaves the device, not about what the file may do on the way in. |
| Server sync pull (same `ProjectMerger`) | yes | **Bounded elsewhere.** Rows are authenticated and pass §4.17/§4.18 server-side; `IdentityTrust.serverAssignsIdentity` disables the email-keyed remap on this path. Clause 4 does not apply — sync overwrites are already recorded to `Sync_Conflicts` by task 10.12. |
| Magic-link identity adoption (`ServerIdentityAdopter`) | yes, **and hard-deletes** | **Was finding K-4. Closed by task 10.75** (§4.20). The row's facts were right and its verdict was *missing*: it recorded the exposure and never said whether the server is different from a file, which is the only question that decides what to do about it. §4.20 says it — the server is the authority on which id names an email and on nothing that follows from it — and enforces the four things that follow: `RowValidator` now runs (it was the last write path in the app that skipped it), an id this device already holds for a different person is refused, several local users sharing an address are no longer fused onto one id (**the honest-path variant, which needs no attacker**), and the superseded `Users` row is captured to `Sync_Conflicts` before the hard delete. |
| Held-column promotion (`UnknownColumnStore.promote`) | yes | **Was finding K-5. Closed by task 10.76.** `promote` now bounds entry count, column-name length and value size, never overwrites a column that already holds a non-null value (the migration-backfill-overwrite harm named in the finding), and quarantines rather than retries any entry it fails to apply (the unrecoverable-brick harm). The store also gained a `project_id` scope, closing the separate cross-project channel the finding named for the three globally-keyed tables. |
| Deep links, URL schemes, file-open and share-extension handlers | — | **The four sub-claims below still hold, but the conclusion they were used to support did not — was finding K-3, closed by task 10.77.** No `CFBundleURLTypes`/`CFBundleDocumentTypes` in the iOS or macOS `Info.plist`, one `MAIN`/`LAUNCHER` intent-filter in `AndroidManifest.xml` and no `VIEW`/`SEND`, and no link-handling package in `pubspec.yaml` — none of that stopped an exported Android activity from accepting an explicit component intent's `route` extra as the initial go_router location, no URL type required. `app_router.dart` now sets `overridePlatformDefaultLocation: true`, and both `AndroidManifest.xml` and `ios/Runner/Info.plist` disable Flutter's own deep-linking receiver explicitly rather than by the absence of a registered URL type. |
| Cloud backup | upload only | **Not "N/A" — a supply route into row 4** (corrected by task 10.73, and it is the same defect shape as row 4's own verdict). The code claim holds and was re-verified: `CloudBackupService` encodes and never decodes, and there is no cloud restore path. What "N/A" then invited the reader to conclude is that this path cannot deliver hostile data, and it can — one hop over. Anyone with write access to the linked folder can drop a file named `TriTrack_<Project>_<timestamp>.zip`, which the user later picks through row 4's file picker *believing it is their own*. The UI is where the mismatch shows: `auto_backup_section.dart` (deleted with the cloud backup, `3a9a2c8`) is three careful paragraphs about who can **read** that folder ("its protection is whatever your cloud provider gives that folder") and says nothing about who can **write** to it. §4.15.1 reasoned about the folder's confidentiality and never about the same archive being a **write primitive against the field record**. Bounded now by §4.19.2's clauses rather than by the absence of a decoder. |

**Gate C's sixth re-run audited this table (2026-08-16). Two corrections, and
they are the gate's own blocking finding and its sharpest non-blocking one.**

- **Row 4 (client backup/restore) is now finding K-1 and is rated blocking**
  (§13.2). The row's facts were right; its *deferral* was wrong twice over.
  `preferIncoming` is not required — the full J-1 damage profile lands under the
  **default** `lastWriteWins` strategy with validation on, because an unbounded
  `revision` wins `MergeResolver` outright. And the exposure argument — "a
  deliberate whole-project act on a file the user chose" — is contradicted by
  copy on the screen that hosts the Import button
  (`data_export_screen.dart:70-72`: *"can be shared via WhatsApp, email, or
  cloud storage"*). Two further facts the row did not have: the merge is not
  scoped to the manifest's project, and `IdentityTrust.emailMatchesPerson` lets
  the file re-attribute its own rows to the victim. One fact in the row's
  favour: `RowValidator` **does** run here (default `validate: true`, no caller
  in the repo turns it off) — and stops none of it.
- **Row 7 (deep links) — the four sub-claims still hold and the conclusion does
  not** (§13.6 K-3). No URL types, no document types, no associated domains, no
  link-handling plugin: all still true. But `AndroidManifest.xml:16` is
  `android:exported="true"`, and an exported activity is startable by any app on
  the device with an explicit component intent — no intent-filter needed.
  `FlutterActivity.getInitialRoute()` returns the caller's `route` extra
  unconditionally and go_router prefers it over `initialLocation`, so
  "All external data enters via an explicit `FilePicker` or the clipboard" is
  false, as is `splash_screen.dart:44-45`'s "non-skippable gate." Bounded by
  §5.4 (a malicious app on the device is a non-goal), so non-blocking — but the
  iOS receiver is armed by default and closed only by the absence of OS
  registration, which is one layer. **Closed by task 10.77**: `app_router.dart`
  sets `overridePlatformDefaultLocation: true` (platform-independent, so it
  also covers macOS), `AndroidManifest.xml` disables
  `flutter_deeplinking_enabled` explicitly rather than relying on exported
  meaning armed, and `ios/Runner/Info.plist` sets `FlutterDeepLinkingEnabled`
  to `false` *before* Phase 11 has a reason to register a URL type — closing
  the single-layer gap this row named while it was still cheap to close.
  `splash_screen.dart:44-45`'s comment no longer claims more than the widget
  itself guarantees.
- Rows 5 and 6 (identity adoption, held-column promotion) were audited and
  remain open with more detail attached — §13.6 K-4 and K-5. Neither is
  blocking; both are unscheduled, which §13.12 argues is the actual defect.
  **Row 5 is now closed by task 10.75** (§4.20), and what it cost to leave
  open is worth recording beside the other three: unlike rows 4, 7 and 9, its
  facts were never contradicted by anything — the row was *right*. What it
  lacked was a **verdict**, because the question it needed to answer ("is the
  server different from a file, and why") is not one of this table's five
  columns. A row can be fully accurate and still decide nothing. **Row 6 is
  now closed by task 10.76**: bounds on entry count, column-name length and
  value size, a never-overwrite-non-null rule against the migration-backfill
  harm, quarantine instead of retry against the unrecoverable-brick harm, and
  a `project_id` scope against the cross-project channel.

**Task 10.73 closed row 4 and, as its brief required, asked whether any *other*
verdict in this table rests on a claim the product's own copy contradicts. One
does, and it is a third instance of the same shape.**

- **Row 9 (cloud backup) — the code claim holds and the verdict drawn from it
  does not.** "N/A. upload only" is true about `CloudBackupService` and invites
  the reader to conclude the path cannot deliver hostile data. It can, one hop
  over: the linked folder is a place a third party can *write* a file the user
  will later pick through row 4's picker. §13.2 already said this in passing
  and the table never absorbed it. The UI is where the mismatch is visible —
  `auto_backup_section.dart` (deleted with the cloud backup, `3a9a2c8`) spends three paragraphs on who can read that
  folder and none on who can write to it, and §4.15.1 reasoned about the
  folder's confidentiality only. Row 9 is corrected above; the consent, clock
  and authorship clauses of §4.19.2 are now what bounds it, rather than the
  absence of a decoder.
- Rows 2 and 3 (pasted `TT1:` → `Tags`, tag CSV import) were re-checked against
  the code and their claims still hold: both mint a fresh `tag_id` and re-stamp
  the sync clock locally, so neither file nor paste can choose identity or the
  merge clock, and `Project_Tags`' `linkOrReactivate` cannot reach an existing
  row behind a freshly-minted id. Recorded as re-verified rather than assumed.

**The pattern across rows 4, 7 and 9 is the finding, not the three rows.** In
each, the *facts* in the "can it modify" column were right and the **verdict**
was drawn from an assumption nobody re-read against the product: that choosing
a file means trusting it, that no registered URL type means no external entry,
that no decoder means no hostile input. §12.11's practice already says a
finding recorded as open must leave with a task number; the sibling clause this
adds is that **a verdict is a claim, and a claim that the UI contradicts is a
finding in its own right** — not a footnote, and not something the next gate
should have to re-derive.

**Gate C's seventh re-run (2026-08-16) audited this table again. Every row's
claim held; the table's *axis* did not, twice — §14.3 and §14.4.**

- **The question this table asks — "can it modify an existing row?" — is
  necessary and not sufficient.** Row 3 (tag CSV import) answers "insert only"
  and is marked **Safe**, correctly on that axis. But an insert-only path with
  no bound is still destructive at scale (a 52 KB archive decoded to 4,000,000
  rows, all inserted, no consent because nothing was overwritten — L-9), and a
  row that is only ever *inserted* is still a weapon **on the way back out**: a
  tag name planted by an archive is written unneutralized into every exported
  CSV, where a spreadsheet formula reads the latitude and longitude columns
  beside it (L-3, blocking, task 10.94). **Export was never on this list.**
  The table enumerates what a file can do to the database and has never asked
  what the database can do to whoever opens what it produces.
- **§4.19's clause 4 exemption list is itself an attack surface — L-2,
  blocking, task 10.93.** `columnsMovedByEveryEdit` exempts `revision` from the
  consent diff on the sound ground that it moves on every honest edit. An
  archive that changes *only* `revision`, to clause 3's legal ceiling, therefore
  applies with no dialog and no visible change — and one honest edit later the
  row can never be restored from the user's own backup again. The exemption
  criterion holds for a column the merge *ignores*; `revision` is the column the
  merge *reads*. **When a control exempts something, the exemption belongs in
  this enumeration as its own row.**

**Clause 6 asked of the same list (task 11.19, 2026-08-21).** The table above
asked five questions because there were five. Clause 6 is a sixth, and the
whole point of task 10.66's rule is that a new clause is asked of every row
rather than of the row that prompted it. Verdicts:

| Path | May the receiver's rights be checked here? | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pasted `TT1:` → `Observations` (`SharedObservationImporter`) | yes | **Enforced by task 11.19.** One check above all three write branches. |
| Pasted `TT1:` → `Tags`/`Project_Tags` (same screen) | yes | **Already enforced**, via `TagRepository.insert` → `BaseRepository.assertRoleMayWrite` (tasks 11.3/11.11). Nothing to add. |
| Tag CSV import | yes | **Already enforced.** `tag_csv_commit.dart` commits through `TagRepository`/`ProjectTagRepository` inside one transaction, so the same guard runs per row. |
| Client backup/restore (`ProjectMerger` ← picked `.zip`) | yes, **and only here** | **Enforced by task 11.20.** One check, first statement inside the merge transaction, resolved in the project the manifest names. This is the one path with no screen gate to pair it with — see below. |
| Server sync pull (same `ProjectMerger`) | **no, and must not be** | Replication, not authorship. The rows are already authorized server-side, and the app's own `MutationActor.replication` bypass exists for exactly this: applying the local gradient to a pull would make a viewer's device refuse to *receive* the project it is entitled to read. |
| Magic-link identity adoption (`ServerIdentityAdopter`) | no | It writes the device's own `Users` row. There is no project, so there is no role to hold in one. |
| Held-column promotion (`UnknownColumnStore.promote`) | no | Same reason as the pull row: the columns arrived through replication that was already authorized. |

**The open instance, closed by task 11.20 (2026-08-21).** `ProjectMerger.merge`
took a `MergeOrigin` and no acting user at all, so a viewer could restore an
archive over a project they may only read. 11.19 declined to patch it because
the question underneath was a **decision**: a restore can legitimately create a
project this device has never held, where there is no membership row to resolve
a role from, and *"check the receiver"* and *"restore a project you do not
have"* had to be told apart before any code was written.

**They are told apart by whether the device has an answer, and the answer is to
abstain when it does not** — clause 6's existing null-permits reading, reused
rather than given a second form. Membership is server-derived, so the
reinstalled phone that restore exists for has no membership rows at all;
refusing there would break the feature's most important use and violate
Phase 10's no-server invariant. What is refused is the case where the device
*does* hold the project and *does* hold an open membership row saying `viewer`.
The full reasoning, the two rejected candidates, and the measured
self-authorization attack that fixes the check's *position* are in clause 6.

**One property of this row is not shared with any other in the table, and it is
why the enforcement had to land in the merger.** Every other import path has a
screen that knows which project it is writing into before the user acts, so it
can withhold the control and the write-path check is a second layer. The import
screen does not know: which project an archive is for is unknown until the file
is picked and decoded. There is no button to gate, so this check is the whole of
the device-side answer.

The residual — a viewer who reinstalls and restores onto a device with no
membership rows still passes, and holds a private divergent copy the server
refuses — is accepted and recorded at §5.10.

#### 4.19.3 What every control here deliberately ignores (task 10.93, finding L-2)

L-2 is not "`revision` was exempt." It is that **an exemption is a decision
nobody re-reads**, and §4.19.1's table had no row for one. The gate's lesson —
*wherever a control deliberately ignores something, that exemption is where the
next problem is* — is discharged by enumerating them, the way §4.19.1
enumerates import paths. This is the list, and a new exemption belongs on it
before it is written into code.

**The corrected criterion, first, because every row below is judged by it.** A
column may be left out of clause 4's consent diff only if **(a) it moves on
every honest edit** *and* **(b) the merge does not read its value.** The first
half alone is what shipped, and it is unsound: exempting a column the merge
*reads* means the one field an attacker most wants to set is the one field the
user is never shown. `revision` is the merge's ordering key and clause 3's
bounded quantity, so it fails (b) — and the exemption is now **derived from the
two halves in code** (`UntrustedImportRules.consentDiffExempt`) rather than
typed out, because a patched list leaves the next reader with a list and no
criterion. That is how K-8 happened inside J-1's own remediation.

| # | The control | What it deliberately ignores | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Clause 4's consent diff | `revision`, `updated_at` — "they move on every honest edit" | **Was finding L-2.** Both fail (b). No longer exempt; judged together as the merge clock and shown when the payload cannot account for the advance (`isUnexplainedRevisionAdvance`). The *noise* property the exemption existed for survives — an ordinary correction still mentions no clock. |
| 2 | Clause 4's consent diff | `last_modified_by` | **Holds, and it is the case that shows the criterion is real rather than convenient.** It moves on every honest edit, the merge never reads it (task 10.10 excluded it from reachability for the same reason — free-text provenance that references nothing), and rule 2 already forbids it from carrying the payload's claim. Its value is never an attacker's choice. |
| 3 | Clause 4's consent diff | `created_at`, `origin_device_id` — until task 10.73 | **Was finding K-8**, and it is the same class one gate earlier. Both fail (a) *and* (b). Not exempt. |
| 4 | Clause 4's destructive predicate | Any `null → non-null` write except `deleted_at` | **Was finding L-12.** `Project_Memberships.end_date` is a second deactivation and the predicate had never been told. Now derives from `SyncTable.deactivationColumns`, and the sweep for a third is a test (`deactivation_columns_test.dart`) rather than a memory. |
| 5 | Clause 4's destructive predicate | Any change where `was == null` — "filling an empty column is an addition" | **Holds.** The exception is exactly the deactivation case in row 4, which is that criterion read correctly rather than a special case. A prompt that always fires is one the user learns to dismiss, which would put the record back where J-1 found it with an extra click. |
| 6 | Clause 3's ceiling | Values *at* the ceiling — the check was `>` | **Was L-2's other half, and the sharper statement.** The ceiling is what the device refuses to *hold*; the value a payload may *carry* has to leave room for what this device does to the row next, or an honest edit takes it past a bound the holder's own export is then measured against. **A bound that admits a value it will later refuse is not a bound** (`maxImportedRevision`). |
| 7 | Clause 4, on the `authenticatedServer` origin | The whole consent gate | **Holds.** A background sync has nobody to ask, and task 10.12's sync-side capture already records the overwrite. Stated as a property of `MergeOrigin` rather than a call-site argument (§4.19.2's "one input, not five"). |
| 8 | Clause 2, on the share path | The sender's genuine third-party `last_modified_by` | **Holds — a named fidelity cost, not an oversight.** §4.19 rule 2 made the trade explicitly: a forgeable audit column is the worse trade. |
| 9 | Clause 1, on the share path | Every column outside `ObservationShare.writableColumns` | **Holds**, and it is asserted against `encode()`'s own output so the two lists cannot drift — which was clause 1's original lesson. |

**The second question, asked of every row above (task 10.109, finding M-17).**
Round 7's lesson produced this table; M-17 is what the table still missed, and
it is a *different question* rather than a missing row. Every verdict above asks
**what** a control ignores. M-17 asks **how much**: the exemption reasoned about
`revision`'s *visibility* — it moves on every honest edit, so showing it would
make the dialog fire on every legitimate import — while the harm lives in its
*magnitude*. `+1` beside one edited column is noise; `+1000` beside one filled
column freezes a field record against its own project. **A presence test cannot
express that, and deleting the exemption is the wrong fix**: a dialog people
learn to dismiss protects nobody, which is the property the exemption existed
for and which §14.3 confirmed is real.

So consent now turns on the advance being **unexplained relative to the changes
the user is being shown** (`UntrustedImportRules.explainedRevisionAdvance`).
`maxUnexplainedRevisionAdvance` survives as the absolute cap — no quantity of
visible changes explains an advance past it — and below it the allowance scales
with the diff. The exemption is untouched, its purpose intact: an ordinary
import still mentions no clock.

Asked of the other rows, and this is the part that earned its keep:

- **Row 1's own second column.** `isUnexplainedRevisionAdvance` judged
  `revision`, so a payload that left `revision` alone and moved only
  `updated_at` — the merge's *tiebreak* — was never judged at all. Measured:
  `updated_at` four minutes ahead of the holder's clock, everything else
  byte-identical, `outcome=applied changes=0`, a falsified timestamp written
  with no dialog. Small (clause 3 caps the lead at five minutes, so it outranks
  only edits made inside that window, and the next edit anywhere bumps
  `revision` past it) and the same defect one column over. The predicate now
  iterates `mergeClockColumns` (`isUnexplainedClockAdvance`).
- **Rows 4 and 5 — the destructive predicate.** The magnitude question is
  *volume*, and it is already on the record with owners rather than newly found:
  one consent-free addition is an addition, four million of them is **L-9**
  (task 10.99), and a change set too large to read is **L-5** (task 10.87),
  whose cut point the file gets to order.
- **Row 7 — the `authenticatedServer` origin.** The largest magnitude exemption
  here: a hostile server rewrites every row with nobody to ask. It holds on the
  same terms it always did — a background sync has no user in front of it and
  task 10.12's capture records the overwrite — and the volume half of that
  capture is task 10.87's second bullet, not a new finding.
- **Rows 2, 6, 8, 9 hold with nothing to add.** `last_modified_by`'s value is
  never the attacker's choice at any size (row 2); row 6 *is* a magnitude
  exemption and was read that way when it was closed; rows 8 and 9 are about
  which columns exist, where "how much" has no meaning.

#### 4.19.4 The outbound question, asked of every format the app writes (task 10.94, finding L-3)

§4.19.1 asks what a file can do to the database. **It never asked what the
database can do to whoever opens what it produces** — so export was not on any
list, and finding L-3 is a tag name planted by a consent-free insert reading the
coordinate columns beside it on a colleague's machine. Reproduced live in
Microsoft Excel; closed and re-measured there (§15.10).

The question every outbound format must now answer: *does the receiving
application interpret any part of this file as instructions?*

| Format | Written by | Interpreted by the recipient? | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Observation CSV | `observation_csv.dart` | **Yes** — every mainstream spreadsheet evaluates a cell beginning `=`, `+`, `-`, `@` | **Was L-3.** Neutralised at `SpreadsheetSafeCsv`, one choke point every encoder passes through. |
| Tag roster CSV | `tag_csv_export.dart` | Yes, same | Same choke point. |
| Non-detection CSV | `non_detection_csv.dart` | Yes, same | Same choke point — including the semicolon-joined `tag_names` column, whose first element leads the cell. |
| Project backup `.zip` (`manifest.json` + `data.json`) | `backup_archive.dart` | **No.** JSON is data to every reader of it, and the only reader is this app's own decoder, which is governed by §4.19.2 | No neutralisation. Recorded so the next reader does not re-derive it. |
| Cloud auto-backup upload | `cloud_backup_service.dart` | Same file as above, one hop further out | Same verdict; the folder's *write* direction is the finding there (§4.19.1 row 9), not its content. |
| `TT1:` share payload (clipboard) | `observation_share.dart` | **No.** Base64 of JSON, pasted into a messaging app as opaque text and parsed only by this app's decoder | No neutralisation. |
| Offline region metadata, DEM tile cache | `offline_region_store.dart`, `dem_tile_store.dart` | **No.** Device-local caches this app writes and reads; they never leave the sandbox | Out of scope, and named so the absence is deliberate. |
| Sign-in email (task 11.287, 2026-09-20) | `smtp_email_sender.dart` | **Two recipients, and both matter.** A mail relay interprets the SMTP envelope; a mail client interprets the message. | **The only caller-influenced bytes in the whole message are one address in one header.** It is checked at the HTTP boundary and **again in the sender before a socket opens** — one `@` between plain ASCII, no brackets, spaces or control characters — because header injection is this format's `=` in a spreadsheet cell and the choke point has to be the writer, not the caller. The body is fixed; the address is not repeated in it. The plan's own payload `a@b.com\r\nBcc: …` is a test asserting an empty relay transcript. |

**Two rules this leaves behind.** A new encoder goes through
`SpreadsheetSafeCsv` — enforced by a grep in
`test/security/csv_export_injection_test.dart`, because a *future* file is the
thing a call-site fix cannot cover. And a new outbound format gets a row here
before it ships.

### 4.20 How far the server is trusted with this device's identity (task 10.75, finding K-4, 2026-08-16)

§4.19 says a payload from an untrusted party may never be trusted with
authorship or with the merge clock. `ServerIdentityAdopter` trusts the server
with **exactly those**: a server-chosen `user_id` becomes a primary key, the
user column of every synced table (`sync_tables.dart`), including `Projects.owner_user_id`, a
`User_Emails` binding and this device's acting identity — each with
`revision + 1`, so it beats every peer's copy — and the superseded local `Users`
row is hard-`DELETE`d.

Row 5 of §4.19.1 recorded that and called it Open. What it did not do — and
what finding K-4 is really about — is say **whether the server is different**.
The answer is *partly*, and leaving that partly implicit is precisely how
§4.19.1's rows went stale: an unstated distinction cannot be re-checked,
because there is nothing on the page to check it against.

#### The distinction, stated

> **The server is the authority on which id names an email. It is not an
> authority on anything that follows from that id.**

The first half is defensible and is not a concession. It rests on three things
a picked file does not have:

- **An authenticated session.** The response comes from a redemption over a
  session the user initiated, on a link delivered to a mailbox they control.
  §5.3 already accepts mailbox compromise as account compromise; this adds
  nothing to that.
- **A design-assigned role.** §4.17/§4.18 make the server the identity
  authority on purpose. `ServerIdentityAdopter`'s own doc comment gives the
  reason: continuous sync between two devices that each resolve an email
  collision locally rewrites `user_id` values *every round, forever*. Someone
  has to be authoritative, and only the server can be.
- **A bound on what the response may say.** `completeSignIn` refuses unless the
  returned address equals the one the **user typed**, so the server can confirm
  an identity the user asserted and never substitute one. That check is real
  and load-bearing — it is why a hostile server cannot reach a colleague's
  records by naming their address.

The second half is where the code was wrong, in four distinct places. Each is
now enforced, and each is a *different* kind of claim:

1. **Naming an id is not vouching for its shape.** `serverUserId` arrived as
   "is a non-empty String" and went into a primary key on eleven tables.
   `RowValidator` never ran on this path — the last write path in the app that
   skipped it, which is §4.19 clause 5, and clause 5 was never a trust
   judgement in the first place. It runs now, on the `Users` row and on the
   derived `User_Emails` row, and `RowValidator` itself gained the shape half
   of the bound it was missing: an identifier must be non-blank, within
   `maxPrimaryKeyLength`, and free of control characters, on **every** table
   and therefore on the merge and archive paths too, not only here.
   `user_email_id` is *composed* from the id and an address, so it is checked
   in its own right — a derived key needs its own bound, not its parts'.
2. **Naming an id is not naming whose rows those are.** The email check bounds
   which local rows adoption may read *from*; it says nothing about the id
   adopted *into*. A server that legitimately confirms `sam@example.com` and
   answers with a colleague's `user_id` had this device rewrite Sam's
   observations onto Alex's `Users` row with a bumped revision that wins the
   next sync — silently, every foreign key intact, the profile screen simply
   showing the wrong name. An existing local row for the server's id is now
   accepted only if it carries the signed-in address, carries a Phase 7
   placeholder (so it names nobody), or already records that address in
   `User_Emails`. Anything else is refused rather than guessed at.
3. **The server never chose the targets at all, and that is where the harm
   actually lives.** The set of local rows folded in is picked *here*, from
   local email anchors. §4.19's frame does not reach it, because there is no
   untrusted payload involved. **The honest-path variant needs no attacker and
   is the one that will happen:** two field researchers sharing an
   institutional mailbox on one device both matched the signed-in address,
   both folded onto one id, and one profile was hard-deleted. The old rule
   folded in *every* local row carrying the address; the rule now is the one
   the prior-address branch beside it has always applied — **ambiguous means
   do not guess.** When several local users claim the address, only the active
   user is adopted and the rest are held back untouched, rows and `Users` row
   alike. The cost is named rather than hidden: a genuine same-person
   duplicate is no longer folded automatically and the user keeps two profiles
   until something merges them. That is recoverable; fusing two people and
   deleting one is not.
4. **Being the identity authority is not authority to destroy.** §4.19 clause
   4's subject is *the person holding the record*, not the trust level of the
   sender — and the superseded `Users` row was deleted with no capture of any
   kind. The hard delete itself stays and the argument for it is unchanged: a
   tombstone would sync the false claim "this user was deleted" and propagate a
   ghost user to every peer. What was wrong is that the argument for **not
   tombstoning** had been read as an argument for **not recording**, which are
   different claims — the first about what to tell other devices, the second
   about what to keep on this one. The row is now written to `Sync_Conflicts`
   before it is deleted, in the same transaction, so the `first_name`,
   `last_name`, `created_at` and `origin_device_id` that existed on exactly one
   device in the world remain readable.

   **On `project_id`.** `Users` is globally keyed, so there is no honest single
   project to file the record under. One row per project is written, because
   the tidier-looking alternative — a sentinel project id — produces a record
   the sync status screen can never show, and a record nobody can read is the
   same as no record, which is the defect being fixed. The sentinel is used
   only on a device holding no projects, where there is no screen either way.

#### What this does not claim

- **A hostile server can still cost you your account.** It can decline to sign
  you in, or mint a fresh id and leave this device correctly adopted onto an
  identity the rest of the team does not share. Nothing here prevents that,
  and nothing can while the server is the identity authority. The guarantee is
  narrower and is the same shape as §4.19's: **the field record is not
  silently destroyed or reattributed**, and any `Users` row that is superseded
  survives in a form the holder can read.
- **The redemption response is not signed.** Under §4.1's TLS requirement an
  on-path attacker cannot forge one; in a **debug** build against a
  private-range host, cleartext is still permitted (F13/§2.5) and there the
  transport is the only thing between a `user_id` and this database. The four
  checks above are what stands behind it, and they are deliberately
  transport-independent for that reason.
- **`heldBack` is reported and not yet shown.** The adoption report names the
  users held back, and no screen renders it. Nothing is lost — those rows are
  untouched, which is the whole point — but a shared-mailbox device ends up
  with two profiles and no explanation of why. Recorded as Discovered Scope,
  not as a closed question.

**Enforced by** `ServerIdentityAdopter` (all four), `RowValidator`
(`isWellFormedIdentifier`, shared with every other write path) and
`CurrentSession.completeSignIn` (the email bound, unchanged).
**Guarded by** `test/security/server_identity_adoption_test.dart` (27 tests),
whose groups map one-to-one onto the four clauses above so a clause deleted
from this section leaves a visibly orphaned group; plus a negative control in
each group, because "refuse everything" would satisfy every adversarial test
here and break sign-in.

**Each clause was neutralized in turn and its own group went red** — §4.19's
discipline, applied here so that no clause is guarded only by tests another
clause also satisfies:

| Clause neutralized | Tests that failed |
| --- | --- |
| 1 — `isWellFormedIdentifier` reduced to "non-empty String" | 9, all in clause 1's group (its negative control still passed) |
| 2 — the collision check skipped | 1, clause 2's adversarial test |
| 3 — the ambiguity branch always taken | 4: clause 3's three adversarial tests, plus the clause 4 test that asserts a held-back user is not captured from |
| 4 — the capture made a no-op | 3, all in clause 4's group ("nothing is captured when nothing is superseded" correctly still passed) |

Clause 3's fourth failure is the only cross-group one and it is the right kind:
that test asserts a *clause 3* property from clause 4's side. Clause 1's
neutralization is also the one that proves the shared bound is shared — the
same edit is what `RowValidator`'s own group asserts against the merge and
archive paths.

**Violated by:** taking any identifier from a network response into a key
column without `RowValidator`; adopting into a local `Users` row this device
attributes to someone else; folding several local users onto one id because
they share an address; and deleting a superseded identity row without first
recording it where the holder can read it.

### 4.21 The role gradient, and the two writes that are grants (task 11.3, 2026-08-20)

**Decision.** A project membership carries a role, and the role decides what
its holder may write. The gradient is enforced **on the server**, per row, in
`RowAuthorizer`; the app enforces the same thing at its repository layer so a
screen cannot offer a write that will be refused. Those are not equal partners.
The server is the boundary; the app is agreeing with it.

| Role | May |
| --- | --- |
| `viewer` | read the project; record nothing, change nothing |
| `contributor` | record observations, edit and delete **their own** |
| `owner` | everything, plus membership, roles and project settings |

**Every row of that column is a write.** Reading is undifferentiated: a `viewer`
sees everything an `owner` sees within a project they both belong to. That is
§4.21.4, added 2026-09-07, and it is a rule rather than an accident of how the
screens happen to be built.

**Reasoning.** Through Phase 10 a project had exactly one member, its owner, and
`ProjectAuthorizer` returned one undifferentiated `member`. Task 11.2 made
non-owner members real and gave them roles — and nothing read them. A person
invited as a `viewer` could record observations, and could write every table the
rule table governs with `anyUser` (tags, triangulation sessions, position
estimates, recovered-tag locations), because that rule permits everyone who gets
as far as being a member. Read-only was a word on an invitation.

**Three things the gradient deliberately does not do.**

1. **It does not replace the rule table.** Two questions compose on every write:
   *may this person write in this project at all* (the gradient) and *may they
   write this row* (`MutationRule`, unchanged). A contributor passes the first
   and is still held to their own observations by the second.
2. **It does not read "contributor writes its own" as "no shared row."**
   Recording one observation also writes a `Triangulation_Sessions` row and may
   link a `Project_Tags` row, and neither table has an author column to be "your
   own" by — they are shared project vocabulary. The stricter reading would
   leave the role unable to do the only thing it exists for.
3. **It does not refuse a viewer's push at the transport.** A blanket `403`
   would refuse the one push a viewer legitimately makes — their own `Users`
   profile row, which is theirs and not the project's — and would turn every
   locally-recorded row into a failed sync rather than a per-row decision. §4.7
   and the data-custody rules require a refused row to be held, counted and
   explained (task 10.28); a per-row `unauthorized` gets that and a `403` does
   not.

**`Tags` is global and is still project data.** A tag is a physical
transmitter a project is tracking, so the gradient applies to it — but the
question "which project vouches for this tag" is answered by §4.13's
tag-reference rules rather than by a `project_id` column, so that is where the
gradient is applied for this one table. A viewer may neither create a tag nor
alter one their project uses. Two consequences to hand on: the *insert* refusal
is narrowed to an explicit `viewer` rather than to anyone without write rights,
because a first publish uploads a project's tags before the `Projects` row that
would give the caller any role at all; and **task 11.11 narrowed tag *editing*
further, to owners only** — **done, 2026-08-21**, in the reachable-tag branch of
`RowAuthorizer._authorizeTagReferences`, where the test is now
`access != ProjectAccess.owner` rather than `!access.permitsProjectWrite`.

**The tag rules in full, after 11.11.** They are deliberately asymmetric, and
the asymmetry is the decision rather than an inconsistency:

| Act on a tag the project references | `viewer` | `contributor` | `owner` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| create | no | **yes** | yes |
| edit (rename, re-tune, recolor) | no | **no** | yes |
| retire (a `status` change, no branch of its own) | no | **no** | yes |

Creating stays open to a contributor because owner-only creation does not
prevent duplicates — two owners each offline create the same collar's tag and
collide identically, since the duplicate comes from working offline rather than
from who may write — while it *does* cost a field tech with no signal the
ability to record the observation at all. That is a permanent loss traded for a
tidiness problem, on the app's primary use case. Changing an existing tag is not
the same act: every observation of that collar references it, so a rename, a
frequency change or a retirement rewrites what already-recorded rows mean, and
those bearings cannot be taken again.

Near-duplicate tags that get created anyway are **warned about, never refused**
(`NearDuplicateTags`, and the warning names the matched tag and what matched),
and reconciled by Phase 12's merge tool. A refusal here would block honest field
data — two collars can legitimately share a nominal frequency if they are never
in range together — which is the same trade the creation rule declines.

**This table is written per-project, and that reads as though a tag belonged
to one — corrected by task 11.27 (2026-08-22).** It does not: `Tags` is
global (stated above) and a **second** project may hold its own `Project_Tags`
link to the exact same row. The "edit" and "retire" rows above are answered
correctly for the caller's own project, but they do not say what a *different*
project using the same tag experiences when that edit happens: nothing warns
it, and its members' already-recorded bearings on that tag now reference a
row that reads differently than it did when they were taken. Task 11.23 found
this had no test and no entry anywhere in this document; task 11.24's own
audit of this section confirmed the same gap. **The condition under which it
is a defect rather than a design trade is exactly which record a bearing
should point to** — a question this document does not answer alone. Task
11.32 answers half of it: `Tag_Versions` freezes what a tag read at the
moment each bearing was recorded, so an edit to the live `Tags` row no longer
changes what any already-recorded bearing, in any project, is understood to
mean — the drift becomes a fact in the history rather than a silent rewrite
of the past. What survives, and is still open, is narrower: two projects
still *share* one `Tags` row, so an edit still changes what the *other*
project's tag list shows today and what its bearings recorded *from now on*
mean, and no notification passes between them. **Task 11.34 (not yet built,
"decouple project tags from the tag log") is the design under consideration
for closing that remainder**, by copying a tag into a project when it is
added rather than sharing the one global row; until it ships, the tag rules
above describe the current, shared-row behavior correctly for one project
at a time and incompletely for two. (Task 11.29, which this paragraph used to
cross-reference, is canceled — tag frequencies drift in the field, so
editing a tag must stay possible; see task 11.32 above.)

**An unrecognized role grants nothing.** `resolveProjectRole` returns null for a
`role` string this build cannot interpret, and every caller reads null as no
rights. The database `CHECK` constraint and `RowValidator` both refuse an
unknown role on the way in, so this is a backstop rather than an expected path
— but the permissive reading is the one that would matter.

**One resolution, both sides.** `resolveProjectRole` lives in
`packages/tritrack_sync` beside `resolveProjectOwners`, for the reason task 11.1
hoisted that one: an app and a server that disagree about somebody's role
disagree about whether their field record exists.

**Violated by:** any write path that consults membership without consulting
`role`; a role check that lives only in a widget; a client-side gradient the
server does not repeat; treating an unknown role as permissive.

**Implemented by:** 11.3. `ProjectAccess` (server), `RowAuthorizer._authorizeRole`
(server), `BaseRepository.assertRoleMayWrite` (app), `ProjectRoleRights`
(shared). Tested in `server/test/integration/member_authorization_test.dart`
over a real socket and `test/data/repositories/role_gradient_test.dart` in the
app.

**And by 11.19 and 11.20 on the two client write paths that reach no
repository.** `SharedObservationImporter` and `ProjectMerger` both write raw
statements inside their own transactions, so `assertRoleMayWrite` never ran in
either and the gradient was enforced by the screen alone — on the restore path,
not even that. §4.19 clause 6 is the same rule on both, resolving the role
through the same query (`readProjectRole`, hoisted out of
`BaseRepository.projectRoleFor` for exactly this). The gradient is asked of the
**receiving user** and never of the identity a payload claims — see clause 6 for
why that distinction is load-bearing rather than pedantic.

**The restore path is where the gradient meets its own limit, and clause 6 says
so out loud.** A role is server-derived, and a restore's most important use is a
device that has not talked to the server yet. So on that path the gradient
governs when the device has been told a rung and **abstains when it has not** —
which is the same reading `assertRoleMayWrite` has always had, arrived at from
the opposite direction. Tightening it there would not harden the gradient; it
would stop a reinstalled phone recovering last season's data.

The tag rows of that table are 11.11's, and are implemented by
`RowAuthorizer._authorizeTagReferences` (server) and `TagRepository.insert` /
`TagRepository.assertMayEdit` (app) — the app needs its own seam here because
`Tags` has no `project_id` column for `assertRoleMayWrite` to resolve a role
against. Tested in the same two files, plus
`test/data/repositories/tag_authorization_test.dart`.

#### 4.21.1 A row whose existence is itself a permission

**Decision.** Every synced table declares `SyncTable.insertIsAGrant`. Three
answer yes, and an insert into one of them is authorized in its own right:

| Table | Why creating a row is a grant | What authorizes the insert |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Project_Memberships` | the row's existence *is* the membership | the caller must name themselves, be a current owner **or** be establishing the project in this same push, and hold no open membership of it already |
| `Projects` | creating one makes the caller its owner | §4.17's naming invariant (the row must name the caller as owner) plus the publish gate in `sync_routes.dart` |
| `Project_Tags` | linking a global tag makes it readable by everyone in the project | §4.13's tag-reference rules (the tag must exist and be claimed by no other project) plus the gradient |

The other nine answer no: `Users`, `User_Emails` and `Tags` are global rows
carrying no rights at all — sign-in identity comes from `auth_accounts`, never
from these — and the remaining six are field records, where a new row is
somebody's data and confers nothing on anybody. (`Observation_Exclusions` is
one of the six, and was missing from this count until task 11.21 — the same
11.7 omission as §4.13's, and the reason the count is now stated as a
subtraction from twelve rather than as two numbers to keep in step.)

**Reasoning.** Phase 8 authorizes edits and deletes and deliberately not
inserts, because creating a row is normally adding your own data. That is right
for an observation and false for a membership, where an unauthorized insert is
not a spurious record but a stranger on the project. Task 11.1 hand-checked
`grantOwner` and task 11.2 hand-checked invite redemption, both in the app;
**neither binds a device that skips the app and puts the row on the wire.**

**The declaration is the control, not the switch.** `insertIsAGrant` is required
on every descriptor, so adding a table is a decision somebody had to write down
rather than one made by omission — the same discipline `tableMutationRules` gets
from having no default entry. Flagging a table without deciding what may create
its rows lands in `_authorizeGrantingInsert`'s unhandled branch, which **denies**.

**What this leaves.** Exactly one membership insert survives on the push path: a
project's own creator bootstrapping their owner row as they publish, or
backfilling it on a project that predates task 8.4. Adding anybody else is not a
push — it is invite redemption, where the server writes the row itself from the
invitation's own `project_id` and `role` (task 11.2's
`SyncService.insertServerAuthoredRow`). That is why the push path needs no
exemption for invitations and must not grow one: a pushed row would name its own
role, its own user and its own project, and the authorizer would have to prove
each matched an invitation. Handing the attacker the pen is the alternative
design, not a simpler version of this one.

**Violated by:** a new table added without declaring `insertIsAGrant`; an
exemption in `_authorizeGrantingInsert` for a row the client proposes; a second
`insertServerAuthoredRow` call site added without the same reasoning.

#### 4.21.2 Cross-project isolation — a verdict per endpoint

***Derived*** — and see the provenance registry at the top of this document.
`test/documentation/permissions_matrix_membership_test.dart` enumerates every
route the server declares, from every file under `server/lib/` that mounts any,
and requires **exactly one row below to cite each of them verbatim** — method,
then path, placeholders spelled as the code spells them — and requires every
route this table cites to be one the server actually declares. A route with no
row fails; a row with no route fails.

**What is derived is that a row exists for every endpoint. The verdict text
itself is prose and no test reads it.** That is the honest split: §2.4's likely
breach is *one endpoint nobody wrote a verdict for*, and that half now cannot
happen silently. Whether a verdict is **right** is still a person reading the
handler.

§4.11 states the rule. This is the enumeration, because the standing rule is
that silence about an endpoint is not a verdict, and because §2.4's breach is
the most likely real one in this system: not a clever exploit, one endpoint that
checks *authenticated* and forgets *authorized for this project*.

"Project-scoped identifier" means a value in the path, body or query that names
a project or something inside one.

| Route | Project-scoped identifier | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /health` | none | **Unaffected.** Unauthenticated by design and returns only `{"status":"ok"}` — §2.2's rule that a chattier health check is free reconnaissance. **It is a LIVENESS probe and nothing else** (task 11.128): a server with no database answers `200` here deliberately, because restarting cannot reach a database that is down. |
| `GET /ready` | none | **Unaffected, and new in task 11.128.** Unauthenticated by design. Returns `{"status":"ready"}` or `503 {"status":"not_ready","degraded":["database"]}` — a closed vocabulary of one word, enforced by an enum. §2.2 carries the disclosure decision and the measurement behind it. |
| `POST /auth/magic-link` | none | **Unaffected.** Pre-authentication; rate-limited per source. |
| `GET /auth/link-status/<requestId>` | none — `requestId` is a server-minted UUID | **Unaffected.** |
| `GET /auth/redeem`, `POST /auth/redeem` | none | **Unaffected.** This is how one becomes authenticated. |
| `POST /auth/sign-out` | none | **Unaffected.** Acts on the presented token only. |
| `GET /auth/sessions` | none | **Unaffected.** The devices you are signed in on, listed from `session.userId` after the bearer token is validated. The route reads no identifier from the path, body or query at all, so there is nothing to aim at another account — the same shape, and the same reason, as `revoke-all` below. |
| `POST /auth/sessions/revoke-all` | none | **Unaffected.** `user_id` from the session, never the body. |
| `POST /auth/sessions/revoke-device` | `device_id` (body) — not project-scoped | **Unaffected.** Keyed `(user_id, device_id)` with `user_id` from the session, so it selects only within the caller's own devices. |
| `POST /sync/push` | `project_id` (envelope) | **Enforced, twice.** `ProjectAuthorizer.resolve` gates the request; `RowAuthorizer` then refuses any row claiming a different project than the envelope, and any row whose stored copy lives elsewhere. Tested against a fabricated project id, not a constant. |
| `POST /sync/pull` | `project_id` | **Enforced.** `!access.permitsSync` → 403, with `absent` deliberately failing so a nonexistent project and a forbidden one answer identically (§4.13). Global tables are narrowed by `ProjectReachability`, so project A's pull cannot carry project B's people or tags. |
| `POST /sync/ack` | `project_id` | **Enforced.** Same gate; the cursor is keyed `(user_id, device_id, project_id)`. |
| `GET /projects/mine` | none | **Enforced by construction.** Lists from `context.session.userId`; there is nothing to aim at. |
| `GET /projects/deleted/mine` | none | **Enforced by construction.** The same shape as the row above: no field on the route at all, and the query is scoped to `context.session.userId` three ways — an open `owner` membership, a tombstoned `Projects` row, and a tombstone whose `last_modified_by` the server recorded as the caller. There is nothing to aim at another person's projects and no identifier to probe with; a caller asking about a tombstoned id they do not hold is answered by the `_requireOwner` routes and by pull identically to a fictional one (measured for a tombstoned id, `deleted_project_directory_test.dart`). §4.28.1 carries the field table and refuses the general listing this is not. Task 11.292. |
| `GET /projects/<projectId>/join-settings` | `projectId` (path) | **Enforced.** `_requireOwner` calls `ProjectAuthorizer.resolve` with the session's `user_id` before anything is read, and refuses anything but `owner`; "not yours" and "no such project" land on the same `403 forbidden` (§4.13). The body carries the live join code, which is §4.2.1's one written exception to §4.2, so the response is `no-store` (§4.7). |
| `POST /projects/<projectId>/join-settings` | `projectId` (path) | **Enforced.** Same owner gate. Nothing in the body names a project: it carries `joining_enabled` and `team_size_limit`, both bounded, and the `UPDATE` is scoped `WHERE project_id = $4` from the path the gate already resolved. |
| `POST /projects/<projectId>/join-code/rotate` | `projectId` (path) | **Enforced.** Same owner gate. `clear_pending` is the design's only bulk operation and it acts solely on rows already scoped `WHERE project_id = $3 AND decided_at IS NULL`, so it cannot reach another project's queue. Grants nothing. |
| `GET /projects/<projectId>/join-requests` | `projectId` (path) | **Enforced.** Same owner gate; the list is `WHERE project_id = $1`. Carries other people's email addresses, hence `no-store` (§4.7). |
| `POST /projects/<projectId>/join-requests/<requestId>/approve` | `projectId` and `requestId` (path) | **Enforced, twice — and this one is a grant.** The owner gate resolves the project from the session; the deciding `UPDATE` then carries `WHERE request_id = $3 AND project_id = $4 AND decided_at IS NULL`, so a request id belonging to a project you do not own is not merely refused, it is invisible — it draws the same `409` as one already decided or one that never existed, which is what stops an owner of A probing for B's request ids. The membership row is built from the request's own `project_id` and `user_id` and the role the owner chose at this moment; **nothing in the body shapes it**, which is why §4.21.1 needs no exemption for it. |
| `POST /projects/<projectId>/join-requests/<requestId>/reject` | `projectId` and `requestId` (path) | **Enforced, twice.** The same owner gate and the same `WHERE request_id = $3 AND project_id = $4` on the deciding `UPDATE`, with the same single refusal. Writes no membership and discloses nothing. |
| `POST /projects/<projectId>/members/readmit` | `projectId` (path), `user_id` (body) | **Enforced, twice — and this one is a grant.** The owner gate resolves the project; both membership probes are then `WHERE project_id = $1 AND user_id = $2`, so the route can only re-admit somebody who **already held a closed membership in this project**. It cannot add a stranger, and "already a member" and "never was" draw one refusal, so it cannot be used to ask questions about a user id either. |
| `GET /projects/<projectId>/deletion` | `projectId` (path) | **Enforced.** Same owner gate (`_requireOwner`) before anything is read; the answer is one row `WHERE project_id = $1` of the server-only `project_destruction` table, plus two numbers from the server's own configuration (the grace period and the backup window). Not a member's read: a contributor is refused identically to a stranger, because the only thing this read is for is deciding to destroy. Task 11.290. |
| `POST /projects/<projectId>/deletion` | `projectId` (path) | **Enforced, and this one destroys.** Same owner gate.
