The body carries an `action` and nothing else — no date, no day count — so the server's clock and grace period decide when, and a device clock cannot move anybody's deadline. `schedule` writes one row keyed on the path's project id and never moves an existing date; `cancel` deletes that row; `immediate` runs `ProjectDestructionService.destroy`, whose every `DELETE` is `WHERE project_id = $1` over the project-scoped tables in `TombstoneRetentionService.purgeableTables`' order and the server's own per-project bookkeeping. After it commits the project has no membership rows, so the same caller is refused on the next request exactly as a stranger would be. Task 11.290. **`restore` (task 11.302) is the one action gated more narrowly than the owner gate**: after `_requireOwner`, the caller must be in `GET /projects/deleted/mine`'s population for this id — `ProjectDirectoryService.isDeletedBy`, built from the same SQL text as the listing, so an open owner membership, a tombstoned row, and a tombstone whose `last_modified_by` is the caller — and anyone else draws the same `403 forbidden`. It withdraws any scheduled destruction and then clears `Projects.deleted_at` for the path's id only (`WHERE project_id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NOT NULL`), bumping the revision and re-stamping `server_seq` so every member's next pull carries it. On a project that is not deleted it writes nothing and answers the standing. A destroyed id cannot be restored and is refused like a fictional one; this route does not name it, and §4.13's written exception is not widened. §4.28.1 records who may restore and why. |
| `GET /projects/join-requests/mine` | none | **Enforced by construction.** Keyed on `context.session.userId` and nothing else; there is no field on the route by which a caller could name another person or another project. `project_id` comes back only for an **approved** request — a pending or rejected one would be telling somebody which project refused them. |
| `POST /projects/join-requests` | none — deliberately | **Enforced by construction.** There is no `project_id` on this route, for the reason the deleted redeem route had none: a route that took one would let a caller ask "does this code work for project X" and read the answer off the difference, which is §4.13's existence oracle in a new costume. The project is selected by the code itself (`WHERE code = $1 AND joining_enabled = TRUE`), and malformed, unknown, joining-switched-off and deleted all draw one refusal. Writes a pending request, not a membership. |
| `GET /diagnostics/health`, `GET /diagnostics/projects`, `GET /diagnostics/projects/<projectId>`, `GET /diagnostics/projects/<projectId>/rows/<table>`, `GET /diagnostics/identities`, `GET /diagnostics/devices`, `GET /diagnostics/auth-events`, `GET /diagnostics/revision-anomalies`, `GET /diagnostics/traffic` | path, on two | **Out of this model, by design — and stated rather than assumed.** The console has no user session: it is gated on a real loopback TCP peer plus a static operator token (§4.10), and it exists so the person who runs the server can read their own database. There is no user identity to isolate one project from another *for*. Two consequences worth writing down: the console is the only place a `project_id` is accepted with no per-project authorization, so **the day it grows a per-user session, this becomes a live gap**; and its blast radius is the operator token, which is why §4.10 keeps the console off by default and off the network. Carried to task 11.9's inventory. |

**Task 11.123 filled this table's gap and made the gap impossible to reopen
quietly.** Four rows had left it on 2026-09-01 with the invitation routes tasks
11.81 and 11.84 deleted, and **ten routes the server declares had no row at
all** — the nine join-settings, join-code, join-request and re-admission routes
that replaced invitations, plus `GET /auth/sessions`, which had been missing
since it was written and which the brief for this task did not know about. The
verdicts above were written by reading each handler, and **every one of them
came back enforced**; nothing here was blessed on the strength of resembling a
row that already existed.

**Two of the ten write a membership** — approve and re-admit — and both are
covered by §4.21.1's granting-insert reasoning, because the server writes those
rows itself rather than accepting them on the push path. The task's brief said
three; the third was miscounted, and rotating a join code or switching joining
on grants nobody anything.

**The diagnostics row is one row citing nine routes, deliberately.** Its verdict
is a single argument about the whole console and repeating it nine times would
invite the nine copies to drift; the derivation still requires all nine
citations to be present and correct, so a tenth diagnostics route cannot appear
without this row being edited.


**Violated by:** a new route that reads a project id without resolving access
from the session; a refusal that differs between a forbidden project and a
fabricated one; a diagnostics route reachable with a user session rather than
the operator token.

#### 4.21.3 A push that writes nothing vouches for nothing (Security Gate B, 2026-08-20)

**Found by Gate B's re-run against task 11.3's own changes, before it shipped.**
Recorded here rather than only in the plan, because the rule it produced is a
general one and the bug was one line.

**What happened.** The tag-reference check gained `if (!changesStoredRow)
continue;` for `Tags` rows, correctly: a push that changes nothing needs no
write permission, and without that clause a `viewer`'s ordinary sync — which
re-offers unchanged rows whenever a receipt is missing — would have accumulated
a permanent refusal for every tag in their project. What it missed is that the
no-op branch it fell through to then called `_noteEstablishedTag`, recording the
tag id in `_establishedThisPush` — the within-push bookkeeping that lets a tag
created and first used in one round be referenced by the rows that use it.

**The exploit, reproduced against a real database.** Two rows for one `tag_id`
in one push. The first carries a losing revision, so it changes nothing and
needs no permission — and vouches. The second carries a winning revision and
short-circuits **all three** guards behind the vouching branch: the role
gradient, the claimed-by-another-project refusal, and the orphan author check.
A `Project_Tags` row in the same batch rides the same vouching to link a
stranger's tag into the attacker's own project, after which
`ProjectReachability` delivers the tag's frequency, notes and deployment dates
on the next pull. Any authenticated user holding a tag's id could rename,
retune or tombstone another team's transmitter record, and read it.

**The rule, stated once.** *Vouching is a claim that this push established the
row.* Only a row that passed authorization **and actually wrote something** may
make it. A refused row must not vouch — that was already true and already
written down — and neither must a row that wrote nothing, which was not.

**Why the obvious alternative is wrong.** Removing the `!changesStoredRow`
clause instead would close the hole and reintroduce the false refusal it was
added for: a viewer, or anyone re-offering an unchanged row, would be told they
may not write something they are not writing. §4.7's data-custody rules make
that a held row with a permanent explanation, which is a lie about the record.
The fix is to stop the no-op vouching, not to start refusing it.

**Violated by:** any future call site that records within-push provenance from a
branch that does not write.


#### 4.21.4 Reading inside a project is not on the gradient (Michael, 2026-09-07)

**Decision.** §4.21's gradient is a **write** gradient. Within a project a
person belongs to, **every role reads everything the project holds** — the
gradient decides what they may change, never what they may see. A screen that
shows a `viewer` less than it shows an `owner` is doing something the model has
not asked for, and needs a reason of its own.

**Asked and answered directly.** On 2026-09-07, shown a viewer who could open a
tag's details page read-only, Michael said: *"A non-owner should be able to read
all the tag's info."* This section exists so that the next reader meets a
written rule rather than an undocumented difference they must read as drift.

**Why this needed writing down at all.** §4.11 fixes the server's *read scope*
— the set of projects a request may read comes from the session, never from the
request — and §4.23 says the app's checks are advisory and the server is the
boundary. **Both are about writes or about scope. Neither says what a screen may
render to a member who cannot write.** Nothing in this document did, and on
2026-09-06 a screen changed that behavior with no instrument able to notice
(see the last part of this section).

**What changed, and the field-by-field argument rather than an assertion.** The
Tag Database's details page (`lib/features/more/screens/tag_database_screen.dart`,
`_TagEditDialog`) used to refuse a non-owner's tap outright: the refusal was
shown and the handler returned. **So the one person who could not edit a tag was
also the only person who could not read it.** It now opens read-only, with that
same refusal — same wording, same `tag_edit_not_permitted` key — as its banner.

The page shows eight fields. Where each already reached a viewer's eyes before
the change:

| Field on Tag details | Tag list row | Map | Record (observation logging) | Project setup tag list | Export tags CSV |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Frequency | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Pulse rate | no (was, until 2026-09-06) | no | yes | no | yes |
| Pulse pattern | no | no | no | no | **yes, and nowhere else** |
| Tag / animal name | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Status | yes, as a grayed icon | no | no | yes | yes |
| Date put on | no | no | no | no | **yes, and nowhere else** |
| Notes | no | no | no | no | **yes, and nowhere else** |
| Color | yes, the swatch | yes | yes | no | yes |

**The reporter's argument was that these fields were already rendered on the map
and the record screen. Three of them were not** — pulse pattern, date put on and
notes appear on neither, and `pulsePattern` and `datePutOn` are rendered nowhere
in `lib/` outside this page. **The conclusion survives, through a different
surface than the one named:** the Tag Database's own **Export tags CSV** button
writes all eight fields for every tag on the device, is gated by nothing
(`refused: null` — "an export reads the tag list out and writes no record, so no
permission governs it"), and has always been available to a viewer. So no field
crossed a boundary it had not already crossed, and the decision Michael was asked
for covers the fields he was actually shown.

**That export is intended and is recorded here so it is not read as an
oversight.** A viewer may export every field of every tag on their device, in one
tap. Under this section's rule that is correct: the data is inside a project they
belong to, and the export writes nothing. It is named explicitly because an
ungated bulk read *looks* like a gap next to a gated bulk import sitting one icon
away.

**Violated by:** a screen that hides project data from a member because of their
role, without a reason stated in
`test/documentation/screen_permission_branches_test.dart` and here; a read
permission enforced only in a widget (which would be §4.23's error in the other
direction — an advisory check with no boundary behind it).

**Implemented by:** the read-only branch of `_TagEditDialog` and the padlock on
`_TagRow`; `project_setup_screen.dart`'s `enabled: isOwner` fields, which are the
same shape; `project_members_screen.dart`, which every member may open (task
11.99).

**The one deliberate exception, and why it is not one.** A non-owner does not see
the join code or the pending-request list on the members screen. **A join code is
a credential, not information about the project** — showing it to a viewer would
hand them the ability to admit strangers, which is a write. Everything else on
that screen, including every member's role and every past stint, is readable by
everybody.

##### What can see a change like this, and what cannot

**Nothing in this repository could have seen it, and that is the larger finding.**
The instruments that exist, and the question each answers:

- **`test/documentation/permissions_matrix_membership_test.dart`** derives
  §4.2 of `PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md` from the server's route declarations, in both
  directions. **It answers what the server returns.** A screen is not a route.
- **§4.21.2's per-endpoint isolation verdicts** and
  `server/test/authz/*` answer the same question on the wire, per row.
- **`test/features/refusal_messages_rendered_test.dart`** renders nine
  `UnauthorizedMutation` messages through real screens. It answers **whether a
  refusal is worded well**, not whether a refusal is the right answer. This is
  exactly how the change hid: the refusal it covered was correct, actionable and
  tested — it was simply the *end of the road*, which is invisible from inside a
  test that checks the message.
- **`reasonedMenuItem` / `DisabledReasonNote`
  (`test/features/disabled_reason_geometry_test.dart`)** answer whether a
  disabled control says why, and whether the sentence fits. Not what is behind it.
- **The `mayWrite*` / `mayCreateTag` / `mayEditTag` providers** answer whether a
  write would be refused, so a screen can avoid offering it. **All three are
  named for writing**, and there is no read-side equivalent because until now
  there was no read-side rule.

**Measured 2026-09-06 before proposing anything.** Of the 64 widget-tree source
files under `lib/features/` and `lib/widgets/`, **13 branch on a permission
signal — 9 of the 25 screens, 3 dialogs, and the shared reason-rendering helper.**
Three of the 13 change what is *rendered* rather than only what is *offered*.
That is a small enough population that a written list with a verdict per file is
an honest instrument, and `test/documentation/screen_permission_branches_test.dart`
is that list, kept true by a derivation: a file that starts or stops branching on
a permission fails the run until somebody writes down what a person without that
permission sees there.

**Its limit, stated where it will be read rather than discovered.** It is a
declaration, not a derivation of behavior. It notices a **file** joining or
leaving the class; it cannot notice a screen already on the list changing what it
shows a viewer. **Both known instances of this class are of that second kind** —
task 11.99's owner-only members screen and this one — **so the new check would
have caught neither.**

**That gap is closed. Task 11.183 built the per-role record**, and it is
`test/documentation/screen_role_view_test.dart`. It holds what an owner and a
non-owner each see on all nine screens, declares the **21** places where a
permission decides what is rendered, and **fails when one of them appears,
vanishes or is reworded** — which is what would have caught both known
instances. **Its verdict on 2026-09-06: no screen hides project data from a
member because of their role.** All nine satisfy this section today.

**And the "one deliberate exception" is now a rule rather than an exemption,
which is the stronger shape.** The members screen may withhold the join code and
the pending-request list **because the server refuses a non-owner both routes** —
`_requireOwner` on `GET /projects/<id>/join-settings` and
`GET /projects/<id>/join-requests` — and the pending list additionally carries
the email addresses of people who are not members of anything. So the general
form, and the one to apply next time:

> **A screen may withhold something from a member only when the server would
> withhold it too.**

**That is checkable and it is checked**: a test reads `_requireOwner` out of
`project_routes.dart` and goes red if either route opens up. **An exception
written as a coupling cannot quietly become a license; one written as prose
can.**

### 4.22 What a mark may name, and why a dangling reference is inert (task 11.9, 2026-08-22)

`Observation_Exclusions` is the table behind "this bearing is superseded" and
"exclude this observation from the analysis." It is the **only write in this
app where one person acts on somebody else's record** — §4.21 sets the two
rungs (superseding is contributor-level on anyone's row, excluding is
owner-only), and §4.13 records that its primary key discloses nothing. Neither
answers the question this section exists for.

**The question.** A mark names the observation it takes out of analysis, in
`observation_id`, and names an optional replacement in
`superseded_by_observation_id`. **There is no foreign key on either side of the
wire** — `schema.dart` gives three reasons, all of them good, the first being
that sync legitimately delivers a mark before the row it names. `RowValidator`
does not check the column either, and `sync_tables.dart` justifies the absence
of an `observationColumns` declaration with one sentence: *"the observation this
row names is always in the same project, so the ordinary project scope already
carries it."* **Nothing enforces that sentence.** So: can a mark name an
observation in another project, or one its writer cannot reach, and if it can,
what happens to the analysis of the project that owns that observation?

**Measured answer, part 1: yes, it can, and the server accepts it.** A
contributor in project P pushing a mark whose own `project_id` is P and whose
`observation_id` belongs to project Q is answered `inserted`
(`scripts/verify_11_9_team_surface.py`, probe 1). So is one naming an
observation id that exists nowhere at all. The check that *does* fire is a
different one: a mark whose own `project_id` is Q is refused
(`crossProjectClaim`), and a mark pushed straight into Q by a non-member draws
§4.13's uniform `403`. **Scope is enforced on the row; the reference is not
checked at all.**

**Measured answer, part 2: nothing happens, and the reason is a second property
rather than the sentence above.** Every consumer of a mark resolves it inside
one project:

- `ObservationExclusionRepository.activeByObservation(projectId)` and
  `withdrawnByObservation(projectId)` both filter on `project_id` before
  keying by observation.
- `AnalysisEligibility.eligible` is handed that already-scoped map together
  with one project's observations, and the two call sites — the position
  estimation screen and the Log/Team tab — each pass a `projectId`.
- Pull delivers a mark only to members of the project the mark's own
  `project_id` names, so a mark aimed at Q's observation never reaches Q.

That is measured, not read: `test/security/exclusion_reference_scope_test.dart`
builds the one state in which a cross-project reference could bite — **the same
`observation_id` present in two projects**, which Phase 6.3's replica import
produces by design when a shared observation keeps its identity — and asserts
that a mark in one project changes nothing in the other. Each test carries its
own positive control in the same body: the identical mark, aimed inside its own
project, must take the observation out. Removing the `project_id` filter from
the repository turns all three tests red, which is how we know they measure
something.

`superseded_by_observation_id` is narrower still: it is written and never read
back. No screen resolves it, and the solver ignores it.

**Disposition: accepted, with the condition made explicit.** A dangling or
foreign reference is inert because the *reads* are project-scoped, **not**
because the write is constrained. Anything that starts resolving
`observation_id` or `superseded_by_observation_id` without a `project_id`
alongside it — a cross-project "where else does this bearing appear" view, an
export that follows the replacement link, a report that joins marks to
observations globally — turns every historical value into a live cross-project
reference. That is the same conditional shape as §5.9(b)'s id-list columns, and
the same instruction applies: **give the column a real check before writing the
feature, not after.**

**Violated by:** any read of `Observation_Exclusions.observation_id` or
`superseded_by_observation_id` that is not scoped by `project_id`.

---

### 4.23 The app's permission checks are advisory; the server is the boundary (task 11.9, 2026-08-22)

Stated here as a general property because it keeps being rediscovered per
feature — task 11.11 raised it for tags, 11.19 and 11.20 for the two import
paths, 11.7 for exclusion marks — and each rediscovery costs a round of
argument about whether it is a finding.

**It is not a finding. It is the design.**

**And it is about writes.** Every check named below stops a *write*. What a
screen may *show* a member who cannot write is §4.21.4's question, and the
answer there is "everything the project holds" — a read is not on the gradient.

Every permission this app enforces is enforced twice, and the two enforcements
are not equal partners:

- **In the app**, `BaseRepository._authorize`, `assertRoleMayWrite`,
  `assertMayMark`, `assertMayEdit`, `receiverMayImport` and the
  `mutation_authorization.dart` verdicts stop a *screen* from offering a write
  that would be refused. They run against this device's own SQLite file.
- **On the server**, `ProjectAuthorizer` and `RowAuthorizer` run against
  Postgres inside the sync transaction, over rows that arrived from an
  untrusted network. **This is the boundary.**

**A person with access to their own device's database file can therefore edit
anything locally.** A viewer can write an observation into their SQLite file
with a text editor; a contributor can set their own membership row's `role` to
`owner`. Neither is a vulnerability, because neither changes what anyone else
sees: the row is refused on the next push, held with an explanation (task
10.28), and never reaches a teammate. What such a person has is a private,
divergent copy of data they were already allowed to read — which is §5.1's
removed-member non-goal and §5.10's restore residual, in general form.

Three consequences worth writing down, because each has been asked separately:

1. **A client-side check that fails open is not automatically a finding.** The
   several `?? true` "permit while the role is still resolving" defaults in the
   UI layer are advisory-layer behavior; what they can produce is a control
   that renders enabled and then fails at the tap, which is a task 11.12
   usability question, not a security one.
2. **A client-side check that fails open where there is no server-side twin
   *is* a finding**, and that is the distinction tasks 11.19 and 11.20 turned
   on. The question to ask of any new write path is not "does the app check"
   but "does the server refuse".
3. **This property is what makes the role gradient meaningful at all.** A
   `viewer` who can write because only the UI stopped them is not a viewer —
   which is why §4.21's gradient is enforced in `RowAuthorizer._authorizeRole`
   and measured on the wire rather than asserted in a widget test.

**Violated by:** any write path where the app's check is the only check.

### 4.24 A control that holds for a different reason than the documented one is fragile in a specific way (task 11.27, 2026-08-22)

Stated here as a general property, the way §4.23 was, because this is its
**third** appearance in two weeks and each time it looked like a different bug:

- §19.2 (task 11.24): `_authorizeExclusionKind` was documented and believed to
  read the stored mark's `kind`. It read the pushed one. A withdrawal that
  flipped `kind` to `superseded` in the same row escaped the owner-only rung
  the comment said was there.
- §18.4's N-4 (task 11.9): `RowAuthorizer._mayReplicate`'s doc comment says it
  "requires write access to the project"; the code returns `access.
  permitsSync`, which is true for a `viewer`. It is safe today only because
  `_authorizeRole` happens to refuse a viewer earlier in the same function —
  a fact about ordering, not about the comment's claim.
- §4.3, `auth_routes.dart` and `server/README.md` (task 11.27, this task):
  three places stated that member removal revokes sessions server-side. What
  actually makes removal immediate is unrelated — membership is re-resolved
  on every request — and the session survives, untouched, exactly as designed.
  A correction of this was written once, in §5.1's discussion, three weeks
  before this task; it corrected the *belief* and never touched the three
  places that stated it, so all three were still there for anyone reading
  §4.3, the code, or the README to find and trust.

- `RowAuthorizer._replicableName` (task 11.46, this instance): the paragraph
  on why clause 2 stays in force for the shared-vocabulary tables ended
  *"That is what keeps a first publish working when the project's tags were
  created by a colleague."* Measured, it does not. Clause 2 vouches only when
  the project **already reaches** the person named, and on a first publish the
  project on the server reaches nobody — it is being created by the request
  asking the question. Such a tag is refused, every time.

  **This one is a variant of the shape below, and the difference is worth
  keeping.** The three above state the wrong *reason* for a control that does
  hold. This states a wrong *outcome*: the case the sentence names does not
  work at all. It survived for the same reason they did — nothing downstream
  visibly broke, because the refusal cascades **cleanly** (the bearing using
  the tag is refused by `_authorizeTagReferences`, held on the device, and
  explained), so the only symptom was records quietly not arriving. It was
  found by task 11.43 *measuring the publish payload*, not by reading the
  comment, which is the general lesson: a false outcome claim is invisible to
  review precisely when the failure it hides is graceful.

**The shape is the same each time.** A person states property A as the reason
a control works. Property B is the real reason, and B happens to hold too — so
nothing visibly breaks, and the wrong belief survives review after review. The
danger is not the moment the comment is wrong; it is the moment somebody
*preserves the documented reason* while refactoring, because they have no way
to know it was never the load-bearing one. Moving `_authorizeRole` below the
replication exemption, or teaching a future removal flow to call
`revokeAllSessionsForUser` "to match what the comment already says," would each
turn a harmless drift into a live defect, on a day when nothing about the
*code path people are reading* told them to check.

**What this means in practice:** when a review finds a comment or a security
model sentence that states *why* a control is safe, checking that the control
fires is not enough. The reason stated must be re-derived from the code that
runs, not read off the comment — and where the two diverge, the comment is the
one that gets fixed, immediately, at its source, not merely noted somewhere
else in the document. Task 11.27's own finding is the proof this rule needs
restating: the correction three weeks earlier addressed the belief and left
the sentence, which is exactly the failure this paragraph exists to name.

**Violated by:** fixing what a control does without fixing what a nearby
comment says it does for; correcting a false claim in one place while the same
claim stands, verbatim, somewhere else; treating "the control happens to hold"
as equivalent to "the documented reason is true."

---

### 4.25 Leaving a project — the one exception to owner-only membership (task 11.28, 2026-08-23)

**Decision.** A person may end **their own** currently-open membership row, and
nothing else. No owner confirmation is required. Michael decided this on
2026-08-22.

**Why this section did not exist before.** It should have. Membership rows are
`MutationRule.projectOwner` — the row *is* somebody's rights, so an owner writes
it and nobody else — and the consequence nobody wrote down is that **a viewer or
a contributor could not get off a project by any means.** Task 11.23 found it as
M8 and called it the most consequential entry in the permissions matrix; the
note attached to it read *"No section of the security model discusses it at
all."* This is that section.

It was not only a missing feature. A device that tried anyway hit an
`UnauthorizedMutation` no screen caught, and if the row reached the wire the
server refused it *forever* — held, re-offered, refused again — so that device
stayed permanently divergent on that row. A refusal that can never become an
acceptance is not a control, it is a stuck state.

**The exception, stated as narrowly as it can be.** `isSelfDeparture`
(`packages/tritrack_sync/lib/src/membership_departure.dart`) is the single
definition both sides apply:

1. The table is `Project_Memberships` and the write is an **update**. An insert
   into this table is a grant and is untouched by this.
2. **The stored row's `user_id` is the caller.** Read from the stored row, never
   from the incoming one, so what the caller claims about the row is irrelevant.
3. The stored stint is **open** — `end_date` and `deleted_at` both null.
4. The incoming row sets `end_date` to a non-empty timestamp.
5. **Every other declared column is byte-identical to the stored row**, and the
   set of "every other" is derived from the shared table spec rather than
   listed. A column added to this table in a future migration is immutable
   during a departure without anybody remembering to say so.

**What it overrides, and what it does not.** Exactly two refusals, at two named
points in `RowAuthorizer.authorizeWrite`: the role gradient (§4.21), so a
`viewer` can leave; and the `projectOwner` rule, so a non-owner can. Everything
else still binds, and the ones that matter are:

- **The last owner cannot leave.** `_authorizeOwnerRemoval` runs on the
  permitting path, not around it, so a departure is subject to the zero-owners
  rule exactly as an owner's removal of somebody else is — including the case a
  single device cannot see, two owners leaving from two offline devices, where
  the second to arrive is refused.
- **The audit column must name the caller** (§4.0 of the permissions matrix,
  task 11.24). A departure is a change, and a change names who made it.
- **Leaving is not a promotion.** `role` is immutable during a departure. The
  closed row confers nothing live either way, so the harm this refuses is
  *attribution*, not privilege: a closed stint is the record that somebody held
  a role on this project between two dates, and that record is what a permit
  report and a publication read.
- **Leaving is not a tombstone.** `deleted_at` is immutable during a departure.
  Ending a stint and erasing it are different acts, and erasing stays
  owner-only.
- **Leaving is not rejoining.** An already-ended stint cannot be reopened. The
  way back onto a project is invite redemption, which the server authors itself.

**The device is left consistent, and that is half the fix.** Three ordered steps
in `MembershipController.leaveProject`: sync that project first, so the
departure is not built from a stale copy of a row an owner changed while this
device was offline; write the departure; and unlink the project **only once the
server has confirmed the row**. The order is the design — unlinking first would
strand the departure on the device forever, so the person would still be a
member everywhere but here. Left linked, the project would go on syncing until
the server refused it with a bare `403`, which is terminal, unexplained, and
indistinguishable from a broken server.

**And the offline case, which on a field device is the normal one.** Somebody
leaves at the end of a track with no signal: the departure is written and
pending, goes out days later, and from the sync after *that* the server refuses
the project — long after the action that caused it. So the refusal itself is
handled: a `403` on a project **this device's own records say the signed-in
person has already left** unlinks it (`SyncController._unlinkIfWeAlreadyLeft`).
The second half of that condition is what keeps it narrow. A `403` alone is also
what a member *removed by an owner* sees, and their membership row still reads
open because the pull that would have closed it is the very thing being refused;
unlinking on the refusal alone would quietly stop syncing a project somebody may
be about to be re-added to. Only sync bookkeeping is cleared — cursor,
last-success, linked flag — never data (task 10.19).

**What leaving does not reach, said out loud.** The copy of the project already
on the leaver's device stays there and keeps working offline. This is the same
limit an owner is shown before they add anybody (`removalDisclosure`), stated
from the other side, and the confirmation dialog says it.

**Violated by:** an exception keyed on "a membership row is being ended" rather
than on *whose* row; reading the subject from the incoming row; permitting any
second column to move in the same write; permitting an insert; bypassing the
last-owner guard by allowing early rather than inside the ownership branch;
unlinking a project before the server has taken the departure.

---

### 4.26 A reference to a refused row costs one row, not the whole request (task 11.46, 2026-08-28)

**The failure.** The server's foreign keys are `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED`
(§10.5's clock and sequencing work). A row that references something the server
does not hold therefore does not fail at the `INSERT` that made it — it fails at
`COMMIT`, after `applyPush` has already decided and reported a per-row outcome
for every row in the batch, and outside the reach of anything that could turn it
into one. The request dies whole: `errorHandlerMiddleware` catches the throw and
answers `internal_error`, and **every row in the push is rolled back, including
the ones that were perfectly fine.**

**It was reachable, and reproduced.** A project built from a colleague's archive
carries rows that colleague last touched. §4.17 refuses those, correctly. The
rows that then break are not those rows — they are the caller's **own** bearings
pointing at them. `Triangulation_Sessions` is the reproduced instance: a session
a colleague last edited was refused by §4.17, and the owner's own observation
naming it through `Observations.(session_id, project_id)` was accepted, so the
push 500'd at commit. The tag path that task 11.43 predicted would do the same
does **not**, because `_authorizeTagReferences` refuses the dependent bearing
first — which is why this had to be measured rather than assumed.

> **The cause used in that reproduction no longer refuses anything (task
> 11.47), and this paragraph is left in the past tense rather than rewritten.**
> An audit name on shared vocabulary is now accepted, so a session a colleague
> last edited does not dangle. **The defect this section fixes is untouched** —
> it was never about *why* a referent was refused, only about what happens to
> the row pointing at it — and every other way to refuse a referent still
> reaches it: a role refusal, an unreachable tag, a malformed row. The
> regression test was re-expressed onto an unreachable tag for exactly that
> reason (`publish_and_join_test.dart`); had it been left alone it would have
> gone green while reproducing nothing, which is the failure mode §0 keeps
> naming.

**The decision: refuse the one row.** `RowAuthorizer._authorizeReferences` now
checks, for every foreign key the schema declares, that what a row points at
either already exists or is being written by this same push. A row that would
dangle is refused as `DenialReason.danglingReference` — one more `unauthorized`
on the wire, indistinguishable from any other per §4.13. It costs that row
nothing it was not already losing (its referent was refused too), it lets the
rest of the push land, and `SyncHeldRowStore` holds and explains it the way
§4.17 already relies on.

**Why this is not an existence oracle**, which is the question §4.13 makes every
server-state check answer. It runs **last**, only on a row authorization has
already allowed, so a caller can only reach it with references they were already
entitled to make: identity columns are narrowed to the caller by §4.17, tag
columns to the project's reachable set by §4.13's D-1 work, `project_id` to the
project in the envelope, and the session key is composite with that `project_id`
— so what shows through is at most whether a row exists **inside a project the
caller can already pull in full**. That argument is written one key at a time,
so it does not automatically extend to a key added later:
`server/test/authz/reference_integrity_test.dart` fails when the built database
carries a foreign key `foreignKeys` does not declare, which is the moment
somebody has to extend it.

**What is deliberately not solved here.** This makes the failure legible and
survivable; it does not make a colleague-authored row publishable. Whether that
condition should stop existing is task 11.34's copy-on-add question, and this
section does not pre-empt it.

**Half of that was answered by task 11.47, and it is worth being precise about
which half.** A colleague-*edited* row is now publishable — that is the audit
column, and §4.17's newest narrowing. A colleague-**authored** row is not, and
will not be: Michael decided on 2026-08-28 that a restored record keeps the
name of the person who made it, so their bearings remain theirs to push. The
two words did most of the work in this whole area and are worth keeping apart.

### 4.27 What the server tells somebody it has just stopped talking to (task 11.60, 2026-08-29)

**Decision.** A caller with **no open membership** on a project is refused
everything about it, with one stated exemption: `POST /sync/pull` returns **the
caller's own `Project_Memberships` rows whose stint is over** — the rows where
`end_date` or `deleted_at` is set — and nothing else. No other table, no other
person's rows, no `Projects` row, and no page beyond the one. Push and ack are
unchanged and still refuse outright.

**The problem it solves, in plain terms.** An owner removes somebody. The
removed person's phone never finds out, because the only request that could
carry the news is the request the server is now refusing. Their app shows an
amber "the server is refusing access", their bearings sit on the device, and the
Delete control does nothing — because the control that lets a departed member
delete their own copy (`MutationExemption.departedMember`) reads the *local*
membership rows, and locally they are still a member. Task 11.57 measured this;
`membership_cycle_matrix_e2e_test.dart` asserted it.

**Why this shape and not a screen fix.** The alternative was to leave the device
knowing nothing and word the screen around it. That could never say *you have
been removed* — it would be false when the real cause was a revoked session, a
rebuilt server, or an outage — so it would have been a workaround for not
knowing, on the one surface Phase 11 spent four tasks making truthful. It would
also have needed a **second way to delete a project**, beside the departed-member
path that already exists. This deletes a special case instead of adding one: once
the device holds its own closed row, the existing exemption is satisfied and
delete works through the path already there. Michael decided this on 2026-08-29,
reversing his own earlier choice the same day and overriding the planning
session's lean.

**What this must be indistinguishable from, which is the security question.**
This is a read that answers a caller the server is otherwise refusing, and that
is the shape existence oracles are made of (§4.13, §7.3 B2). The property is:

> **A caller who holds no closed membership row on the named project cannot
> tell, by any observable, a project that does not exist from one that exists
> and is not theirs.** Same status, same body, same query sequence.

Three things make that true, and each is a thing that was done rather than
assumed:

1. **The exemption is keyed on a row only the server can produce.** The
   disclosure fires when `Project_Memberships` holds a closed row for
   `(project_id, this session's user_id)`. A prober cannot manufacture one for a
   project they were never on — the row is written by an owner's push or by
   invitation redemption, both of which are authorized elsewhere. So the only
   callers who can observe the exemption at all are callers for whom the server
   already holds a durable record that they were a member, and who therefore
   already knew the project existed.
2. **The lookup runs on every refusal, not only on the ones that will succeed.**
   A forbidden project, a fictional project and a closed stint all execute the
   same query before the answer is chosen, so the refusal branch does not become
   shorter than the disclosure branch.
3. **`ProjectAuthorizer.resolve` no longer returns early for a project that does
   not exist.** It used to run one query for `absent` and two for `none` —
   a difference in *work done* between "does not exist" and "not yours" that
   predates this task and that this task removed, because adding a third query on
   top of it would have widened it.

`server/test/security/closed_membership_disclosure_test.dart` demonstrates the
property rather than asserting it: it compares the full response — status, headers and
body bytes — across a fictional project, a real project the caller was never on,
and a real project the caller was removed from *while holding a closed
membership on a different project*, so the caller is one who can reach the
exemption and still learns nothing about the ids they have no row for.

**What the row itself discloses, stated rather than waved past.** The row is the
caller's own, and it carries `end_date` (when their stint ended) and
`last_modified_by` (which account ended it). The task brief said "not who
removed them, not when", and this ships both — deliberately, and the reasoning
is the useful part. `end_date` **is** the news; without it the row says nothing.
`last_modified_at` is the merge clock, so a row stripped of it cannot be merged
at all. `last_modified_by` could have been blanked, and was not, because a row
that differs from the server's copy is a row this device will disagree with the
server about forever — a second, unmergeable representation of a row, which is
the class of defect `packages/tritrack_sync` exists to prevent. **The residual:
a removed member learns which account removed them.** They were a member, so
they already held that project's membership list and its owners' ids; the one
case where the id is new to them is an owner promoted after their last
successful pull, and the `Users` row for that id is *not* delivered, so it
resolves to no name on their device. This is the part of the exemption most
worth attacking.

**What it does not do.** It does not restore any access: `permitsSync` is still
false for a closed stint, the same enum value governs push and ack, and the
disclosure is a branch taken *after* that check fails rather than a widening of
it. It does not deliver an open membership row — including the fail-closed case
where a role string this build cannot interpret leaves somebody with an open row
and no access. That person still sees "the server refused access" and is not
helped by this section; it is a smaller gap than the one being closed and it is
recorded here rather than fixed quietly.

**Where the exemption lives, on purpose.** One function,
`ClosedMembershipDisclosure.rowsFor`, in a file named after it, with one call
site — the same discipline as `SyncService.insertServerAuthoredRow`, and for the
same reason: a second caller should be visible in a grep rather than hidden
behind a permissive default. **This project's findings come from exemptions**, so
this one is written down here, attacked in
`server/test/security/closed_membership_disclosure_test.dart`, and carried on the
trust-boundary inventory as entry 28 with an Open verdict until Gate C attacks it
(task 11.49).

**Fixed 2026-09-18: the device undid this section on the owner's own screen
(task 11.280).** §4.27 is the server's half — it tells a person whose stint is
over that it is over. **The device threw that answer away.** A repair in
`ProjectMembershipRepository`, reached from `currentProjectProvider`,
`projectByIdProvider` and `allProjectsProvider`, re-inserted a **fresh open owner
membership row** whenever it read a project whose `owner_user_id` matched the
signed-in user. So an owner who left or was removed from a project they had
created was quietly restored **on the next screen build**, every time, and would
never learn from the app that their access had ended.

**Only an owner of a project they personally created could reach it.** The repair
keys on `Projects.owner_user_id`, so contributors and viewers were never affected
— stated here so nobody re-derives it as still open.

**It is not dated, on purpose.** It has presumably been true since whichever of
tasks 8.4/11.1 and 11.54/11.60 landed second, and task 11.280 did not try to
narrow that further because **the fix does not depend on when it started** and a
date written from inference is the kind of number this project has been wrong
about before.

**How it was found is worth as much as the fix.** Nobody reported it. A
*screenshot* of the Sync Status screen could not be taken — the harness waited
twenty seconds for "you're not on this project" and the screen never said it —
and the task that chased that timeout found the round had classified correctly
and something else had undone it on the next build. **A picture that cannot be
taken is a finding.** Covered now by
`test/core/providers/app_context_provider_test.dart`.

### 4.28 What a row of `GET /projects/mine` may carry (task 11.64, finding P-1, 2026-08-29)

***Derived*** — `test/documentation/project_directory_field_set_test.dart` diffs the field table below against the fields the route returns. A sixth field cannot appear without this section being updated. *(Said "fifth" until 2026-09-24; task 11.290 added the fifth, `destroy_at`, on 2026-09-20 and this sentence was not carried — found by task 11.310.)*

**Why this section exists at all.** `/projects/mine` has been on the inventory
since Gate C's first run, folded into entry 15, and it has only ever been
attacked as a *route*: can a stranger reach it, does a revoked session still
work, does a removed member still see the project. All three hold. What nobody
had ever written down is **what the answer contains** — and without that
sentence, "does `/projects/mine` leak?" is not a question anybody can answer,
because there is no statement to falsify. Task 11.49 found this, recorded it as
finding P-1, and deliberately stopped there under §6's stopping rule. This is
the sentence.

**The rule.** A row of `GET /projects/mine` carries exactly five fields, and a
sixth is a disclosure decision that amends this section:

| Field | What it is | Why the caller may have it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `project_id` | The project's identifier | The caller has an open membership in it; every sync request they make already names it |
| `project_name` | Its name | Shown on the project list and the join screen. The caller is a member; they see it in the app already |
| `owner_user_id` | **Another person's identifier** | See below — this is the only field that needed a decision rather than a sentence |
| `role` | *The caller's own* role in that project | A fact about the caller |
| `destroy_at` | When the server will destroy the project, or null (task 11.290) | A fact about the project, not about any member: an owner scheduled its destruction and every member's records go with it. The rows are the projects the caller holds an open membership in, so the caller is exactly the person the date is addressed to — a contributor cannot cancel it, and the one thing they can do is export before it arrives, which needs the date. Set by the server's clock from the server's grace period; no device writes it. It is not a "timestamp belonging to another member" in the sense of the list below: it belongs to the project |

**`owner_user_id` is kept, and here is the reasoning rather than a shrug.** It
is another person's `user_id`, which is exactly the class of value entry 27's
attacks searched the sessions response for and did not find. It is kept here
for one reason: **every caller of this route already holds it.** The rows are
projects the caller has an *open membership* in, so the same caller may
`POST /sync/pull` that project and receive its `Projects` row, whose
`owner_user_id` column is the same value. Removing it from this response would
narrow nothing — it would move one disclosure from a route where it is written
down to a route where it is not.

What it is **not** is an excuse for the next field. `Users.email` is *also*
reachable by that same pull, and it must not appear here, because this route
answers before a device has joined anything and its response is what the join
screen renders. The test is not "could they get it another way"; it is "is this
field needed by what this route is for, and is it already theirs".

**What may never appear here**, stated so a future field has something to be
checked against: any email address, any device identifier, any token or token
hash, any session or membership dates, any source address, any count or
timestamp belonging to another member, and any of the server's own bookkeeping
columns (`server_seq`, `revision`, `updated_at`).

**How this is kept true.** Two checks, in two places, because a rule with no
instrument is the shape §4.7's retention sweep had for six gates:

- `test/documentation/project_directory_field_set_test.dart` reads the table
  above out of this file at run time and compares it to `ProjectSummary`'s own
  `toJson`. Adding a field to the class without amending this section turns it
  red, and so does amending this section without changing the class.
- `server/test/integration/member_authorization_test.dart` asserts the same
  five keys on a **live** response from a real server, so a field added by the
  route rather than by the model is caught too.

**Amended by task 11.290 (2026-09-20), a code task, because the section itself
says a new field amends it and the field-set test refuses the field until it
does. Read and adopted by the planning session on 2026-09-21** — the row above
is the decision, not a placeholder waiting for one.

**The distinction it turns on, stated so a later field can be measured against
it:** `destroy_at` is a fact about the *project*, not about any member, which is
why it may travel to a contributor who cannot act on it and whose only remaining
move is to export before it arrives. Every other row here is either the caller's
own fact or one already visible to them in the app. **A sixth field that cannot
be defended on one of those two footings does not belong on this route**, and the
place to argue it is here rather than in the task that wants it.

**The three bounds this route was also missing**, closed by the same task and
recorded here because they are the reason P-1 was filed rather than merely
noted:

- **No `LIMIT`.** `ProjectDirectoryService.listFor` now takes one
  (`maxListedProjects`, 200) with a deterministic `ORDER BY`. The row count is
  caller-influenced: a signed-in caller can publish projects.
- **No per-user rate limit**, while `/auth/sessions` — the same shape of
  authenticated read — got one under task 10.56.
  `RateLimitPolicy.projectListPerUser` closes it, at the same 60 per 15
  minutes and keyed on the authenticated user, which cannot collapse behind a
  proxy the way an address can (§4.4.1).
- **No `cache-control: no-store`**, which the sessions listing has sent since
  task 11.35. A list of somebody's projects is not something to leave in a
  shared cache (§4.7).

**Why 10.56's sweep missed all three.** That task bounded *every field on every
route*, and this route has no fields at all — no body, no query, no path
segment. A sweep keyed on "what does this route read from the caller" cannot
see a route that reads nothing, and the thing 10.56 was actually defending
against — an unbounded read available to anyone with a session — was present
here the whole time. **The class, not the instance:** the question to ask of a
route is "what does answering it cost, and who may ask", not only "what does it
parse".

#### 4.28.1 The second route: what a row of `GET /projects/deleted/mine` may carry (task 11.292, 2026-09-21)

***Derived*** — the same test, `project_directory_field_set_test.dart`, diffs the
second field table below against `DeletedProjectSummary.toJson`, and requires
the line above each table to name the route it belongs to, so the two tables
cannot be silently swapped.

**Why a second route exists.** Task 11.289 made an owner's plain *Delete* in the
app reach the server as a **tombstone** — `Projects.deleted_at` set, every record
kept — and the route above leaves a tombstoned project out for everybody, which is
right for a list of projects to sync. Task 11.290 built destruction, reachable
from that list and from the join screen. **Between them, a tombstoned project was
on no screen of any device, including its owner's**, and the only way to destroy
it was an operator `INSERT` over `psql` (written into `server/README.md` by task
11.292). Michael met exactly this on 2026-09-20: seven projects he had deleted on
his Mac sat on his server as tombstones that nothing could name.

**Two designs were on the table and both amend this section, so the decision is
recorded here.**

- **A sixth field on `/projects/mine`** — carry tombstoned projects too, with a
  `deleted_at`. **Refused**, for two reasons that are about this section rather
  than about code. Every existing reader of that route (the join list, the
  deletion-notice refresh, the relink path) would receive rows it was never
  written to see; and the rows would have been present on a *row-level*
  condition — owner, and the tombstone's author — that the field table above
  has no column for, so the section's one-field-at-a-time defense would have
  stopped describing what the route does.
- **A second route, carrying exactly one kind of row.** Adopted. Every consumer
  is new, and every field is defended once, below.

**The rule for the second route.** A row of `GET /projects/deleted/mine` carries
exactly four fields, and a fifth is a disclosure decision that amends this
subsection:

| Field | What it is | Why the caller may have it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `project_id` | The project's identifier | The caller holds an open **owner** membership in it; a pull of the project by that caller already delivers its `Projects` row, tombstone and all. Same footing as the table above |
| `project_name` | Its name | Same footing as above: already the caller's through a pull, and shown on the Projects list until the moment they deleted it |
| `deleted_at` | When the caller's device deleted it | **The caller's own act.** The route lists a tombstone only when the server recorded *the caller* as its sender — `Projects.last_modified_by`, which §4.17 requires to be the caller's own id on an update, so the server can stand behind *"you deleted this on"* rather than repeat a device's claim |
| `destroy_at` | When the server will destroy it, or null | The same field, on the same footing, as the table above: a fact about the project, set by the server's clock, and here addressed to the one person who can cancel it |

**Who is listed, stated as three conditions that all have to hold** — and each
one has a test that goes red without it (`server/test/integration/deleted_project_directory_test.dart`,
watched failing on 2026-09-21 with each clause removed in turn):

1. **An open `owner` membership**, the same membership join the route above
   uses, narrowed to the owner role. So every row here is one `_requireOwner`
   admits to the deletion routes — `ProjectAuthorizer` never reads
   `Projects.deleted_at`, measured rather than read off its comment — which is
   what makes the listing actionable rather than a report. An owner demoted
   *after* deleting drops off the list the moment the deletion routes would
   refuse them.
2. **A tombstoned row.** A destroyed project has no `Projects` row left and
   cannot appear, so the list empties itself as *delete now* runs.
3. **The caller sent the tombstone.** A co-owner who did not delete it is not
   told about it here; a tombstone with no audit name (a build older than the
   stamp) is not listed either. **The operator path is the reach for both.**

**Refused, in writing: a general "show me deleted projects" listing.** Every
tombstoned project the caller can see, or every tombstoned project on the
server, in any form — a field, a route, a query flag. **It is a question about
the server's history, not about the caller's own projects**, and it fails both
footings this section allows: the rows are not the caller's own fact, and a
project the caller does not hold an open membership in is not one they already
hold. §4.13's reopen trigger names this shape by name — *a listing, a search* —
and a listing that named a tombstoned or destroyed id to somebody who does not
already hold it would be that trigger fired. The narrow route above takes **no
identifier at all**: it cannot be used to ask about an id, and a caller who
wants to ask about a tombstoned id they do not hold is answered by the
`_requireOwner` routes and by pull identically to a fictional one — measured for
a *tombstoned* id on 2026-09-21 (the destroyed case was measured by 11.290; the
tombstoned one had never been).

**What may never appear here** is the list above, unchanged, plus two that are
specific to this route: **`owner_user_id` and `role`**, which the route above
carries and this one does not — owner-only by construction, both would only
ever say the caller's own id and the word `owner`, and a field that can say
only one thing is a field to leave off.

**Bounds.** The same `LIMIT` (`maxListedProjects`), a deterministic `ORDER BY`,
`cache-control: no-store`, and **the same per-user rate-limit bucket as
`/projects/mine`** rather than a second one: it is the same question asked of
the other half of the same table by the same screen, and a second bucket would
double the allowance for a read nobody needs more of.

**The way back — built by task 11.302 (2026-09-24), Michael's decision of
2026-09-21.** Until then a delivered deletion had no route back from any device,
and the row this route feeds offered only to *finish* it. It now also offers
**Restore**, which is `POST /projects/<projectId>/deletion` with the action
`restore` (§4.21.2 carries the verdict). **No new route and no new field** — so
nothing in this subsection's field table changed, and nothing any route returns
grew. Four decisions, recorded here because this is the section a person reads to
learn who is told about a deleted project, and a fifth added 2026-09-27:

1. **Who may restore is exactly who is listed here, derived rather than
   restated.** The route asks `ProjectDirectoryService.isDeletedBy`, which is
   built from the same query text as this listing; the server tests read what
   each caller may do off the listing's own answer for them. So the screen never
   offers a restore the server refuses, and the server never permits one no
   screen can show.
2. **Owner-only, and narrower: the owner who deleted it.** The delete it undoes
   is owner-only; the restore follows it and then keeps the author clause,
   because widening restore to any co-owner means widening *this listing* to
   co-owners too — a co-owner cannot restore what no screen shows them — and
   that is a change to footing, not to a button: *"you deleted this"* is the
   caller's own fact, while *"a colleague deleted this"* is a fact about the
   project's history. **Nothing measured says a co-owner needs it**: no report of
   a co-owner wanting to undo a colleague's delete exists, and a co-owner today
   can ask the deleting owner, who can restore from any device they sign in on.
   **Reopen trigger:** the first report of a co-owner who needed to undo a
   colleague's deletion buys widening this listing and the restore together, as
   one decision amending this subsection.
3. **Unconditional while the tombstone stands; impossible once the project is
   destroyed.** A tombstone keeps every record, so nothing about the passage of
   time makes restoring less correct, and a separate "restore window" would be a
   second clock beside the destruction one. The only end is destruction, which
   the row already shows as a countdown when one is scheduled; restoring
   **withdraws any scheduled destruction in the same transaction** (a restored
   project still counting down would be restored in name only), and the sweep
   re-reads the schedule under a lock before destroying, so a restore that lands
   after the sweep read its list is honored. Once destroyed, the restore is
   refused exactly as for a fictional id; the app then asks pull, which names a
   destroyed id under §4.13's existing written exception, and says the project is
   gone with nothing left to restore. **This route does not name it** — the
   exception is not widened.
4. **What every device does is decided by the data, not by a message.** The
   server clears `deleted_at`, bumps the revision (so the restored row beats the
   tombstone every device holds under the shared merge rule, whatever their
   clocks say), and re-stamps `server_seq` (so it re-enters every member's delta
   window). A device that holds the project's tombstone and is not itself
   waiting to send a change to that row finds the project on `/projects/mine`
   again and fetches it on its next foreground; see `restored_project_arrival.dart`
   in the app. **A member learns nothing about the restore that they could not
   already pull** — the row they receive is the project's own row, which a member
   already receives.
5. **A deleted project still accepts its members' records** (decided by the
   planning session, 2026-09-27; found by task 11.313). Neither the device's
   push nor the server's push route reads `Projects.deleted_at`; only a
   **destroyed** project is refused. **Kept that way, on purpose.** An app
   deletion is reversible, and a member hears of it only when their device next
   syncs. Refusing would punish a member for an owner's act they could not yet
   know about: their field records, made while they still held the project,
   would be refused and stranded on the device. Accepted, those records sit on
   the server hidden with the project, come back with it on a restore, and go
   with it on destruction. **No access is widened:** the membership check is
   unchanged, so only a current member can write, exactly as before the
   deletion. It is also what makes the member's notice true ("nothing you have
   recorded here is lost"). **Reopen if** a deleted project ever becomes
   impossible to restore while it still exists on the server, or if deletion
   gains a meaning of "frozen."


---

### 4.29 What one member of a project may see about the others (task 11.99, 2026-08-31)

**Why this section exists.** Until this task the members screen was owner-only —
the route to it was rendered on the projects list inside `if (isOwner)`. That
was never a decision anybody wrote down; it was a consequence of the screen
having been built, in task 11.2, as *the owner's membership dashboard*. Nothing
recorded whether a non-owner was being kept off it because showing colleagues'
names is a disclosure, or merely because nobody had needed to build the other
half.

The cost of leaving that unwritten was paid by the person least able to absorb
it. **The only place TriTrack ever named somebody's own role to them was inside
a failure message, after they had already tried something they were not allowed
to do.** A field technician whose position estimate would not save could not
tell whether that was their role or a fault in the app, and could not see who to
ask. `/w-03` found it writing the roles page for the user guide: it had to
publish a table the app could not show to most of the people it applies to.

**The decision. A non-owner may open the members screen and read the current
member list — names and roles — and their own role. Everything on that screen
that is an *action* stays owner-only:** the join code, the pending-request
queue, changing a role, removing somebody, and putting a past member back.

**The reasoning, which is the part that had to be written rather than assumed.**
This screen discloses nothing to a member that they do not already hold. Three
independent routes, and the third is decisive:

1. **Sync already sends it.** `Users` and `Project_Memberships` are ordinary
   synced tables. Every member's device receives every other member's row for a
   project they belong to, and has since Phase 10. Withholding the screen
   withheld the information from the *person*, never from the device.
2. **Another screen already shows it.** The log screen renders every
   observation's observer by name to every member, and offers a filter *by
   observer* — which is a list of the project's contributors, presented as a
   control.
3. **Any member can already export the lot.** The data-export screen is not
   role-gated (§4.15.2 records what an export carries and why), and
   `ProjectExporter` collects the `Users` row of every person referenced by the
   project's records — `email` column included. **A viewer can take a backup
   archive and read every member's address in it.** That is a wider disclosure
   than this screen makes, it is by design, and it was accepted in writing on
   2026-08-30.

Given (3), a rule that hid the member list would not have been a confidentiality
control. It would have been an inconvenience that read as one — which is the
worse outcome, because somebody would eventually rely on it.

**"Roles yes, member list no" was the other candidate and was rejected on the
evidence above**, not on preference. It would narrow nothing real while leaving
"who do I ask" unanswerable, and the task's own framing allowed it explicitly.
Recording that it was considered matters as much as the answer: the next person
to ask this question should not have to re-derive that the export path exists.

**What this section does *not* license.** The bound is *a current member of that
project*, resolved the same way every other read is — the screen's own
`projectMembershipsProvider` reads local rows for a project this device holds,
and the server's rules are unchanged by this task, which touched no server code.
In particular:

- **A non-member learns nothing.** There is no route to this screen for a
  project this device is not on, and the local database holds no membership rows
  for one.
- **The pending-request queue stays owner-only**, and that is a real line rather
  than symmetry. A pending requester is not a member. Their address is on that
  list precisely so an owner can decide whether to trust them, and showing an
  address to people who have no say in that decision widens the disclosure past
  what it is for.
- **The join code stays owner-only.** §4.2.1 makes it the one written exception
  to the plaintext rule so an *owner* can re-read it; it is a capability, not a
  fact about the project, and holding it is what lets somebody ask to join.

**How this is kept true.** `test/features/more/project_members_screen_test.dart`
asserts that a non-owner reads their own role and the member list and gets
neither the join code nor the pending list nor a working role control, and
`test/features/more/project_row_actions_test.dart` asserts that the route is
offered to a contributor at all — the specific thing that did not exist.

### 4.30 A member can pin a row against every later correction, and that is an accepted risk of write access — but never a silent one (task 11.159, 2026-09-05)

**The shape.** `MergeResolver` decides last-write-wins on `revision` first. A row
pushed at a very large `revision` therefore wins **every** future merge. A
teammate's genuine correction arrives at `revision: 8`, loses, and their device
tells them *"Unchanged (local was newer)"*. Nothing on the server refuses it, and
nothing anywhere says the record has become unamendable. Task 11.158 gave
`revision` a floor and deliberately flagged this ceiling rather than guessing at a
number for it.

**Decision, and it is two decisions.**

1. **The pin itself is an accepted risk of trusting somebody with writes.** The
   person who can do this is already a contributor or an owner on that project —
   somebody who can already overwrite the same row's contents with anything they
   like, tombstone it, or fill the project with fabricated observations. Pinning
   is not a new capability; it is a more permanent rendering of one they have.
   §4.21's role gradient is what decides who may write at all, and §4.23 states
   the general form: **the app's checks are advisory and the server is the
   boundary — but the boundary is "may this person write here", not "is what they
   wrote sensible".**
2. **What is *not* accepted is that it happens invisibly.** A silent permanent
   loss of a field record is the harm this project ranks highest (§1), and until
   this task nothing on the server could answer *"is anybody's correction being
   discarded forever?"* — not the diagnostics console, not the traffic log, not a
   query anybody could write. That gap is closed.

**Why the server does not refuse instead.** **A ceiling cannot be both safe and
effective, and that is a fact about the harm rather than about any number.**
Unovertakability begins many orders of magnitude below any bound that would be
safe to enforce — `revision: 1000000` pins an observation exactly as permanently
as `2^62` does — so a bound high enough that no honest row trips it does not
prevent the pin, and a bound low enough to prevent it is a guess about how many
times a row is edited over its life. Guessing low strands an irreplaceable field
record behind a red bar nobody can clear.

Bounding the **increment** rather than the value was the alternative considered.
`test/data/sync/offline_revision_burst_test.dart` measured it before anything was
designed, and it does not survive:

- The push offers a row's **current state**, never an edit log. Fifty corrections
  made in a dead zone arrive as **one row advanced by fifty** — so the delta is
  "how long was this person off the network", a ceiling wearing a different hat.
- A batch limit bounds how many *rows* a push carries, not how far one row has
  moved. There is no history on the wire to split.
- **A delta is blind exactly where the pin is cheapest.** A row the server has
  never seen is an insert, and an insert has no stored revision to be measured
  against. A first push at `2^62` passes a delta bound without it being consulted.
- The app itself admits `revision: 3999000000` on the share/import path (§4.19
  clause 3's own ceiling) and pushes it verbatim, so any server ceiling below that
  number would refuse a row the app consented to hold.

**The asymmetry, stated because it is the whole argument.** Refusing wrongly
strands a field record, silently and permanently. Noticing wrongly costs one row
in a server-only table. The likelier cause is a client bug — an uninitialized
value, an overflow, a bad import — and **the person holding the broken client is
not an attacker; stranding their data helps nobody.**

**Implementation.** `server/lib/src/sync/revision_plausibility.dart` classifies
every incoming row and never changes the merge: the question it asks is not *"is
this number too big"* but **"could this many edits have been made in the time the
row itself claims they took"**, answered from the row's own `created_at` /
`updated_at` span, so the only parameter is an edit rate bounded by what a person
can physically do rather than a judgement about a record's lifetime.
`server/lib/src/sync/revision_anomaly_log.dart` records what it finds in
`revision_anomalies`, a server-only table (no `latestSchemaVersion` bump), one row
per affected record. `GET /diagnostics/revision-anomalies` reads it.

**A pin already in place is caught too, and by a different door.** The register
would otherwise hold only pins pushed since this shipped, and a count of zero
would read as *"there are none"* while meaning *"none since Tuesday"*. So a push
that **loses** last-write-wins to a stored row whose own revision is
unexplainable is recorded as well (`observed_as = 'blocking'`) — which is also
the exact moment the pin starts costing somebody a correction. On such a row the
attribution columns name **the person whose edit was discarded, not whoever
pinned it.**

**Violated by:**

- Refusing a push on the strength of its `revision` alone, at any threshold. That
  is the stranding this section exists to reject; if it is ever wanted, it needs
  its own decision here with a measurement of what it would refuse.
- Letting the classification change which row wins. It is an observation, and a
  merge that consulted it would be a second implementation of the merge rule —
  the thing `packages/tritrack_sync` exists to prevent.
- Recording row **content** in `revision_anomalies`. It holds a primary key and
  numbers, the same bound `sync_traffic_log`'s `lost_detail` keeps (§4.7 rule 6).

**Residual, named rather than implied.** A member who wants to pin a row quietly
can still do it *below* the rate this detects — a revision of a few thousand on a
row a few days old is unovertakable in practice and explainable on paper. **This
is an instrument, not a control**, and it is aimed at the client bug rather than
at the determined insider, because §4.21 already grants that insider the write.
The count is also only visible through the diagnostics console, which is off by
default (§4.10); putting it in `scripts/operator_status.sh`, the command an
operator actually runs, is recorded as Discovered Scope by task 11.159.

**How this is kept true.** `server/test/sync/revision_plausibility_test.dart`
(the rule, including every legitimate field shape that must stay silent) and
`server/test/integration/revision_anomaly_test.dart` (the whole push path,
asserting **both halves** — the row is stored *and* the register says so, so a
build that quietly started refusing would fail). The burst measurement that
licenses all of it is `test/data/sync/offline_revision_burst_test.dart` in the
app, which prints what it measured on every run.

## 5. Non-goals

Stated plainly so nobody later assumes protection that was never built. Each is
a deliberate scope decision, not an oversight.

### 5.1 A removed member's retained local copy

Setting `end_date` stops future syncs and blocks server access immediately
(§2.3). It cannot delete the copy already in their local SQLite, and no
offline-first system can. Everything they synced while a member, they keep,
permanently.

**Accepted conditional on disclosure** (2026-08-01): the owner must be told this
**at the moment they add a member**, in the flow, not in a help page. For
projects tracking poaching-target species, precise historical locations in a
departed member's offline copy are a real disclosure surface, and the person
adding them should know that before they do it. Task 11.2 owns the wording; keep
it factual — this is a property of the software, not a warning about the person.

**Built by task 11.2 (2026-08-20), as a control rather than a sentence.** The
text is `removalDisclosure` in `project_members_screen.dart` and it appears in
two places: the add-member sheet, where the "Create invite code" button is
**disabled until the owner acknowledges it**, and the removal confirmation,
which is the moment somebody is most likely to believe removal took the data
back. Both are asserted in `test/features/more/project_members_screen_test.dart`
— including that the button is disabled with a valid address entered and enabled
only after the acknowledgement, because a disclosure that does not gate anything
is documentation with a checkbox next to it.

**What "immediately" means, corrected by task 11.2 and then again by task
11.27.** §4.3 used to say of `revokeAllSessionsForUser` that it is "what task
11.2's member removal calls". **It was not, and 11.2 never called it.** That
sentence was written when a user had one project; session revocation is per
*user*, so calling it on removal would sign a field tech out of the two other
studies they are on because one of them ended — the assumption Phase 11
explicitly forbids. The mechanism is narrower and already built: the server
resolves project access from membership on **every** request and caches no
decision, so a closed stint is refused on the removed member's very next
request, on their existing unexpired session, for that project only. §4.3's
database-backed sessions are still what make this possible; they are just not
the thing being revoked. Both halves are pinned in
`server/test/integration/membership_and_joining_test.dart`.
**Task 11.9 recorded that this correction had never reached its source** —
§4.3 itself, `auth_routes.dart`'s comment and `server/README.md` still stated
the false version three weeks after this paragraph was written to correct it.
**Task 11.27 fixed all three (2026-08-22).** The general lesson — a correction
written *about* a claim, rather than *into* it, leaves the claim itself
standing for the next reader to trust — is stated once, as a property, in
§4.24.

### 5.1.1 The invitation token (task 11.2, 2026-08-20)

**Decision.** An invitation is an 8-character code from a 32-character alphabet
(Crockford Base32: digits and letters, minus `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), stored as a
SHA-256 hash, single-use, expiring in 14 days, revocable, and **bound to the
address the server has authenticated for the redeeming session**.

| | Magic-link token (§4.2) | Invitation code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entropy | 256 bits | 40 bits |
| Delivery | email, by the server | a person, out of band |
| At rest | SHA-256 hash only | SHA-256 hash only |
| Lifetime | 15 minutes | 14 days |
| Single-use | yes, atomically | yes, atomically |
| Bound to | the mailbox it was sent to | the address the invite names |

**Reasoning on the entropy, because 40 bits looks wrong next to §4.2's 256.**
Guessing an invitation is worth nothing on its own. A code redeems only for a
session authenticated as the address the invitation names, so a correct guess is
useful only to somebody who *has already been invited*. What the entropy bounds
is nuisance — an authenticated user grinding at codes issued to themselves —
and a per-user rate limit (§4.4) bounds that too. The binding is the control;
the length is a bound on noise.

**Reasoning on the length and alphabet — the constraint is the field, not
aesthetics.** Invitations travel out of band (decided 2026-08-17): written on a
whiteboard, texted, said out loud in a truck, read over a radio. A 36-character
UUID fails that badly enough that people photograph it instead, which puts a
credential in a camera roll and a cloud backup. The excluded letters are the
ones misread as `1` and `0`; canonicalization folds `I`/`L`→`1` and `O`→`0` on
input, so a reader who typed the letter still lands on the code that was
printed. `U` is excluded so no generated code spells anything an owner would be
embarrassed to read out, and its presence on input is treated as a misreading
rather than a fixable typo.

**Reasoning on 14 days rather than §4.2's 15 minutes.** A magic link races an
email; an invitation races a person who may be in the backcountry for a week.
Fifteen minutes would make the feature unusable and push owners toward leaving
