one code live indefinitely. Fourteen days still means a photograph of last
season's whiteboard grants nothing.

**The code is shown exactly once.** It is stored only as a hash, so an owner who
loses it revokes and re-issues — one tap — rather than the database holding
working grants to a project whose rows are the locations of collared animals.

**Every refusal is the same refusal.** Expired, revoked, already used, never
existed, malformed, and *issued to somebody else* answer identically (§4.13).
The last one is why: distinguishing it would tell a caller a fact about a third
party's address. The one exception is "you are already a member", which is a
fact about the caller, is reachable only by the invited person holding a live
code, and does **not** consume the code.

**Violated by:** a code that works for whoever holds it; storing a code in
recoverable form; a redemption that matches against an address from the request
rather than from `auth_accounts`; a refusal that says which reason it was; a
`SELECT`-then-`UPDATE` consumption path; a membership row created from anything
the redeeming request supplied.

### 5.2 A member who deliberately exfiltrates data they are authorized to see

Anyone who can see a project's observations can screenshot them, export a CSV,
or type coordinates into a text message. This is the §2.1 social-engineering
path's terminal step and it is not technically preventable in a tool whose
purpose is showing people where animals are.

What partially addresses it is not a control but a record: attribution
(`last_modified_by`, preserved authorship), the data-access audit log (§4.7),
and Phase 11's membership stint history make after-the-fact investigation
possible. Detection and accountability, not prevention. Do not let a future task
claim prevention.

### 5.3 Email channel security

Magic-link authentication means **mailbox compromise equals account
compromise**. There is no second factor. Anyone with read access to a team
member's email can sign in as them.

Accepted, with reasoning: the alternative — passwords — trades this for a
credential that can be phished, reused across sites, and leaked in someone
else's breach, against the actor most likely to try phishing (§2.1). The
mailbox is also usually better defended than a password TriTrack would store,
because it is behind an institutional identity provider with its own MFA.
Bounded by the 15-minute single-use window (§4.2), so it is *current* mailbox
access that is required, not a historical archive.

**If this becomes insufficient**, the answer is a second factor or institutional
SSO as an *option alongside* magic links — not instead of them, since NAU SSO
was already rejected for v1 because it excludes the non-NAU collaborators who
are the common case.

### 5.4 A compromised device or a malicious app on it

Root/jailbreak, a malicious app with filesystem access, a keylogger, or physical
access to an unlocked device. §4.8 explains why device-local encryption does not
change this. No integrity attestation, no jailbreak detection, no anti-tamper.

### 5.5 Targeted or state-level adversaries

Device implants, CA-level TLS interception, supply-chain attacks specifically
aimed at TriTrack, coerced disclosure. Out of scope at this scale.

Relatedly: **no certificate pinning.** Pinning would break the LAN development
workflow and every self-hosted deployment, and the threat it stops — a
CA-level MITM — belongs to this actor class, not to §2.1–§2.5. Standard platform
trust-store validation, with no `badCertificateCallback` override anywhere in
the codebase, ever.

### 5.6 Denial of service

Rate limits (§4.4) exist to stop email bombing and enumeration, not to keep the
server up under attack. There is no DDoS protection, no traffic scrubbing, no
capacity planning for hostile load. This is acceptable precisely because of
asset ranking §1.5: the app works fully offline, so an unavailable server costs
delay and nothing more.

### 5.7 Protection of data the user exports on purpose

A backup zip, a CSV, or a `TT1:` share payload leaves TriTrack's control the
moment it is written. Backups are unencrypted zips by design (they must be
restorable and mergeable by other TriTrack installs), and the share payload is
base64, which is encoding rather than encryption. Once a user has put a file in
a cloud folder or pasted a payload into a messaging app, its confidentiality is
that service's, not ours.

The one place this deserved more than a non-goal is the *automatic* cloud backup
path, because there the export happens on a schedule without a person deciding
to do it each time. §4.15 resolves the specific question of defaulting that path
to on; archive encryption for it remains open, see §6.

### 5.8 Third-party disclosure through map tile requests

Fetching map tiles and elevation data discloses the project's areas of interest
to OpenStreetMap, OpenTopoMap, Esri, and AWS — a bounding box, and by request
pattern, the areas being worked. Existing behavior, unavoidable for an online
tile-based map, and partly mitigated in practice by the offline tile
pre-download that field use depends on anyway. Not addressed further; worth
knowing it exists, since it is a disclosure of asset 1 at reduced precision that
no control in this document touches.

### 5.9 Two narrow `RowAuthorizer` gaps — re-derived against a real team (task 11.3, 2026-08-20)

Found during Gate B's 2026-08-03 re-review of task 10.10's code. Both were
judgment calls made explicitly because **in Phase 10 every project had exactly
one member: the owner.** Task 11.3 destroyed that assumption and was named here
to re-derive both against the population that replaced it — contributors,
viewers, and removed-but-still-locally-holding-data former members. Re-derived
2026-08-20. **Both are on task 11.9's list by name, whatever the outcome below**,
so neither can be rediscovered as new.

**(a) An orphan `Tags` row — one no project references — was writable by anyone
who knew its id.** `RowAuthorizer` treated "referenced by no project" as
"nobody's," so a caller holding an unreferenced tag's opaque UUID could push a
stale copy, receive the server's current copy back as a conflict loser
(permitted because `Tags` is `anyUser`-ruled), link it into their own project,
and thereafter update or tombstone it.

**Re-derived: the entry ran two worries together, and only one of them was ever
about orphans.**

- *The viewer.* **Real, and now closed.** A `viewer`'s whole grant is read-only,
  and this path let them rewrite or tombstone every tag their project used.
  Closed by §4.21's gradient: a tag the caller's project references is that
  project's data, so writing it needs write rights — and, since task 11.11
  (2026-08-21), owner rights specifically for a *change* to an existing tag.
  **Not** closed by anything
  about orphans — the tags a viewer can see are claimed ones.
- *The removed member (§2.3), who keeps every tag id they saw.* **Does not
  apply.** Every id they hold is one their old project's rows reference, which
  makes it *claimed*, not orphaned, and a departed member has no access to vouch
  for it — the existing claimed-elsewhere refusal already stops them. The orphan
  clause was never what protected against this.

**So the orphan case is unchanged by Phase 11, and is deliberately kept open —
with a narrower rule and a different reason than 2026-08-03's.**

**Corrected by task 11.218, 2026-09-10, from task 11.34's measurement
(`CLAUDE_DOCS/TAG_COPY_ON_ADD_DESIGN.md` §1.5): the flow this residual was
kept open to protect does not work, and never has.** The paragraph below is
kept, struck through, because a corrected reason and the reason it replaced
are both useful to a later reader.

~~Kept open because an unlinked tag is a supported product state, not an
accident: the tag dialog offers "None (unlinked)" outright, and the tag
database is a lab's global list of transmitters, so a tag not yet on any
project still has to replicate between one person's phone and their laptop.
Refusing that would hold somebody's own tag hostage on their own device — a
data-custody failure traded for a disclosure that requires guessing a v4
UUID.~~

**Measured: sync is per-project on both sides, and an unlinked tag belongs to
no project, so no request — push or pull — can ever carry one.** The device
narrows a global table to a project's own tag ids before queuing a push;
the server narrows `Tags` to `ProjectReachability`'s tag set before answering
a pull. An orphan tag is in neither set, on either side, for any project. **So
a device's own orphan tag never leaves that device by sync at all — there is
no flow here to protect, and no data-custody failure to trade against a
disclosure.**

Narrowed anyway, because it was free: **only the user the stored row already
names (`last_modified_by`) may maintain an orphan.** That drops "anyone who
knows the id" to "the person who last wrote it," and costs the legitimate flow
nothing, since the only way an orphan reaches this server is somebody pushing
it, and that push stamps them. A null stamp permits, on the same contract
`MutationRule.permits` states for a null governing value — rows predating
identity capture (Phase 7) have no author to compare against, and stranding real
data over a column nobody filled in is the worse error.

**CLOSED BY CONSTRUCTION, task 11.219, 2026-09-10 (schema v14, schema major
3).** ~~What remains open, corrected: an orphan tag can still be *linked*
into a project by anyone holding its id, and thereby adopted — that write
path stays open, for the reason above (it is how a tag becomes a project's at
all).~~

**There is no such thing as an orphan `Tags` row any more.** Copy-on-add made
`Tags` project-scoped: `project_id` is `NOT NULL` and half the primary key,
so a tag row cannot exist without a project on either side of the wire. The
three things this residual was about all stop being reachable, and none of
them by a check somebody has to remember:

- **"A tag no project references" cannot be pushed**, because the row itself
  carries the project and the ordinary scope check at the top of
  `RowAuthorizer._decide` refuses a row claiming a project the caller cannot
  reach. There is no orphan branch left to narrow — the whole of
  `_authorizeTagReferences`, `_tagIsClaimedElsewhere`, `_tagRowExists` and
  `_noteEstablishedTag` is deleted.
- **Linking an unclaimed tag into a project is not an operation.** Adding a
  tag to a project *copies* it: a new row, in the caller's own project, with
  a fresh id. Nothing widens what a project may read, which is also why
  `Project_Tags` lost its `insertIsAGrant` flag and then the table itself.
- **What the person keeps instead is device-local.** The lab's list of
  transmitters is `Tag_Library`, in neither `syncTables` nor `tableSpecs`, so
  no push, pull, merge or archive carries a row of it. That costs nothing
  that worked — see the measurement above, which is what made the design
  possible.

**Finding F4 closes with it**, and for the same reason: its *read* half was
"knowing a tag's UUID lets anyone link it into their project and read its
name, frequency and notes." There is no link, and a `Tags` row a caller
pushes must claim a project they can already reach — so the id buys nothing
it did not already buy for that project's other rows.

**Accepted-and-closed; owner: task 11.9's inventory**, where it stays listed
by name rather than being deleted, so a later reader can tell *closed* from
*never considered*.

**(b) Two delimited-id-list text columns have no foreign-key check and can name
another project's rows.** `Non_Detections.tag_ids_listened_for` and
`Estimated_Positions.observation_ids_used` are free-text columns holding
delimited id lists — not in `tagColumns`, not checked by the tag-reference
rules, no FK on either side. A caller can store another project's ids there.

**Re-derived: the acceptance holds, and its condition is now enforceable rather
than merely written down.**

The 2026-08-03 acceptance rested on two things. One was the single-owner
population, which is gone. The other was that **neither column feeds
reachability** — nothing computed from them decides which rows a pull delivers —
so a foreign id stored in one is a dangling reference and not a disclosure. That
second reason survives the change of population intact, and it is the load-
bearing one: the columns are written by people who already hold the project's
data, and no read filter consults them. Multi-member reachability does not touch
them, because reachability is computed from `identityUserColumns` and
`tagColumns`, and these are in neither.

**Not given a foreign-key check, and the reason is a real cost, not laziness.**
The server authorizes every row of a push *before* writing any of them, so a
position estimate and the observations it cites, pushed in one batch, would be
judged against a snapshot in which those observations do not yet exist. The
within-push bookkeeping that solves this for tags (`_establishedThisPush`) would
have to be built twice more, to close a gap that discloses nothing today.

**The condition is what got enforced instead.** §5.9(b) previously said "decide
whether these columns need a real check *before* any future feature folds them
into reachability" — and a sentence in a document cannot enforce a *before*.
`assertSealedColumnsFeedNoReachability` — named
`assertUnvalidatedIdListColumnsFeedNoReachability` until task 11.219 widened
it — now fails if either column is ever declared in `userColumns`,
`tagColumns` or `emailColumns`, which are the three declared sets every
reachability, naming and archive-collection computation walks. The day
somebody builds "which observations does this estimate depend on" as a
first-class relationship, that test goes red and points here — because on that
day every value ever written under the unchecked assumption becomes a live
cross-project disclosure vector, not on the day the column itself changes. The
test carries a positive control that fires in the same run.

**Accepted; owner: task 11.9's inventory.**

**Task 11.219 widened the same assertion and left this clause alone.** Schema
v14 added two **provenance** columns to `Tags` — `lineage_id`, which says
which physical collar a row is a copy of, and `copied_at` — and §2.3 of
`CLAUDE_DOCS/TAG_COPY_ON_ADD_DESIGN.md` requires that nothing live ever read
a lineage into a decision about which rows travel. That is a design property
rather than an accepted risk, but it is **one edit away from being false in
exactly the same way**: adding the column name to a declared set. So both are
checked by the one assertion, which names which of the two reasons the caller
has broken. Its positive control fires on each.

**What did *not* change here, said out loud because it looks like it should
have.** `Non_Detections.tag_ids_listened_for` still holds bare tag ids, and
tags became project-scoped in v14 — but for a tag in one project the v14
migration leaves its `tag_id` exactly as it was (§3.2), so no value in this
column was invalidated and no reference that resolved before stopped
resolving. ~~The design's §3.3(3) anticipated a *forked* project's
non-detections keeping the original tag's id and being newly dangling; **no
fork ran** — the migration refuses that case rather than performing it — so
that consequence has not arisen and this clause needs no new sentence about
it. If a fork is ever written, it does.~~

**The fork was written (task 11.224, 2026-09-10), because the refusal fired
on Michael's iPhone: two collars were held by two projects each.** So the
sentence is now owed, and this is it. **When schema v14 forks a tag that two
or more projects hold, the project that adopted it first keeps the original
`tag_id` and every later project gets its own copy under a fresh id; that
later project's bearings, sessions, estimates and truth points move to the
copy — and its "no signal" entries do not.** `TagScopeMigration.fork` leaves
`tag_ids_listened_for` untouched, which task 11.224 confirmed against the
code rather than the design: `Non_Detections` declares no `tagColumns`, the
column is in `unvalidatedIdListColumns`, and
`assertSealedColumnsFeedNoReachability` goes red the day it is declared in
any set that decides what a project reaches. Re-pointing it in a migration
would be the first code in the repository to treat the list as a relationship
that has to resolve, which is the thing this clause's acceptance is
conditional on nobody doing.

~~**The consequence, stated as what a person sees rather than as a property.**
In the project that received the copy, a "no signal" entry that listened for
the shared collar still names the original id, which now belongs to the other
project. The Log shows that entry without the collar's frequency (it says "no
tags recorded"), the map's no-signal marker has no color for it, the CSV
export writes the bare id where the frequency and name would go, and the
Log's per-collar filter no longer finds the entry. The row itself is intact
and nothing is deleted. **This is exactly the dangling reference the column
was already permitted to hold** — a foreign-project id in a text column that
nothing resolves — arising from the migration rather than from a caller. The
migration counts these rows and prints the count in its own log line
(*"Non_Detections rows in forked projects still naming the original tag id"*),
so the number is on the device rather than in this paragraph; on Michael's
phone it is whatever that line says. **It discloses nothing** — the id it
names is one the same person's other project holds, on the same device — and
nothing reads it into a reach set, so the acceptance above is unchanged.
**If a later task wants those entries to show the collar again, the honest
fix is a per-project re-pointing that reads the column as an id list
deliberately, with the reachability check this clause says such a reader
owes first** — not a quiet `LIKE` in a migration.~~

**Struck and dated, 2026-09-10 (task 11.225): true from the fork (task
11.224) until this migration, and no longer.** Michael decided to fix the
consequence rather than leave it, and schema v15 (`NonDetectionRelinkMigration`,
`lib/data/db/non_detection_relink_migration.dart`) is the "honest fix" the
struck paragraph named — a reader that treats
`Non_Detections.tag_ids_listened_for` as a relationship deliberately, for
every project and every listened-for id: if the id no longer names a `Tags`
row in that row's own project, and that project holds a `Tags` row with the
same `lineage_id`, the id is rewritten to that row's. **The reachability
check this clause said such a reader owes is discharged structurally, not by
declaration**: `assertSealedColumnsFeedNoReachability` still returns
normally with this migration in the tree (it declares
`tag_ids_listened_for` in none of `userColumns`, `tagColumns` or
`emailColumns`), and every lookup the reader makes is filtered to the row's
own `project_id` — it can ask "does *this* project hold a same-lineage row",
never "which projects hold this lineage", which is the question that would
actually leak. `test/data/non_detection_relink_migration_test.dart` asserts
both. Derived from `lineage_id` rather than from what the fork did, so it
gives the same answer whether it runs right after v14's fork or, as on
Michael's device, weeks later — and it is idempotent, since after one pass
every id already resolves locally.

**One more consequence of the fork, corrected rather than struck, because
the earlier paragraph's reasoning was measured and found not to carry for
this column (task 11.225).** The re-pointed *bearings, sessions, estimates
and truth points* keep their `updated_at`, and that reasoning holds for
them: the server has refused a second project's claim on a tag since task
11.3, so those rows were never accepted under the shared id and have no
receipt to leave stale. **`Non_Detections.tag_ids_listened_for` is
different, and this is the "later task" that measured it rather than
assuming the same argument carried.** The column is unvalidated and feeds
nothing — that is the whole reason it is sealed — so nothing ever stopped a
`Non_Detections` row from being accepted by the server while the same
collar's bearings were refused. `SyncEngine`'s pending selection
(`_pendingClause`) offers a row only when `Sync_Row_Receipts.acked_updated_at`
does not match the row's current `updated_at`; rewriting the data without
moving `updated_at` would leave an existing receipt's match intact, and the
correction would never be offered again. So task 11.225's migration measures
this per row rather than assuming an answer — it checks whether
`Sync_Row_Receipts` already holds a receipt for the exact row being
rewritten, and bumps `updated_at` (and `revision`) exactly when one is
found; a row with no receipt is already pending regardless, so leaving it
alone costs nothing.

### 5.10 A viewer's private divergent copy, restored onto a device with no membership rows (task 11.20, 2026-08-21)

**The residual of §4.19 clause 6 on the archive-restore path, written down here
rather than left as a gap for a later gate to rediscover.**

Clause 6 refuses a restore when this device holds an open membership row saying
`viewer`. It **permits** when the device cannot resolve a role at all, because
membership is server-derived and the case restore exists for — a reinstalled
phone, a replacement one recovering last season's archive — has no membership
rows by definition. So the check is evaded by clearing the app's data first: a
viewer who reinstalls and then restores an archive of a project they may only
read passes it.

**Accepted, and the reasoning is a trade rather than an oversight.**

- **Nobody else's record is reachable.** Every row they write is refused at the
  server on the next sync (§4.21), so the divergence is confined to their own
  device. What they end up holding is a private, edited copy of a project they
  were **already entitled to read** — this discloses nothing they did not have.
- **The alternative costs more than it buys.** The only local signal that
  distinguishes the evasion from the honest reinstall is the same absent
  membership row, so any check strict enough to catch it also refuses the
  genuine restore — the owner recovering a field season on a new phone. That
  trades irreplaceable data for a view on one device, and it breaks Phase 10's
  first invariant (the app works fully with no server) on the one feature that
  invariant exists for.
- **It does not meet §4's bar** (`SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md`): no silent or
  unrecoverable loss — K-1's consent gate still shows the user field-by-field
  what a restore would replace; no disclosure of coordinates or observer
  identity beyond what the person could already read; no authorization bypass
  affecting anyone else, since the server refuses the rows; and no claimed
  control failing to fire — clause 6 fires exactly where this document says it
  does, which is where the device has an answer.

**Confirmed by the planning session, 2026-08-21, with one argument the entry did
not make and which is the strongest of them.** A viewer who wants a private
edited copy of a project they may read does not need this path at all — **they
can export the CSV**, which they are entitled to do, and edit it in a
spreadsheet. The residual grants no capability they did not already hold; it
only offers a more laborious route to it. An acceptance that rests on "the
alternative costs more" is weaker than one that rests on "the attacker gains
nothing", and this one rests on both.

**What would change this.** If a device ever gains a locally-verifiable
statement of its own membership — a signed grant it can check without the
server, which is the same key-custody problem archive signing needs — the
abstain-on-null reading becomes unnecessary and this entry should be re-decided
rather than re-accepted. Recorded so that day is a decision and not a surprise.

**Accepted; owner: task 11.9's inventory.**

## 6. Discovered scope

Items found while writing this document, filed under Phase 10's Discovered Scope
in `DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md`. None blocks task 10.0.

1. **`.gitignore` has no secret patterns** — no `.env`, no `*.key`, no
   `secrets*`. §4.6 requires them, and they must land *before* 10.3 creates the
   first file that would hold a credential.
2. **10.6's spec does not name secure storage.** §4.8 makes keychain/keystore
   storage of the session token mandatory and it is the highest-value control in
   that decision. 10.6 needs the dependency and the acceptance criterion.
3. **`latestSchemaVersion` is not a constant in `schema.dart`** — it is derived
   as the max of the migration list in `migrations.dart` (currently 5). Task
   10.1 says to move it from `schema.dart`; the extraction is slightly different
   from what the plan describes.
4. **The auto cloud backup path is the largest existing disclosure surface**
   (§3.7, §5.7) and it predates the server entirely: unencrypted zips containing
   every name, email, and full-precision coordinate for a project, written on a
   schedule into a third-party cloud folder. **Partially addressed by task
   10.19 (§4.15, 2026-08-06):** the in-flow statement of what leaves the device
   now exists, and the decision to default the path to on is recorded rather
   than assumed. **Still open:** optional encryption of the archive — deferred
   in §4.15 point 4 on the grounds that the destination is user-owned storage,
   not a hostile network hop, but not accepted as permanent. Needs its own task
   if this changes (e.g. a passphrase-encrypted archive option) or once
   real-world usage shows the risk is being underweighted.
5. **`TT1:` share payloads are unauthenticated** (§3.7, §4.12): no signature or
   MAC, so claimed author, `origin_device_id`, and `revision` are
   attacker-controlled inputs to last-write-wins. Bounded server-side by §4.11
   but real client-side. Needs a task to decide whether to sign them.
6. **`device_id` is forgeable and is the final LWW tiebreaker** (§3.7, §4.12).
   **Closed by task 11.27 (2026-08-22), registered as N-8 (§18.4): Michael
   accepted it in writing, with the reason and the condition that would
   reopen it.** This item sat exactly as "probably acceptable" for six weeks
   with no task number, which is task 10.72's failure shape.
7. **Rate-limit storage must move out of process** before any multi-instance
   deployment (§4.4). A deployment precondition, not a Phase 10 code task, but
   it needs to be written down somewhere that is checked.
8. **The backup private key needs a custody arrangement** (§4.9) — an offline
   copy and a second holder — before the first backup that matters. An
   operational task, not a coding one.
   **Decided by task 10.24 (2026-08-09): see §4.9.1.** Two holders with their
   own `age` identities and a paper offline copy each; the pipeline exists
   because the arrangement does, not the other way round. The one part still
   outstanding is naming holder 2, which needs a real deployment to be about —
   §4.9.1 makes that the trigger for the first backup of real data, and the
   backup job warns on every run until it happens.

## 7. Verdicts — Security Gate C (task 10.16, 2026-08-07)

### 7.0 Gate result: **FAILED. The server does not listen beyond localhost.**

This gate re-ran §2 and §3 against what was actually built, not against what
this document says should have been built. It found drift, which is what it
exists to do. **Five blocking findings are open**, four of them reproduced
against a live server over raw HTTP rather than argued from code.

The localhost-only restriction stays in force. Per the plan's framing, failing
items block exposure; they do not become future work that ships alongside the
thing they block. They are filed as blocking Discovered Scope in
`DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md` and this gate must be re-run once they are closed.

**The single most important result is not any one bug.** It is that
`RowAuthorizer` reasons about **who owns the row being written** and never
about **who the row names**. Every one of B1's four instances is that one
omission surfacing in a different column. Point-patching the four columns would
leave the class open; the invariant needs stating once and enforcing everywhere.

Gate B found and closed two instances of exactly this class — it dropped
`last_modified_by` from reachability (`sync_service.dart:370-377`) and refused
`Project_Memberships` rows naming anyone but the caller
(`row_authorizer.dart:169-180`), and the second of those carries the comment
"it makes that stranger's `Users` row reachable from the attacker's project."
The reasoning was right and was applied to two columns rather than derived as a
rule. That is the drift.

### 7.1 Were Gates A and B actually run, and their findings closed?

**Checked in the record, not assumed.**

| | Run | Re-verified | Findings |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Gate A** (after 10.6, auth) | Yes — adversarial pass, 7 findings, 5 fixed | `/security-review` re-run 2026-08-02; re-reviewed against the actual commit `02edc65` on 2026-08-03 | 5 fixed, 2 recorded-not-fixed (the `link-status` behavior oracle, carried into §7.6 below; the transaction wiring, since fixed). Postgres half closed for real on 2026-08-02 when Docker became available: 19 integration tests, all passing. |
| **Gate B** (after 10.10, authz) | Yes — two adversarial passes | `/security-review` re-run 2026-08-02; re-reviewed against commit `d52b4c8` on 2026-08-03, confirming no later commit touched the authorization boundary | 4 fixed. 2 sub-threshold items accepted and recorded as §5.9. |

Both gates were genuinely run and their findings genuinely closed. **Neither
was wrong about what it examined.** B1 is not a regression of a Gate B fix — it
is an adjacent column Gate B never looked at. This is the argument for having a
summative gate at all: A and B each verified their own scope correctly, and the
class-level pattern was only visible from outside both.

### 7.3 Adversarial pass — every attempt and its recorded result

Run against a live `docker compose` stack (real Postgres, real bound socket,
real magic links read off disk) using a raw HTTP client — no client code, no
mocks, no in-process shortcuts. 27 attempts. **24 controls held; 3 attacks
succeeded.** A follow-up pass escalated the three successes and independently
verified two further findings from the code review.

**The six attempts task 10.16 names by name:**

| # | Attempt | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Cross-project access with a session scoped to a different project of the same user | **Held.** One user owning P1 and P2: a pull for P2 returned only P2's rows; a pull for P1 never disclosed P2's observation; a row body claiming `project_id = P2` pushed through P1 applied nothing and never appeared in P2. |
| 2 | Reuse a consumed magic link | **Held.** `400 invalid_or_expired_link`, no session issued. A guessed 43-character token gets the identical response. |
| 3 | Act on an explicitly revoked session | **Held.** Session worked (200) → `revoke-all` → the same token returned 401 on both `/projects/mine` and `/sync/pull`. Per-device revocation killed only the named device and left the sibling device at 200. |
| 4 | Reach the diagnostics console off-host | **Held.** From this machine's real LAN address (`192.168.0.88`), with the correct token: `403 diagnostics_console_local_only`, on both `/diagnostics/health` and `/diagnostics/projects`, while `/health` answered 200 from the same address — so the refusal is the console's gate, not a connectivity artifact. |
| 5 | Enumerate registered addresses | **Held.** A registered and an unregistered address both return `202` with an identical key set. No status, body, or key difference. |
| 6 | Mutate another user's observation over raw HTTP, bypassing the client | **Held for a stranger.** A non-member's push against the victim's project: `403`, and the victim's stored latitude was unchanged afterwards. **Not held for a legitimate user against their own project — see B1d.** |

**Other attempts that held:** unauthenticated `/sync/pull` (401); a stranger's
self-granted `Project_Memberships` row into a foreign project (403, and the
follow-up pull still 403); oversized `batch_size` against a foreign project
(403); a 40 KB unauthenticated body (400); SQL injection through `project_id`
and through the diagnostics table path segment (no injection — server and
tables intact afterwards, confirmed by a subsequent legitimate pull returning
its rows); token guessing from one source (429 after the §4.4 limit, honest
because a redemption attempt carries no third party's address).

**Two controls confirmed working by accident, worth recording:** a hand-crafted
`Projects` row with `coordinate_format: "decimal_degrees"` was rejected as
`invalid` — the shared `RowValidator` genuinely stops a raw request inserting
what the client's forms would reject. And a push referencing a nonexistent
parent row produced an opaque `500` with a `trace_id`, with the server log
recording only `ForeignKeyViolationException on POST /sync/push` — the
exception *type* and nothing else, which is §4.13 and §4.7 rule 6 working
exactly as designed on a path nobody wrote a test for.

**Attacks that succeeded — the blocking findings.**

#### B1 — Row authorization never checks who a row *names*

Four instances of one omission. All four reproduced live.

**B1a — identity disclosure by forged authorship (`Observations.user_id`).**
An authenticated user pushes an observation **into their own project** whose
`user_id` names a victim they have no relationship to. The rule check denies
it, then the replication exemption (`row_authorizer.dart:193` — inserts of
`author`-ruled rows by someone with project access) allows it. `user_id` is a
genuine reachability edge, so the attacker's next pull of their own project
returns the victim's full `Users` row. Observed:

```
baseline attacker pull -> Users: [attacker only]
forged insert          -> inserted
after forgery          -> Users: [victim: Victim Person <pv-…@example.org>, attacker]
```

Because `_globalFilters` maps `User_Emails` by `user_id`, the same pull also
returns the victim's **prior address history**, not only their current address.
Asset 4 (§1) disclosed to any registered user who knows a `user_id` — and
`user_id` travels in every `TT1:` share payload, every CSV export, and every
synced row's `last_modified_by`.

**B1b — the same thing through `Non_Detections.user_id`.** Identical path,
identical outcome. Recorded separately because a fix aimed at `Observations`
would not close it.

**B1c — the same thing through `Projects.owner_user_id`, on update.**
Authorization compares the **stored** row (correctly, per §4.12 — checking the
incoming copy would let a caller seize any row). But that means an owner may
rewrite their own project's `owner_user_id` to name a victim: at the instant of
the check the attacker still owns it. The victim becomes reachable, and the
attacker does not lose access, because their own `Project_Memberships` row
keeps them at `ProjectAccess.member`.

**B1d — authorship forgery, one-way and irrevocable.** The severest of the
four, and a *different class*: integrity, not disclosure. `RowAuthorizer`'s own
class doc states that updating a row attributed to someone else "is forgery …
Always denied, with no exemption." That is true in one direction only. An
attacker creates an observation they legitimately author, then updates it to
name a victim. Observed:

```
1. attacker creates own observation   -> inserted
2. attacker rewrites author -> victim -> updated
3. server's authoritative copy        -> user_id = <victim>
   notes: 'FABRICATED: victim reported this animal at this location'
4. attacker tries to revert           -> unauthorized
```

The attacker chooses the coordinates, the time, the tag, and the notes, stamps
someone else's name on it, and is then **locked out of the row they
fabricated** — so there is no later edit by them to point at. For a telemetry
record that may support a permit, a publication, or a regulatory finding, this
is the highest-impact item in this gate. It is asset 2 (§1), and §0's argument
that a falsified bearing silently corrupts published science is precisely this.

**Suggested shape of the fix — one invariant, not four patches.** An incoming
row may not name a user other than the caller, on any table, on insert or
update, unless a real replication provenance backs it. Note that disclosure is
only possible when the named `Users` row **already exists on the server**; if
the id is unknown, inserting it discloses nothing. That distinction is probably
where a fix that preserves legitimate first-publish replication lives.

> **Closed by task 10.20 (2026-08-09).** The invariant is recorded as §4.17 and
> implemented as `RowAuthorizer._authorizeNaming`. The seam guessed at above is
> the one that worked. All four reproductions were re-run over raw HTTP against
> a live stack and refused; `scripts/verify_c1_row_naming.py` is that run, and
> it was checked against a build with the invariant removed, where all four
> still succeed and B1d writes the fabricated record verbatim. Gate C's verdict
> stands as recorded until task 10.25 re-runs it in full.

#### B2 — Project existence oracle (violates §4.13)

`ProjectAccess.absent.permitsSync` is `true`, deliberately, for the publish
case. The consequence was not traced: a nonexistent project passes the gate,
finds nothing, and returns **200 with an empty row set**, while an
existing-but-forbidden project returns **403**. Verified live on both pull and
push:

```
pull(real foreign project id) -> 403
pull(nonexistent project id)  -> 200
push(real foreign)=403   push(nonexistent)=200
```

§4.13 states the requirement in the exact terms this fails: "Wrong project,
wrong user, and nonexistent are indistinguishable from outside." §4.13's
`Violated by:` list names this failure mode first. Task 10.10 rejected the
row-level version of this oracle by name; the project-level one was never
closed. Impact is existence-only — no row content — and project ids are v4
UUIDs, so blind enumeration is impractical. It matters because ids leak through
legitimate channels: share payloads, exports, screenshots, support tickets.
Confirming a project exists on this server is itself the reconnaissance §2.1
and §2.4 are about.

> **Closed by task 10.21 (2026-08-09).** `ProjectAccess.absent` no longer
> permits sync; publish is permitted by the *shape of the request* instead, and
> the mechanism plus its one irreducible residual are recorded in §4.13. Pull,
> push and ack were re-run over raw HTTP against a live stack and answer a real
> foreign project and a fabricated id identically;
> `scripts/verify_c2_existence_oracle.py` is that run, and it was checked
> against a build with the seam removed, where all five comparisons diverge —
> including two that leak through a `500` rather than the recorded `200`. Gate
> C's verdict stands as recorded until task 10.25 re-runs it in full.

#### B3 — The cleartext exemption can ship, and by default does

§4.1 permits cleartext only when **both** conditions hold: a debug build, *and*
a loopback or private-range target. **Only the first half was built.**
`security_config.dart` implements the `TRITRACK_ENV` check and contains no
private-range check at all. `TRITRACK_ALLOW_CLEARTEXT_LAN=1` with
`TRITRACK_ENV=development` binds `InternetAddress.anyIPv4` in cleartext on a
public host, prints a warning, and serves.

And `docker-compose.yml:54-55` makes that the default:
`${TRITRACK_ALLOW_CLEARTEXT_LAN:-1}` and `${TRITRACK_ENV:-development}`, with
`ports: "0.0.0.0:${SERVER_PORT:-8080}:8080"`. Confirmed from the running
container's own startup log:

```
!!! Serving CLEARTEXT HTTP on all interfaces. Session tokens and observation
coordinates are readable by anyone on this network.
```

The warning is honest and the refusal under `TRITRACK_ENV=production` is real.
But §4.10's own reasoning — "the default is what gets deployed" — was applied
to the diagnostics console and not to this file. §2.2's closing claim, "the
localhost-only restriction stays in force until task 10.16 passes," is
currently enforced by documentation rather than by code.

> **Closed by task 10.22 (2026-08-09), in three places.** §4.1's second
> condition now exists as `isPrivateNetworkAddress` in `tritrack_sync`, shared
> so the two enforcement points cannot drift: the server refuses to start when
> cleartext-on-all-interfaces would be served from a machine holding a public
> address, and the app's URL validator refuses `http://` to a non-private
> target **in every build**, not only release ones — the client had built the
> same half of the same sentence and no one had noticed. `docker-compose.yml`
> now publishes to `127.0.0.1` by default and no longer defaults `TRITRACK_ENV`
> to `development`; reaching a phone is `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` in
> `.env`, one deliberate documented line.
>
> Verified live by `scripts/verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py`, which reproduces
> the finding rather than asserting against a mock: it starts the real server
> image on a Docker network whose subnet is `203.0.113.0/24`, so the container
> genuinely holds a public address, and requires it to exit `78` with a
> readable refusal naming that address. It also reads the defaults back out of
> `docker compose config` — Docker's own resolution, `.env` applied — and
> confirms a running stack answers on `127.0.0.1` and **not** on this machine's
> LAN address. Recorded from the run: `192.168.0.88:8080` refused,
> `127.0.0.1:8080` answered `200`.
>
> **One gap remains open by construction, and it is named rather than closed.**
> A container cannot see its host's addresses — inside Docker every interface
> is the private bridge — so the startup refusal cannot fire on a public VPS.
> What confines exposure there is the compose publish default, which is a
> default and not a control: an operator who sets `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0`
> on a publicly-addressed host gets cleartext on the internet and no refusal.
> `.env.example` says so at the point where that line is typed, and
> `server/README.md` says so in the transport section. §4.1's actual answer for
> that deployment is TLS. Gate C's verdict stands as recorded until task 10.25
> re-runs it in full.

#### B4 — §4.9 encrypted backups: still unimplemented

No `pg_dump`, no `age`/GPG, no backup script anywhere in `server/`. Already
recorded as open by task 10.14 with the reason (§6 item 8: no key custody
arrangement, and encrypting to a key with no custody story makes recovery risk
worse). **10.16 must not treat it as satisfied, and does not.** It stays
blocking for a deployment that holds real data, because §2.1's control list
names it against the actor this whole document is organized around.

> **Closed by task 10.24 (2026-08-09), custody first.** The precondition was
> the finding, so §4.9.1 — two holders with their own `age` identities, an
> offline paper copy each, a stated blast radius for a lost key, and no
> break-glass copy on the server — was written before any code. The pipeline
> then followed: `server/backup/` runs `pg_dump | age` wholly inside one
> container so plaintext never touches a filesystem, and the `backup` compose
> profile keeps it a one-shot job rather than a long-lived container mounting
> every historical snapshot.
>
> **Proven by restoring, not by asserting.** `scripts/backup_restore_drill.sh`
> stands up a throwaway stack, lets the *server's own* migration code build the
> schema (21 tables), seeds an observation carrying coordinates, and then runs
> nine checks. Recorded from the run of 2026-08-09: the job **refuses** with no
> recipients configured and writes nothing; the archive carries an `age` header
> and none of the seeded coordinates, email, project name or note appear in it
> in the clear; an **unrelated private key is refused** (`no identity matched
> any of the recipients`); the correct key restores into a fresh database whose
> every column of every table matches the original by name and type, with the
> seeded observation and its coordinates returned identically; a `pg_dump`
> against a nonexistent database **leaves no archive behind**, which is the
> `pipefail` case that would otherwise yield a well-formed archive of a
> truncated dump; and `TRITRACK_BACKUP_KEEP=2` prunes the *oldest* archives and
> their checksums, keeping the newest.
>
> **What is not closed, and is a deployment step rather than code:** holder 2 is
> unnamed, because no server holding real data exists yet. §4.9.1 makes filling
> that in the trigger for the first real backup, and the job warns on every run
> while only one recipient is configured. Gate C's verdict stands as recorded
> until task 10.25 re-runs it in full.

#### B5 — Authorization denials are never audited

`auditDenial` constructs `AuthAuditLog` on the raw `Connection` while the sync
handler's `db.runTx` is still open. `postgres` 3.5.12 refuses a query on a
connection inside a transaction, and `record`'s catch swallows the exception.
Verified directly against the database after this gate generated many 403s:

```
SELECT event, count(*) FROM auth_audit_log GROUP BY event;
 rate_limit_tripped | 29
 link_requested     | 22
 session_created    | 19
 link_redeemed      | 19
 redemption_failed  | 17
 session_revoked    | 3

SELECT count(*) FROM auth_audit_log WHERE event = 'authorization_denied';  ->  0
```

Every other audit event works. The one that records someone probing other
people's projects does not, and fails silently. An attacker can probe
indefinitely and `/diagnostics/auth-events` — the stated answer to "was my
account compromised" — shows a clean history. This is a control that is present,
tested for its own logic, and inert in production; §4.7's `Violated by:` list is
about what must never be logged, but a security log that silently writes nothing
is the same failure from the other end. No test covers it: `grep
authorizationDenied server/test` returns nothing.

> **Closed by task 10.23 (2026-08-09).** The root cause was the executor, not
> the catch: `postgres` 3.5.12 refuses a second statement on a connection
> while that same connection's own `runTx` is open, and `auditDenial` shared
> its connection with the sync handler's transaction. `bin/server.dart` now
> opens a dedicated `auditDb` connection that never has a transaction of its
> own to collide with — see [AuthAuditLog]'s doc comment in
> `server/lib/src/security/audit_log.dart`. Separately, `onError` on
> `AuthAuditLog` is now a required constructor argument rather than optional:
> a write failure still cannot be allowed to fail the request (§1's
> availability ranking, still last but not zero), but nothing can construct
> the class anymore without deciding what happens when one is lost, so the
> old "wired to a `print` nobody reads" shape is at least a choice made in
> the open. `server/test/security/audit_log_test.dart` reproduces the
> original collision directly against Postgres (shared connection loses the
> row; a dedicated one does not), and
> `server/test/integration/sync_audit_test.dart` closes the coverage gap this
> finding named: a stranger's denied push now leaves a real
> `authorization_denied` row, proven end to end over a bound HTTP socket, and
> reverting the dedicated-connection wiring reproduces zero rows and fails
> that test. Gate C's verdict stands as recorded until task 10.25 re-runs it
> in full.

### 7.4 Secrets in git history

**Verified across the whole history, not the working tree.** All 68 commits,
`git log --all -p`.

- No `.env` object has ever existed in the repository. `.env.example` is present
  in every version with every value empty.
- No PEM or private-key block anywhere. The single `-----BEGIN` match in the
  entire history is the detector string inside
  `test/security/no_committed_secrets_test.dart`.
- No provider credential patterns (AWS, GitHub, Slack, Google, OpenAI, JWT).
- No Postgres URI carrying a password.
- Every historical `docker-compose.yml` uses `${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?...}`
  required-markers; no version ever carried a literal.
- 111 candidate `password|secret|token|key` assignment lines reviewed
  individually: all are code, test fixtures with transparently fake values, or
  environment lookups.

**Verdict: clean.** This closes the full-history gap that
`no_committed_secrets_test.dart` explicitly left for 10.16 — that test checks
`git ls-files`, i.e. the current tree only.

Recorded for the record: task 10.14's near-miss, where a draft of the
placeholder-rejection list contained this machine's real local Postgres
password. Catching that before it landed is why §4.6's control has the reasoning
written into the code rather than only the list.

### 7.5 The §4.15 cloud-backup default — required verdict

**Was it decided explicitly, or defaulted into? Decided explicitly.** §4.15 is a
dated decision that names the tension (asset 1 confidentiality against asset 2
availability), argues the trade rather than asserting it, states what it does
*not* cover, and carries a `Violated by:` clause. It is exactly the recorded
decision 10.16 asked to confirm. **This item passes.**

**The archives' own protection — verdict: accepted, with one part of the
reasoning now falsified.**

- **Encryption at rest: none.** The archive is a plain `ZipEncoder` output, no
  password. Accepted in §4.15 point 4 on the grounds that the destination is
  user-owned storage rather than a hostile network hop.
- **Retention: 10 archives deep**, in the user's linked folder.
- **What a compromised cloud account exposes:** every name, every email, every
  full-precision coordinate for the project — asset 1 and asset 4 together, in
  a form that needs no TriTrack credential to read. The `isLinked` gate holds
  (verified: nothing leaves before a folder is picked), so §4.15's stated
  invariant is intact.

**The falsified part, and it is new since §4.15 was written.** §4.15's central
argument is "the destination is storage the user already owns and already
trusts." That holds for the user's *own* data. It does not hold for anyone
else's. Since task 10.9 shipped publish-and-join, a member's local database
holds every other member's `Users` row and full `User_Emails` history. With
auto-backup on by default, the next foreground write puts colleagues' names,
current *and prior* email addresses, and precise coordinates into **one
member's personal cloud folder** — without those colleagues consenting, being
notified, or being able to revoke it. §4.15 point 2 reasons about a
single-user trust boundary that publish-and-join had already widened.

This does not overturn the decision, and it is not blocking at localhost. It
does mean §4.15 needs re-deciding against a multi-member population before
Phase 11, on the same schedule as §5.9's two accepted gaps — filed as
Discovered Scope.

> **Re-decided by task 10.60 (2026-08-15) — see §4.15.1.** Default stays on,
> payload stays unencrypted under a time-bounded acceptance with the
> key-custody design named as the blocker, disclosure copy rewritten to name
> other people's data. §4.15.1 also corrects this section's dating: the
> widening is not 10.9's, it is Phase 6 share import's, and it is therefore
> live in the app as shipped rather than pending on the server.

Not blocking for a localhost-only prototype. Several become blocking the moment
the server is exposed or Phase 11 adds a second member; each says which.

| # | Finding | Why it is not blocking now |

"fix" by setting `TRITRACK_DIAGNOSTICS_ALLOW_REMOTE=true`. Given B3, that
combination puts every project's coordinates in a browser over cleartext, with
the console token in a readable header. Worth a note in the README before
someone reaches for it.

### 7.7 Residual-risk summary, in plain language

*Written for a reader who is not working on this code — NAU's information
security office, an IRB reviewer, or a future maintainer. Current as of
2026-08-07.*

**What this system is.** TriTrack is a field-research app for tracking radio-
collared wildlife. A biologist walks a transect with a radio receiver, records
bearings to a collared animal, and the app triangulates the animal's position.
It works fully offline, on the phone, with no server. A server component has
just been built so that a research team can sync one project across several
devices. **That server has never been exposed to any network beyond the
developer's own machine, and this assessment is the gate that decides whether
it may be.**

**The decision: it may not, yet.**

**Why this data is more sensitive than it sounds.** The app stores precise,
timestamped locations of individual collared animals. For endangered or
commercially trafficked species, that dataset is directly useful to poachers.
Targeting researchers' telemetry data is a documented pattern in conservation,
not a hypothetical. A leak has a physical-world consequence that a leaked
spreadsheet does not, and it cannot be undone by rotating a credential. The
system also holds researchers' names and email addresses, which matters in
enforcement contexts where being identifiable as the person who located an
animal carries its own risk.

**What was done.** A threat model was written before any server code existed.
Three review gates were run: one after authentication was built, one after
authorization, and this one — a summative gate before any exposure. This gate
re-tested the original threat model against the software as actually built,
attacked a live server over raw HTTP as an attacker would rather than reviewing
the code as an author would, and searched the project's entire version-control
history for accidentally committed credentials.

**What holds up well.** Authentication is sound. There are no passwords to
steal or reuse: sign-in is a single-use emailed link, and the resulting
credential is stored in the phone's hardware-backed keychain, never in ordinary
app storage. Credentials can be revoked immediately, either for one lost device
or for every device at once, and revocation takes effect on the very next
request. The database is not reachable from any network. No credential has ever
been committed to version control — verified across the full history, not just
the current files. The system resists being used to discover whether a given
email address is registered. Attempts to inject database commands through the
web interface failed. A user's separate projects are properly isolated from each
other, and an outsider cannot read or modify a project they have no relationship
to — both tested against a running server, not merely reviewed.

**What does not hold up — the reasons this gate failed.**

1. **Any registered user can attach another person's name to a record, or pull
   another person's contact details.** The permission system correctly asks "do
   you own the record you are changing?" but never asks "whose name are you
   putting on it?" A user can create a record in their own project, stamp a
   colleague's name on it, and thereby both fabricate a scientific observation
   attributed to that colleague and cause that colleague's name and full email
   history to be delivered to them. The fabrication is one-way: having done it,
   the attacker can no longer edit the record, so there is no later edit to
   point at. This was reproduced against a live server. It is one design
   omission appearing in four different places, and it needs to be fixed as a
   single rule rather than patched four times.

2. **The server tells any logged-in user whether a given project exists**, even
   one they have no access to, by answering differently for "not allowed" and
   "no such thing." No project contents are exposed. It is a reconnaissance
   aid, and it contradicts a rule this system set for itself.

3. **The bundled server configuration serves unencrypted traffic on all network
   interfaces by default.** The design permits unencrypted traffic only on a
   home or lab network during development; only half of that restriction was
   actually implemented, and the ready-to-run configuration file turns the
   permissive setting on by default. Anyone on the same network could read
   session credentials and animal coordinates in transit. This is why the
   server must not be exposed until it is fixed.

4. **Server database backups are not encrypted, because they do not exist yet.**
   This was a deliberate, recorded decision — encrypting to a key with no
   custody arrangement makes data loss more likely, not less — but it means
   there is currently no backup story for a deployed server.

5. **Security logging for permission denials silently does nothing.** Every
   other security event is recorded correctly. The one that would show someone
   probing other people's projects fails due to a database-transaction bug and
   discards its own error. Confirmed by querying the database directly: zero
   such records after this assessment generated many denials. An operator asking
   "has anyone been poking at my data?" would see a clean history.

**Known risks accepted on purpose.** Several things are deliberately not
defended against, and are documented as such: a departing team member keeping
the copy of the data already on their own phone; a person authorised to see the
data choosing to leak it; the security of email itself, which is outside this
system's control; a phone that is already compromised at the operating-system
level; and targeted attack by a well-resourced state adversary. The app also
does not encrypt its local database file, relying instead on the phone's own
disk encryption and app sandboxing — a decision made explicitly, though one
supporting safeguard for it (warning a user whose phone has no passcode) was
never built and should be.

**One thing worth flagging beyond the server.** The app can back itself up
automatically to the user's own cloud storage folder, and this is on by default
once a folder is chosen. The archive is not encrypted. This was a deliberate
trade — losing a phone destroys a field season's data as irreversibly as a leak
discloses it — and the archive goes to storage the user already owns. But now
that projects can be shared between team members, one member's automatic backup
carries their *colleagues'* names, email addresses, and coordinates into that
member's personal cloud account, without those colleagues' knowledge. That
reasoning needs revisiting before team features ship.

**Bottom line.** The foundations — authentication, credential storage,
revocation, database isolation, secret handling — are solid, and were built
before the features that depend on them rather than retrofitted. The permission
layer has one systematic gap that a code review found and a live attack
confirmed, plus a transport-configuration default that would expose traffic on a
shared network. Neither is subtle once seen, and neither requires a redesign.
Until both are fixed and this assessment is re-run, the server stays on the
developer's machine, reachable by nothing else.

**What we would most value a second opinion on:** whether the permission fix
described above is the right shape; whether the accepted risks listed here are
reasonable ones to accept for research data of this sensitivity; and what NAU
requires of a system holding location data for protected species if it is ever
to run on university infrastructure or be named in a data-management plan.

### 7.8 On outside review

`/security-review` and a Claude-assisted audit catch a great deal — this gate is
evidence of that, having found five blocking issues that two earlier gates and
309 passing tests did not. Neither is equivalent to a professional review of an
internet-exposed system holding poaching-sensitive data. **NAU's information
security office reviews §7.7 before any deployment reachable beyond
localhost** — they exist for it, the review is free, and an institutional
sign-off is independently useful if this ever touches IRB, grant compliance, or
a data-management plan.

**Status:** §7.7 written and ready to send; the request to NAU is drafted and
awaiting the developer's review. Not yet reviewed by NAU. **This item is not
closed, and the gate cannot pass until it is.**

> and unsent, its recipient line still blank. See §8.9.

> **Superseded in part by §9** (the second re-run, 2026-08-13). D-1, D-2's size
> arm, D-3 and E-1 are closed and re-verified there; E-2 and E-3 are not, and
> two of this section's claims were overstated — see §9.4 G-2, §9.4 G-3 and
> §9.5 G-4. Read §9 for current state; this section stands as the record of

### 8.0 Gate result: **FAILED AGAIN. The server still does not listen beyond localhost.**

**C-1 through C-5 are genuinely closed.** All five were re-run live and all five
are refused; three of the five were additionally checked against a build with
the fix reverted, where each reproduces the original finding verbatim. That work
holds up, and §8.2 records it.

The gate fails on other things. Six items block, and they are independent — no
one of them is the reason:

| # | Blocking item | New? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **D-1** | **C-2 was closed at the status code; the per-row `outcomes` map answers the same question.** A general existence oracle for users, tags and arbitrary row keys — and 10.20 added a new arm to it. §4.13's own words. **Closed by task 10.29 (2026-08-13)** for arms (a) and (b), and **fully closed by task 10.35 (2026-08-13)**: arm (c) was the client-chosen-primary-key collision, and project-scoped keys remove the collision rather than bounding it. All three arms now verify as indistinguishable against a live server (`scripts/verify_d1_per_row_oracle.py`, arm (c) included). **Overstated — corrected at §9.5 (G-4):** arm (c) is closed for the six project-scoped tables, and the script's arm (c) case tests one of them. `User_Emails` is still keyed globally and still answers, and no other rule covers it. | new |
| **D-2** | **The C-5 fix turned denial auditing into an unbounded attacker-controlled write.** 10 requests, 0.9 s, 10 MB on disk, no rate limit on the route, §4.7 retention still unscheduled. | new |
| **D-3** | **A refused row is silently lost and the app says "Synced."** The exact case task 10.25 said to check, failing the exact way it predicted. **Closed by task 10.28 (2026-08-13)** — refusals are held durably, counted, explained and retryable; publish had the same defect and was fixed with it; live-on-device check still owed. | new |
| **E-2** | **The e2e override reopens C-3 through two documented steps.** It declares no `ports:`, so it inherits `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS` — and adds disabled per-source rate limits and a mount of live magic-link tokens. One line. | new |
| **F13** | **The client's `https` requirement is form validation, not transport enforcement.** §7.6 already called this "Blocking before any real deployment." Still open — and its compensating control is weaker than §7.6 recorded. | carried |
| **TLS** | **Cannot be verified, because there is nothing to verify it on.** 10.25 required confirming TLS terminates in front of the server on the real host. No host, no proxy, no deployment exists. | carried |
| **NAU** | **The institutional review still has not happened.** Drafted 2026-08-07, unsent, recipient line blank. §7.8's terms are unchanged. | carried |

The localhost-only restriction stays in force. Two further items do not block
exposure but must be fixed before the *next* re-run can claim anything: **E-1**,
because the regression tests guarding C-1, C-2 and C-5 default to inert without
a database, and **E-3**, because the documented in-place restore drops the live
database before it knows the archive can be decrypted.

**The result worth carrying forward this time** is not D-1, D-2, D-3 or E-2
individually. It is that **every one of them was introduced by, or left visible
by, the remediation of the previous gate's findings** — and that a pass which
only re-ran C-1…C-5 would have found none of them. 10.25's spec insisted on
repeating the whole adversarial pass rather than spot-checking the five, on the
grounds that C-1 had been invisible to two scoped reviews and 309 passing
tests. That instinct was right twice over: the scoped thing to check was the
five findings, and the five findings were all fine.

**Second result, about the shape of security fixes.** D-1 and D-2 are the same
story told twice. A fix changes one branch of a two-branch behavior and the
branches become distinguishable (D-1). A fix revives a code path that was dead,
and the path had never been reviewed as a live one because it had never been
live (D-2). Before 10.23, every denial write was silently discarded — the bug
was, in this one narrow respect, load-bearing. E-2 is a third variant: a fix
for a *test-harness* problem inherited a production default nobody re-read.
**Repairing a security control is a change to the attack surface and needs to
be attacked as one.** None of these is a defect in the reasoning of 10.20,
10.23 or 10.26; all are what those tasks did not think to look at afterwards.

### 8.1 What was re-run, and how

The whole of 10.16, not a spot-check. Everything below was run against a live
`docker compose` stack — real Postgres, real bound socket, real magic links off
disk — using raw HTTP, no client code and no mocks, which is the methodology
that surfaced C-1 in the first place.

| | Result |

| `flutter test` | **703 passed**, 26 skipped |
| Server suite (`scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh`) | **347 passed** — but plain `dart test` with no database is 197 / 139 skipped / **11 failed**, see E-1 |
| `flutter test test/e2e --tags e2e` | **26 passed, in a single pass** |
| C-1…C-5 live reproductions | **all refused** (§8.2) |
| Adversarial pass, 24 attempts | **20 held, 4 failed** (§8.3) |
| Secrets across the whole git history | **clean**, 78 commits (§8.7) |
| `/security-review` on the remediation diff | §8.4 |

The client and e2e suites are green on a clean checkout with no special
knowledge required — task 10.26's acceptance criterion, and the precondition
for this gate being able to read its own instruments. At the last gate the
client suite was red and the e2e suite could not complete a run. **The server
half of that criterion is not met** (E-1): green requires the Docker script,
which is the special knowledge, and the plain path is both red and — more
importantly — mostly skipped.

None after** |

**C-5 had no live verification script and now does.** C-1 through C-4 each got
one; C-5 was closed on the strength of two Dart tests. Those tests are good —
`sync_audit_test.dart` proves the behavior over a bound socket — but both
build their own two-connection wiring, which is the thing under test. They
would still pass if `bin/server.dart` regressed to one shared connection. That
gap is why the reversal control above is the row that matters: it exercises the
artifact that actually gets deployed.

While writing that script, its first draft asserted three properties with
`all(...)` over the result rows. `all([])` is `True`, so on the reverted build
— where there are no rows, which *is* the finding — three checks reported
**PASS**. Fixed before use, and recorded here because it is the same silent
success this finding was made of, reproduced in the tool built to detect it.

### 8.3 The adversarial pass, re-run in full

`scripts/gate_c_adversarial_pass.py`. Three groups: the six attempts 10.16
names by name, the other attempts §7.3 recorded as held, and — the part that
found things — **new attacks aimed at the remediation itself.**

**20 controls held, 4 failed.** Everything §7.3 recorded as holding still
holds:

- Cross-project access with a session scoped to another project of the same
  user: a pull for P1 never discloses P2's observation, and a row body claiming
  another project never lands there.
- A consumed magic link and a guessed one are refused **identically** (`400`,
  byte-for-byte).
- A revoked session is refused `401` on both `/projects/mine` and `/sync/pull`.
- No diagnostics route answers from this machine's LAN address.
- A registered and an unregistered address are indistinguishable (`202`, same
  key set).
- A stranger cannot mutate the victim's observation (`403`, latitude unchanged).
- Unauthenticated pull refused; a self-granted membership creates no access;
  an oversized `batch_size` against a foreign project refused; SQL injection
  through `project_id` leaves 21 tables intact and a legitimate pull working.
- **New:** the row-naming invariant holds on `Observations`, `Projects` and
  `Project_Memberships` alike, and on `last_modified_by` — it behaves like a
  derived rule, not four patches, which was the point of 10.20.
- **New:** audit-log injection through `project_id` forges no row; the `event`
  column still holds only the closed enum; no error body carries a coordinate,
  an address, a project name or a user id.
- **New:** a real foreign project and a fictional one are not distinguishable
  by *timing* either (5.1 ms vs 4.0 ms) — C-2 was closed at the status code,
  and closing it there did not just move the tell.

Two of the four initial failures were the harness's own bugs, found by reading
them rather than believing them: a wrong route name (`/auth/revoke-all` for
`/auth/sessions/revoke-all`), and a losing `revision` that made the merge
discard a row before authorization was ever consulted — which would have
reported "held" for the wrong reason. Both fixed; both then held. **The
remaining failures are D-1 and D-2, plus a re-confirmation of §7.6 F10** (an
unauthenticated malformed body still answers `500`, not `401` — unchanged,
still non-blocking for the reason §7.6 gives, still live).

### 8.4 The new blocking findings

#### D-1 — The `outcomes` map is a general existence oracle

**C-2 was closed one level too high.** Task 10.21 made the *HTTP status code*
uniform, and it did that correctly — §8.2 confirms pull, push and ack answer a
real foreign project and a fabricated id identically, including by timing. But
a push also returns a per-row `outcomes` map, verbatim, inside every `200`.
That map answers the question the status code no longer does.

Three arms, all reproduced live. In each, the attacker is **an ordinary
registered user with no relationship to anything they are asking about**:

**(a) Does this person have an account here — and have they published a
profile?** A global-only push, naming a `project_id` that is a random UUID
which has never existed. No project ownership, no publish, nothing:

```
published Users row (victim)  -> 200  ['lost_to_server']
account only, never published -> 200  ['unauthorized']
never seen by the server      -> 200  ['inserted']
```

A clean three-way read of a stranger's registration status. **This arm is new,
and 10.20 created it.** Before the row-naming invariant, naming a known foreign
user was *permitted* — that was C-1's disclosure — so both cases answered
`inserted` and there was no differential. Fixing the disclosure turned the
branch into a signal.

**(b) Does this tag id exist on this server?**

```
a tag referenced by the victim's project -> 200  ['unauthorized']
a tag id that exists nowhere             -> 200  ['inserted']
```

**(c) Does this row primary key exist anywhere on this server?** Mallory pushes
an observation into **her own project** carrying the victim's `observation_id`:

```
an observation_id in the victim's project -> 200  ['unauthorized']
an observation_id that exists nowhere     -> 200  ['inserted']
```

Arms (b) and (c) are **not** products of the remediation — they come from
`_isForeignTag` and the `crossProjectCapture` rule, both of which predate it.
They were missed by Gate B, by Gate C, and by 10.21, which found this exact
channel, patched the instance it was looking at, and recorded in §4.13 that
"the outcome map answered the question the status code no longer did." That
sentence was right and was applied to project reachability rather than derived
as a rule. **This is C-1's pattern a second time**: a correct piece of
reasoning applied to the instance in front of it instead of to the class.

**What does not leak: content.** Verified — the victim's observation survives
the (c) probe unchanged, in the victim's project, still attributed to the
victim. The authorization is doing its job. Only *existence* escapes.

**And none of it is audited.** Every probe above returns `200`, so none reaches
`auditDenial`, which is wired only to the three project-level `403` paths
(`sync_routes.dart:199, 487, 551`). Measured across a full run of these probes:
`authorization_denied` rows `194 -> 194`. §7.3 B5's complaint — *"an attacker
can probe indefinitely and `/diagnostics/auth-events` shows a clean history"* —
is **still literally true for this attack**, after the task that closed it. See
D-4.

§4.13 states the bar in the exact terms this fails: wrong project, wrong user,
and nonexistent must be indistinguishable from outside. §4.13's own
justification for treating C-2 as blocking applies here without modification —
"not blind enumeration; it is confirmation, of an id that reached the attacker
through a `TT1:` payload, an export, a screenshot." Every id above travels that
way: `user_id` is in every share payload, every CSV export and the
`last_modified_by` of **every synced row**; tag ids are in share payloads;
observation ids are in exports. §1 ranks researcher identity as asset 4, and
§2.1 is organized around an actor for whom "which of these researchers has an
account on this server" is reconnaissance.

Given the same-class-as-C-2 reading, **this is blocking.** The fix is not a
patch: making the unknown case answer `unauthorized` too would close arm (a)
but also break the first-publish replication seam C-1's fix was built on. The
two branches have to converge on one answer, and choosing it is a design
question. If it proves irreducible without breaking publish — which is
plausible — then it must be **stated and bounded in §4.13 and §4.17 the way the
publish-collision residual already is**, not left as an unexamined consequence.

One more reason this survived: **the current test suite asserts it as correct.**
`authorization_test.dart:642-653` pins `inserted` for an observation naming a
user the server has never heard of, and `:1007-1030` pins `unauthorized` for
the same shape naming a registered user. Both assertions are right about
authorization and together they are the oracle, written down as expected
behavior.

> **Closed by task 10.29 (2026-08-13), at the level the answers leak.** The
> `outcomes` map itself was left alone — patching what is *reported* is the
> mistake this finding is about — and the three forking branches inside
> `RowAuthorizer` were converged instead. The rule now sits in §4.13: no per-row
> outcome may depend on server state the caller has no other way to observe, and
> where authorization must consult such state both branches answer the refusal,
> because the permissive branch performs a write and a write cannot be concealed.
>
> - **Arm (a) closed.** §4.17's "the server has never heard of them" clause is
>   gone; a row may name only the caller or someone the project already reaches.
>   The three-way collapses to one `unauthorized`. The third value —
>   `lost_to_server` for a stale copy of a real user's row — is closed
>   separately: a no-op now checks whether the caller may be told the stored row
>   exists, at the reachability bar, so the routine re-offer every sync performs
>   is unaffected. **The design question this finding posed was answered by
>   refusing**, and the cost is recorded in §4.17: an imported colleague's work
>   does not replicate until they are on the project. Task 10.28's held-row
>   machinery is what makes that payable — the rows are kept, counted and
>   explained, not lost.
> - **Arm (b) closed.** A tag may be referenced only where pull would already
>   deliver it, asking `ProjectReachability` — the same computation the read
>   filter uses — instead of the old "is some other project using it?" test that
>   permitted orphans and refused claimed tags. The `Project_Tags` row that
>   claims a tag for a project is the one operation allowed to widen a project's
>   reach, and there too a tag id that names nothing and one another project
>   holds are a single refusal.
> - **Arm (c) was the residual, and is now closed too — task 10.35
>   (2026-08-13) made primary keys project-scoped**, so a key another project
>   holds no longer collides and there is nothing left to answer. The
>   verification script's arm (c) check is an equivalence like the others, and
>   passes. The paragraph below records what the residual was while it stood.
>   It was originally stated in §4.13 as a property of
>   client-chosen primary keys on every table rather than of `Projects` alone,
>   with its bound checked rather than asserted: existence escapes, the victim's
>   row does not move, change, or come back. Closing it means project-scoped
>   primary keys — a schema change filed under Phase 10's Discovered Scope.
>
> **Worse than recorded, in one respect.** Reproducing the finding over raw HTTP
> turned up a fourth shape the write-up did not name: where the "server does not
> hold it" branch left a dangling foreign key, the push answered **`500`** while
> the held id answered `200` — a status-code-level oracle, on the routes C-2 was
> supposed to have made uniform. It is closed by the same change, because the
> reference is now refused before any write is attempted.
>
> **Both cited assertions were corrected upward, and checked as corrected.**
> `authorization_test.dart`'s "first publish may still carry an unknown
> colleague" now asserts the refusal and says in the test itself that its old
> expectation *was* the oracle. Seven new cases are written as **equivalences** —
> two pushes differing only in a fact about the server's contents must come back
> the same — because pinning each answer separately is precisely what let this
> survive two gates. Reverting `row_authorizer.dart` fails four of them, and
> `scripts/verify_d1_per_row_oracle.py` (the C-2 verifier's method one level
> down, over raw HTTP against a live stack) reports six distinguishable pairs
> against the pre-fix build and none after.

#### D-2 — Denial auditing is an unbounded attacker-controlled write

The C-5 fix made `authorization_denied` actually record. `auditDenial` writes
the caller's `project_id` into `auth_audit_log.outcome` — deliberately and
correctly, since an operator needs to know which project was refused
(`sync_routes.dart:171-175`). `project_id` is entirely caller-controlled and
nothing bounds its length. The sync body limit is 8 MB
(`sync_routes.dart:51`), and `/sync/pull` has no rate limit at all — §4.4's
limits are on magic links and redemptions.

Measured live, with incompressible content so TOAST compression does not
flatter the result:

```
10 denied pulls, 1 MB of project_id each: status 403, 0.9s
auth_audit_log on disk: 10 MB
```

~11 MB/s of attacker-chosen bytes, from one ordinary registered user, on a
route that answers `403` the whole time. §7.6 already records that §4.7's
retention is a mechanism nothing schedules, so nothing removes it either. That
is asset 5, and it is the kind of finding that only exists *because* the
control was repaired: before 10.23 every one of these writes was silently
discarded.

Neither of the two obvious guards is present: the value is not truncated on the
way in, and the column is `TEXT` with no length bound
(`audit_log.dart:26-37`). What does hold: injection through the same field
forges nothing, the `event` column still admits only the closed enum, and no
coordinate or note from the refused row reaches the log — §4.7's never-log
