rules survive the path becoming live, which was the thing most worth checking.

#### D-3 — A refused row is silently lost, and the app reports "Synced"

Task 10.25 named this case in advance: *"10.20's invariant denies a case Phase
6's observation-sharing flow can legitimately hit… Confirm that fails visibly
and says something useful."* It does not, and the failure is worse than
invisible.

The path, traced end to end and confirmed against a live server for the
server half:

1. A user saves a colleague's `TT1:` payload. The importer writes a faithful
   replica — the observation *and* a local `Users` row for the colleague. The
   app says **"Observation saved, attributed to the original observer."**
2. On the next sync both rows are pushed. If the colleague has a server account
   but is not on this project, `_authorizeNaming` refuses — correctly, this is
   C-1's invariant working. The server answers `200` with the row's outcome set
   to `unauthorized`. Confirmed live in §8.4's D-1 transcript: this is the
   `200 unauthorized` line.
3. `SyncEngine._push` reads the outcomes and keeps only `lostToServer`
   (`sync_engine.dart:201-202`); `unauthorized` and `invalid` hit the
   `continue`. `SyncRunReport` (`sync_engine.dart:11-44`) has no field for
   either, so nothing downstream can see them.
4. The push watermark has already advanced, unconditionally
   (`sync_engine.dart:195-197`). A replica preserves the sender's clock
   verbatim by design (task 6.3), so its `updated_at` sits below the new
   watermark and `_collectChangedRows`' `updated_at >= watermark` predicate
   (`sync_engine.dart:396-399`) will never select it again. **The row is not
   retried, and is not counted as pending.**
5. The user sees **"Synced just now."** and a green `Icons.cloud_done_outlined`
   headline reading **"Synced"**, with no pending count and "No overwritten
   edits."

So the server permanently refuses a primary scientific record, the client
permanently stops offering it, and the app affirmatively tells the researcher
it is safely on the server. That is asset 2. `SyncRowOutcome`'s own doc comment
says the enum exists because "silence about a loss is the failure mode this
whole field exists to prevent" — the value is on the wire and in the response;
it is simply never read.

**This is the sign-in bug's shape exactly**, which is why 10.25 asked for it:
correct server, passing tests, and a user-facing surface that says the opposite.
No test covers it — the fake transport in `sync_engine_test.dart` never denies
a row, and there is no widget test for `SyncStatusScreen` or `SyncStatusBanner`
at all.

The report already carries enough to detect it: `pushed - applied -
lostToServer.length` is the refused count. Nothing consumes it, and there is no
surface to show it on.

> **Closed by task 10.28 (2026-08-13).** A refusal is now a durable local record
> (`Sync_Held_Rows`), written *before* the push watermark moves, counted by
> `SyncStatus.heldCount`, and shown as `SyncHealth.rowsRefused` — a red banner
> reading "1 record isn't on the server", never "Synced", plus a "Not synced to
> the server" section on the status screen carrying a client-authored reason and
> a per-row "Try again". Outcome classification is an exhaustive switch, and an
> offered row the server says *nothing* about is held rather than assumed
> applied. `ProjectPublisher.publish` had the same defect in a worse form —
> outcomes ignored entirely, watermark set to `now`, a count of rows *sent*
> reported as rows uploaded — and follows the same rules now.
>
> **One deviation from the finding's own prescription, recorded because it is a
> judgment call, not an oversight:** the watermark is clamped to the earliest
> refusal for the round that learns of it, and is then allowed to move past it on
> later rounds. Pinning it below a refusal *permanently* — which is what the
> literal reading asks for — re-offers every row written after that refusal on
> every subsequent sync, forever, and wedges any project larger than one batch;
> and it contradicts the same finding's requirement that the outcome be "held and
> explained, not retried forever." The enforced invariant is therefore **no path
> advances past a refusal that has not been durably recorded and counted.**
>
> Both testing gaps this finding named were part of the fix: `FakeSyncTransport`
> can now deny and ignore rows, and `SyncStatusBanner`/`SyncStatusScreen` have
> widget tests for the first time. 751 client tests green. **Not yet verified
> against a live server on a device** — that check is still owed, and is the one
> §7's own instruction for this case asked for.
>
> **The deviation above was retired by task 10.33 (2026-08-13), which removed
> the push watermark entirely.** That clamp was the most a single per-project
> timestamp could do about a permanent refusal, and it existed only because the
> watermark could not represent "everything except this one row." Selection is
> now a join against `Sync_Row_Receipts` — one durable receipt per row the
> server has confirmed — so a refused row is pending because it has no receipt,
> nothing is dragged back into the window alongside it, and no project size
> wedges the push. Step 4 of the transcript above no longer describes any code:
> there is no watermark to advance, and the replica whose older clock put it
> permanently out of reach is now selected like any other unconfirmed row.
> 10.33 was opened because that same clock behavior turned out to strand rows
> **with no refusal involved at all** — the D-3 asset reached by a second,
> independent route.

#### D-4 — C-5's fix covers project-level denials only, not row-level ones

Not blocking, but it qualifies the C-5 closure and belongs next to it.
`auditDenial` has exactly three call sites — `refusePush`, the pull `403` and
the ack `403` (`sync_routes.dart:199, 487, 551`). Those are the *project*-level
refusals, and §8.2 confirms all three now write.

**Every row-level `unauthorized` writes nothing.** That is where all four of
C-1's original exploits lived, and where D-1's probe lives. The push returns
`200`, `auditDenial` is never reached, and the only server-side trace is the
aggregate `rows_rejected` integer on `sync_traffic_log` — no user id, no row
key, no named subject, and behind the same diagnostics console D-5 covers.
Measured: a full run of D-1's probes moved `authorization_denied` from 194 to
194.

This is arguably in-spec — §4.7 assigns "rejected by authorization" to the
180-day data-access log rather than the one-year authentication log — which is
why it is not rated blocking. But B5's stated failure mode was "an attacker can
probe indefinitely and the console shows a clean history," and for the
row-naming probe that sentence is still true. **The C-5 closure note should say
which half it closed.**

**Re-weighed at task 10.34, against 10.29's fallout: non-blocking classification
confirmed, priority and the shape of the eventual fix both change.**
10.29 closed D-1, and that is what actually settles the "probe indefinitely"
half of this finding — the probe now teaches an attacker nothing, because every
arm answers the same opaque `unauthorized` regardless of the truth, audited or
not. Auditing the row-level channel would improve *forensics*, not close a
live information leak; there is no leak left for it to close. So this stays
non-blocking on the same grounds it was filed on, not weaker ones.

What changed is the operational picture the classification was implicitly
assuming. §4.7's "in-spec" argument pictured row-level denials as the rare,
often-adversarial event B5 was worried about; 10.34 established they are now
the **routine result of an ordinary workflow** — every push of an imported
colleague's observation, every push cycle, until 11.2 gives that colleague a
way onto the project. That does not make the finding blocking (nothing is
disclosed either way), but it means two things for whoever picks D-4 up:

1. **The console gap now hides routine operation, not just attack traffic.**
   An operator trying to answer "why hasn't my colleague's data shown up"
   currently has only the aggregate `rows_rejected` integer — no user id, no
   row key, no reason — for what is, post-10.29, the single most common
   authorization outcome the server produces. That is a real cost to fix,
   independent of the security argument.
2. **A fix must be bounded from its first commit, not retrofitted.** The
   project-level channel `maxAuditFieldLength` bounds stayed low-volume because
   a project-level `403` requires a caller with no relationship to the project
   at all (§4.7 addendum above). A row-level channel has no such rarity to lean
   on — it is the expected shape of an ordinary multi-device season — so
   logging it one row per denial the way `auditDenial` does today would
   recreate D-2's growth curve on a route with no attacker required to trigger
   it. **Aggregation (one row per held identity, updated on repeat, the same
   shape `SyncHeldRowStore` already uses client-side) rather than an
   append-only event log is the right default to start from**, not a size cap
   on an unbounded stream of writes.

#### D-5 — The audit rows are written, and nobody can read them

Also not blocking on its own, and also a qualification of C-5 rather than a new
defect. §7.6 already recorded that inside Docker the server sees the bridge
gateway as the peer, never `127.0.0.1`, so the diagnostics console is
unreachable through the published port **even from the host**. That is
unchanged: `_requireLocalUnlessAllowed` is a peer-address check
(`diagnostics_routes.dart:67-83`), the console is off by default, and the
server image carries no `curl`, `wget` or `psql` for an in-container escape
hatch.

So the read path for everything 10.23 now writes is: disabled by default;
unreachable from the host when enabled; and documented with a command that
returns `403` (`README.md:324-326` and `server/README.md:162-163` both tell the
operator to `curl` `/diagnostics/auth-events`). The only working read is
`docker compose exec postgres psql`, which appears in no document. §7.6 said a
README note was owed here. **It is still owed, and 10.23 made it matter more:
there is now something in that table worth reading.**

#### E-1 — The regression tests for C-1, C-2 and C-5 default to inert

Not an exposure finding. It is a finding about **this gate's own evidence
base**, and it has to be fixed before the next re-run can claim anything.

`dart test` in `server/` on a clean checkout, with no `POSTGRES_*` set:

```
197 passed, 139 skipped, 11 failed
```

The 11 failures are all `LateInitializationError` from
`tombstone_retention_test.dart`, the one Postgres-dependent file that does not
carry the `skip: _skipReason` guard the other eleven use. Fixing those is
trivial — **and fixing them is the trap.** Add the guard and the suite goes
green at roughly 150 silent skips, including every C-1 reproduction
(`authorization_test.dart`'s "Gate C — the row-naming invariant" group), every
C-2 oracle test, and the C-5 denial-audit test. Nothing anywhere asserts that
the Postgres suite actually ran. The finding this document says was "invisible
to two scoped code reviews and 309 passing tests" would then be guarded, on the
default path, by nothing at all — and the run would say so in green.

The database-backed suite is genuinely green (347 passed, §8.1) via
`scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh`. That is the "special knowledge" task
10.26's own acceptance criterion said should not be required, so **that
criterion is not actually met for the server half** — recorded here rather than
reopening 10.26, because the fix is a guard test asserting the suite ran, not a
change to what 10.26 did.

*A claimed version of this said the suite "exits 0 and prints All tests
passed." It does not — it fails, which is how the 11 unguarded tests were
found. The correction matters: today the signal is loud and wrong, and the
obvious repair is what makes it quiet and wrong.*

#### E-2 — The e2e override reopens C-3 through two documented steps

`docker-compose.e2e.yml` declares no `ports:` of its own, so it inherits
`${SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}` from the base file. Both of these are
documented workflows in the README:

1. Set `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` in `.env` so a phone can reach the
   server (the LAN walkthrough — the deliberate, documented one-line opt-in
   10.22 built).
2. Run the e2e suite per `README.md:387`.

Verified with Docker's own resolution:

```
host_ip: 0.0.0.0     published: "8080"
TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED: "1"
TRITRACK_DEV_MAGIC_LINK_DIR: /e2e_magic_links
```

Cleartext on every interface, **with §4.4's per-source magic-link and
redemption limits raised to `1<<30`**, and a bind-mounted directory of live
magic-link tokens, for as long as the stack is up. That is C-3's condition —
"the artifact people actually run is cleartext on every interface" — recreated
by 10.26, which is why it is rated the way C-3 was.

`docker-compose.server-test.yml:18` already shows the right pattern: it
hardcodes `127.0.0.1:` rather than deriving from `.env`. One line.

Related, and non-blocking: `rate_limiter.dart:61-65` says the flag "is refused
outright rather than let a copy-pasted `.env` line quietly disable a real
control." The refusal fires only on `TRITRACK_ENV == 'production'`, which ships
empty — so in the shipped configuration that guard does not fire. What actually
protects it is that the base compose never declares the variable, so Compose
will not forward it (verified, §8.4). Correct behavior, mitigations the
comment does not name, and one named that does not hold. **And
`bin/server.dart:131-139` catches that `StateError` and degrades to the strict
defaults rather than refusing to start**, so "refuses outright" is loose twice
over. The behavior is right; fix the sentence.

#### E-3 — The restore drops the live database before it knows the archive can be read

`server/backup/restore.sh:59-84`, in order: check the database exists →
**`DROP DATABASE`** → `CREATE DATABASE` → *then* `age --decrypt | psql`.
Nothing validates the identity against the archive, or that the age header even
parses, before the destructive step.

The scenario is the one §4.9.1 was written for. An incident, the documented
in-place path (`TRITRACK_RESTORE_REPLACE=I_UNDERSTAND`, target =
`$POSTGRES_DB`), and the operator mounts holder 2's identity by mistake — or
the archive was truncated copying it back from off-site storage. The live
database is dropped, and only then does `age` report `no identity matched any
of the recipients`. Live data gone, backup unreadable.

Compounding: there is no `--single-transaction`. `age` authenticates per STREAM
chunk, so a truncated archive decrypts a valid prefix and *then* aborts, and
that prefix is already committed statement by statement. The comment at
`:72-77` correctly claims `ON_ERROR_STOP` prevents "a database that exists,
answers queries, and is missing rows" — for **SQL** errors. A mid-stream
decrypt abort produces exactly that outcome and is not covered.

The drill does not catch it: `backup_restore_drill.sh:179-186` runs its
wrong-key check against `drill_wrongkey`, a database that does not exist, so
the drop path is never exercised with a bad key. That is why nine green checks
and this finding coexist.

Asset 2, not asset 1 — no disclosure. But §4.9 exists to make recovery
possible, and this is the one path where using it can destroy the thing it is
meant to recover. Fix: decrypt to `/dev/null` (or read and verify the header)
before dropping, restore into a temporary name and rename, and add
`--single-transaction`.

#### Other new findings, recorded, none blocking

- **`revision` is unbounded.** `RowValidator` range-checks coordinates,
  bearings, frequencies and enums but never `revision`, and `MergeResolver
  .compare` is a plain `>`. Any row a caller may write can be pinned at
  `2^63-1` and never legitimately overwritten again. Two places that reaches
  past the attacker's own data: an orphan `Tags` row (writable by any
  authenticated caller by design, §5.9/F4) can be tombstoned at max revision
  and never un-deleted; and a `Users` row planted through the replication seam
  — which §4.17 already records as surviving if the id later becomes held —
  becomes a permanent squat rather than merely first-in. The account path
  itself is closed, since `auth_accounts.user_id` is server-generated at
  redemption. **Recommend a sanity bound on `revision` in `RowValidator`.**
- **A failed first publish is distinguishable from a refusal by timing.**
  `attemptPublish`'s savepoint exists so those two look identical, and on the
  wire they do. But a free project id runs the whole batch through `applyPush`,
  `SET CONSTRAINTS ALL IMMEDIATE`, an owner `SELECT` and a `ROLLBACK TO
  SAVEPOINT` before answering `403`, while a taken or forbidden id answers
  after a single `resolve` `SELECT`. With a deliberately large malformed batch
  the gap is attacker-amplifiable. §8.3 measured no timing difference on the
  *ordinary* pull path (5.1 ms vs 4.0 ms); this is the publish path
  specifically. Belongs in §4.13's residual paragraph beside the collision
  signal.
- **The private-range check runs once, at startup.** `TransportSecurityConfig
  .resolve` is called only from `bin/server.dart:40`. A laptop that boots on a
  private LAN and later acquires a public address keeps serving cleartext.
  The *container* blind spot is documented at `security_config.dart:111-117`;
  this one is not.
- **`docker-compose.yml`'s `TRITRACK_ENV` comment credits a control that is not
  there.** 10.22 changed `${TRITRACK_ENV:-development}` to `${TRITRACK_ENV:-}`
  and the comment at `docker-compose.yml:76-81` describes this as moving the
  safe posture to "the one nobody had to remember." Verified: `TRITRACK_ENV` is
  only ever compared `== 'production'` (three call sites), so both forms are
  behaviorally identical and both already honoured `TRITRACK_ENV=production`
  from `.env`. The real C-3 fix was the loopback publish default plus the
  private-range refusal. **Correct the comment**, so a future reader does not
  count a no-op as a control — this document's whole method is that the
  reasoning has to be true, not just present.
- **Backup: the SSH-recipient path is dead code.** `for r in $(printf '%s'
  "$RECIPIENTS" | tr ',' ' ')` word-splits `ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3…` into two
  tokens, and the first hits the `ssh-ed25519|ssh-rsa) fail` arm, so the
  `ssh-*)` accept arm below it can never be reached for a real SSH key. It
  fails loudly and writes nothing, so this is a usability defect rather than a
  security one — but §4.9 offers SSH recipients as a supported option and they
  do not work.
- **Backup: the restore identity mount is declared on the shared service.**
  `${TRITRACK_RESTORE_IDENTITY:-/dev/null}:/identity/key.txt:ro` sits on the
  `backup` service, so an operator who leaves `TRITRACK_RESTORE_IDENTITY` set
  in `.env` after one restore binds the age **private** key into every
  subsequent backup container — the one box §4.9 is built so it cannot read its
  own backups. The `/dev/null` default is correctly rejected by restore's own
  `[ -f ]` check, so the shipped state is fine; the failure needs an operator
  to leave a variable set.

**Checked and found safe**, recorded so the next pass need not redo them:
`isPrivateNetworkAddress` is correct in the dangerous direction on every class
tested — `172.16-31` bounds, `100.64/10`, `169.254/16`, `127/8`, `::1`,
`::ffff:0:0/96` unwrapping, `fc00::/7`, `fe80::/10` correctly excluding
deprecated `fec0::/10`, and everything unhandled falling to "public, refuse".
`SyncTable.userColumns` is complete against every `TableSpec`. The update arm
of the naming invariant has no bypass — ownership is checked against the
*stored* row, project transfer is refused, and a member cannot self-promote
because `_governingValue` resolves the real owner rather than inferring it.
`PushResult.lost` never crosses the wire. The savepoint's `SET CONSTRAINTS`
is transaction-scoped and correctly undone. The backup pipeline writes no
plaintext to disk: `pg_dump | age` is one in-process pipe, the `.part`-then-
rename plus header check means no non-ciphertext file survives, and restore
decrypts straight into `psql` with no temp file. And 10.26's rate-limit escape
hatch is **not** reachable in a real deployment: `docker-compose.yml` does not
declare the variable at all, so Compose will not forward it from a
copy-pasted `.env`, and when the production refusal does fire
`bin/server.dart:131-139` falls back to the strict defaults.

### 8.5 F13 — the finding the last gate already called blocking

§7.6 recorded F13 with the verdict **"Blocking before any real deployment."**
It is unchanged, and 10.22 says so in its own code: `server_config_provider
.dart:92-94` carries the comment *"This remains a validator, not transport
enforcement — §7.6 F13 records that gap and 10.22 does not close it."*

Verified independently here: `validateServerUrl` has exactly one non-test call
site, a `TextFormField` `validator:` (`server_config_screen.dart:85`); `setUrl`
persists whatever it is handed; `build()` reads it back with no scheme check;
and `kReleaseMode` appears in exactly one place in all of `lib/` — that
validator's own default argument. An `http://` URL stored by a debug build
survives into a release build and carries the 90-day bearer token in cleartext.

**And the compensating control §7.6 leaned on is weaker than recorded.** That
rationale rested on the platform layers — Android's debug-variant-only
cleartext config, which does hold, and iOS/macOS App Transport Security, which
probably does not apply at all. `pubspec.yaml` pulls plain `http` with no
`cupertino_http`, so `http.Client()` resolves to `IOClient` over `dart:io`,
which opens sockets directly rather than through `NSURLSession`. ATS gates
CFNetwork traffic. **This was not verified empirically and should be, on a
device, before either platform is counted as a mitigation** — it is the
difference between "cleartext to a LAN address on iOS" and "cleartext to any
address on iOS."

10.22 did real work adjacent to this: §4.1's private-range condition now exists
on both sides from one shared predicate, in every build. That closes what the
*field* accepts. It does not close what an already-configured client connects
to.

### 8.6 TLS termination on the real host — cannot be verified

10.25 required: *"Verify TLS actually terminates in front of the server on the
real host… confirm it exists and works — do not rely on the app's own check,
which is structurally blind there."*

**There is no real host.** No reverse-proxy configuration of any kind exists in
the repository — no nginx, Caddy, Traefik, certbot or ACME config — and
`TRITRACK_TLS_CERT_PATH`/`TRITRACK_TLS_KEY_PATH` are empty everywhere they
appear. The server has never been deployed anywhere.

This item is therefore **not failed but unverifiable**, and that distinction
does not help: it was on the gate because the protection it names is the one
that actually operates on a public deployment, C-3's container blind spot
(§7.3 B3) being structural. The gate cannot confirm a control that has not been
built. **Whatever deployment is eventually proposed, the reverse proxy is part
of it and is in scope for the gate that approves it** — it is not a thing to
add afterwards and mention in a README.

**The artifact now exists (task 10.49, 2026-08-15).** `docker-compose.tls.yml`
adds a `caddy` service that terminates TLS on 443 and reconfigures `server` so
it is no longer reachable from outside the compose network except through it;
`proxy/Caddyfile` is the whole proxy configuration, four lines. **Verified
locally, end to end, with a self-signed certificate:**

- `server` starts with `TriTrack server listening on https://…` — its own
  TLS satisfied via a second, separate self-signed pair
  (`TRITRACK_TLS_ORIGIN_CERT`/`_KEY`), because `TRITRACK_ALLOW_CLEARTEXT_LAN=1`
  (hardcoded in the base file) combined with `TRITRACK_ENV=production` (which
  this overlay sets, matching what a real deployment should run with) is
  already a documented refusal (`server/README.md`'s own table) — the origin
  certificate is the file's own documented way out of that refusal, not a
  workaround invented for this task.
- Caddy's log shows `"certificate obtained successfully"`, `"issuer":"local"`
  for `TRITRACK_TLS_DOMAIN=localhost` — its own internal CA, chosen
  automatically because Caddy recognizes `localhost` as not a public name,
  with no code difference from the real-deployment path, which would show
  `"issuer":"acme"` against a real domain instead.
- `curl --cacert <Caddy's exported local root> https://localhost/health`
  returns `{"status":"ok"}` with the certificate **chain verified**, not
  `-k` — real termination, real forwarding to the origin, not merely "a
  response came back."
- **task 10.48's actual client code**, both branches of
  `createPlatformHttpClient`, exercised against the live proxy in a real
  `flutter test` network round trip: `http.Client()` (Android/Linux/Windows)
  accepted the connection once Caddy's root was trusted via `HttpOverrides`;
  `CupertinoClient` (iOS/macOS) correctly **refused** the same certificate,
  because `HttpOverrides` has no effect on `NSURLSession`, which only trusts
  the platform keychain — deliberately not modified for this run. That
  refusal is confirmation the client's certificate validation is genuinely
  active on that path, not a gap in the verification: a real deployment's
  Let's Encrypt certificate is already in the platform trust store by
  construction, so nothing on the client needs to change for it to work
  there.

**What stays unverifiable, on purpose — named as its own step rather than
folded into the above.** Everything just described ran on loopback against a
certificate this verification minted itself. The real-host check 10.25
required — DNS for a real domain pointed at a real host, ports 80/443
actually reachable from the internet, Caddy's log showing `"issuer":"acme"`
rather than `"issuer":"local"`, and an unmodified device reaching the real
domain and trusting what it gets back — still has no host to run it against.
`server/README.md`'s "TLS termination" section names this explicitly as the
separate, human step it is; this document does the same, rather than letting
"verified locally" above be read as covering it.

**Certificate custody checked against task 10.43's, not assumed separate.**
The two use disjoint key material — Caddy's ACME account key and issued
certificates (real or internal), held in the `tritrack_caddy_data` named
volume; the origin's self-signed pair, generated once outside the
repository; and 10.43's `minisign` backup-signing key, mounted only into the
`backup` service. No file or volume is shared between them, and nothing
about this task changed §4.9.2's custody arrangement. Checked because the
task asked for the check, not because either system suggested an overlap on
its own.

### 8.7 Secrets in git history — still clean

Re-run across the whole history, all **78 commits** (68 at the last gate),
`git log --all -p`, 142,936 lines.

- No `.env` object has ever been tracked. Every historical `.env.example` has
  every value empty.
- No PEM or private-key block. The only two `-----BEGIN` matches in the entire
  history are the detector string in `no_committed_secrets_test.dart` and §7.4's
  own sentence about it.
- The single `AGE-SECRET-KEY-1` match is `no_committed_secrets_test.dart`'s
  detector constant, added by 10.24 for the key class it created.
- No AWS, GitHub, Slack, OpenAI or JWT patterns. No Postgres URI carrying a
  password. Every historical compose file uses the `${VAR:?}` required-marker.
- 126 candidate assignment lines reviewed: all code, environment lookups, or
  transparently fake fixtures — `hunter2` (the secrets detector's own planted
  secret), `live-secret-token-value` (a test asserting a token is *not*
  logged), `drill-only-not-a-real-secret`.

**Verdict: clean.**

**Superseded as the mechanism, 2026-09-04 (task 11.150), and the reason matters.**
This section is the last time the *manual* review was actually run — **78 commits.**
Task 10.58 built `test/security/no_committed_secrets_test.dart`'s history pass to
replace it, and the manual review has not been run since. **But the replacement was
not covering it either:** in CI it ran under a checkout of depth 1, so it scanned one
commit while its own vacuity guard (more than 100 blobs) passed on the tip tree alone.
**Nothing established this claim between 78 commits and 652.** Task 11.150 ran the
full scan — 652 commits, 4,744 distinct blobs, 4,246 of them read for content (the
rest are over the 512 KB bound no detector has ever looked past) — and the verdict is
unchanged: **clean.** The scan now takes about five seconds and runs on every push
with `fetch-depth: 0`, and it fails loudly rather than quietly if the clone is ever
shallow again. **The manual `git log --all -p` review is not needed each round; what
is needed is that the offline suite is green and its checkout depth intact.**

**One thing this section broke, and the fix is the point.** Writing the
paragraph above turned `no_committed_secrets_test.dart` red: its `age` detector
matched the bare prefix `AGE-SECRET-KEY-1`, and §8.7 writes that prefix out in
order to report that no key is committed. Task 10.24 hit exactly this and
reworded its own sentence; task 10.26 then fixed this class properly in the
assignment regex — and did not carry the fix to the age detector beside it, so
half the class stayed open. 10.24's note had predicted precisely this: *"a
scanner that cannot tell prose from a value will keep finding the documentation
that describes it, so 10.26 should fix the detector, not the sentences."*

Fixed here the same way: the detector now requires the prefix **plus 20
characters of bech32 body** — far more than any sentence puts after it, far
less than a usable key, so a truncated or line-wrapped paste is still caught.
Two tests were added beside 10.26's, one planting a syntactically real identity
to prove the detector still fires and one holding the prose form to prove it
does not. Small, but it is this gate's own subject in miniature: a security
check that is red for a reason nobody can act on is a check people stop
reading, and then a real finding hides in the noise.

### 8.8 §7.6 re-verified: one closable, one blocking, the rest intact

Every finding in §7.6 was re-checked against the code as it stands.

**Closable: F5 only.** `Users` row pre-emption is closed by 10.20 —
`_serverHoldsIdentity` queries `auth_accounts` as well as `Users`
(`row_authorizer.dart:372-382`), which is precisely the window F5 described,
and `authorization_test.dart:1334-1357` pins it.

**Still open and blocking: F13** (§8.5).

**Still open, rationale intact, non-blocking:** F4 (narrowed by 10.21's
`vouching` change, orphan case unchanged), F6, F10, F11, §4.12 requirement 1,
§4.8 control 2, Postgres TLS hard-disabled (now three call sites, 10.23 added
one), `quoted()` not escaping. **`sendMagicLink` returning `void` left this
list on 2026-09-20 (task 11.287): the SMTP sender it was waiting for arrived
and the signature turned out to be the mitigation.**

**Should close before exposure, though individually sub-threshold — and two are
no longer the "one-line fix" §7.6 called them:**

- **The diagnostics cluster is one defect, not four.** F9 (router mounted as a
  catch-all, so an unauthenticated caller learns the console is enabled), F12
  (`changeme` starts cleanly as the console's entire authentication), §4.10's
  unenforced production refusal, and `allowRemote` uncoupled from TLS. Today
  the only thing between an exposed server and "a scanner finds the console,
  then authenticates to it with a placeholder, and reads every project's
  coordinates" is an operator not setting three environment variables. **The
  README note §7.6 said was owed is still owed** — `README.md` still documents
  `TRITRACK_DIAGNOSTICS_ALLOW_REMOTE=true` neutrally.
- **§4.10's fix is no longer one line.** The obvious form — refuse when
  `TRITRACK_ENV=production` — is now weak, because 10.22 deliberately ships
  `TRITRACK_ENV` blank (correctly, that was part of closing C-3). A refusal
  keyed on it fires only for an operator who set it, who is the same operator
  who would not have enabled a remote console. It should be keyed to the same
  public-bind/no-TLS predicate §4.1 already uses. That is a design call.
- **The rate limiter's per-source collapse is elevated by exposure.** §7.6
  records that behind Docker's publish every client presents as the bridge
  gateway, collapsing §4.4's per-source bucket into one global one. On
  localhost that is theoretical. On an exposed server it means a botnet is not
  per-source limited at all, *and* one abusive source exhausts the shared
  bucket and 429s every legitimate sign-in — a trivial sign-in denial of
  service. Needs a shared store or an explicit trusted-proxy
  `X-Forwarded-For` path.
- **§4.7's purge job should be scheduled before exposure**, not after — and D-2
  makes that sharper than it was.

**Fix regardless of the gate:** F15. `scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh` still
has no `-p`, so `trap cleanup EXIT` runs `down -v` against the developer's own
project name. **It fired during this gate run and destroyed
`tritrack_tritrack_postgres_data`.** It is now git-tracked, so the "untracked,
never reviewed" half of its rationale no longer holds. One flag.

Two things noticed while re-verifying, neither a finding on its own:

- `session_store.dart:74-76` uses `KeychainAccessibility.first_unlock`, which
  does **not** require a passcode to be set, while the doc comment above it at
  `:62-64` says both stores are "gated on the device passcode." The comment
  overstates the iOS side. Relevant because §4.8's whole case for skipping
  SQLCipher rests on platform protection, and control 2 (§7.6) was the thing
  that would have surfaced a passcode-less device.
- 10.26's rate-limit escape hatch is refused under `TRITRACK_ENV=production`,
  but `bin/server.dart:131-139` **catches that `StateError` and degrades to the
  real defaults** rather than refusing to start. That is the correct fail-safe
  direction; the doc comment's "refuses it outright" reads as "the server will
  not start," which is not what happens. Worth correcting the comment, not the
  code.

### 8.9 The NAU information-security review — still has not happened

`CLAUDE_DOCS/NAU_infosec_review_request.md` is unchanged since 2026-08-07:
drafted, **not sent**, recipient address deliberately blank. §7.8's terms are
unchanged and they are not something this gate can satisfy on its own:

> **NAU's information security office reviews §7.7 before any deployment
> reachable beyond localhost.** … **This item is not closed, and the gate
> cannot pass until it is.**

This is a human action — sending the request and receiving a response — and no
amount of testing substitutes for it. §7.7 remains the document to send;
§8.10 records what has changed underneath it since it was written, and the
draft should carry that delta rather than being sent as-is.

**Independently of every other finding above, the gate cannot pass until this
happens.**

### 8.10 What changed in the residual-risk picture since §7.7

§7.7 stays as written — it is the document that goes to NAU, and it was
accurate on 2026-08-07. This is the delta a reader needs alongside it.

**Fixed, and verifiable:** all five of §7.7's numbered failures. In its own
plain-language terms — a user can no longer attach a colleague's name to a
record or pull their contact details; the server no longer reveals whether a
project exists; the bundled configuration now serves only to the operator's own
machine and refuses to start unencrypted on a public address; database backups
exist, are encrypted to keys the server does not hold, and have been proven by
restoring rather than asserted; and permission-denial logging now actually
records, on the deployed wiring, checked by reverting the fix.

**New, and it belongs in front of a reviewer:**

1. ~~**The server tells any logged-in user whether a given person has an account
   on it** — and whether a given tag or record id exists on it (D-1).~~ This is
   the same class of leak as the project one that was just fixed, one level
   down, where fixing the status code did not reach. Existence only; no names,
   no coordinates, no record contents. It matters because the ids being tested
   travel in exactly the documents a research team circulates — shared
   observations, spreadsheet exports — so it turns "here is a shared record"
   into "here is a roster of who uses this server."

   **Fixed, in two steps, both on 2026-08-13.** Task 10.29 stopped the server
   answering whether a person has an account here and whether a tag id exists.
   That left one arm, which was written up here as something a reviewer should
   still be told about: a logged-in user could learn whether a given record id
   was already in use on the server, by attempting to create a record under it
   and seeing the attempt refused. The cause was that record ids are chosen by
   the app rather than the server, so removing it meant changing how every
   table is keyed — **which is what task 10.35 then did.** Record ids are now
   scoped to their project, so an id another project happens to use does not
   collide and the server has nothing to refuse. Verified live: all three arms
   answer identically (`scripts/verify_d1_per_row_oracle.py`).
2. **A logged-in user can fill the server's disk** by making refused requests
   (D-2), at roughly 11 MB/s, because the refusal is now recorded and nothing
   bounds or removes what it records.
3. **The app can tell a researcher their observation is synced when the server
   has permanently refused it** (D-3). This is the one to lead with for a
   research-integrity reader: it is a silent loss of a primary scientific
   record, and it is reachable through an ordinary, intended workflow —
   receiving a colleague's shared observation.
4. **The unencrypted-cloud-backup concern §7.7 flagged is unchanged**, and
   §7.5's falsified premise still stands: one member's automatic backup carries
   colleagues' names, current and prior email addresses, and precise
   coordinates into that member's personal cloud account.
5. **The phone-side transport gap (F13) is probably wider than §7.7 implies**
   on iOS and macOS, pending a device check (§8.5).

**The honest summary for a reviewer is unchanged in shape from §7.7's:** the
foundations are solid and were built before the things depending on them; the
five findings that failed the last gate were fixed properly, at the level of
the rule rather than the instance; and re-attacking the result found three more,
two of them created by the fixes. That is what a gate is for, and it is an
argument for the gate rather than against the work.

### 8.11 On the process this gate keeps validating

Three gates and two re-runs now agree on one thing: **the live adversarial pass
finds what code review and passing tests do not.** 703 client tests, 347 server
tests, 26 e2e tests, a clean `/security-review` of the remediation diff and
three targeted reviews did not surface D-1, D-2 or D-3. A crafted `curl`, a
`psql` count, and reading four lines of `sync_engine.dart` did.

Two additions to that, from this run specifically:

- **Verify the verifier.** Three of this gate's checks passed vacuously in
  their first draft, and one of its four initial "failures" was a wrong route
  name. Every reproduction script in `scripts/` is now checked against a build
  with its own fix reverted, because a security test that has never been seen
  to fail is not evidence.
- **Re-attack the fix, not just the finding.** This is the durable lesson.
  D-1 and D-2 exist only because C-1 and C-5 were fixed. Nothing in the
  remediation was wrong; what was missing was a pass over the new code with the
  same hostility the original was given.

## 9. Verdicts — Security Gate C, second re-run (task 10.25, 2026-08-13)

### 9.0 Gate result: **FAILED. The server still does not listen beyond localhost.**

**D-1, D-2's size arm, D-3 and E-1 are genuinely closed**, and this run
re-verified all of them live rather than taking the remediation tasks' word for
it. C-1 through C-5 remain closed and were re-run again. The three suites are
green in one pass — 764 client, 357 server, 30 e2e — the first of which is up
from 703 and the last of which now includes the live refused-row check §8
recorded as owed to "the next device session."

The gate fails on six items. They are independent; no one of them is the reason.

| # | Blocking item | New? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **G-1** | **The e2e suite reports success when it runs nothing.** `flutter test test/e2e --tags e2e` with the environment unset prints "All tests skipped" and **exits 0**. That is E-1's exact shape, on the one suite that exercises the wire protocol, the schema-major boundary and the refused-row path against a real server — and 10.31's guard was built for the server only. | new |
| **G-2** | **E-2 is not closed. 10.32's `ports:` does not replace the base file's — Compose merges them.** With the LAN opt-in taken, `docker compose config` still renders `0.0.0.0:8080` *alongside* the override's loopback mapping. The stack currently fails to start rather than exposing, but that is Docker's bind ordering, not a control, and the file asserts a guarantee it does not provide. | carried, and worse than recorded |
| **G-3** | **E-3, reproduced destructively.** The documented in-place restore dropped a live database holding the only copy of an observation before verifying the replacement archive at all — the real defect, and the one this row is about. The archive used in this reproduction was **deliberately truncated by the harness** to exercise that gap; `age` refusing it afterward is the control working, not a second defect (§9.4 corrects an earlier compressed reading of this same run that took the refusal for "the archive would not decrypt," full stop). Recorded as must-fix-before-this-gate at the last run; never given a task. Asset 2. | carried, now proven |
| **F13** | **The client's `https` requirement is still form validation, not transport enforcement.** Unchanged in every particular, including the seam where the fix belongs (`serverHttpClient`) still doing no scheme check. §7.6 and §8.5 both already rated this blocking. | carried |
| **TLS** | **Still nothing to verify.** No reverse-proxy configuration of any kind exists anywhere in the repository. | carried |
| **NAU** | **The institutional review still has not happened.** Unchanged since 2026-08-07: drafted, unsent, recipient line blank. | carried |

**The result worth carrying forward.** The last gate's lesson was *repairing a
security control is a change to the attack surface*. This one adds the sharper
half: **three of the six blocking items are places where a fix was recorded as
landed and the thing it was supposed to close is still open.** E-2 was closed by
a task that read the file instead of rendering it. E-3 was written down as
blocking and then simply never scheduled. D-1's arm (c) is recorded in §4.13 and
§8.4 as "closed outright" and survives on `User_Emails` (§9.5, G-4). None of
these is a new mistake in reasoning; all three are the *record* getting ahead of
the code. A gate that trusted the plan doc's Status fields would have passed all
three.

Two further items do not block exposure and are not new work in the sense the
others are, but they change what the next run can measure: **D-2's row-count arm
is still open** (its size arm is closed, and the measured amplification is down
roughly 90-fold), and **D-5 is worse on inspection than recorded** — the only
configuration that can read the audit log is the one §4.10's network gate exists
to prevent.

### 9.1 What was re-run, and how

The whole of 10.16 again, not a spot-check. Everything below ran against a live
`docker compose` stack — real Postgres, real bound socket, real magic links off
disk — over raw HTTP with no client code, except where the point was explicitly
to exercise the client.

| | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `flutter test` | **764 passed**, 30 skipped (the e2e groups, by design) |
| Server suite (`scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh`) | **357 passed**, zero skips |
| Server suite with no database | **fails loudly** — 10.31's guard, confirmed |
| `flutter test test/e2e --tags e2e` | **30 passed, in a single pass** |
| C-1…C-5 live reproductions | **all refused** (§9.2) |
| D-1 live reproduction, all three arms | **all indistinguishable** (§9.2) |
| Backup/restore drill, incl. 10.36's marker | **all green** (§9.2) |
| Adversarial pass, 33 attempts | **28 held, 5 failed** (§9.3) |
| Secrets across the whole git history | **clean**, 89 commits (§9.6) |

**The stack ran under its own Compose project name** (`-p tritrack-gate`), not
the default. F15 destroyed the developer's data volume during the first gate
run; 10.27 fixed that for the test script, and this extends the same discipline
to the gate itself, which 10.27 did not cover.

### 9.1.1 The gate's own instruments had silently rotted

Before any of the above could run, four of the five `verify_*.py` scripts and
the adversarial pass were still sending `schema_major: 1`. Task 10.35 moved the
server to major 2 on 2026-08-13. **Every request they make would have been
refused `409` before reaching a single control**, and the scripts' own checks
would then have read `None` out of an empty `outcomes` map — which, for the
checks phrased as "is this refused?", is indistinguishable from the control
holding.

This is exactly the item 10.35's own Discovered Scope filed: *"a major bump
silently invalidates every one of them that is not exercised in the same
session… cheap now, confusing in a year."* It was one day, not a year.

Fixed as part of taking the measurement, and fixed at the level the finding is
about: **`scripts/gate_wire.py` parses** the envelope out of
`schema_constants.dart` and `sync_protocol.dart`, and every table's primary key
out of `sync_tables.dart`. A future bump updates the tools by definition rather
than by somebody remembering. It raises at import if the declarations it reads
have moved, rather than falling back to a stale default — the failure it exists
to prevent.

Two things surfaced while doing it, both worth more than the chore was:

- **`verify_c1_row_naming.py`'s regression check was asserting the opposite of
  current behavior.** Its final section, "legitimate first-publish replication
  still works," expects an imported colleague's `Users` row to be `inserted`.
  Task 10.29 converged that branch on the *refusal* — deliberately, as D-1's
  design decision, paying the replication seam as the price. Nobody re-ran the
  script after 10.29 landed, so the inversion sat there. Now retitled and
  inverted, with the reasoning inline, plus a check that the caller's *own*
  rows still publish (which is what that section was really protecting).
- **`server/backup/restore.sh` has the same rot in a place the drill cannot
  see.** Task 10.36 added `SCHEMA_MIN=1` / `SCHEMA_MAX=2` as shell literals with
  a comment saying to "update both bounds together whenever either constant
  moves." That is the same hand-maintained coupling, one bump away from
  refusing a restorable archive or accepting an unrestorable one, and
  `backup_restore_drill.sh` asserts the sidecar's value without ever comparing
  it to `schemaMajorVersion`. Filed, not fixed — it is a task, not a gate
  chore.

### 9.2 C-1…C-5 and D-1: still closed, re-verified live

| Finding | Script | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **C-1** row naming | `verify_c1_row_naming.py` | All four B1a–B1d refused; the caller's own publish unaffected |
| **C-2** existence oracle | `verify_c2_existence_oracle.py` | Pull, push, ack, a malformed first publish and a no-rows push all answer a real foreign project and a fabricated id identically |
| **C-3** cleartext defaults | `verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py` | Server exits 78 on a public address; compose publishes loopback only; the LAN address does not reach the running stack while `localhost` answers 200 |
| **C-4** encrypted backups | `backup_restore_drill.sh` | All green, including a restore into a fresh database, a wrong-key refusal, retention pruning oldest-first, and 10.36's schema sidecar (present, marker-less archives treated as major 1, an out-of-range major refused by name) |
| **C-5** denial auditing | `verify_c5_denial_audit.py` | Push, pull and ack denials each leave an `authorization_denied` row carrying caller, project, source address and trace id; the never-log rules hold on that path; other event types unaffected |
| **D-1** per-row oracle | `verify_d1_per_row_oracle.py` | All three arms indistinguishable — registration status (three cases), tag existence (reference and claim), and arm (c)'s key collision, which 10.35's project-scoped keys removed rather than bounded |

The adversarial pass adds an independent line on the same ground: the row-naming
invariant refused on every table and column tested, a real user and a fictional
one were indistinguishable, and a real foreign project and a fictional one were
not separable by timing (4.2 ms vs 4.0 ms).

### 9.3 The adversarial pass, re-run in full

`scripts/gate_c_adversarial_pass.py`, now four groups: 10.16's six named
attempts, §7.3's other held attempts, group C's attacks on the *first* round of
remediation, and **a new group D aimed at the second round — tasks 10.28
through 10.36**, none of which existed when group C was written.

**28 controls held, 5 failed.** Everything §7.3 and §8.3 recorded as holding
still holds, and group D's new ground held on the parts that matter most:

- **The composite primary key is caller-supplied on both halves now**, so a row
  key can name one project while the envelope names another. Neither direction
  lands: a key naming the victim's project does not write there, and a push
  aimed at a foreign project is refused `403` before it can write into the
  caller's own.
- **10.29's converged refusals are genuinely uniform.** An unreachable user, an
  unreachable tag and a user the server has never seen produce the same status,
  the same response key set and the same outcome string. The oracle converged;
  it did not move one field down, which is the failure mode D-1 was.
- **10.35's major check runs in front of authorization and refuses uniformly** —
  a real foreign project and a fabricated one get byte-identical `409`s — and a
  refused-major push applies no rows.

The five failures:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ce2** | A denial flood still grows the audit store without bound. §9.4 |
| **Ch** | §7.6 F10 again: an unauthenticated malformed body answers `500`, not `401`. Unchanged, still non-blocking for the reason §7.6 gives, still live |
| **Dc** | `User_Emails` is still a global-key existence oracle. §9.5 |
| **Dg** | E-2 is not closed. §9.4 |
| **Dh** | A row can be pinned at `revision = 2^63-1` and never legitimately updated again — recorded non-blocking at the last gate by reading, now reproduced live: the pin is `inserted`, and a later edit at revision 2 does not apply |

**One of this run's own checks passed vacuously in its first draft**, and it is
worth recording for the same reason §8.2 recorded its predecessor. `Dc` compared
a key already in use against a free one, and read the in-use key with a `psql`
query whose quoting was wrong. The query returned nothing, the comparison
short-circuited on the empty case, and the check printed **HELD** — against the
finding it was written to catch, which was live. Found by reading the detail
line (`taken=(None, None)`) rather than the verdict. Third time in three gates
that a verification tool has reported success for the absence of its own input.

### 9.4 The blocking findings

#### G-1 — The e2e suite reports success when it runs nothing

```
$ flutter test test/e2e --tags e2e
00:00 +0 ~28: All tests skipped.
$ echo $?
0
```

No database, no server, no environment variables — and an exit code that a
person, a script, or a gate reads as "the end-to-end suite passed."

This is **E-1 verbatim**, one suite over. Task 10.31 closed E-1 properly and the
fix is good: `server/test/support/database_coverage_guard_test.dart` fails —
never skips — when no Postgres is configured, and a no-database `dart test` now
exits non-zero. Confirmed live this run. But the guard was written for the
server suite, and `test/e2e/support/e2e_env.dart` has the identical structure
with no equivalent: `e2eSkipReason` is non-null whenever the two environment
variables are unset, every group carries it, and nothing anywhere asserts that
the suite ran.

**Why this is rated blocking rather than filed as tidy-up.** The e2e suite is
the only thing in the repository that exercises the wire protocol end to end
against a live server: the schema-major boundary 10.35 introduced, the
serialization fidelity 10.35's Discovered Scope flagged as analyzer-verified
only, and — as of this run — the refused-row visibility path that three separate
tasks deferred to "the next device session." All of it is invisible on the
default path. §8.1 recorded "26 passed, in a single pass" as a gate result; the
command that produces that number produces `0` and "All tests skipped" just as
readily, and nothing in the output distinguishes them at a glance.

This run measured it correctly — 30 passed, environment set, against the live
stack — so it does not invalidate anything above. It is rated with E-1's own
rating, which the last gate stated as *blocking the next re-run's ability to
claim anything*.

**The fix is E-1's, applied symmetrically**: a guard test that fails rather than
skips when `E2eEnv.isConfigured` is false, landed *before* anything else, since
the standing rule 10.31 wrote into `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md` — "a test
that cannot run must not look like a test that passed" — is now on its fourth
instance in Phase 10.

#### G-2 — E-2 is not closed: Compose merges `ports:`, it does not replace it

Task 10.32 added a `ports:` block to `docker-compose.e2e.yml` hardcoding
loopback, with this comment:

> Hardcoded to loopback here, deliberately not reading the variable, so no
> `.env` value can change it.

That is not what happens. Compose **merges** sequence-valued keys from later
files into earlier ones rather than replacing them, so the base file's
`${SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}` mapping survives alongside the override's.
Rendered with the LAN opt-in taken — E-2's own stated precondition, an operator
who followed the README's LAN walkthrough and then ran the e2e suite:

```
$ SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0 docker compose \
    -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.e2e.yml config
    ports:
      - host_ip: 0.0.0.0        <-- the base file's, still there
        published: "8080"
      - host_ip: 127.0.0.1      <-- 10.32's
        published: "8080"
```

Brought up for real, the two mappings collide and the stack **fails to start**:
`failed to bind host port 127.0.0.1:8080/tcp: address already in use`. So there
is no exposure today. But:

1. **The safe outcome is incidental.** It is Docker's port proxy refusing a
   second bind on the same port, not any control this project built. It is not
   asserted anywhere, not tested, and not what the file claims is happening.
2. **The repair path leads back to C-3.** An operator hits an opaque
   "address already in use" while following two documented procedures, and the
   obvious fix — delete the override's `ports:` block, which is the newer and
   stranger-looking of the two — is precisely E-2's original configuration:
   cleartext on every interface, §4.4's per-source limits raised to `1<<30`,
   and a bind-mounted directory of live magic-link tokens.
3. **The base file alone still behaves correctly**, verified this run: with the
   opt-in set and no override, the LAN address answers `200`. So the deliberate
   one-line opt-in 10.22 built is intact; it is only the override that is
   broken, and broken in the direction of an unexplained failure.

**Verified fix, tested this run and then reverted** (a gate does not repair its
own findings): `ports: !override` renders exactly one mapping, on loopback,
with the opt-in set. One token. The comment above it needs rewriting too, since
it currently documents a guarantee the file does not make.

**Rated as E-2 was, which is as C-3 was.** The last gate closed C-3 and rated
its reopening at the same severity; that reopening has not been closed, and the
task that was supposed to close it verified the fix by reading the file rather
than rendering it — which is the same distance between "the code looks right"
and "the artifact behaves right" that this gate keeps finding things in.

#### G-3 — E-3, reproduced: the documented restore destroys live data before it knows the archive is readable

E-3 was recorded at the last gate under *"Must fix before the NEXT gate
re-run… Neither blocks exposure. Both block the next gate being able to claim
anything."* E-1 got task 10.31. **E-3 got nothing** — no task, no entry, no
status. `server/backup/restore.sh` is unchanged in the respect that matters:
`DROP DATABASE` → `CREATE DATABASE` → *then* `age --decrypt | psql`.

Task 10.36 added a pre-flight, which is real progress — the schema-version
sidecar is read and can refuse before the drop — but it validates the *marker*,
not the *ciphertext*, and the marker is a plaintext file an operator can copy
between archives (this run did exactly that, to build the truncated case).

Reproduced live, `scripts/verify_e3_restore_replace.sh`, new this run:

```
1. live database 'tritrack' holds the canary observation
2. truncated copy: 12656 of 37969 bytes        [FAULT INJECTED BY THIS HARNESS —
                                                 not something that happened to
                                                 the archive; see note below]
3. stopped the server (an operator restoring in place does this first)
   running: TRITRACK_RESTORE_REPLACE=I_UNDERSTAND against 'tritrack'
   | Archive schema major: 2 (this build supports 1 through 2)
   | Dropping existing database 'tritrack'...
   | age: error: failed to decrypt and authenticate payload chunk,
   |      file may be corrupted or tampered with   [EXPECTED — age correctly
   |      refusing the truncated STREAM from step 2, not a decryption defect]
   | RESTORE FAILED — decrypt/restore failed.
   DATA LOST  the canary is gone — the live database was dropped before the
   DATA LOST  archive was known to be readable. Rows remaining: <database gone>
```

**Labeled per task 10.40, after task 10.37 verified it:** step 2's truncation
is deliberate fault injection, built by this harness to prove the drop-before-
verify ordering is exploitable — it is not evidence that encrypted backups
cannot be decrypted. A good archive was separately confirmed to decrypt and
restore cleanly on both paths, canary intact, before anything above was
changed. The one real defect is `DATA LOST`: the database was dropped before
the archive — corrupted or not — was ever read. That ordering is what this
finding is about, not the archive's readability.

**Two details that matter for the fix.** First, the harness initially reported
the data as *surviving*, because the running server held connections and
`DROP DATABASE` failed with "is being accessed by other users." That looks like
a control and is not one — it is Postgres refusing a busy database, and it
disappears the moment the operator does the obvious correct thing and stops the
server first. Second, **the drill cannot catch this and could not have.** Every
target it restores into is a fresh name (`drill_restored`, `drill_legacy`,
`drill_toofar`, and a `drill_wrongkey` that never existed), so it never types
`TRITRACK_RESTORE_REPLACE=I_UNDERSTAND` at all. Nine green checks and this
coexist because the drill exercises the path that cannot destroy anything.

The fix is the one E-3 already named — verify the decrypt before the drop,
restore into a temporary name and rename, add `--single-transaction` so a
mid-stream abort cannot commit a valid prefix — plus the drill case, which is
now written and can be folded in rather than authored from scratch.

#### D-2 — the size arm is closed, the row-count arm is not

Task 10.30 capped every free-text field `AuthAuditLog.record` writes at 500
characters, at the API boundary rather than the one known call site. That works
and it is the right level: verified live, the widest `outcome` any caller can
store is exactly 500 characters, injection through `project_id` forges no row,
and the `event` column still holds only the closed enum.

Re-measured with 100 KB of incompressible content per request:

| | Last gate | This gate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 200 denied requests | ~200 MB | **200 KB** |
| sustained rate | ~11 MB/s | **~122 KB/s** |

A ninety-fold reduction, from one ordinary registered user, while the server
answers `403` throughout. What has not changed: `/sync/pull` carries no rate
limit (§4.4 limits magic links and redemptions only, confirmed in
`rate_limiter.dart`), the row count grows 1:1 with requests, and **§4.7's
retention sweep is still a mechanism nothing schedules.**

**Not blocking.** §5.6 makes denial of service an explicit non-goal on the
stated grounds that the app works fully offline, so an unavailable server costs
delay and nothing more — and 10.28/10.33 now make that literally true for the
push path, since the client retains and re-offers anything the server did not
confirm. §4.7's re-derivation at 10.34 is also correct as far as it goes: a
*project-level* `403` still requires a caller with no relationship to the
project, which the ordinary import workflow does not produce.

**But §4.7's own `Violated by:` list names "retention that quietly grows
without bound"**, and that is still the state: a decision recorded as 1-year
retention, implemented by nothing. The remaining work is the purge schedule,
not another cap.

#### D-5 — sharpened: the only way to read the audit log is to disable the control protecting it

Verified live this run, which §8 did not do:

| Configuration | `/diagnostics/auth-events` from the host |
| --- | --- |
| Shipped default (console off) | **404** |
| `DIAGNOSTICS_ENABLED=true`, correct bearer token | **403** `diagnostics_console_local_only` |
| …plus `DIAGNOSTICS_ALLOW_REMOTE=true`, correct token | **200** |
| …plus `ALLOW_REMOTE=true`, no token | **401** |

The shipped default now answers `404` rather than the `403` §8.4 recorded,
which is the better answer — a disabled route should not announce itself. The
substance is unchanged and worse than "unreachable" conveys: under Docker every
request from the host arrives from the bridge gateway, never loopback, so
§4.10's network gate refuses the operator along with everyone else. **The only
configuration that can read the rows C-5 exists to create is the one §4.10
built the gate to prevent**, leaving the bearer token as the sole control.

The undocumented alternative — `docker compose exec postgres psql` — works and
appears in no README. §7.6's owed README note is still owed, and now has a
second thing to say.

**Not blocking** (nothing is exposed; this is a control that cannot be
*consumed*), but it means C-5's remediation has not yet delivered the thing C-5
was about, which was an operator being able to see denials.

#### D-4 — unchanged

`auditDenial` still has exactly three call sites, all project-level
(`sync_routes.dart:199, 487, 551`). Every row-level `unauthorized` — which is
where C-1's exploits, D-1's probes and, since 10.29, the ordinary import
refusal all live — writes nothing. §7.3 B5's complaint is still literally true
for exactly those requests. Recorded non-blocking as before; §4.7's note on what
a future fix must budget for still stands, and D-2's row-count arm above is the
reason that budget matters.

### 9.5 G-4 — `User_Emails` is still a global-key existence oracle, and the record says otherwise

From an ordinary session with no relationship to anything being asked about,
naming **the caller themselves** so the row-naming invariant is satisfied and
the only variable is the primary key:

```
push User_Emails with a user_email_id another user already holds
  -> 200 {"outcomes": {"User_Emails/<id>": "unauthorized"}}
push User_Emails with a fresh user_email_id
  -> 200 {"outcomes": {"User_Emails/<id>": "inserted"}}
```

That is **D-1 arm (c), unchanged**: *"does this key exist anywhere on this
server."*

Task 10.35 scoped the six project-scoped data tables to `(<id>, project_id)`.
~~`Users`, `User_Emails` and `Tags` remain keyed globally. Two of the three are
covered anyway by rules that do not depend on keying — `Users` by §4.17's
naming invariant, `Tags` by 10.29's reachability rule, both re-verified
indistinguishable this run.~~ **The `Tags` half of that sentence was wrong when
it was written and is now moot** — H-3 (§10.7) found that 10.29's reachability
rule covered nothing of the kind, and task 11.219 then gave `Tags` a
`project_id` in its primary key, which closes it the same way 10.35 closed the
other six (measured 2026-09-10, task 11.220; see §4.13). **As of 2026-09-10 only
`Users` and `User_Emails` are still keyed globally**, and `Users` is covered by
§4.17's naming invariant. `User_Emails` is covered by neither: its
`userColumns` check passes when the caller names themselves, and there is no
membership edge to consult, so the key collision is the whole of the
answer. **G-4 is what is left of this finding, and it is a one-table question
now rather than a three-table one.**

**The disclosure is negligible and that is why this is not blocking**: a
`user_email_id` is a client-generated UUIDv4, it appears in no share payload,
and probing one means guessing 122 bits. It is also a *write* collision, but
UUIDv4 makes accidental collision a non-event.

**What is not negligible is that the record claims this is closed.** §4.13 and
§8.4's D-1 row both now read that arm (c) was "fully closed by task 10.35" and
that "all three arms now verify as indistinguishable" — and
`verify_d1_per_row_oracle.py`'s arm (c) case tests a project-scoped table, which
is exactly the case 10.35 fixed. The next person to read §4.13 will believe the
property holds for every table, because that is what it says.

This is the same shape as C-1 and as C-2→D-1, for the third time: **the fix was
applied to the instances that had reproductions, and the sentence describing it
was written as though it had been derived as a rule.** 10.35's reasoning was
sound and its bump was justified on grounds independent of this. What is missing
is the sweep over the tables nobody had written a probe for.

Two ways out, and it is a decision rather than a patch: scope `User_Emails` by
its natural owner (`(user_email_id, user_id)`, another major bump, almost
certainly not worth it), or ~~restate §4.13's residual honestly as *"closed for
project-scoped tables; a client-chosen global key still answers on `Users`,
`User_Emails` and `Tags`, of which only `User_Emails` is not covered by another
rule."*~~ restate §4.13's residual honestly. **The wording proposed here was
itself wrong** — it named `Tags` as still answering, which stopped being true on
2026-09-10, and §10.7's H-3 entry had already said this paragraph's `Tags` claim
was derived by reading rather than probing. **§4.13 now carries the restatement,
measured**: closed for every project-scoped table, `Users` covered by §4.17,
`Projects` a stated residual, `User_Emails` the one gap.

### 9.5.1 G-5 — one malformed row fails the whole push with `500`

Live, as an authorized caller pushing to their own project:

| Row | Response |
| --- | --- |
| Valid | `200`, `inserted` |
| Valid plus an unknown extra column | `200`, `inserted` — 10.18's preservation working |
| Missing a `NOT NULL` column | **`500 internal_error`** |
| Wrong type on `latitude` | **`500 internal_error`** |
| One valid row batched with one bad row | **`500`**, and the valid row does not land |

The protocol has a per-row `invalid` outcome — `HeldRowReason.forOutcome`
handles it explicitly — and this path never produces one. A single unserializable
row fails every push that carries it, indefinitely.

**Non-blocking, and genuinely low severity**: it is not an oracle (it requires
being authorized already), it discloses nothing (`Ci` confirms the body carries
only `internal_error` and a trace id), it is unreachable through the app's own
serializer, and 10.28's rule 2 means the client holds everything rather than
losing it — silence is treated as a refusal, which is the fail-safe direction.
Recorded because it is F10's family on the routes every fix has rewritten, and
because "one bad row and this device can never sync again" is a support call
with a `500` and no explanation at the end of it.

**Closed by task 10.46 (2026-08-14).** `SyncService._tryWrite` (`sync_service.dart`)
wraps every row's `_insert`/`_update` in its own `SAVEPOINT`: Postgres aborts
the *whole* enclosing transaction on any statement error, so without one, one
bad row poisoned every statement after it — including the good rows already
queued — and the final `COMMIT` (or the outer transaction's own rollback)
discarded the lot, which is exactly "one valid row batched with one bad row →
`500`, and the valid row does not land" above. A failed write now rolls back
to its own savepoint, reports `SyncRowOutcome.invalid` (the same outcome
`RowValidator` uses — the caller cannot tell which check caught it, which is
the point), and the rest of the batch proceeds normally. Reproduced live —
both the missing-`NOT-NULL`-column and the wrong-type-on-`latitude` cases —
in `server/test/integration/sync_envelope_typing_test.dart`.

### 9.6 Secrets in git history — still clean

89 commits, whole history, `--all`. Every hit is a variable reference
(`PGPASSWORD="$POSTGRES_PASSWORD"`), a test fixture (`'right-token'`), or a
literal placeholder. No `.env`, no key material, no certificate or identity file
has ever been committed. `no_committed_secrets_test.dart` is green, including
its own plant-a-secret proof that the detector still catches a real one.

### 9.7 The user-facing check 10.25 asked for — mostly closed, for the first time

10.25's instruction was to check the surfaces the fixes touched *on a device*,
naming the case where a colleague's `TT1:` payload is refused because they are
not on the project: **"Confirm that fails visibly and says something useful…
This is a code-review blind spot by construction."** Tasks 10.28, 10.34 and
10.35 each verified their own half at the widget-tree level and deferred the
rest to "the next device session."

That gap is now mostly closed, by
`test/e2e/refused_row_visibility_e2e_test.dart` — new this run, and the reason
the e2e suite is 30 tests rather than 28. It drives the **real `SyncEngine`
against the real server**, produces a genuine refusal through the ordinary
import workflow (a `Users` row for a colleague plus an observation attributed to
them, both carrying the sender's clock verbatim as task 6.3 requires), and
asserts on what a user is shown:

- the replica is recorded in `Sync_Held_Rows` by the real server's refusal;
- the observation still exists locally, unchanged, still attributed correctly;
- `heldCount` is non-zero — the number that forbids reporting a clean sync;
- the reason is `notPermitted`, and its client-authored copy says the record is
  safe, that it is waiting on project membership, and what to tap;
- `applied < pushed` — the refusal is not counted as success;
- a following round does **not** re-offer the held row (held, not retried
  forever), and releasing it does.

That is everything up to the pixels. **What still needs a human with a phone**:
that the sentence reads correctly at a glance in the actual workflow on a small
screen, which is what 10.34's residual was about and what a `flutter test`
process cannot answer; and F13's ATS question, which needs a build on iOS.

The other two surfaces 10.25 named are in better shape. **10.22's startup
refusal is visible** — the server prints the full `!!! Serving CLEARTEXT HTTP…`
warning naming the variable and the section, and exits 78 with a specific
message on a genuinely public address (`verify_c3`). **10.23's audit path is
not** — the rows are written and, per D-5 above, cannot be read by any
documented means. A correct refusal nobody can see is exactly the support call
10.25 predicted.

### 9.8 On the process, again

Three gates, three re-runs. The live adversarial pass keeps finding what code
review and passing tests do not, and this run adds a specific corollary about
*documentation*:

**The plan doc's Status fields are not evidence.** Three of six blocking items
here are places where the record and the code disagree — E-2 marked Done with
the exposure still rendering, E-3 written down as blocking and never scheduled,
D-1 arm (c) described as closed outright and live on `User_Emails`. Each was
found by running the thing, and each would have been missed by any process that
started from "10.32 is Done, so E-2 is closed."

The two older lessons held up under their own test:

- **Verify the verifier.** Group D's `Dc` printed HELD against a live finding
  because its own SQL returned nothing. Third gate running, third vacuous pass.
  The habit that catches these is reading the detail line, not the verdict.
- **Re-attack the fix.** Group D existed only because tasks 10.28–10.36
  happened, and it is where G-2, G-4 and the live confirmation of `Dh` came
  from.

One new one, from §9.1.1: **a gate's instruments rot faster than its findings
do.** A schema major bumped on 2026-08-13 invalidated five of this gate's six
tools within a day. Tools that speak a versioned wire should derive their
constants from the source of truth rather than restate them, which is now what
`scripts/gate_wire.py` does — and `server/backup/restore.sh` is the remaining
place that does not.

## 10. Verdicts — Security Gate C, third re-run (task 10.25, 2026-08-14)

### 10.0 Gate result: **FAILED. The server still does not listen beyond localhost.**

**The three findings this round was scheduled to close are closed, and all
three were verified the way they were found rather than the way they were
reported.** G-1's e2e skip guard fails an unconfigured `--tags e2e` run and its
file-count assertion catches a deliberately removed file; G-2's `!override`
renders exactly one loopback mapping with the LAN opt-in taken; G-3's restore
verifies the whole decrypted stream and restores into a staging database before
any live data is touched, and the drill that could not previously reach that
path now exercises it in four destructive cases. C-1…C-5 and D-1 refuse again.

The gate fails on seven items. Four are new — two of them the most serious
findings any of these three re-runs has produced, both in the backup path, both
reachable by the one party §4.9 deliberately chose to trust — and three are
carried, unchanged, each now rated blocking at three consecutive gates.

| # | Blocking item | New? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **H-6** | **The restore path authenticates integrity, not origin.** An archive forged with nothing but the *public* recipient string — which §4.9 says may appear in a commit — passes the checksum, the schema marker and the decrypt-verify, has its SQL executed as the Postgres **superuser**, and is renamed into the live database name. Reproduced live, `scripts/verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh`. 10.37's rename-aside means the real database survives and is recoverable; nothing else stops it. §10.5.1 | new |
| **H-7** | **Retention deletes by filename, so write-only access to the archive directory destroys every real backup.** `backup.sh:150-155` keeps the lexically-highest `KEEP` names; 30 planted files dated 2999 make the next legitimate backup run delete the entire genuine history, checksums and sidecars included. No key, no read access, executed by the backup job itself. §10.5.2 | new |
| **H-1** | **10.39's guard turns the default `flutter test` run red.** The new `test/e2e/e2e_coverage_guard_test.dart` is tagged `e2e`, but nothing excludes that tag from a plain `flutter test`, so the suite that Phase 10 invariant 5 exists to keep green with no server and no network now exits 1 on a clean checkout. G-1 is genuinely closed; it was closed by breaking the guarantee next to it. §10.4 | new |
| **H-2** | **Every one of the gate's five wire-speaking instruments aborted before running a single control.** 10.40's new `gate_wire.preflight()` asserts `200` on a `/sync/pull` whose designed answer is `403`. The gate could not measure anything until it repaired its own tools — the same lost cycle §9.1.1 recorded, with the sign reversed. §10.5 | new |
| **F13** | **The client's `https` requirement is still form validation, not transport enforcement.** `lib/core/providers/server_http_client_provider.dart` contains no scheme check of any kind; `cupertino_http` is still absent from `pubspec.yaml`, so the ATS compensating control still probably never applies. Unchanged in every particular. Rated blocking by §7.6, §8.5 and §9.0. | carried ×3 |
| **TLS** | **Still nothing to verify.** A fresh sweep for `nginx`, `caddy`, `traefik`, `certbot`, `letsencrypt` or any reverse-proxy configuration across every `*.yml`, `*.conf` and `Dockerfile` in the repository returns nothing outside `CLAUDE_DOCS/`. | carried ×3 |
| **NAU** | **The institutional review still has not happened.** `CLAUDE_DOCS/NAU_infosec_review_request.md` is untouched since the commit that created it (`831a269`, task 10.16): "drafted 2026-08-07, **not sent.** Recipient address deliberately left blank." | carried ×3 |

**The result worth carrying forward, part one.** Every previous round of this
gate attacked the sync API, because that is where the findings were. H-6 and H-7
came from attacking the **backup path**, which C-4 closed at the first gate and
which nothing had adversarially probed since: three tasks (10.24, 10.36, 10.37)
have worked on it, each correctly, and all three were reasoning about *accidents*
— corruption, truncation, a wrong key, an ordering that destroys data. Nobody
asked what an adversary who can write a file into that directory can do, and
§4.9's own decision that the public recipients need not be secret makes that
adversary cheap. **A control designed against accident is not a control against
an adversary, and the two get written down in the same sentence.**

**Part two.** §9's lesson was that the record gets ahead of the code. This
round adds: **the last three remediation tasks each did what they were asked,
and two of them broke the instrument that would have noticed if they hadn't.** 10.39 closed a
"tests must not pass by skipping" finding and left the default suite failing.
10.40 added a self-check to five tools that speak the wire and never ran one of
them against a live server — the check asserts a status code the server is
designed not to return. Neither is a reasoning error. Both are the same
omission: *the fix was never executed in the configuration it ships in.*

Nothing found this round is a *network* exposure: the five C-findings, D-1, and
every control §7.3 and §8.3 recorded as holding still hold, and the adversarial
pass is the largest it has been (40 checks). H-6 and H-7 are not network
findings either — they are integrity and availability findings against asset 2,
reachable by whoever holds the off-site copy. And two of the three carried items
are human actions nobody has taken in seven days, while the third is a one-seam
code change three gates have now asked for.
