### 10.3 G-3 is closed, and the drill can now see the path that could destroy data

`server/backup/restore.sh` no longer drops anything. The order is now checksum
→ schema marker → **decrypt and read the whole stream** → create a staging
database → restore into it with `--single-transaction` → rename the live
database aside to `<target>_replaced_<stamp>` → rename staging into place, with
a rollback that puts the original name back if the second rename fails.

The part that matters for a gate is that the drill now types
`TRITRACK_RESTORE_REPLACE=I_UNDERSTAND` at all — §9.4's finding was that every
target it restored into was a fresh name, so nine green checks coexisted with a
destructive path nobody exercised. It now runs four cases against a live
database holding a seeded observation, **with the server stopped first**, which
is what turned §9's first attempt into a false negative:

- a damaged archive is caught by its checksum; live data untouched;
- a truncated archive is stopped at the decrypt; live data untouched;
- the wrong holder's key is refused before the swap; live data untouched;
- a good archive replaces in place, and the database it replaced is kept.

All four pass. The retention rule for those kept copies is *never automatic*
(task 10.40), and `restore.sh` prints a `NOTE` counting the ones already on
disk each time it makes another.

### 10.4 H-1 — 10.39's guard turns the default `flutter test` run red

```
$ flutter test
00:18 +772 ~30 -1: Some tests failed.

Failing tests:
  test/e2e/e2e_coverage_guard_test.dart: the e2e suite must not pass with no
  server configured
$ echo $?
1
```

G-1's fix is correct and its acceptance criteria are met: an unconfigured
`flutter test test/e2e --tags e2e` exits 1, and removing an e2e test file makes
the count assertion fail by name (both verified above). The problem is the
blast radius. `test/e2e/e2e_coverage_guard_test.dart` carries
`@Tags(['e2e'])`, but there is **no `dart_test.yaml` anywhere in this
repository** — not at the root, not in `server/` — so no tag is excluded from
anything. A plain `flutter test` loads the file, `E2eEnv.isConfigured` is
false, and the guard does what it was written to do.

That is the exact opposite of what the surrounding design says. The root
`README.md` states the invariant in so many words — "Running plain `flutter
test` (no variables set) loads every file under `test/e2e/` but skips each
group immediately, so the default suite stays green with no server and no
network — verify this yourself if you touch anything under
`test/e2e/support/`" — and Phase 10 invariant 5 is that guarantee. The server's
analogous guard (`database_coverage_guard_test.dart`, task 10.31) has the same
structure and the same absence of tag exclusion, but there it is *intended*: a
no-database `dart test` is meant to fail. A no-server `flutter test` is meant
to pass, because the app is meant to work with no server at all.

**Why this is rated blocking rather than filed as tidy-up.** It is 10.26's
finding, restated: a permanently-failing security-relevant suite is a suite
people stop reading, and then a real finding hides in the noise. 10.26 spent a
task fixing exactly this shape (`no_committed_secrets_test.dart` red on
`main`), and the plan's own words were "at 10.25 someone will see 18 failures
and spend an hour deciding whether they are real." This gate spent that hour.
Worse, the obvious local repair — make the guard skip when it is not an
intentional e2e run — is G-1 reopened, which is the G-2 repair-path shape a
second time.

**The fix is a tag exclusion, not a change to the guard.** The guard's
condition is right; what is missing is a `dart_test.yaml` that keeps
`e2e`-tagged tests out of the default run, so that `--tags e2e` is the only way
to load them and the guard only ever fires on a run that meant to be an e2e
run. That also makes the README's claim true again rather than aspirational.
**A gate does not repair its own findings, and this one is left in place.**

### 10.5 H-2 — the self-check added to protect the instruments disabled all five of them

```
$ python3 scripts/verify_c1_row_naming.py
PREFLIGHT ABORT: the version handshake failed — /sync/pull with this script's
envelope ({... 'schema_version': 6, 'schema_major': 2}) returned 403
({'error': 'forbidden'}) instead of 200.
$ echo $?
1
```

Identical output from `verify_c2_existence_oracle.py`,
`verify_c5_denial_audit.py`, `verify_d1_per_row_oracle.py` and
`gate_c_adversarial_pass.py`. Five for five, against a healthy server that
answered `200` on `/health` and went on to pass every control below.

`gate_wire.preflight()` signs in a brand-new account and pulls a **random
project id**, then requires `200`. The designed answer to that request is `403
forbidden` — §4.13's uniform denial, which is precisely what C-2's remediation
made it and what `verify_c2` asserts three lines later. The check's own error
message tells the reader to update the parsed constants, which are correct.

The envelope was never the thing being tested here: 10.35's major check runs in
front of authorization (§9.3 De), so a stale `schema_major` is a `409` and a
`403` already proves the server understood the envelope. Accepting `403` keeps
every bit of the check's purpose. That one-line correction, with its reasoning,
is now in `scripts/gate_wire.py`, and the repaired check was itself re-verified
by forcing a stale major in-process and confirming it still aborts. **The
instruments were repaired; the finding stands as a finding**, on the §9.1.1
precedent that a gate fixes its own tools and records that it had to.

Three gates, three instrument failures, and the trend is the point. §8.2 found
a check that passed vacuously. §9.1.1 found five tools sending a stale schema
major. §9.3 found `Dc` printing HELD against a live finding because its own SQL
returned nothing. This round: a self-check written to end that pattern, added
to five tools, **never once run against a live server before being recorded as
done**. The plan entry for 10.40 states it was "wired into all five
wire-speaking scripts"; that is literally true and none of them worked.

### 10.5.1 H-6 — the restore path authenticates integrity, not origin: a forged archive is promoted over the live database and runs as superuser

> **Closed by task 10.43 (2026-08-14), custody decision first.** §4.9.2 is the
> arrangement, written before the wiring, because §4.9's own precedent is that a
> key with no custody story is worse than no key. Every archive is now signed
> with `minisign` on the machine that produced it; the verifying key is
> configured with the restore procedure and never read from beside the archive;
> and one signature binds the ciphertext, the recorded checksum and the schema
> marker, so the three files H-6's attacker authored are no longer three
> independent opinions.
>
> **The refusal that closes it is not the check, it is the rule**: an archive
> whose origin cannot be established is never promoted over an existing
> database, under any combination of flags. Unsigned archives — every one
> written before this task — still restore, into a name of their own.
>
> `scripts/verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh` was kept and extended into a
> regression test: it now runs the forgery against **both** configurations, with
> and without a verifying key set, because the second is the state every
> deployment is in on the day the fix lands. It refuses in both and the live row
> survives. **Confirmed load-bearing by a negative control** — with the origin
> gate alone neutralised and every other check left in place, the forgery
> reproduces exactly as recorded below (`forged row now live: 1`, `real row
> still live: 0`, superuser table created), which is the only way to know the
> refusal comes from the new gate and not from some unrelated check firing
> first. The drill covers it at steps 7h–7j, including an archive signed by an
> untrusted key and a genuine signature paired with substituted bytes.

**Reproduced live**, `scripts/verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh`, new this run. This
one is not a fault injected to prove an ordering; the archive in it is a
*genuine, valid* archive that the operator's own key decrypts, authored by
someone who never had that key.

§4.9 chose public-key backups so that the machine taking the backup and the
off-site destination holding it cannot read the contents, and it says plainly
that the recipient strings are not secrets: *"The **public** recipient strings
are not secret. They live in `.env` … it is fine for them to appear in
documentation, tickets, or a commit."* That decision is about **reading**.
Nothing in §4.9, `backup.sh` or `restore.sh` says anything about who may
**write** an archive the restore path will trust.

`restore.sh` gates a restore on three things, and an entity with write access
to the archive directory authors all three:

| Gate | Why it passes |
| --- | --- |
| `<archive>.sha256` (`restore.sh:100-107`) | A plain checksum file beside the archive. The attacker writes it. Absent, it is a `NOTE`, not a refusal (`:108-111`) |
| `<archive>.schema` (`:129-144`) | Cleartext marker, no cryptographic binding to the ciphertext. The attacker writes `schema_major=2` |
| `age --decrypt \| awk` (`:204-208`) | The file really *is* encrypted to the operator's public key — anyone holding the public half can do that — and the content test is two literal `pg_dump` comment lines |

The transcript, with the attacker holding **only** the public recipient:

```
  | Checksum: matches the value recorded at backup time.
  | Archive schema major: 2 (this build supports 1 through 2)
  | Verifying the archive decrypts and is a complete dump (nothing changed yet)...
  | Verified: decrypts with the mounted key, and the dump is complete.
  | Restoring into 'tritrack_restore_20260814T132427Z'...
  | Renaming the existing 'tritrack' aside to 'tritrack_replaced_...' (not dropping it)...
  | Restored into 'tritrack' — 2 tables.

  restore exit status        : 0
  forged row now live        : 1
  real row still live        : 0
  attacker's table created   : 1
```

The forged SQL is piped into `psql` as `POSTGRES_USER`, which the
`postgres:16-alpine` entrypoint creates as a **superuser** — so the content of
the archive is not merely data, it is arbitrary SQL with superuser rights
(`COPY … FROM PROGRAM` is in that set). Then it is renamed into the live
database name.

**What limits it.** 10.37's rename-aside means the real database survives as
`tritrack_replaced_<stamp>` and is recoverable, which is the difference between
this and a catastrophe; the operator has to notice. And the attacker needs write
access to the archive directory — which is precisely the party §4.9 decided to
trust: `docker-compose.yml:133-139` makes it a host bind mount described as *"the
directory you sync to encrypted-at-rest storage"*, and `restore.sh`'s own error
text invites an operator mid-incident to *"fetch another copy"*.

**Rated blocking.** It is asset 2 (integrity of the field record) plus code
execution, in the control C-4 created, reachable without any secret, and the
comments asserting otherwise are load-bearing: `restore.sh:98` says *"the
decrypt below authenticates the bytes regardless"* and `:200-202` says the
header *"proves this is a database dump at all, and not some other file that
happens to be encrypted to the same key."* Against an accident, both are true.
Against an adversary, age's AEAD proves the bytes were not altered *after*
encryption and says nothing about who encrypted them.

The shape of the fix is a signature the backup box can produce and the restore
box can verify — `age` has no signing mode, so this is `minisign`/`signify` or
an SSH-key signature over the archive plus its sidecars, with the verifying
public key living with the restore procedure rather than beside the archive. The
decision belongs with §4.9's custody arrangement, not with a patch.

### 10.5.2 H-7 — retention deletes by filename, so write access to the archive directory destroys every real backup

`backup.sh:150-155`:

```sh
# Timestamps are ISO basic UTC, so lexical order is chronological order.
ls -1 /backups/tritrack-*.age 2>/dev/null | sort -r | tail -n +$((KEEP + 1)) \
  | while read -r old; do rm -f "$old" "${old}.sha256" "${old}.schema"; done
```

The comment is true only if every matching filename was written by this script.
Retention keeps the `KEEP` lexically-highest names and deletes the rest, so an
entity with **write-only** access to the directory plants
`tritrack-29991231T235959Z.age` and 29 siblings, and **the next legitimate
backup run deletes every real archive**, its checksum and its sidecar — executed
by the backup job itself, with no key and no read access. `backup.sh:85` refuses
to overwrite an archive it would write, and places no constraint on files it did
not write.

**Rated blocking, on the same reasoning as H-6 and for the same asset**: total
loss of the backup history, by the party §4.9 trusts with ciphertext, through
the mechanism §4.9 built. It is not a denial-of-service exclusion under §5.6 —
§5.6 covers server availability, and asset 2 is the field record itself.

Fix candidates, in the order they should be considered: prune only files this
run can account for (a manifest the backup box keeps, or names matched against
the archive's own decryptable timestamp), and treat an unexpected name as a
refusal to prune rather than an instruction to delete something else.

### 10.5.3 F13 — the client's `https` requirement is now transport enforcement, not a form check

> **Closed by task 10.48 (2026-08-14), enforcement moved to the seam.**
> `validateServerUrl` was, and remains, the settings field's `validator:` — but
> it was also the *only* place a cleartext URL was ever rejected, so `setUrl`
> persisting an unvalidated value, a migration writing `baseUrl` directly, or a
> future import path all bypassed it silently, exactly as §7.6/§8.5/§9.0 named.
> `serverHttpClientProvider` — the one seam task 10.2 already made every sync,
> auth and project-link call site pass through to get a client at all — now
> calls `requireValidServerUrl(config.baseUrl!)` on the *stored* value before
> constructing anything, and throws `InvalidServerUrl` rather than silently
> handing back a client. There is no longer a second way in: `AuthClient`,
> `HttpSyncTransport` and the project-link flow all resolve their client
> through this provider, and nothing in `lib/` constructs `http.Client()`
> directly for server traffic.
>
> `requireValidServerUrl` re-runs `validateServerUrl`'s exact rule rather than
> a second copy of it, so the field and the seam cannot drift the way the field
> and "the seam" (which did not exist) had already drifted.
> `server_http_client_provider_test.dart` proves the refusal for a URL written
> straight through `setUrl`, which is precisely "any saved value... bypasses
> it" reproduced as a test, not narrated.
>
> **The ATS question is settled, not restated a fifth time.** §8.5 found that
> `pubspec.yaml` pulled plain `http` with no `NSURLSession`-backed client, so
> `NSAllowsLocalNetworking` in both platforms' `Info.plist` (task 5.1) had no
> CFNetwork traffic to apply to — a compensating control credited on paper with
> nothing underneath it. `cupertino_http` is now a dependency, and
> `createPlatformHttpClient()` routes iOS and macOS through `CupertinoClient`
> (backed by `NSURLSession`) instead of the raw `dart:io` socket the plain
> `http.Client()` opened; every other platform is unchanged. This makes ATS a
> real second enforcement point behind `requireValidServerUrl` — a cleartext
> connection to anything outside what `NSAllowsLocalNetworking` permits is now
> something the OS itself has traffic to refuse, not a policy with nothing
> wired to it.
>
> **What this does not close, and is explicitly not claimed to close:** nothing
> here has run on a physical iOS or macOS device, in a release build, against a
> real network. `flutter test` on this machine confirms `CupertinoClient`
> constructs and the app compiles against it; it cannot confirm ATS actually
> refuses a cleartext connection to a public host in the field, because the
> `flutter_tester` harness is not sandboxed the way a shipped app is and ships
> no `Info.plist` of its own. **That verification needs a device and is
> Michael's to run**, the same way §8.6 named TLS termination as needing a real
> host before the gate could credit it.

**Closed by task 10.50 (2026-08-15).** `integration_test/ats_transport_security_test.dart`
is a committed, re-runnable test — not the throwaway button the task warned
against — driven by `scripts/verify_ats_transport_security.sh`. It runs as
the real, sandboxed app bundle (via `flutter drive`, which installs and
launches the genuine `.app`/`.ipa` with its real `Info.plist`, not the
`flutter_tester` harness `flutter test` uses), and calls
`createPlatformHttpClient()` directly — the exact function
`serverHttpClientProvider` calls — never a `CupertinoClient` constructed
inline, and deliberately below task 10.48's own scheme check (which would
otherwise refuse request #2 before a packet moved and make the test pass
while proving nothing).

The three requests, all required together — #1 is what makes #2 evidence
rather than a coincidence with an unreachable host, and #3 proves
`NSAllowsLocalNetworking` still works:

| # | Request | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `https://example.com` | succeeded |
| 2 | `http://example.com` | refused — error text contains "App Transport Security policy requires the use of a secure connection", asserted exactly, not merely that something threw |
| 3 | `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` (a throwaway loopback responder, started outside the sandboxed app under test) | succeeded |

**Run for real, three times, all three requests passing every time:**

| Platform | OS | Build mode | Tool | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| macOS (desktop, this Mac) | macOS 26.6 (25G72), darwin-arm64 | Debug | `flutter test integration_test/… -d macos` (builds and launches the real `.app`) | **PASS** |
| macOS (desktop, this Mac) | macOS 26.6 (25G72), darwin-arm64 | Profile (AOT) | `flutter drive --profile` | **PASS** |
| iOS Simulator, iPhone 17 Pro | iOS 26.5 | Debug | `flutter drive` | **PASS** |
| Michael's iPhone (physical, USB) | iOS 26.5.2 (23F84) | Profile (AOT) | `flutter drive --profile` | **#1/#2 PASS, #3 not completed** — see below |

Proved the test was real, per the task's own instruction, by pointing request
#2 at `https://example.com` instead and confirming it then succeeds (the ATS
assertion fails as expected) — a test that "passes" regardless of what URL
#2 targets would be exactly the kind of decoration §4.1 warns against.

**A genuine "Release" build could not be produced, and this is recorded
rather than worked around.** `flutter drive` (the only tool that installs and
runs the actual compiled app, which `integration_test` needs for ATS to
apply at all) refuses release mode outright for every non-web target:
*"Flutter Driver (non-web) does not support running in release mode. Use
`--profile` mode for testing application performance."* This is a Flutter
toolchain constraint, not a shortcut taken here. **Profile mode is
equivalent evidence for ATS specifically, and here is why:** `macos/Runner/Info.plist`
and `ios/Runner/Info.plist` are each a single file, shared by every Xcode
build configuration (Debug/Profile/Release) — only the *entitlements* files
differ per configuration, and ATS is governed entirely by `Info.plist`'s
`NSAppTransportSecurity` dictionary, read by `NSURLSession` at the OS level.
Nothing about `kReleaseMode` vs `kProfileMode`, JIT vs AOT, or which
entitlements file was linked changes what ATS itself does. A profile build
exercises the identical plist a release build would.

**A genuine iOS Simulator *profile* run could not be produced either, for a
different, unrelated reason**, also recorded rather than worked around:
Flutter's own build step failed with *"release/profile builds are only
supported for physical devices. attempted to build for simulator"* — AOT
compilation targets physical-device architectures only. This is why the
Simulator row above is Debug: it is the only mode the Simulator supports at
all, and per the same Info.plist reasoning above, still exercises real ATS.

**The physical-device run — attempted repeatedly, and the load-bearing half
completed twice, said plainly rather than rounded up or down.** Michael
connected his iPhone (first over wireless, then USB) and the run was tried
seven times across two sessions. What actually happened:

- **Requests #1 and #2 — the entire ATS claim — passed on the physical
  device, independently, twice** (a `flutter clean` separated the two runs,
  so the second was not a cached repeat of the first). This is the strongest
  evidence in this section: not a simulator, not this Mac, the real hardware
  ATS is named for.
- **Request #3 (the local-network control) did not complete, for two
  different infrastructure reasons, neither an ATS question:**
  1. First pass: the script pointed it at `127.0.0.1`, which is correct for
     macOS/Simulator (they share this machine's network stack) but wrong for
     a physical device — a phone's own loopback is itself, not the Mac. Its
     own `NSURLErrorDomain` code `-1004` ("could not connect") reproduced
     this exactly. Fixed in `verify_ats_transport_security.sh`: it now
     detects a physical Apple device (`emulator: false` in `flutter devices
     --machine`) and targets this machine's real LAN address instead.
  2. Second pass, address fixed and confirmed correct by Michael directly
     (not inferred): the phone still could not reach it —
     `NSURLErrorDomain` code `-1009` ("appears to be offline") — with Wi-Fi
     confirmed on the same network as this Mac. Not diagnosed further within
     the session.
  3. Three further attempts (two after the address fix) stalled at Xcode's
     install/launch handshake before the test ever ran at all — "Xcode is
     taking longer than expected to start debugging the app" — a device
     deployment reliability issue, unrelated to networking or ATS, that did
     not reproduce on macOS or the Simulator.
- **Not left as a silent gap.** `verify_ats_transport_security.sh`'s LAN-address
  detection fix is committed regardless of whether request #3 itself ever
  passed on hardware — it is correct for the next attempt, on this device or
  another, and was verified to compute the right address (confirmed against
  Michael's own report of this Mac's LAN IP) even where the phone's route to
  it did not work this session.

**Why this closes F13 rather than leaving it open.** The task named the
residual risk precisely: *"if that's the only thing left unrun, say so
precisely rather than leaving F13 open."* What is left unrun is request #3 on
a physical device specifically — a check of `NSAllowsLocalNetworking`, which
exists so a LAN dev server keeps working, not a check of the refusal F13 is
about. That refusal is now proven on physical hardware, twice, independently
— not merely simulated. The remaining gap is named, not hidden, and is a
reasonable next session's five minutes, not an open security question.

**F13 is closed.** The ATS claim §10.48 substantiated is now backed by real,
passing runs across every platform the finding named — including physical
hardware for the exact request that matters — with the ATS
error text asserted exactly rather than merely "something threw," and the
one residual — request #3's local-network reachability on this specific
physical device, blocked by device-deployment flakiness this session could
not run down — is named as Michael's optional next step, not claimed as
done.

### 10.6 The adversarial pass, re-run in full — and a fifth group

`scripts/gate_c_adversarial_pass.py` now has five groups: 10.16's six named
attempts, §7.3's other held attempts, group C against the first round of
remediation, group D against the second (10.28–10.36), and **a new group E
aimed at ground no previous group covered**.

**33 controls held, 7 failed.** Everything §7.3, §8.3 and §9.3 recorded as
holding still holds, and one previously-failing check has flipped:

- **`Dg` holds.** With `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` set — E-2's own stated
  precondition — `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f
  docker-compose.e2e.yml config` renders exactly one mapping, `host_ip:
  127.0.0.1`. **G-2 is closed**, and closed the way G-2 asked: by rendering the
  merged config, not by reading the file.

The four carried failures are the four §9.3 recorded, all previously rated
non-blocking and all unchanged in substance: **`Ce2`** (a denial flood still
grows the audit store — 40 denied requests in 0.2 s added 44 rows; §4.7's
one-year retention is still implemented by nothing, confirmed again by the
absence of any sweep in `audit_log.dart` beside the tombstone service that does
have one), **`Ch`** (§7.6 F10: an unauthenticated malformed body answers `500`),
**`Dc`** (G-4, `User_Emails`), and **`Dh`** (a row pinned at `revision =
2^63-1`).

Group E's three new failures are in §10.7. Group E also confirmed, as held:
malformed and future envelopes are refused and apply nothing, and their
refusals disclose no project existence; naming the server's own tables
(`auth_audit_log`, `sync_cursors`, a SQL-injection-shaped name) in `rows`
writes nothing, forges no audit row and drops no table; and degenerate paging
values (`batch_size` 0, −1, 2⁴⁰; `cursor` −1, 2⁶³−1) never produce a `500`.

**Two of group E's checks were wrong in their first draft, in opposite
directions**, and both are recorded here because that is now the most reliable
finding this gate produces. The envelope-uniformity check compared raw response
bodies and so reported a disclosure that was nothing but the per-request
`trace_id` in a `500` body — a check that cannot tell an oracle from a trace
id. The forbidden-table check demanded a non-`200` status and so reported a
finding against a server that had in fact ignored every attempt and written
nothing. Both now compare the thing that matters (error shape with the trace id
stripped; rows actually written) and both are in the repository in their
corrected form.

### 10.7 New non-blocking findings

#### H-3 — `Tags` is a global-key existence oracle, and §9.5 says it is covered

From an ordinary session, in the caller's own project, with no relationship to
the victim or their project:

```
attacker claims a tag_id the victim's project already holds
  -> 200 {"applied":0,"outcomes":{"Tags/<id>":"lost_to_server"}}
attacker claims a fresh tag_id
  -> 200 {"applied":1,"outcomes":{"Tags/<id>":"inserted"}}
```

That is **D-1 arm (c) again**: *does this key exist anywhere on this server.*

§9.5 reasoned that of the three tables 10.35 left keyed globally, `Users` is
covered by §4.17's naming invariant and **`Tags` by 10.29's reachability
rule**, leaving `User_Emails` (G-4) as the only uncovered one. `Users` had a
probe (`Cc`) and `User_Emails` had one (`Dc`). **`Tags` had none** — the claim
that covered it was derived by reading, which is the exact provenance G-4 was
filed to complain about. This is that probe, and the claim is wrong: 10.29's
rule governs whether a caller may *reference* a tag they cannot reach, not what
the conflict resolver says when they *claim its primary key*.

Confirmed by inspection that this is disclosure only and not an integrity
problem: the victim's row is untouched (`VICTIM-TAG|150.1|1` in the database
after the attempt), the attacker's value never lands, and neither party's tag
content appears in the other's pull.

**Non-blocking for G-4's reason, which applies unchanged**: a `tag_id` is a
client-generated UUIDv4, so probing one means guessing 122 bits, and the answer
is one bit about a key nobody can predict. **What is blocking-adjacent is the
pattern.** This is the fourth instance of *fixing the instances that had
reproductions and writing the sentence as though the rule had been derived* —
C-1, C-2→D-1, D-1 arm (c)→G-4, and now G-4's own carve-out. §9.5 offered two
ways out and recommended restating §4.13's residual honestly; that restatement
would have been wrong too, because it names `Tags` as covered. The sweep over
tables nobody wrote a probe for is still the missing work, and it is now
overdue by two gates.

**The missing work was closed by task 10.45 (2026-08-14), and that is all it
closed.** `scripts/verify_h3_existence_oracle_sweep.py` is that sweep: every
table in `sync_tables.dart`, probed the same way, in one committed script rather
than one gate's worth of ad hoc reproductions. **It made the finding measurable;
it did not make the oracle go away**, and this entry read as though it had for
four months. See §4.13's citation of it for the result.

**The oracle itself is CLOSED as of 2026-09-10 — task 11.219, measured by task
11.220, and not by anything aimed at this finding.** Task 11.219 made a tag
belong to one project for a product reason: adding a collar to a project now
copies it rather than linking a shared row. The key became `(tag_id,
project_id)` — and `Tag_Versions` became `(tag_version_id, project_id)` with it
— so the attack above no longer has a target. **A stranger claiming the victim's
`tag_id` inside their own project names a different row**, which is precisely
how task 10.35 closed arm (c) on the six project-scoped tables. Re-probed live
on 2026-09-10: both tables answer `inserted` whether the id is held or free.
**Both came off the sweep's `RECORDED_FINDINGS`, so a future schema change that
un-scoped either key would now fail the run rather than print an accepted
finding.**

**Worth keeping in view: this was closed by a product decision, not by a
security one.** Nobody set out to close H-3; §11.7 had accepted it. The
schema change that closed it was chosen for how field teams share collars.
**The reverse is the thing to watch for** — a product decision that quietly
*re-opens* one of these — and the sweep, with the two tables off its accepted
list, is what would say so.

#### H-4 — a wrongly-typed envelope field is a `500`, on the check that runs in front of everything

| Envelope | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| `schema_major` absent | `400 malformed_envelope` |
| `envelope` name absent | `400 malformed_envelope` |
| `schema_major: 3` (future) | `409 schema_version_mismatch` |
| **`schema_major: "2"` (a string)** | **`500 internal_error`** |

Three malformed envelopes get the uniform `400` §4.13 requires; the right value
with the wrong JSON type gets a `500`. It is uniform across project existence
(both a real foreign project and a fabricated one answer `500`, and the bodies
differ only in the trace id), it discloses nothing, and no row lands — so it is
F10's family (§7.6) and G-5's (§9.5.1), not a new class. It is recorded because
of *where* it sits: 10.35 put the version check in front of authorization on
every sync route, which makes this the first code an authenticated caller can
reach anywhere in the protocol, and F10 is now three gates old on the same
argument.

**Closed by task 10.46 (2026-08-14), together with F10 and G-5** — same code,
same owner, same fix. `SyncEnvelope.fromJson` already rejected a string
`schema_major` correctly (`schemaMajor is! int` catches a string exactly like
it catches an absent field); the `500` never came from there. It came from
`sync_routes.dart`'s `handle()`, which read four fields *for logging only* —
`project_id`, `device_id`, `schema_major`, `schema_version` — with `as
String?`/`as int?`, a cast that tolerates `null` but throws on anything else
wrongly typed, and did so **before** `withSyncContext`'s authentication check
even ran. That is the same defect as F10 (an unauthenticated caller reaching
uncaught code before the session check) at a second, adjacent site, which is
why the entry above says "closed together": fixing the logging casts
(`_asString`/`_asInt`, returning `null` on a wrong type instead of throwing)
let the *real* validation already in `SyncEnvelope.fromJson` run and produce
the `400 malformed_envelope` it was always designed to. `schema_major: "2"`
now answers `400`, reproduced live in
`server/test/integration/sync_envelope_typing_test.dart`.

#### H-5 — a table this server does not know is dropped without a word

```
push rows: {"NotATable": [...]}  -> 200 {"applied":0,"outcomes":{}}
```

Nothing is written — that is `Ec`, which holds. But nothing is *said* either.
10.18 decided that unknown *columns* are preserved rather than discarded, on
the grounds that a newer client must not lose data to an older server; an
unknown *table* is discarded silently, and the protocol has a per-row `invalid`
outcome (`HeldRowReason.forOutcome`) that this path never produces. A push
carrying one unknown table and one good row returns `200` with an outcome for
the good row only.

**Non-blocking**, and the client is safe today for the reason 10.28 built:
rule 2 treats a row with no confirmation as refused and holds it, so nothing is
lost locally. It is the same gap as G-5 seen from the other side — the one
outcome the protocol defines and never emits — and the case that reaches it is
a newer client against an older server, which is precisely what schema-major
compatibility exists for.

**Closed by task 10.46 (2026-08-14).** `decodeRows` (`sync_protocol.dart`)
still drops an unrecognized table name silently, on purpose — that policy is
unchanged, and rightly so (§10.18's reasoning applies identically to a whole
table). What changed is that `sync_routes.dart`'s push handler now also reads
the **raw** body — before `decodeRows` filters it — and reports one
`SyncRowOutcome.invalid` per unrecognized table name, keyed `<table>/?` (the
same placeholder `sync_service.dart` already uses for a row it recognizes but
cannot key). `push rows: {"NotATable": [...]}` now answers `200
{"outcomes":{"NotATable/?":"invalid"}}` instead of an empty map, and a push
mixing one unknown table with one good row reports both. Reproduced live in
`server/test/integration/sync_envelope_typing_test.dart`.

### 10.7.1 H-8 — the weak-assertion sweep missed six, and five of them are in the gate's own instruments

Task 10.40's substantive half was a repo-wide sweep for checks that cannot
distinguish success from their own failure, and it reported **"zero new
instances found beyond the five known ones."** This gate re-ran that sweep
independently — 206 candidate sites across `lib/`, `server/lib/`, `packages/`,
`test/`, `server/test/`, `scripts/*.sh`, `scripts/*.py` and `server/backup/*.sh`
— and the claim does not hold. Each of the six below was confirmed by reading
the code, and the first by executing it:

| | Site | Why it is weak |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **W-1** | `test/e2e/e2e_coverage_guard_test.dart` | H-1 above, found independently: no `dart_test.yaml` exists, so `flutter test` runs the guard and the default suite is red. Also means **`scripts/run_offline_suite.sh` — task 10.15's headline "full Flutter suite, green, with the server stack down" — now fails** |
| **W-2** | `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py:341` | `all(v == "unauthorized" for v in vals)` is `True` when `vals` is empty, so a `200` with an empty `outcomes` map read as "every table refused the forged row" — a vacuous pass on **C-1**, the severest Gate C finding. The four `verify_*.py` instruments compare positively (`outcome_for(...) == "unauthorized"`, `set(outcomes) == {"inserted"}`) and were already immune; this one was missed. **Fixed this run**, and `Ca` still holds under the strict form |
| **W-3** | `verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py:150-152` | If the stack is not up, the live-reachability section prints `SKIP`, appends nothing to `failures`, and the script exits `0` printing *"C-3 closed … the shipped compose defaults reach this host only"* — having never checked that the LAN address does not answer, which is C-3's actual reproduction. 10.40 exempted this script from `preflight()` because it does not speak the wire; the skip-to-pass it leaves behind went unmentioned |
| **W-4** | `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py:245` | `held_check("A4 no LAN address to test from", True, "skipped")` increments the HELD tally for a control that was never exercised. Honestly labeled in its own line, indistinguishable in the total this document quotes |
| **W-5** | `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py:404-406` | `all(re.fullmatch(...) for e in events)` is `True` on an empty `auth_audit_log` — i.e. on C-5 regressing. Two failures must coincide, so it is low, but it is the named shape |
| **W-6** | `run_offline_suite.sh:12` | `docker compose down … \|\| true`, then the script asserts *"the suite is fully green with no server running"* without ever checking that nothing is listening. "Could not bring the stack down" and "the stack was never up" reach the same branch |

**One class-level observation, worth more than any single row.**
`gate_c_adversarial_pass.py:75` returns `(0, repr(e))` on a connection-level
failure, and every *negative* assertion in the file — "the secret is not in the
body", "the victim's id is not in the response", "STALE-MAJOR did not land" —
is satisfied by a server that stopped answering. `preflight()` guards the start
of a run; a mid-run crash or container restart silently converts the remainder
into HELDs. The gate's instruments need a liveness re-check at the end of a run,
not only at the beginning.

**What the sweep confirmed as genuinely fine**, because a negative result is
only useful if it is specific: all 74 Dart `catch` sites (every `catch (_)` body
is a documented policy decision or a defined fallback — `auth_routes.dart:221`'s
deliberate uniform `202`, `sync_routes.dart:252`'s catch-all so the exception
type cannot become an oracle, `postgres_database.dart:170`'s `ROLLBACK` then
`rethrow`); `audit_log.dart:212`, where a swallowed audit insert is guarded by an
`onError` that is a *required* constructor parameter, so silence is a compile
error; all 59 `skip:` sites and 36 `testDatabaseConfig == null` early returns,
each backed by a guard test that `fail()`s; `no_committed_secrets_test.dart:47-51`,
whose `expect(trackedFiles.length, greaterThan(100))` exists precisely because
"a check that scans zero files always passes"; and
`backup_restore_drill.sh:236-238, 298-299`, which insist on the *specific*
refusal string — the fix for one of the original five.

### 10.7.2 H-9 — three unproven edges left in the restore path, and a detector that blesses one of them

> **Closed by task 10.43 (2026-08-14), all four.**
>
> - **The staging drop is guarded.** One `SELECT 1 FROM pg_database` before the
>   `CREATE`, and the trap armed only *after* it — the previous order meant a
>   `CREATE` that failed on a taken name ran a trap that dropped the database it
>   had collided with. `:79-82`'s claim is now enforced rather than asserted.
> - **The trap is disarmed before the swap, not after it.** From the moment the
>   staging database holds a verified restore, every way the script can fail is
>   a way an operator needs it to still exist. `INT` and `TERM` are trapped for
>   the window *before* the swap, which is safe precisely because of the guard
>   above. Every swap-failure message now names both surviving databases.
> - **The rollback runs.** `TRITRACK_RESTORE_FAULT` is a drill-only seam that
>   can only make a rename fail, and the drill uses it for both the single
>   failure (rollback succeeds, live database comes back) and the double failure
>   (both copies survive and are named). It had never executed once.
> - **The detector is no longer only a grep.** `restore_ordering_test.dart` now
>   asserts the *guard* — collision check before `CREATE`, trap armed after it,
>   trap disarmed before the first `ALTER DATABASE` — and the old grep carries a
>   comment naming what it cannot prove and pointing at the drill step that can.
>   It also gained an `isNotEmpty` assertion, because a grep over zero matching
>   lines passes.
>
> The staging collision is forced deterministically at drill step 7m: the
> staging names for the current second and the next four are created *inside the
> same container* that then runs the restore, so the collision does not depend
> on how long `docker compose run` takes to start. The restore refuses, and all
> five planted databases are still there afterwards.

10.37's ordering is right and G-3 is closed. These are the edges around it,
found by reading the file rather than running it, and none of them is reachable
by an attacker — they are operator-luck cases:

- **The staging drop is the one drop nothing checks.** `restore.sh:162-169`
  queries `pg_database` for `$TARGET` and refuses without
  `TRITRACK_RESTORE_REPLACE`. There is no equivalent check for `$STAGING`, and
  the EXIT trap armed at `:233` runs `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS "$STAGING"` with
  output suppressed — a database this run did not necessarily create. Reaching
  it needs a name collision to the second (two concurrent restores of the same
  target, or a clock stepped back over a surviving leftover), so it is not
  likely; but `:79-82` *asserts* that the script only ever creates "something
  new under a name nobody is using", and one `SELECT 1 FROM pg_database` before
  the drop would make that true. **Provably safe from the `_replaced_` copy**:
  `"_restore_"` and `"_replaced_"` cannot collide for any target name.
- **The worst-case swap failure discards the verified restore, silently.** The
  trap stays armed across the swap. If the rename-aside succeeds, the promote
  fails, and the rollback also fails, `fail` prints the correct manual
  instructions naming `$DISPLACED` — and then the trap drops `$STAGING`, the
  fully verified restored copy, without mentioning it. Ctrl-C inside the swap
  window does the same; only `EXIT` is trapped, not `INT`/`TERM`.
- **The rollback has never run.** The drill's four destructive cases cover
  checksum mismatch, truncation, wrong key and success. Nothing forces a rename
  to fail, so `:276-283` — the code that protects against the bullet above — is
  untested.
- **And the detector for this file is a text grep.**
  `test/security/restore_ordering_test.dart:80-95` asserts that every
  non-comment line containing the literal `DROP DATABASE` also mentions
  `$STAGING`. A drop assembled in a variable passes it, and the unguarded
  staging drop *satisfies* it — so the test currently certifies the one drop
  worth questioning.

### 10.7.3 The compose merge sweep 10.38 asked for, completed

10.38's widened criterion was to check every compose key that merges rather
than replaces. Done, by rendering rather than reading. **`ports: !override` is
real** — with and without `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0`, the merged config
carries exactly one mapping, `host_ip: 127.0.0.1`, and the stack starts cleanly
and answers on loopback while the LAN address does not (verified live on a
throwaway project name). Two latent instances of the same class, both harmless
today and both one commit from mattering:

- **`docker-compose.e2e.yml:47-48` `volumes:` merges.** Harmless only because
  the base `server` service has no `volumes:`. The base file already declares
  `TRITRACK_TLS_CERT_PATH` / `TRITRACK_TLS_KEY_PATH` (`docker-compose.yml:79-80`)
  with no mount behind them; the moment §4.1's certificate mount is added to the
  base service, this override inherits it rather than replacing it — G-2's exact
  class.
- **`docker-compose.server-test.yml:17-18` `ports:` has no `!override`.**
  Harmless only because the base `postgres` has no `ports:`. That file's comment
  reads as a replacement guarantee and is a concatenation.
- **Cleared:** `environment:` (map merge is key-wise, override wins, no
  shadowing), `profiles:` on the backup service (render-verified intact, so
  neither override un-gates the `/identity/key.txt` mount), `healthcheck.test`,
  long-form `depends_on`, and every other sequence/map key — `command`,
  `entrypoint`, `cap_add`, `env_file`, `expose`, `labels`, `networks`,
  `security_opt` — which appear in no compose file in this repository. There are
  three compose files, no `docker-compose.override.yml`, and no `COMPOSE_FILE`
  usage in `scripts/`.
- **One real residual:** `!override` needs Compose ≥ 2.24, and nothing in the
  repository records a minimum version. `README.md:216-217` says to verify with
  `docker compose version` and states no floor. The gate's own check is
  defended against this (`Dg` asserts `published != []`, so an older Compose
  erroring on the tag fails rather than passing on empty output); an operator's
  run is not.
- **And `docker-compose.e2e.yml:41-44`'s new comment is already stale**: it says
  the tag "was verified once during the Gate C re-run, then reverted before the
  gate ran again", while the tag is present two lines below it. That sentence
  described 10.25's second run and reads, in the file as it now stands, as
  though the fix is absent.

**Closed by task 10.47 (2026-08-14).** Both latent instances now carry
`!override`, verified by re-rendering the merged config — with and without
`SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` for the e2e file, and with the base
`docker-compose.yml` layered under `docker-compose.server-test.yml` — rather
than by reading the files, on the same reasoning this section's own opening
line states and G-2 was twice missed by. Neither render changed: one
mapping/mount survives in each case, exactly as before, because there is
still nothing on the base side to concatenate with — the tag is there for the
day there is. The stale comment is corrected to describe what the file does
now rather than narrate 10.25's specific run. `README.md`'s prerequisites now
state the ≥ 2.24 floor `!override` requires, with the reasoning: an older
Compose fails to *parse* these files rather than silently merging them
wrong, which is the safe direction, but only for a reader who knows to expect
the parse failure rather than assume a broken install.

`verify_c5_denial_audit.py` and `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py` now default
`COMPOSE` to `-p tritrack-gate` — naming, in code, the project name §9.1's
discipline previously only existed as an instruction a gate operator had to
remember to type. `scripts/gate_smoke_test.sh` needed the matching change
(its own stack now also comes up under `-p tritrack-gate`): it invokes both
scripts without setting `COMPOSE` itself, so it and they have to agree on the
same default, and before this task they only did by coincidence — both
happened to default to no `-p` at all, which is exactly the ambiguity being
closed. Re-run live end to end via `gate_smoke_test.sh`: every instrument
reached the right container under the new name; `gate_c_adversarial_pass`
still reports 36 held / 4 failed, and all four are the same pre-existing,
already-recorded, non-blocking findings this document names elsewhere
(`Ce2`/D-2 §10.8, `Dc`/G-4 §9.5, `Eb`/H-3 §10.7, `Dh` §10.6) — not a new
failure and not a connection error, which is what would have appeared if the
project-name change had reached the wrong (or no) stack.

### 10.9 On the process, again

Three re-runs, and the failure has migrated each time. §8: repairing a control
changes the attack surface. §9: the record gets ahead of the code. §10: **the
fix was never run in the configuration it ships in.**

H-1 and H-2 are the same mistake in two different tasks on the same day. 10.39
verified its guard with `--tags e2e` and never ran plain `flutter test`. 10.40
wired a self-check into five instruments and never ran one of them against a
live server. Both tasks recorded accurate, specific completion notes — 10.39's
even says "a configured run against a live server was not re-verified here (no
server was brought up in this session)", which is exactly the gap, written
down, and passed over. **A remediation that changes a signal must be executed
in every configuration that reads that signal**, and for this repository that
means at minimum: the default suite, the tagged suite, and against a live
stack.

The older lessons held again. Group E existed only because 10.37–10.40
happened, and it is where H-3, H-4 and H-5 came from — *re-attack the fix*
paying out for the third consecutive gate. And two of group E's own checks were
wrong before they were right, caught by reading the detail lines rather than
the verdicts, which is now four gates in a row that this habit has caught
something.

And one correction to the shape of the last two gate summaries, which both
said in effect *nothing found here is an exposure, the rest is process*. That
was true of §8 and §9. It is not true of this one. **H-6 is a real attack with a
live reproduction**: forge a file, and an operator's own documented recovery
procedure installs it as the field record and runs it as superuser. It was
missed by three consecutive gates for a reason worth naming — every previous
round attacked the HTTP API, because that is where the previous round's findings
were, and a gate that re-runs the last gate's ground plus the last gate's
remediation will keep finding things in the same two places. The backup path had
been touched by three tasks and adversarially probed by none.

So, plainly: the sync surface is in good shape and has now held three
adversarial passes, twice against builds with the fix reverted. The severest
findings *on that surface* are one-bit oracles on 122-bit client-generated
UUIDs. What is keeping the gate closed is a different list: **two findings in
the backup path, two broken signals, and three carried items nobody has
acted on in seven days** — F13, the reverse proxy, and the NAU review, none of
which any adversarial pass can close.

### 11.0 Gate result: **FAILED. The server still does not listen beyond localhost.**

**All ten scheduled remediations landed and nine of them hold.** H-1 is closed —

guarantee §10.4 recorded as broken. H-2 is closed — all seven instruments ran
against a live server and reported real results, the first gate in four where
the tools worked on the first attempt. H-4, H-5, G-1, G-2 and G-3 hold under
re-attack. F13 is closed at the seam and ATS was proven on physical hardware.
The reverse proxy §4.1 has asked for at three consecutive gates now exists,
and `verify_tls_termination.sh` passes **7 checks** with `server: ports=None`
in the rendered config — verified independently by re-rendering the merged
compose, not by trusting the drill.

The gate fails on three items. **Two are new and both were found by attacking
ground the previous four rounds never touched: the deployment topology itself,
and the retention half of the backup path.** The third is the NAU review, now
carried and unactioned at four consecutive gates.

| # | Blocking item | New? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **I-1** | **§4.4's per-source rate limit is a single global bucket, and every audit row records one constant address.** Reproduced live in **both** the shipped `docker compose` and the mandated TLS/Caddy production deployment: **10 unauthenticated requests deny magic-link sign-in to every user of the deployment**, and all 12 events recorded `source_address` = the proxy's container IP. C-5's forensic content is void in the same stroke. §11.3 | new |
| **I-2** | **H-7 is not closed — retention verifies bytes, not names.** Reproduced live on the current build with the remediation fully configured: 30 copies of **one genuine `(archive, .minisig)` pair** renamed to 2999 all verify as authentic, retention does not refuse, and the next legitimate backup run **deletes the entire genuine history**. The survivors are valid, signed and restorable, so a later restore silently rolls the database back to a stale snapshot. §11.4 | new |
| **NAU** | **The institutional review still has not happened.** `NAU_infosec_review_request.md` has been revised twice and sent zero times. Recipient still blank. This is the one item on this gate no amount of engineering closes. | carried ×4 |

**The result worth carrying forward.** Every previous round of this gate
attacked *the server*. This round attacked **the configuration the server is
deployed in**, and both new findings live there. I-1 is not a bug in
`rate_limiter.dart` — that code is correct, well-reasoned, and its own doc
comment at `request_identity.dart:33-37` predicts this exact failure. I-2 is
not a bug in `minisign` — the signature verifies precisely what it claims to.
Both are properties of the *seam* between a correct control and the topology it
runs in, and a seam is nobody's file. The recurring lesson has been "the fix
was never run in the configuration it ships in" (§10). This round sharpens it:
**the control was never run in the configuration it ships in, and the
configuration changed underneath it without the control being re-measured.**

**Part two, and it is the reason I-1 survived four gates.** The gate's own
stack is brought up with `docker-compose.e2e.yml`, which sets
`TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED=1`. **No adversarial pass has ever
observed the per-source limiter doing anything**, because it has never been
switched on in a stack the gate attacked. The one control that claims to cover
it — `Cf` — is a negative `grep` over `docker compose config` **stdout whose
return code is never checked** (§11.5), so it reports HELD when the command
fails outright. A control measured only by a text search against a stack where
it is disabled is not a measured control.

`docker-compose.tls.yml`'s `ports: !override []` was verified by rendering the

### 11.3 I-1 — the per-source rate limit is a global bucket, live in both deployments

§4.4 states the requirement plainly: *"Both keyings are required, not
alternatives. Per-email alone lets one attacker bomb a thousand different
colleagues. Per-source alone lets a botnet bomb one colleague."* The per-source
key is `peerAddressOf(request)`, which reads the real TCP peer and deliberately
never reads `X-Forwarded-For` (`request_identity.dart:26-31`) — correct, and
correct for the right reason.

**In the shipped `docker compose`** (base file, no overrides, limiter enabled):

```
attacker-1 … attacker-10  -> 202     (10 distinct emails, unauthenticated)
attacker-11, attacker-12  -> 429
innocent-biologist@nau.edu -> 429     {"error":"rate_limited"}
source_address recorded for all 13:  172.19.0.1
```

**Behind Caddy, in the deployment §4.1 mandates** (`docker-compose.tls.yml`,
`TRITRACK_ENV=production`, real TLS):

```
a1 … a10 -> 202 ; a11 -> 429 ; innocent@nau.edu -> 429
source_address recorded for all 12:  172.20.0.4   (the proxy's container)
```

Ten unauthenticated HTTP requests deny magic-link sign-in to **every user of
the deployment** for 15 minutes, and 60 sustain it for an hour. The per-source
rule written to stop a botnet bombing one colleague instead hands one attacker
a lever on everybody. And because the recorded address is a constant, the
`authorization_denied` and `link_requested` rows C-5 exists to produce cannot
say who did it — 158 events in the gate database, one distinct
`source_address` between them.

**This was predicted, filed, and then overtaken.** The 2026-08-07 Discovered
Scope entry from task 10.14 says whoever puts a proxy in front "must either
refuse `/diagnostics/*` at the proxy and accept the rate-limit merge, or
introduce a trusted-proxy header with all the care that needs." Task 10.49
shipped the proxy and did neither, and recorded no acceptance. The filing was
correct; nothing connected it to the task that made it real.

Two things it is **not**. It is not a `X-Forwarded-For` spoofing hole — the
server's refusal to read that header is right and must stay. And the
diagnostics console's loopback gate **fails closed** here, better than the
2026-08-07 prediction: Caddy reaches the origin from a bridge address, not
`127.0.0.1`, so `diagnostics_routes.dart:74` still refuses. Verified, not
assumed.

### 11.4 I-2 — retention authenticates bytes, and the attack is on names

10.44 replaced H-7's lexical prune with a signature predicate, and the
predicate is real: `backup.sh:250-263` refuses to prune anything unless
**every** `tritrack-*.age` in the directory carries a `.minisig` that verifies.
The lexical `sort -r | tail` survives only in the branch where all files have
just verified. That is a sound structure, and finding I-2 is not that the
structure is wrong.

**A minisign signature covers bytes. Filenames are not bytes.** Copy one
genuine archive and its signature to any other name and the copy verifies
perfectly. Live, on the current build, keys configured:

```
1. genuine backup            -> tritrack-20260815T174540Z.age (+ .minisig)
2. attacker copies that ONE pair to 30 names dated 2999
   /backups now holds 31 archives — all 31 verify
3. next legitimate backup run:
     Retention: removing /backups/tritrack-20260815T174543Z.age
     Retention: removing /backups/tritrack-20260815T174540Z.age
4. real archives left:     0
   planted archives left: 30
```

No `RETENTION REFUSED`. The entire genuine history is gone, deleted by the
backup job itself, and what remains is thirty copies of one stale snapshot that
pass every check `restore.sh` applies — so the next restore succeeds and
silently returns the database to an old state. Availability and integrity
against asset 2, with no alarm at any point.

The attacker needs write access to the archive directory **and one genuine
`(archive, .minisig)` pair**. That is a narrowing of H-7's original write-only
attacker, and it is not much of one: it is an exact description of the off-site
copy destination, the party §4.9 deliberately chose to trust with ciphertext
on the grounds that it cannot read it. It cannot. It can still destroy the
history.

**The fix is already latent in the data.** `backup.sh:197` writes
`archive=<basename>` into the signed trusted comment, and retention never reads
it back — the binding it needs was authored and then not consulted. Verify the
signature *and* require the signed comment's `archive=` to equal the actual
basename, and a renamed copy stops verifying.

`backup_restore_drill.sh` plants only an **unsigned** file, so this variant has
never been exercised.

### 11.5 The gate's own instruments, again — four vacuous-pass paths

§10.7.1 found six weak assertions, five of them in the gate's own tools. An
independent sweep this round found four more, and **I confirmed each by
demonstration rather than by reading**:

- **`verify_tls_termination.sh:157` cannot distinguish what it measures.** Its
  "the origin is not directly reachable" check probes a hardcoded
  `http://localhost:8080` while the script `source`s `.env` under `set -a`,
  where `SERVER_PORT` lives. **False alarm, observed live:** the first run this
  gate made reported `FAIL … ports: !override [] did not take effect` when the
  override was working perfectly and an unrelated stack held 8080. **False
  clear:** with `SERVER_PORT=8081` the check probes an empty port and passes
  while the origin is published. It also probes `http://` against a listener
  that only speaks TLS, so it fails for the wrong reason either way.
- **`verify_tls_termination.sh:150` cannot fail.** `curl --cacert /dev/null`
  against a host with nothing listening exits 7, and against an unresolvable
  name exits 6; the check treats any non-zero exit as "correctly refused."
  Demonstrated against port 9443 and `no-such-host.invalid`. It proves nothing
  about chain verification, which is the one thing it was added to prove.
- **`gate_c_adversarial_pass.py:473-476` (`Cf`) reports HELD when compose
  fails.** The `subprocess.run` return code is never checked and the assertion
  is a negative substring test over stdout. Demonstrated: pointing it at a
  non-existent compose file gives `returncode=1`, empty stdout, and
  `Cf -> HELD`.
- **`verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh` never writes a `.minisig`.** Both of its
  arms — "with a verifying key configured" and "without" — therefore fall out
  of `restore.sh:153` with `SIGNED=0` and die at the identical unsigned-archive
  refusal. `minisign -V` is never reached in either. H-6's refusal is real (the
  script passes, and it passes for a correct reason), but the *two
  configurations* it claims to cover exercise one branch twice, and the
  present-but-invalid-signature branch — the fatal, non-overridable one that is
  the heart of 10.43 — is exercised by no instrument at all.

Also: `verify_h3_existence_oracle_sweep.py` is run by **nothing**. It is absent
from `gate_smoke_test.sh`'s instrument list and from its `WIRE_INSTRUMENTS`
self-test, though both landed in the same commit (`5edfafc`) — so 10.42's claim
that "the tools work is now a command, not a belief" excludes the newest tool.

### 11.7 The `User_Emails` / `Tags` accept-or-scope decision, settled

> **Update 2026-09-10 — half of this decision has been overtaken by events, and
> the half that remains is unchanged.** Task 11.219 made tags project-scoped and
> gave `Tags` and `Tag_Versions` a `project_id` in their primary keys; task
> 11.220 measured the oracle gone on both. **So the `Tags` half was closed by
> the structural fix this section calls "unavailable" below** — not because that
> paragraph was wrong about the reachability model of the day, but because
> copy-on-add replaced that model. **`User_Emails` is what is left**, and every
> word of the reasoning below still applies to it. **This is one table now, not
> three.**

Task 10.45 recorded these and deliberately left the decision to Opus. **Decision:
accept both, and amend §4.13 to say what it actually guarantees.**

The reasoning: both keys are random client-generated UUIDs
(`sync_tables.dart:103,120` — `user_email_id`, `tag_id`), not emails and not
anything a person types. The oracle answers "does this 122-bit value exist
here", which is not enumerable; to use it an attacker must already hold the
UUID, which means they already had access to the row or an artifact derived
from it. The marginal disclosure over what such a party already knows is *"it is
still present on this server."* The structural fix — 10.35's project-scoped
keys — is **unavailable** here and `sync_tables.dart:78-80` says why: these
three tables have no project column and cannot get one without breaking the
reachability model that pull's read filter is built on. Closing this is a
redesign of the identity tables, not a patch.

What must change is the **rule**, not the code. §4.13 as written ("no response
distinguishes existence from absence") is wider than this design can deliver,
and it has now been "corrected" three times while the build kept violating it in
the same three places. A rule that gets restated after every gate is a rule
that was never scoped. §4.13 should carry the exception explicitly: globally-keyed
identity tables, random-UUID keys, confirmation-only, not enumerable — and the
residual named in the NAU letter's accepted-risk list.

### 11.8 New non-blocking findings

- **I-3 — a latent identity-forgery path that Phase 11 will arm.** The server
  never compares a pushed `Users.email` to the authenticated account's address;
  `RowValidator` requires only that it be non-empty. **Live: an attacker's push
  claiming another user's email returned `200 'updated'`.** The client merger's
  tier-1 dedup then treats a matching current email as proof of identity —
  `project_merger.dart:184-190`, *"tier 1 always wins outright"* — and
  `_applyUserRemap` rewrites `user_id`, `owner_user_id` and `last_modified_by`
  on **every row of the page**. The harm is C-1's exactly (an attacker's
  observations attributed to a colleague), reached through the email column
  instead of the id column. **It is not reachable today**, and I confirmed why:
  cross-user project membership does not exist in Phase 10, so the attacker's
  `Users` row is never delivered to the victim — a self-granted membership is
  still refused (`B2`, held). **Phase 11's stated purpose is to open exactly
  that door.** Fix it server-side before then, cheaply: refuse a `Users.email`
  that does not match the authenticated account, or that another `user_id`
  already holds.

  > **Closed by task 10.55 (2026-08-15), on both sides of the wire.** The
  > server-side rule is §4.18, stated over `SyncTable.emailColumns` rather than
  > at the two call sites, with exactly one permitting branch: the address must
  > be the one `auth_accounts` holds for that `user_id`. The suggested "or that
  > another `user_id` already holds" was deliberately **not** written as a
  > second clause — it would have made the outcome map answer "is this address
  > registered here?", which is D-1's shape on a new column, and the single
  > branch above refuses that case anyway.
  >
  > **The client assumption was the other half, and it is not left standing.**
  > A server check is not an answer to "the merger believes an email"; it only
  > answers "our server won't hand it one". `ProjectMerger.merge` now takes an
  > `IdentityTrust`, and `SyncEngine` passes `serverAssignsIdentity` for every
  > pulled page: **no tier of the email dedup runs on server-delivered rows.**
  > It buys nothing there — §10.6's `ServerIdentityAdopter` already makes the
  > server authoritative for the `user_id` behind an address, behind proof of
  > mailbox control — while leaving a whole-page id rewrite keyed on an
  > unauthenticated string. The file-import path is untouched, where the rule
  > is load-bearing and where nobody assigned the ids.
  >
  > **`User_Emails` came with it.** Tier 2b matches an incoming user's *claimed*
  > prior address against a local user's current one — the same remap, the same
  > harm — and a prior address is unverifiable by construction here. So it falls
  > under the same rule, which in practice ends its replication; the boundary is
  > the address, not the table (a row naming your own current authenticated
  > address still lands, and asserts nothing new). `RowAuthorizer._mayReplicate`
  > already refused this table for *other* people and had no answer for the
  > caller's own row.
  >
  > **Proven, not just written.** `scripts/verify_i4_email_forgery.py` was run
  > against a build with `_authorizeEmailClaim` removed and failed five checks,
  > reproducing I-4 verbatim — including the registration oracle, which showed
  > up in that run as `'updated'` for a registered address against
  > `'lost_to_server'` for one nobody holds. Restored, it passes. Four existing
  > instruments had to be corrected in the same pass: `verify_c1_row_naming`,
  > `verify_c2_existence_oracle`, `verify_d1_per_row_oracle`,
  > `verify_c5_denial_audit`, `verify_h3_existence_oracle_sweep` and
  > `gate_c_adversarial_pass` all built their fixture `Users` rows with an
  > invented address, so all six aborted on a `403` the moment the rule landed
  > — loudly, which is what they are for. `Dc` (G-4) and the sweep's
  > `User_Emails` arm needed more than a fixture edit: with an invented address
  > both probes are refused for the *address*, so the key equivalence would have
  > held for a reason it was not written for. Both now push the pusher's own
  > authenticated address, and both still report G-4 as the recorded finding it

  > same four failures (`Ce2`, `Dc`, `Dh`, `Eb`).
- **I-4 — an oversized `device_id` answers `500`.** A 2 MB `device_id` on
  `/sync/push` returns `internal_error` rather than a typed refusal. Nothing

  > **Closed by task 10.56 (2026-08-15), swept rather than patched.**

  (`:35`). The gate criterion is "the whole history, not just the working tree",
  and the gate does that scan by hand each round — clean again, 107 commits —

  > **Closed by task 10.58 (2026-08-15).** `no_committed_secrets_test.dart`
  > now runs its same detectors (the PEM check, the age-key pattern, the

  > any ref (`git rev-list --objects --all` + a single batched

### 11.9 The 10.19 cloud-backup default, re-verdicted

Confirmed again that the decision was explicit (§4.15) rather than defaulted
into, and confirmed again in code: `cloud_backup_settings_provider.dart` (deleted with the cloud backup, `3a9a2c8`)
sets `enabled = true`, and `backup_archive.dart:41` writes a plain
`ZipEncoder()` archive with no encryption. So the client ships an **unencrypted
copy of asset 1 egressing to consumer cloud storage, on by default**.

The verdict that matters is not "was it decided" but "does the reason still
hold". §4.15's justification was a single-user trust boundary, and §7.5 already
recorded that 10.9's publish/join falsified it. **Four gates later nothing has
revisited it.** This is now the largest accepted risk in the product that is not
tracked as an open finding, and it is accepted on a rationale the record itself
marks as false. It belongs in front of NAU as a question, not in the model as a
settled decision.

> **Re-decided by task 10.60 (2026-08-15) — §4.15.1.** The three questions are
> now answered explicitly: default **stays on** (§7.5 falsified an argument
> about whose confidentiality is at stake, not asset 2's exposure, and
> off-by-default would not have removed the harm anyway — a user who links a
> folder still exports colleagues' details); the payload **stays an unencrypted
> zip**, but under an acceptance that is time-bounded and whose blocker is
> named — client key custody that survives total device loss, required before
> the beta field season; and the **disclosure copy is rewritten** to state that
> the file carries other people's names and prior email addresses, and that
> those colleagues are neither asked nor able to remove it. §11.9's "accepted
> on a rationale the record itself marks as false" no longer holds; the
> unencrypted payload is accepted on a stated, different, and falsifiable
> ground. The question stays in the NAU letter with §4.15.1 attached as the
> answer rather than as an open item.
>
> §4.15.1 also corrects this section's dating: the trust-boundary widening is
> **Phase 6 share import's, not 10.9's** (`project_merger.dart:226`, `:216`),
> so it is live in the app as shipped rather than pending on the server.

### 11.10 Residual risk, in plain language

*This supersedes §7.7, which was written before four rounds of findings.*

**What this system protects.** Precise, timestamped locations of individual
radio-collared animals, some of them protected or trafficked species; the names
and email addresses of the researchers who recorded them; and the scientific
record of who observed what, which has to be trustworthy to be worth anything.

**What is genuinely solid.** The network-facing sync API has now held five
adversarial passes, twice against builds with a fix deliberately reverted to
prove the test could still see it. Authentication has no passwords to steal:
links are single-use, 15-minute, 256-bit, stored hashed, and revocation takes
effect on the next request rather than the next hour. A user cannot read, write,
or name a row outside a project they belong to — the class of finding that
opened this gate (C-1) has been re-attacked at four consecutive gates and refuses
every time. Errors disclose nothing; a wrong guess and a real record are
answered identically. The server has never listened beyond localhost, and the
default configuration still serves only the machine it runs on.

**What is not solid, honestly.** Three things.

*Anyone can switch off sign-in for everybody, with ten requests and no account.*
The limit meant to stop that is counted per source address, and in every way
this system is actually deployed every request arrives wearing the same address.
Nothing is disclosed and nothing is destroyed — but the team cannot log in, and
the log cannot say who did it.

*Whoever holds the off-site backups can destroy the backup history.* Not read
them — the encryption holds, and that was checked again. But the copies are
verified as genuine by a signature over their contents, and a signature does not
care what a file is called. Thirty renamed copies of one real backup are thirty
real backups as far as the system can tell, and the next backup run deletes
everything older to make room. The database itself is untouched; the ability to
go back in time is not.

*An unencrypted copy of the field data is uploaded to consumer cloud storage by
default,* on a justification the record already notes is no longer true now that
projects can be shared between people.

**What is deliberately out of scope**, unchanged and stated so it is not
mistaken for an oversight: a departing colleague's existing local copy of data
they legitimately had; the phone's local database, which relies on device disk
encryption rather than its own; and confirming, if you already hold a
random 122-bit identifier, that it still exists on the server.

**The judgement.** Nothing here is a reason to think the data has leaked, and
nothing found in four rounds has been a network exposure. Two of the three open
problems are about *availability and recoverability* rather than confidentiality
— someone stopping the team working, or destroying the ability to restore —
and one is a default that sends data somewhere it was never re-justified.
I would not put this on the internet this week. I would fix the two, re-decide
the third, and get an outside opinion, which is the last item below and the one
that has not moved.

### 11.11 The NAU review — the item four gates have not closed

**Not done, and not doable from here.** The residual-risk summary §11.10 asks
for is written, current, and plain-language. The cover note is revised. What
remains is a human sending an email to an institution, and that is a real-world,
outward-facing act that belongs to Michael rather than to this session — no
mail channel is authorized here, and sending correspondence to NAU on his
behalf is not something to do unilaterally.

Recorded plainly so it is not quietly re-deferred a fifth time: this is now the
**longest-standing blocking item on the project**, it has been rated blocking at
four consecutive gates, it is the only one no amount of engineering will close,
and it is perhaps twenty minutes of work — find the address, attach §11.10, send
`NAU_infosec_review_request.md`. The letter itself has been revised twice by
gates that could not send it. **The gate cannot pass until it is sent and
answered.**

### 11.12 Task 10.54 — I-3 closed, the instruments repaired, and the class swept

**I-3 itself.** `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py`'s `Cf` never checked the
`docker compose config` subprocess's return code, so it reported `HELD`
against a non-existent compose file (`returncode=1`, empty stdout, substring
absent). Fixed to check the return code and to parse the resolved
`--format json` environment for the actual key, rather than grep the whole
text blob. Re-run live: `Cf` still `HELD` against the real compose file.

`Cf`'s own job stays a **static** check — does the artifact a real deployment
resolves carry the escape hatch — deliberately, not a live-behavior check: this
script attacks the already-running e2e stack, which sets
`TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED=1` *on purpose* (task 10.26), so it
cannot cheaply prove the limiter's live behavior without bringing up a second
stack mid-run. That proof already exists and is the right shape for it:
`scripts/verify_i1_source_identity.sh` (task 10.52) attacks
`docker-compose.tls.yml`, where the limiter is ON, with a negative control.
`gate_smoke_test.sh` runs both in the same pass, so the artifact and the
enforced behavior are each proven by the instrument suited to it.

**§11.5's instrument defects, fixed:**

- `verify_tls_termination.sh`'s "no trust anchor" check used `--cacert
  /dev/null` and treated any non-zero curl exit as "correctly refused" —
  demonstrated unable to fail (exit 6 against an unresolvable host, exit 7
  against a closed port, neither about chain verification). Fixed to use a
  genuine, unrelated throwaway CA certificate and assert curl's specific
  exit 60 (certificate verification failed). Re-running the *original* fix
  live surfaced a second, platform-specific defect the plan text didn't
  anticipate: `--cacert /dev/null` makes some curl/TLS-backend combinations
  fail to load the CA file at all (exit 77, on this host's LibreSSL-backed
  curl) before any handshake is attempted — also not chain verification. The
  unrelated-certificate approach is what makes exit 60 portable.
- The same script's "origin not directly reachable" check probed a hardcoded
  `http://localhost:8080`, wrong when `.env` sets a different `SERVER_PORT`
  and, even at the right port, satisfiable by any unrelated stack holding
  that host port — a false alarm §11.5 observed live. Fixed to ask Docker
  directly whether *this project's own* `server` service publishes anything
  (`docker compose port server 8080`) rather than probe the host over HTTP.
  Docker Compose v5.3.1 answers a genuinely unpublished port with exit 0 and
  the literal string `invalid IP:0`, not emptiness or a non-zero exit — both
  are now checked for.
- `verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh` planted only an **unsigned** archive in both
  its arms, so both fell out of `restore.sh` at the identical no-signature
  refusal and `minisign -V` was never called. Added a third arm: the attacker
  generates their *own* minisign key pair (free, unlike the operator's
  signing key) and signs their forgery with it. Restored against the real
  operator's `TRITRACK_BACKUP_VERIFY_KEY`, this reaches `minisign -V` for
  real and must fail it — refused unconditionally, with no override, unlike
  the no-signature case. Re-run live: 7 checks, passes, and the new arm's
  refusal message is confirmed to name the actual reason (`does NOT verify
  against any key`), not a coincidental one.
- `verify_h3_existence_oracle_sweep.py` was absent from `gate_smoke_test.sh`'s
  instrument list and its `WIRE_INSTRUMENTS` self-test, though it landed in
  the same commit (`5edfafc`) as the other four wire-speaking probes — task
  10.42's "the tools work is now a command, not a belief" excluded the
  newest tool. Wired into both. Re-run live as part of the full smoke test:
  `PASS`.

**The disabled-control sweep**, asked for either way. Every setting found
that weakens or disables a control, and whether an instrument exercises the
control in the configuration it actually ships in:

| Setting | Where | Shipped enabled/on? | Exercised in its shipped (control-ON) form? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED=1` | `docker-compose.e2e.yml` only | No — absent from the base compose | **Yes.** `verify_i1_source_identity.sh` (10.52) attacks the limiter live, enabled, behind the mandated proxy, with a negative control. `Cf` (this task) confirms the shipped artifact doesn't carry the flag |
| `TRITRACK_BACKUP_VERIFY_KEY` unset (retention's key) | `.env` default, everywhere | N/A — retention silently prunes nothing without it (fail-safe) | **Closed by task 10.59 (2026-08-16), finding I-10 in this section's own numbering.** `backup_restore_drill.sh` step 8b now runs a backup in exactly this shipped configuration and confirms it succeeds, prunes nothing, and the NOTE says so recurs on every run — the gap this row named, not fixed here at the time, is fixed there |
| `TRITRACK_ALLOW_CLEARTEXT_LAN=1` | `docker-compose.yml`, the **base** file, hardcoded | Yes — this is the shipped default (§4.1's deliberate C-3 exemption) | Partially. `verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py` proves both halves (public-address refusal live; the resolved compose stays loopback-only) — **but it is not wired into `gate_smoke_test.sh` or any other automated run**, so C-3 stays proven only when someone runs it by hand. Logged as Discovered Scope below, not fixed here: wiring it in means giving it its own compose lifecycle inside the smoke test, the way `verify_i1_source_identity.sh` and `verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh` already do, which is scope beyond this task's named list |

Verdict: not applicable |
