## 12. Verdicts — Security Gate C, fifth re-run (task 10.25, 2026-08-15)

### 12.0 Gate result: **FAILED. The server still does not listen beyond localhost.**

**All nine scheduled remediations landed and every one of them holds where it
was aimed.** I-2 is genuinely closed — a renamed copy of a genuine signed pair
now draws a loud `RETENTION REFUSED` and no genuine archive is pruned, proven
by the drill's new step 10c rather than by reading `backup.sh`. I-4, I-5, I-6,
I-7, I-8, I-9, I-10 and I-11 hold. C-1…C-5 and D-1 refuse again. All four
suites are green in one pass — **792 client / 420 server / 32 e2e / offline** —
and **all ten instruments ran against a live server**, the second consecutive
gate where the tools worked on the first attempt.

**And one thing this gate proved that no previous gate had.** §11.6's standing
note that a different proxy "that forwards a caller's own header unchanged is a
proxy that lets the caller pick their own rate-limit bucket" was never measured
against the proxy this repository actually ships. It is measured now: a forged
`X-Forwarded-For` sent through the shipped Caddy — five variants, including one
naming the proxy itself and one naming `127.0.0.1` — reached the origin as
**nothing at all**. Every audit row named the real client; a flood exhausted
the bucket and rotating forged addresses did not lift the `429`. 10.52's one
load-bearing assumption about a component this repo does not author is true
(§12.3).

The gate fails on three items. **Two are new, and they are the same failure
twice: a fix that was correct for the configuration it was written against, in
a project that ships two configurations.**

| # | Blocking item | New? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **J-1** | **A pasted `TT1:` share payload silently overwrites an observation the device already holds** — moves its coordinates, reassigns authorship, forges `last_modified_by`, and **NULLs the nine fields that make the bearing reconstructible**. Reproduced end to end. No server involved; reachable in the app **as shipped**; the UI reports it as *"You already had this observation — updated it to the newer version."* This is silent loss of irreplaceable field data, the highest-ranked concern in this project. §12.2. **Closed by 10.61**, rule first: §4.19, with §4.19.1 asking the same question of every other import path | new |
| **J-2** | **I-1 is live in the base deployment.** 10.52 closed it behind the proxy. The README's LAN walkthrough has no proxy, and there the source key collapses again: two genuinely distinct callers recorded **one** `source_address`, and twelve requests from one returned `429` to an unrelated caller. The collapse is described, correctly, **inside the remediation's own file** — as a justification for a test escape hatch — and was never connected to the deployment it also describes. §12.4 | new |
| **NAU** | **The institutional review still has not happened.** `NAU_infosec_review_request.md` is byte-for-byte unchanged since the last gate, recipient still blank, "Still not sent." Rated blocking at five consecutive gates. | carried ×5 |

**The result worth carrying forward.** §10's lesson was "the fix was never run
in the configuration it ships in." §11's was "the control was never run in the
configuration it ships in, and the configuration changed underneath it." This
round sharpens both into something narrower and more useful: **this project
ships more than one configuration, and a remediation aimed at one of them is
not a remediation.** J-2 is 10.52's fix, correct and well-built, covering the
deployment §4.1 mandates and not the deployment `README.md` walks a field team
through. And the second configuration is not undiscovered — it is written down,
accurately, in `rate_limiter.dart:62-79`, as the reason a test escape hatch
exists.

**J-1 is the same shape one level out.** Five gates have attacked the server
and, latterly, the topology around it. The `TT1:` import path is neither. It is
the one place where a string chosen by somebody else is parsed straight into
the field record, and no gate had looked at it, because it is not the server
and the server is what a security gate looks at. It has no authorization step
by construction (`mutation_authorization.dart:34-45` documents the bypass), no
`RowValidator`, and an attacker-chosen merge clock.

### 12.2 J-1 — a pasted share payload overwrites the field record, and the app calls it an update

`SharedObservationImporter._upsertReplica`
(`lib/data/sharing/shared_observation_importer.dart:190-235`) looks up
`(observation_id, project_id)`, and when the incoming clock wins it issues a
`txn.update` of **every non-key column**. Both clock inputs are attacker-chosen
and effectively unbounded: `revision` is accepted for any `int >= 0`, and
`updated_at` has no upper bound at all
(`observation_share.dart:370-381`). `revision: 9223372036854775807` therefore
always wins `MergeResolver.compare`.

The replica is assembled from the ~20 fields the wire format carries
(`:146-175`), but `toColumns()` emits the **full** column set. Every column the
payload cannot carry is written as `NULL` over whatever was there.

Reproduced against a real in-memory database, one genuine observation, one
hostile payload carrying the same `observation_id`:

```
BEFORE  lat=35.1983 lon=-111.6513 user=user-victim rev=4
        magBearing=145.0 magStart=140.0 magEnd=150.0
        trueStart=150.2 trueEnd=160.2
        declination=10.2 wmm=WMM2025
        antenna=yagi_3el gain=3.0 agl=1.5
        captureMethod=rangeCapture bearingMethod=peak

OUTCOME SharedObservationImportOutcome.replicaUpdated

AFTER   lat=0.0 lon=0.0 user=user-attacker rev=9223372036854775807
        magBearing=145.0 magStart=null magEnd=null
        trueStart=null trueEnd=null
        declination=null wmm=null
        antenna=null gain=null agl=0.0
        captureMethod=null bearingMethod=null
        lastModifiedBy=user-victim

rows in Observations: 1
Users rows now: [user-victim/victim@nau.edu, user-attacker/attacker@example.com]
```

Read that list again. The location moved. The **sweep endpoints, the
declination used to convert them, and the WMM model version** are gone — which
is to say the bearing can no longer be reconstructed or re-derived, only
believed. `user_id` now names the attacker, so Phase 8's author-only rule locks
the real author out of their own record. `last_modified_by` names the
**victim**, because the payload set it. And a `Users` row of the attacker's
choosing was inserted as a side effect (`:301-313`), which is an identity
anchor for a later file-import merge to match on.

There is one row afterwards. The original is not preserved anywhere.

**Four things make this worse than a merge bug.**

1. **The user is told it went well.** `replicaUpdated` renders as *"You already
   had this observation — updated it to the newer version."*
   (`observation_sharing_screen.dart:268-269`). This is precisely the failure
   shape 10.25's own checklist has demanded be checked at every gate since the
   first: *a correct-looking message that hides harm.* It was checked for the
   server's refusals. Nobody checked the success path.
2. **No authorization runs.** The importer writes raw SQL and is a documented
   repository bypass. Nothing checks that the pasting user may write to the
   project, and nothing checks the payload's author may write that row.
3. **`RowValidator` never runs on this path** — it is the only write path in
   the app that skips it — so the row that lands can be one the server will
   later refuse, wedging the project's sync through the very machinery 10.28
   built for refusals.
4. **It propagates.** The forged row and its forged provenance go to the server
   and to every other device on the next push.

The precondition is one TT1 string the attacker got the victim to paste, plus
an `observation_id` — which every TT1 payload carries, so anyone the team has
ever shared an observation with already holds one.

**Why this is rated blocking on a gate about server exposure**, stated
plainly because it is a fair question: the gate's remit is asset integrity, and
§2 ranks the field record first. 10.60 already established that a finding
affecting the app as shipped belongs on this gate. And the harm does not stay
on the device — the forged row is pushed. A gate that lifted the localhost
restriction while this stood would be widening the network reach of a data
store that a single pasted string can rewrite.

### 12.3 The forged-header attack on 10.52's seam — held, and it had never been measured

`verify_i1_source_identity.sh` is a good drill and its negative control is
real. It attacks with **honest clients only**. The whole trusted-proxy scheme
rests on one assumption about a component this repository does not author —
that Caddy's `header_up X-Forwarded-For {remote_host}` *replaces* a
caller-supplied header rather than appending to it — and the script's closing
note names the danger without testing for it.

Measured, against the shipped `docker-compose.tls.yml` + `proxy/Caddyfile`,
from a container at a fixed address:

```
X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.77                  -> 202
X-Forwarded-For: 198.51.100.9, 203.0.113.77    -> 202
X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1                     -> 202
X-Forwarded-For: <the proxy's own address>     -> 202
X-Forwarded-For: not-an-address                -> 202

audit source_address values, all 6 requests:   172.31.244.50   (the real client)
rows carrying an attacker-chosen source_address: 0
```

and then, after exhausting the bucket:

```
flood 1..4  -> 202 ; flood 5..12 -> 429
forged-source request 1..4 (rotating 203.0.113.x) -> 429 429 429 429
```

The header is discarded at the first trusted hop, exactly as
`proxy/Caddyfile`'s comment claims. **The claim is now measured rather than
asserted**, and `ports: !override []` was confirmed in the same run — `docker
compose ps` shows the origin with no host mapping and the proxy as the only
published service. This belongs in the drill; filed under Discovered Scope.

### 12.4 J-2 — I-1 is closed behind the proxy and open in front of the laptop

§4.4.1's scheme resolves a caller through `X-Forwarded-For` **only** from a
declared trusted peer. `README.md`'s LAN walkthrough — the documented way a
field team uses this today — is the base compose file with
`SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0`, a phone on the Wi-Fi, and **no proxy
anywhere**. There is no header for the scheme to read, and
`TrustedProxies.fromEnvironment` does not refuse, because that deployment is
not `TRITRACK_ENV=production`.

Two genuinely distinct callers — this host, and a container on an unrelated
Docker network reaching the host's real LAN address `192.168.0.88`, standing in
for the phone:

```
host  request 1,2       -> 202 202
phone request 1,2       -> 202 202

auth_audit_log source_address:   192.168.65.1   (4 events, ONE distinct value)

phone flood x12         -> 202 202 202 202 202 202 429 429 429 429 429 429
host (unrelated) after  -> 429
```

Twelve requests from one caller denied magic-link sign-in to a different
caller, and every audit row names a gateway rather than a person. That is
finding I-1, verbatim, in the deployment this project documents.

**Three things about it that matter for the fix.**

- **`RequestSource.direct` is assumed distinguishing, unconditionally**
  (`request_identity.dart:111-114`). 10.52 built a genuine fail-safe — suspend
  the per-source rule when the key cannot tell callers apart — and wired it to
  the *one* way a key can be degenerate that the server can detect, a declared
  proxy naming nobody. A key can also be degenerate because the network path
  rewrote it, and in that case the server believes it is `direct` and enforces
  the merged bucket. The fail-safe cannot fire where it is most needed.
- **It is written down in the fix.** `rate_limiter.dart:62-79` describes this
  exact collapse — "Docker's port proxy, which rewrites every connection's
  source address to the same Docker-bridge address before it reaches
  `SourceIdentity` — the same collapse as finding I-1, one hop earlier and with
  no HTTP proxy in the path to carry a forwarding header, so §4.4.1's
  trusted-proxy scheme does not reach it." It is offered as the justification
  for `TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED`. The sentence is correct and
  the conclusion drawn from it was "so the e2e suite needs an escape hatch"
  rather than "so the LAN deployment is still broken."
- **Stated honestly about platform.** `192.168.65.1` is Docker Desktop's VM
  gateway; on a Linux host with iptables DNAT the client address usually
  survives. So the *severity* varies by host — but nothing in the deployment
  measures which case it is in, the walkthrough is written for a laptop, and
  this project is developed on macOS. A control whose correctness depends on an
  unmeasured property of the host is not a control, which is §11.0's own
  sentence.

**Resolved by task 10.62 (2026-08-16), and it found more than it was sent for.**
§4.4.2 is the design. The proxy-less exposed deployment is **removed and
refused**: `README.md`'s step 4 no longer tells anyone to set
`SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0`, the compose files pass the host's publish
address into the container so the server can finally see the difference between
the loopback default and an exposed listener, and an exposed listener with no
declared source identity exits 78. `TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES=none` — an
unverifiable claim about the network path — is no longer accepted for a
reachable deployment; `peer-verified` replaces it and is gated on
`scripts/verify_source_identity.sh`, a probe that measures the publish path
from two distinct off-host callers and carries a negative control so it can
fail.

**The premise 10.62 was briefed on was itself wrong, which is the finding worth
carrying forward.** The task file said 10.52's fix "holds behind the proxy — the
gate confirmed it." The gate confirmed that forged `X-Forwarded-For` headers do
not reach the origin, which is a different claim. Measured directly: through the
real Caddy directive, three distinct callers arriving over a *published host
port* all present as `X-Forwarded-For: 192.168.65.1`. The proxy forwards
faithfully; the address it sees is already collapsed. `verify_i1_source_identity`
never saw this because its client containers sit on the compose network and
reach the proxy container directly, crossing no publish path — the one caller
shape that survives.

So J-2's own remediation reproduces J-2's structure exactly one layer out: a
control verified in the configuration the instrument could reach, described as
verified generally. It is left **open** rather than closed quietly, because the
server cannot see its proxy's publish path and refusing on it would be a guess —
the same guess §4.4.1 says not to make. Filed as discovered scope with the
measurement attached.

### 12.5 J-3 — the server's own database connection is a Postgres superuser

Task 10.59 (I-10) closed the restore path's superuser problem properly: a
`NOSUPERUSER NOLOGIN` role, `SET ROLE`-ed before the archive's own SQL runs,
with a correct explanation of why `NOSUPERUSER` and not a `GRANT` is what
removes `COPY … FROM PROGRAM`. That reasoning applies unchanged to the
connection that is open all day and answers the network — and was not applied
to it.

The server connects as `POSTGRES_USER`, which the official `postgres` image
makes a superuser. Live, on the gate stack:

```
SELECT current_user, usesuper;          ->  tritrack | t

CREATE TEMP TABLE probe(line text);
COPY probe FROM PROGRAM 'id; hostname';
SELECT line FROM probe;
  ->  uid=70(postgres) gid=70(postgres) groups=70(postgres)
      5f61adf5c344
```

Arbitrary command execution on the database container, from the credentials the
internet-facing process holds.

**Not blocking, and I want to be exact about why.** There is no reachable path
to it: every identifier in `sync_service.dart` comes from the static
`tableSpecsByName` registry, every value is a bound parameter, and an unknown
table never reaches SQL at all. This is a privilege boundary, not an open door.
What it costs is the blast radius of any future injection, driver bug, or
process compromise — which today is "the data" and would otherwise be "the host
and the audit log." The same role can `DELETE FROM auth_audit_log`, so C-5's
forensic record is erasable by whatever compromises the process that writes it.
Rated the same way I-10 was, and it should get I-10's treatment.

### 12.6 J-4, J-5 — untyped 500s and a row that vanishes

Task 10.46 typed the envelope errors; task 10.56 said it had bounded "every
field on every route, not the two named here." Probed live, from an ordinary
authenticated account:

```
/sync/pull  cursor: "abc"      -> 500 internal_error
/sync/pull  cursor: 1.5        -> 500
/sync/pull  cursor: {"a":1}    -> 500
/sync/pull  cursor: true       -> 500
/sync/pull  batch_size: "x"    -> 500
/sync/pull  batch_size: {}     -> 500
/sync/push  device_id  with a NUL byte  -> 500
/sync/push  project_id with a NUL byte  -> 500
```

against `schema_major: "2"`, which 10.46 *did* fix, answering a clean `400
malformed_envelope`. **J-4 is H-4's class, on the fields beside the one H-4
named** — the fifth time in this record that a finding's instances were fixed
and the sentence written as though the class had been. Severity is low (no
write, no unbounded growth, transaction rolls back) and the precondition is any
account, which anyone can create. What it is really evidence of is the sweep.

**J-5:** a non-Map entry inside a *known* table is dropped without a word —
`{"rows": {"Observations": ["hello", 1, null]}}` answers `200`, `applied: 0`,
`outcomes: {}`. Task 10.46 fixed exactly this silence for unknown table *names*
and left the per-row case, where the `invalid` outcome the protocol defines is
still emitted by nothing. The harm is bounded on the client side by 10.28 rule
2 — silence on an offered row is treated as a refusal and held — which is that
task's design working as intended against a defect nobody had found yet.

**Two claims I chased and could not reproduce**, recorded because a gate that
only reports its hits is not a measurement: an 8 MB body is *not* read and
parsed before authentication (`401` in 0.06 s with no credentials), and a
wrongly-typed `user_id` on a pushed row does *not* reach the `as String?` cast
— project authorization refuses first, on all four type variants.

### 12.7 J-6 — the gate's own instruments, again, and one of them is 10.54's own repair

Each demonstrated, not read.

- **`verify_tls_termination.sh:189-192` cannot fail.** `PUBLISHED="$(… ||
  true)"` discards the return code and empty output PASSES. Demonstrated: the
  same command against a project that is not up, and against a nonexistent
  compose file, both print nothing — so the step reports *"docker compose
  reports no published port for the origin in this project; the proxy is the
  only way in."* This is `Cf`'s exact defect, **reintroduced by 10.54 in the
  step it rewrote to fix a different defect in the same check.**
- **`gate_smoke_test.sh`'s self-test cannot detect a missing instrument.**
  `SELFTEST_OK` iterates over the instruments that *ran* and asks whether each
  is in `WIRE_INSTRUMENTS`; it never asks whether each `WIRE_INSTRUMENT` ran.
  Demonstrated with the loop lifted verbatim and `verify_h3` absent: prints
  `SELFTEST PASSED`. **`verify_h3` being absent from that list is the precise
  omission §11.5 reported and 10.54 was written to fix** — 10.54 added the
  missing name and not the check that would have caught it, which is J-4's
  pattern in the gate's own tooling. (`:188` still says "all five" for a list
  of seven.)
- **`verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py` exits 0 while reporting failure.** §10.7.1
  found it exiting 0 with "C-3 closed" against a down stack; that is genuinely
  fixed — it now SKIPs, names the skipped check, and prints *"C-3 is NOT
  confirmed closed by this run."* The text is honest and the **exit code is
  still 0**, which is the only thing any harness reads.

### 12.8 What holds, re-verified rather than assumed

C-1…C-5, D-1 and I-4 all refuse again; the 40-check adversarial pass held 36,
and the four failures are `Ce2`, `Dc`, `Dh` and `Eb` — **the same four §10 and
§11 recorded, no new ones**. I-2 is closed, and closed the way it was found:
drill step 10c plants a renamed copy of a genuine signed pair and the run
refuses loudly, naming the file, pruning nothing. I-6's poll limit fires (30 ×
`200`, then `429`). The diagnostics console's token is compared in constant
time and the console still fails closed behind the proxy. TLS terminates, 7
checks, certificate chain verified through Caddy's internal CA. Secrets are
clean across all 116 commits, now by a committed test rather than by hand.

### 12.9 Residual risk, in plain language

Unchanged from §11.10 in every particular except two, and both are worse:

**The app can be made to destroy field data by a message.** Until J-1 is fixed,
a TriTrack user who pastes a share payload from someone they do not fully trust
can lose the location and the bearing reconstruction of an existing
observation, and be told the paste succeeded. This is the only risk in this
document that is live for users of the app **today**, independent of any
server, and it should be treated as the most urgent item in the phase.

**Sign-in can be denied to a whole team by one person on the Wi-Fi.** In the
LAN deployment, twelve unauthenticated requests deny magic-link sign-in to
every user for fifteen minutes, and the audit log cannot say who did it. Not a
disclosure; an availability and accountability failure, in the deployment the
documentation recommends.

Everything else in §11.10 stands: no protected-species location has ever left a
device except to a user's own cloud backup (§4.15.1's accepted, time-bounded
default) and to a server that listens only on localhost.

### 12.10 The NAU review — the item five gates have not closed

`CLAUDE_DOCS/NAU_infosec_review_request.md` is unchanged since commit `3333cb0`,
the fourth gate's own record. Status line still reads "Still not sent."
Recipient still blank. The residual-risk summary it points at now needs
updating to §12.9, which is a five-minute edit and not the obstacle.

The obstacle is that this is a human action and it has not been taken at five
consecutive gates while nine engineering findings were opened and closed around
it. It is worth saying once more, since the letter itself says it: **do not
wait for the gate to pass before sending this.** Nothing is exposed. The letter
has now been revised three times by three gates that could not send it, and
each revision has been a smaller change than the last.

### 12.11 On the process

Four rounds have now each found their blocking findings on ground the previous
round had no reason to look at: the server's authorization, then the row-level
oracles, then the backup path, then the deployment topology, and now **the
second deployment and the client**. The pattern holding across all five is not
that the fixes were wrong. Every remediation in this phase has been correct
about what it aimed at. What keeps failing is the scope of the aim — a finding
gets fixed where it was reproduced, and the sentence that gets written is about
the class.

That is now six recorded instances (§9.5's `User_Emails`, §10.7's `Tags`,
§11.5's instrument sweep, J-4's typed fields, J-6's self-test, and J-2's second
deployment). It is worth naming as a standing practice rather than re-deriving
it every gate: **when a finding is fixed, the acceptance criterion should name
the other places the same shape could be, and the instrument should measure one
of them.** 10.52's drill is the model — it carries a negative control that fails
loudly when it proves nothing, and that control caught a vacuous pass during its
own authoring. It was still aimed at one deployment.

One more, in the gate's favour: reading the detail lines rather than the
verdicts has now caught something at five consecutive gates. This time it was
two claims from a code-reading pass that did not survive contact with a live
server (§12.6), and one instrument whose §10.7.1 defect was genuinely fixed
while the exit code it reports was not (§12.7).

**One more clause, added at task 10.72 after the sixth gate found its
blocking findings already written down as open:** naming a class and
recording a verdict is not the same act as scheduling the work, and the gap
between them is where K-1 and K-2 spent six weeks unnoticed. **A finding
recorded as open must leave the session that recorded it with a task number,
or it has not been recorded — it has been described.** "Open" is not a
resting state; it is a to-do item without an owner, and it must become one of
two things before the session that wrote it ends: a task number, or an
explicit accepted-risk entry naming who accepted the risk and why (§11.7's
`User_Emails`/`Tags` decision is the model). Silence — an "Open" with neither
— is the failure this clause exists to name.

## 13. Verdicts — Security Gate C, sixth re-run (task 10.25, 2026-08-16)

### 13.0 Gate result: **FAILED. The server still does not listen beyond localhost.**

**All nine remediations from the fifth round landed, and the server-side ones
are the cleanest set this record has seen.** J-4 and J-5 are genuinely closed by
enumeration and not by example: 132 typed probes across every field of both sync
routes — wrong type, wrong shape, null, NUL byte, oversized — returned **zero**
untyped `500`s, and all eight cases §12.6 listed by name now answer `400
malformed_envelope`. J-3 is closed and measured live: the server's own role is
`NOSUPERUSER`, and `COPY … FROM PROGRAM` under it is refused by Postgres itself.
J-6's instrument defects are fixed, with a static detector that proves both
halves of its own claim. J-1's fix on the paste path held every probe I put to
it, including the two exemptions its own design creates. 10.62's refusal is real:
an exposed listener with no declared source identity **exits 78**, and the
message names the denial of service it is preventing. **All four suites green in
one pass — 832 client / 455 server / 32 e2e / offline — and all twelve
instruments ran against a live server**, the third consecutive gate where the
tools worked first time.

**And one thing this gate did that no previous gate had.** §10.5.3 built the ATS
hardware test and every gate since has recorded it as "run by nothing
automated." It was run here, as a real profile-mode app bundle on a real Apple
platform (macOS 26.6): **2 checks pass** — and then **neutralized, to prove it
can fail**, which it did, loudly. F13's last unmeasured half is measured.

The gate fails on three items. **Two are the same finding this record has now
made seven times, and the more important one is that both were already written
down in this document as open.**

| # | Blocking item | New? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **K-1** | **The picked-`.zip` backup restore is J-1, in full, on a file the app tells users to WhatsApp.** Reproduced end to end through `BackupArchive.decode` → `ProjectMerger.merge`: an observation moved to (0,0), `user_id` reassigned to the attacker, `last_modified_by` forged to name the victim, declination and WMM model version erased, a second observation tombstoned, the project's owner reassigned, an attacker `Users` row planted — **under the default merge strategy, with validation on, reported to the user as "Updated: 3."** `Sync_Conflicts` rows afterwards: **0**. §13.2. **Closed by task 10.73** (§4.19.2) | recorded open by §4.19.1; **never given a gate verdict, and its stated mitigation is false** |
| **K-2** | **Source identity collapses in the deployment §4.1 mandates.** The repository's own probe, run without `--report-only`, returns `COLLAPSED` for the TLS overlay's off-host callers and passes its negative control in the same run. That is finding I-1 — one rate-limit bucket for every user, every audit row naming a gateway — live in the only deployment this project permits to be exposed. §13.3 | predicted and left open by §12.4; **still open, now measured as a gate verdict rather than a note** |
| **NAU** | **The institutional review still has not happened.** `NAU_infosec_review_request.md` is byte-for-byte unchanged since commit `3333cb0` — the *fourth* gate's own record — recipient still blank, "Still not sent." Rated blocking at six consecutive gates. | carried ×6 |

**The result worth carrying forward, and it is not the one I expected to
write.** §12.11 asked for a standing practice: "when a finding is fixed, the
acceptance criterion should name the other places the same shape could be, and
the instrument should measure one of them." Task 10.66 adopted exactly that, and
**it worked** — §4.19.1 is that rule applied honestly, and it is how K-1 came to
be written down at all. It enumerated every import path, asked the five
questions of each, and recorded three as **Open**. Then the phase closed the one
that had been reproduced and shipped.

So the failure this round is not the old one. The class *was* named, the sites
*were* enumerated, and the verdicts *were* written — and the gate still fails on
one of them, because **enumerating a class and closing one instance of it leaves
the class open, and the enumeration then reads like coverage.** §4.19.1's table
has "Open" in three rows and the phase moved on. A written "Open" with no task
against it is indistinguishable, six weeks later, from a written "Closed."

**And the second half of that, which is worse:** the reason K-1 was left is
recorded in §4.19.1 itself — *"a restore is a deliberate whole-project act on a
file the user chose, not a casual paste."* That sentence is false, and it is
falsified by copy on the very screen that hosts the Import button
(`data_export_screen.dart:70-72`): *"A full project backup (.zip, ~100–250KB)
can be shared via WhatsApp, email, or cloud storage and restored on any
device."* The exposure argument that deferred the finding was contradicted by
the app's own words, in the same repository, and nothing checked.

### 13.2 K-1 — the backup restore is J-1, and the reason it was deferred is false

`data_export_screen.dart:139-172` is the whole path: `FilePicker.pickFiles`
→ `File.readAsBytes` → `BackupArchive.decode` → `ProjectMerger(db.raw).merge`.
Reproduced against a real in-memory database holding one victim project, three
genuine observations and a real `Users` row, with a hand-built `.zip` — **default
`MergeStrategy.lastWriteWins`, default `validate: true`**:

```
report: inserted=1 updated=3 skipped=0 invalid=0 issues=[]

Projects.owner_user_id = user-evil   rev=9223372036854775807  updated_at=2999-01-01
obs-1: lat=0.0 lon=0.0   user_id=user-evil  last_modified_by=user-victim
       declination=null  wmm=null  rev=9223372036854775807
obs-2: deleted_at=2999-01-01T00:00:00.000Z
Users rows now: [user-victim/victim@example.org, user-evil/mallory@evil.test]

Sync_Conflicts rows: 0
```

Read that against §12.2's transcript. It is the same list: the location moved,
the **declination and WMM model version are gone** so the bearing can no longer
be re-derived, `user_id` names the attacker so Phase 8's author-only rule locks
the real author out, `last_modified_by` names the victim because the file said
so, and a `Users` row of the attacker's choosing was planted. J-1 destroyed one
observation; this destroys **every table**, adds project ownership, and adds a
tombstone. The user is shown `Inserted: 1` and `Updated: 3` and an OK button.

**Three things make it worse than §4.19.1 records, and each was reproduced.**

1. **`preferIncoming` is a red herring.** The full damage lands under the
   **default** strategy. An unbounded `revision` is sufficient — `MergeResolver`
   is consulted, and `9223372036854775807` wins it. `RowValidator` **does** run
   (better than §4.19.1 says) and stops none of it, because it has never
   inspected `revision`, `updated_at`, `deleted_at` or authorship. Removing the
   "Overwrite with backup" button would fix nothing.
2. **The merge is not scoped to the manifest's project.** A file whose manifest
   names project A rewrote the owner of an unrelated local project B.
   `manifest.projectId` is read only for the "Switch to this project"
   affordance.
3. **The file can attribute the attacker's rows to the victim.**
   `IdentityTrust.emailMatchesPerson` is in force on this path, so a `Users` row
   in the archive claiming the victim's address caused every incoming row's
   `user_id` to be remapped onto the victim's real local id.

And `MergeStrategy.preferIncoming` is worse than "the file wins": with it
selected, a row carrying `revision: 0` and `updated_at: 1971-01-01` overwrote
the victim's `revision: 4` row. The local clock is rolled **backwards**, which
no honest sync state can produce.

**On exposure, which is the part §4.19.1 got wrong.** The verdict deferred this
as "a file the user chose." The same archive format is produced by export, by
auto cloud backup and by server publish, and the app itself tells the user to
send it to people (`data_export_screen.dart:70-72`), as do
`TriTrack_Technical_Context.md:456` and `:732-733`. Two documented routes to a
hostile one: a colleague who has legitimately received a project backup holds
every `project_id`, `observation_id` and `user_id` needed to target rows
precisely and can return an edited file as "here's the merged version"; and
anyone with write access to the linked cloud folder can drop a file with the
expected `TriTrack_<Project>_<timestamp>.zip` name, which the user later picks
believing it is their own. §4.15.1 reasoned about that folder's
**confidentiality** and never about the fact that the same archive is a **write
primitive against the field record**.

**Closed by task 10.73 (2026-08-16).** §4.19's five clauses were moved into the
shared package (`UntrustedImportRules`) and applied to this path, plus a sixth
that this path needs and the share path did not — the merge is scoped to
`manifest.projectId`. Each of the gate's four measured facts is answered by a
named clause rather than worked around: (a) the damage under the *default*
strategy is stopped by the clock bound and the consent gate, not by removing a
button, which is why the button is still there; (b) `RowValidator` still stops
none of it and the clock check is deliberately *not* folded into it, because
the server runs `RowValidator` too and its answer to a bad clock is different
on purpose (`ClockSkew.classify`); (c) is the sixth clause; (d) the email dedup
still fires — it is load-bearing here — and now reports a count. The exposure
argument is corrected on §4.19.1's row 4 rather than quietly dropped, and the
sweep it prompted found the same shape in row 9. Reproduction transcript and
per-clause neutralization: `test/security/backup_restore_overwrite_test.dart`.

**Why blocking.** §12.2 already settled the principle: the gate's remit is asset
integrity, §2 ranks the field record first, and a finding live in the app as
shipped belongs on this gate. Everything said there applies here with more
force, because this path reaches every table rather than one row, keeps no prior
version at all, and is reached by a workflow the documentation recommends.

### 13.3 K-2 — the deployment §4.1 mandates has no per-source rate limit

Task 10.62 did what it was asked and did it well. Verified live, on a stack
brought up for the purpose: the base compose with `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0`
and no declared source identity **refuses to start, exit 78**, and the refusal
names the consequence rather than the variable —

> *"the per-source limit becomes ONE BUCKET SHARED BY EVERY USER: ten
> unauthenticated requests from a stranger deny magic-link sign-in to the entire
> deployment for 15 minutes, and every audit row records a gateway instead of a
> person."*

That closes J-2 as filed. It does not close what J-2 *is*, and §12.4 said so
when it filed the remainder as open. Run as a gate rather than in
`--report-only`, the repository's own probe answers:

```
direct   (base compose, published port):      COLLAPSED
proxied  (TLS overlay, off-host caller):      COLLAPSED
negative control (proxied, on-network):       distinct callers stayed distinct
```

The control passing in the same run is what makes the two FAILs measurements
rather than a broken tool. The second line is the finding: `docker-compose.tls.yml`
is the deployment §4.1 *requires* before anything is exposed, and every caller
that is not already inside the compose network crosses a host publish path that
rewrites their address before Caddy ever sees it. Caddy then forwards that one
gateway address faithfully, the origin's allowlist accepts it as authentic, and
`RequestSource` believes it is distinguishing callers. `verify_i1_source_identity.sh`
does not see this because its client containers reach the proxy from *inside*
the network — the one caller shape that survives.

**Why this is blocking rather than a carried note.** The gate's question is
whether the server may listen beyond localhost. On this host it may not, because
in the only deployment it is allowed to do so from, §4.4's controls do not
function: twelve requests from one person deny sign-in to a whole team, and
`auth_audit_log.source_address` cannot say who did it. That is finding I-1
verbatim, and I-1 was rated blocking. Nothing has changed except which
configuration it lives in — for the second gate running.

**Stated fairly about scope**, because the fix is a deployment decision and not
a patch: the probe's own closing text is correct that on Docker Desktop *no*
configuration fixes this, and on a Linux host with iptables DNAT the client
address usually survives. So the honest position is that this project has no
exposable deployment **on the machine it is developed on**, and may have one on a
Linux host that nobody has measured. The instrument to measure it exists and
carries a negative control; what does not exist is a deployment that has passed
it.

**Closed by task 10.74 (2026-08-16), option 1 — §4.4.3.** The exposable
deployment is now qualified by a passing probe run on the host it will run on,
enforced by a startup refusal rather than by prose: an allowlist in
`TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES` additionally requires `TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY`
to be `probe-verified` (measured `proxied: PRESERVED` on this host) or
`on-network-only` (nothing off-host reaches the proxy). The other two options
were refused with reasons recorded: no publish path on this host preserves
addresses, and accepting the collapse means accepting a repeatable remote
denial of service on sign-in for the whole deployment plus unattributable audit
rows. The gate's own framing is preserved rather than softened — **on Docker
Desktop there is now no deployment that can be exposed at all**, and the
qualification is a probe verdict on a machine, never an operating system.

### 13.4 J-3 — closed, and measured under the role the server actually uses

`SET ROLE "tritrack_app"` then, on the gate stack's live database:

```
rolname       rolsuper  rolcreatedb  rolcreaterole  rolcanlogin  rolbypassrls
tritrack      t         t            t              t            t
tritrack_app  f         f            f              f            f

current_user = tritrack_app,  session_user = tritrack

COPY probe FROM PROGRAM 'id; hostname';
  ERROR:  permission denied to COPY to or from an external program
```

§12.5's reproduction is refused by Postgres itself, for the reason 10.59 gave:
`NOSUPERUSER`, not a `GRANT`. The demotion is applied to the connection that is
open all day, which is what 10.59 left undone.

One thing this does **not** close, recorded because §12.5 named it: the same
role can still `DELETE FROM auth_audit_log` — demonstrated, 310 rows. C-5's
forensic record remains erasable by whatever compromises the process that writes
it. Not blocking (the audit log is not a control against the process that owns
it) but it is the untouched half of §12.5's paragraph, and no task carries it.

### 13.5 J-4 and J-5 — closed by enumeration, and it shows

Task 10.64 was told not to fix three cases. It did not. Re-attacked from an
ordinary authenticated account, every field of both sync routes against
`{wrong type ×3, wrong shape ×2, null, NUL byte, oversized 100 KB}` — 112
probes:

```
§12.6's eight named cases:      all 400 malformed_envelope   (were 500)
pull:  project_id device_id cursor batch_size envelope
       protocol_version schema_version schema_major          no 500s
push:  project_id device_id rows envelope
       protocol_version schema_version schema_major          no 500s
body-level: not JSON / array / string / empty                400 malformed_body
J-5:  rows.Observations = ["hello", 1, null]
        -> 200 applied=0 outcomes={'Observations/?': 'invalid'}
```

The `invalid` outcome the protocol defines is finally emitted by something. This
is the first finding-class in this record to be closed on the first re-check
after being told to enumerate rather than patch, and it is worth naming as
evidence that the instruction works.

**One survivor, recorded rather than rounded off (K-6, non-blocking).** The
enumeration covered every *field*; it did not cover every *container*. A `rows`
value that is not a map, or a table whose value is not a list, is accepted
silently:

```
rows: "x" | 1.5 | [1] | null                     -> 200 applied=0 outcomes={}
rows: {"Observations": "x" | 5 | null | {...}}   -> 200 applied=0 outcomes={}
```

No `invalid`, no `malformed_envelope`, indistinguishable from an honest empty
push. That is J-5's exact shape one level up, after the pass that closed J-5.
Harm is bounded to nil today (no write, and 10.28 rule 2 holds an unanswered row
client-side), and I record it mainly because it is the smallest possible version
of this document's recurring pattern, found immediately below a genuine success.

**Closed by task 10.78.** `sync_routes.dart` reports `rows/?: invalid` when the
container itself is not a `Map`, and `_malformedRowOutcomes`'s per-table check
now flags a known table's value that is not a `List` at all, not only a `List`
holding a non-`Map` entry — both container-level, same `invalid` mechanism
J-5 already established. `decodeRows` is unchanged and still deliberately
tolerant (a standing unit test asserts it never throws); the fix is at the
outcome-reporting layer that sits above it, matching the finding's own framing
of this as "J-5's shape one level up."

### 13.6 The other new findings, none blocking

**K-3 — §4.19.1's deep-link row is false as written, and so is a comment
in the code it protects.** §4.19.1 asked the next gate to re-check the claim
rather than re-derive it. Re-checked: its four literal sub-claims are all still
true — no `CFBundleURLTypes`/`CFBundleDocumentTypes` in either `Info.plist`, no
associated-domains entitlement, no extension targets, one `MAIN`/`LAUNCHER`
intent-filter, no link-handling plugin in `pubspec.lock`. **Its conclusion is
not.** `android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:16` is `android:exported="true"`,
and an exported activity is startable by any app on the device with an explicit
component intent — an intent-filter is irrelevant to that. Flutter's
`FlutterActivity.getInitialRoute()` returns the caller-supplied `route` extra
*unconditionally*, ahead of any deep-linking flag, and go_router 17.3.0's
`_effectiveInitialLocation` **prefers the platform default over the configured
`initialLocation`** unless `overridePlatformDefaultLocation` is set, which this
app does not set.

Reproduced, hops 2 and 3, with a negative control:

```
platformDefault = /project-setup/attacker-chosen
  -> effective initial location: /project-setup/attacker-chosen   (SPLASH skipped)
no platform route
  -> effective initial location: /splash                          (control)
```

So `splash_screen.dart:44-45` — *"This is a non-skippable gate: there is no path
into the rest of the app that bypasses this check"* — is false on Android, and
the check it names is Phase 7's first-run identity capture. **Not blocking**: the
precondition is a malicious app already on the device, which §5.4 declares a
non-goal, and iOS is closed today because nothing routes a URL to the app. But
the iOS *receiver* is armed by default (`FlutterDeepLinkingEnabled` absent =
enabled), so the day anyone adds a URL type — a magic-link deep link is the
obvious Phase 11 reason to — route injection is live there too with no second
control. Two false written claims and a single-layer defense on the platform
where it is thinnest.

**Closed by task 10.77.** `app_router.dart`'s `GoRouter` now sets
`overridePlatformDefaultLocation: true`, so `_effectiveInitialLocation` can no
longer prefer a platform-supplied route over `/splash` on any platform this
app ships. `AndroidManifest.xml`'s `MainActivity` now carries
`flutter_deeplinking_enabled = false`, closing the live Android path directly
rather than relying on the router alone. `ios/Runner/Info.plist` now sets
`FlutterDeepLinkingEnabled` to `false` explicitly, closing the single-layer
gap *before* Phase 11 gives it a reason to matter rather than after.
`splash_screen.dart:44-45`'s comment was rewritten to describe what the widget
itself guarantees and to name the platform-layer controls that close the rest,
instead of asserting a guarantee those controls, not the widget, provide.

**K-4 — `ServerIdentityAdopter` takes an unvalidated server-chosen id and hard-
deletes on it.** The redemption-time email check (`auth_provider.dart:101-103`)
is real and load-bearing: it bounds the *targets* of the rewrite to rows the
device already attributes to the address the user typed, so a hostile server
cannot reach a colleague's records. It constrains nothing about `serverUserId`,
which arrives as "is a non-empty String" and is written into a primary key, into
the user column of all 11 synced tables including `Projects.owner_user_id`, into
a `User_Emails` binding, and into the device's acting identity — each with
`revision + 1` so it beats every peer's copy. The superseded local `Users` row is
then `DELETE`d with **no capture of any kind**: no `Sync_Conflicts`, no
tombstone, and its `first_name`/`last_name` survive only on the branch where the
server named an id the device had never seen. `RowValidator` never runs on this
path; no authorization check exists. Preconditions are a hostile or compromised
server, or an on-path attacker in a **debug** build to a private-range host —
F13's enforcement closes the rest. There is also an honest-path variant needing
no attacker: two people sharing an institutional mailbox on one device are
fused and one profile is destroyed. No test drives a hostile `serverUserId`.

**Closed by task 10.75 (2026-08-16), rule first.** The finding's real content
was not any one of those defects but the missing sentence underneath them —
**§4.19 forbids trusting an import with authorship and clocks, and this code
trusts the server with both, and nowhere said why that was or was not
different.** §4.20 is that sentence: *the server is the authority on which id
names an email, and is not an authority on anything that follows from that id.*
The first half is upheld, with its three grounds written down (an authenticated
session, a design-assigned role §4.17/§4.18, and `completeSignIn`'s bound to
the address the **user typed**). The second half is enforced in the four places
the code had conflated with it: `RowValidator` runs on this path — it was the
last write path in the app that skipped it, and the validator itself gained the
shape half it was missing (non-blank, length-bounded, no control characters) on
**every** table, so the merge and archive paths get it too; the derived
`user_email_id` is bounded in its own right; an id this device already holds
for a different person is refused rather than adopted into; and the superseded
`Users` row is written to `Sync_Conflicts` before the hard delete, which itself
stays — a tombstone would sync the false claim that the person was deleted.
**The honest-path variant is fixed by a different rule and it is the one worth
naming:** several local users sharing one address are no longer fused, because
`_resolveLocalUserIds` now applies to current addresses the same
*ambiguous-means-do-not-guess* rule the prior-address branch beside it always
applied. That defect was never about the server at all — the server names an
id, the device chooses the targets — which is why it survived a section written
entirely about untrusted payloads. 27 tests in
`test/security/server_identity_adoption_test.dart`, grouped one-to-one onto
§4.20's four clauses, each group carrying a negative control. Residual, named
rather than closed: `heldBack` is reported and no screen shows it (Discovered
Scope).

**K-5 — `UnknownColumnStore.promote` is unguarded, and latent rather than
prevented.** It writes stashed values into real columns from `onOpen`, on every
launch, after migrations and before any screen reads: no `RowValidator`, no
authorization, no clock, no conflict capture, no bound on entry count,
`column_name` length or `value_json` size. Nothing an attacker stashes today can
promote — promotion requires the column to be unknown at stash time and declared
at promote time — and that timing accident is the whole of the mitigation. Two
harms arm on the next additive schema bump: a stashed value overwriting a
migration's own computed backfill (schema v4's `Tags.color_hex` `UPDATE` is the
exact shape), and a value that cannot be written — a JSON object, or `null` into
a `NOT NULL` column — throwing inside `onOpen`, where the entry is only deleted
*after* a successful update, so the failure repeats on every launch and the
database never opens again. The store is also not project-scoped; 10.35's keys
confine the project-scoped tables, but `Users`, `User_Emails` and `Tags` are
globally keyed and are a live A→B channel. Held values ride outward on every
push and every export, so a stash spreads device-to-device without the server.

**K-8 — §4.19 rule 4's consent gate has a hole exactly the shape of J-1's
fourth defect, and the message claims a consent that never happened.**
`clockColumns` excludes five columns from the was→becomes diff. The
justification written beside it is sound and covers **two** of them —
`revision` and `updated_at` do move on every honest edit, and prompting on them
would train the dismissal. It does not cover `created_at` or
`origin_device_id`, which do not move on an honest edit, are taken verbatim from
the payload, and are excluded anyway. Reproduced against a real database, with
`confirmChanges: false` — the user was never asked:

```
OUTCOME              replicaUpdated
changes reported     0
destructiveChanges   0

BEFORE  created_at=2026-07-01  rev=4           origin=device-victim-phone
AFTER   created_at=2026-08-15  rev=4000000000  origin=zzzz-attacker-wins-every-tie
```

A payload identical to the victim's own row in every carried field, differing
only in the clock, is written with **no dialog**, and
`observation_sharing_screen.dart:387-391` then renders *"Your copy was replaced
**as you confirmed** — **0 values were changed.** Your previous version is kept
and can be reviewed."* Both halves of that sentence are false in the same
breath. `origin_device_id` is the documented final last-write-wins tiebreaker
(`postgres_schema.dart:21`), so a lexically-high forged value wins every future
tie against the victim's genuine edits; `created_at` is falsified provenance.

**Not blocking**, and I want to be exact about why: the observation's
substantive fields are untouched, the prior row *is* captured to
`Sync_Conflicts` (that call is unconditional on the update path, so clause 4's
recoverability half holds), and nothing about the bearing is destroyed. What is
broken is the *visibility* half — which is the half §4.19 says is the whole of
the defense against an unauthenticated payload. And it is J-1's fourth listed
property, *a correct-looking message that hides harm*, reproduced inside J-1's
own remediation. The clause-3 bound did its job in the same run: `created_at`
set to 1999 was refused outright with *"Sync clock is out of range."*

**Closed by task 10.73** (folded in with K-1, since it belongs to the same
code). Both halves: the exemption list now has one written criterion — *does
this column move on every honest edit?* — which `created_at` and
`origin_device_id` fail and which is why `last_modified_by` legitimately
passes; and `replicaUpdated`'s message reads the outcome instead of assuming
it, so an update that destroyed nothing no longer claims a consent nobody was
asked for. The list is shared with the archive path
(`UntrustedImportRules.columnsMovedByEveryEdit`) rather than living on the
share encoder, which is what made it reachable by only one path in the first
place. Guarded on both paths: `share_payload_overwrite_test.dart` (the
in-range clock-only forgery is now held at the gate) and
`observation_sharing_messages_test.dart` (an unconfirmed update may not borrow
the confirmed sentence).

**K-9 — 10.69's race, reintroduced in shell in the same round it was fixed in
Dart.** `server/backup/backup.sh:65-68` (landed by task 10.63, commit `58cb20d`)
does check-then-`CREATE ROLE` with no locking — the exact shape 10.69 replaced
in `ensureServerAppRole` with an unconditional `CREATE ROLE` swallowing both
`42710` and `23505`, after reproducing the failure 30/30 at 8-way concurrency.
`server/backup/restore.sh:547` has it too (pre-existing). Fails closed — the
loser aborts under `set -eu`, so the outcome is a backup that does not run
rather than a bad backup — but two backups on one host, or a cron run
overlapping a manual one, is not exotic. **This is the sixth-round instance of
the pattern task 10.66 was adopted to stop, inside the round that adopted it.**

**Closed by task 10.78.** Both `backup.sh` and `restore.sh` now do the same
unconditional `CREATE ROLE`-and-swallow `ensureServerAppRole` does, adapted to
shell: the role creation always runs, and only a failure whose stderr matches
Postgres's own `already exists` (42710) or `duplicate key value violates
unique constraint` (23505) wording is treated as "someone else just created
it" rather than a real failure. Why the enumeration missed it in the first
place: 10.66's rule was applied to fix the one instance 10.69 was scoped to
(`ensureServerAppRole`, in Dart) — adopting a rule and grepping the repo for
every other instance of the pattern it generalizes are different acts, and only
the first happened in the commit that also introduced the rule.

**K-10 — the test guarding J-3 cannot tell a refusal from a broken harness.**
`server/test/integration/server_app_role_test.dart:100` asserts
`throwsA(anything)` on `COPY … FROM PROGRAM`. A syntax error, a dropped
connection, or a missing temp table all satisfy it. Task 10.69 spent a whole
task making this test deterministic; the assertion it stabilized is the
weak-assertion class H-8 swept for. Asserting SQLSTATE `42501` would make it a
measurement. The sibling assertion in the same file (`rolsuper` is false) is
sound, which is why J-3's closure is not in doubt — but this test on its own
would pass against a server that had never been demoted.

**Closed by task 10.78.** The assertion is now
`isA<ServerException>().having((e) => e.code, 'SQLSTATE', '42501')` —
`insufficient_privilege`, Postgres's own name for exactly the property this
test exists to prove. Confirmed passing against a live Postgres, in isolation
and as part of the full server suite. Why the enumeration missed it: 10.69's
acceptance criterion was "the test stops flaking," and a test becoming
deterministic was taken as evidence it was also measuring the right thing —
determinism and precision are different properties, and fixing the first gave
no reason for anyone to separately ask what a now-reliably-repeatable
`throwsA(anything)` actually establishes.

**K-11 — two scope gaps in the new tooling and the new sweep.** (a)
`verify_instrument_unchecked_returns.py` scans `scripts/*.sh` only,
non-recursively: `server/backup/backup.sh` and `restore.sh` are never read, and
neither is any Python instrument — including `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py`, the
file `Cf` was found in and which the detector's own docstring names as the
origin of the class. Its regexes also miss the inverted spelling
(`[ -n "$VAR" ] && fail`), which is the dominant idiom in this very directory.
Its `0 findings` is true of a subset and its success line claims the set. (b)
10.67's cast sweep enumerated eleven directories and **`lib/data/sync/` is in
neither column** — not fixed, not "verified unaffected". `project_merger.dart:218,227`
reads `row['user_id'] as String` off an imported archive inside
`_buildUserRemap`, which runs *before* the `RowValidator` loop the sweep names
as its mitigation. Crash, not bypass — but it is the class the sweep said it had
enumerated, on the path K-1 is about.

**Closed by task 10.78, both halves.** (a) `verify_instrument_unchecked_returns.py`
now also scans `server/backup/`, gained a second pattern for the inverted
`-n ... && fail` spelling (proven both to catch it and to leave the safe,
dominant `-n ... || fail` idiom alone — new selftest fixtures for each), and
its success line names the directories it read and states outright that
Python instruments are not in scope, rather than implying a complete sweep.
(b) `project_merger.dart`'s `_buildUserRemap` no longer casts `backup`'s rows
with naked `as String?`/`as String`; new module-level `_asStringOrNull`/
`_asStringOrEmpty` helpers skip a malformed row for remap purposes only,
leaving `RowValidator` in `_plan` — which runs after, and which this bug
reached *before* — to actually rule on it. Confirmed the pre-fix cast throws
(`type 'int' is not a subtype of type 'String' in type cast`) before writing
the fix, and added a test that a non-string `user_id` in an archive is
refused rather than crashing the whole merge. Why the enumeration missed
both: neither tool was checked against itself. (a)'s own scan scope was never
audited the way it audits its target — `scripts/*.sh` was where the one known
instance lived, not a scope derived from "everywhere this class of file could
exist." (b) 10.67's "Method" paragraph named `lib/data/sync/**` as one of the
directories its parallel research agents covered, but the verdict table that
same task's own acceptance criterion requires — "a table of every site" —
has no row for it; the paragraph's claim was never checked against the table
it was supposed to summarize.

**K-7 — two instrument notes.** `verify_ats_transport_security.sh`'s own header
recommends `macos --release` as "the cheapest real run"; that invocation cannot
work — `flutter drive` refuses release mode for non-web — and the script reports
`FAIL` for a reason that has nothing to do with ATS. It fails loudly rather than
passing, which is the right direction, but the documented command is broken and
the working one (`--profile`) is the one F13 needs anyway. Separately,
`verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py` is **still** not wired into
`gate_smoke_test.sh` — 10.65 filed that as its own discovered scope and no task
carries it, so C-3 stays proven only when a person remembers to run it. It was
run by hand here: 16 checks, no skips.

### 13.7 Every §2 actor and §3 surface — round 6 verdict (superseded)

**Superseded by §14.10**, which is current as of task 11.217, 2026-09-09. Contents below are left

### 13.10 Residual risk, in plain language

Unchanged from §12.9 except in two particulars, and one of them replaces the
other:

**J-1 is fixed, and the same harm is still live by a different route.** A
TriTrack user who imports a project `.zip` from someone they do not fully trust
— the app tells them this file is shareable by WhatsApp — can lose the location,
the authorship and the bearing reconstruction of observations they already hold,
across every table, with no prior version kept and a success dialog reporting a
count of rows "updated." This is the only risk in this document that is live for
users of the app **today**, independent of any server, and it should be treated
as the most urgent item in the phase, exactly as J-1 was.

**Sign-in can still be denied to a whole team by one person on the network.** In
every deployment this project can currently be exposed in, twelve unauthenticated
requests deny magic-link sign-in to every user for fifteen minutes, and the audit
log records a gateway rather than a person. Not a disclosure; an availability and
accountability failure, and it is now measured rather than argued.

Everything else in §12.9 stands: **no protected-species location has ever left a
device except to a user's own cloud backup (§4.15.1's accepted, time-bounded
default) and to a server that listens only on localhost.**

was not made. Its status line still says "revised again 2026-08-15 after the
fourth Gate C re-run. Still not sent." Recipient still blank.

The letter is repointed at §13.10 as part of this gate, which is the third gate to
revise a letter it cannot send. That is the whole of what engineering can do
here. **It has now been rated blocking at six consecutive gates while eighteen
engineering findings were opened and closed around it**, and the letter's own
text says the thing worth repeating: *do not wait for the gate to pass before
sending this.* Nothing is exposed, nothing will be exposed before the review, and
every gate that defers the letter defers it by another full cycle.

### 13.12 On the process

Five rounds each found their blocking findings on ground the previous round had
no reason to look at. This round found its blocking findings on ground **this
document had already written down as open** — which is a different failure and,
I think, a more instructive one.

Task 10.66's rule worked. §4.19.1 exists because of it, and §4.19.1 is a genuinely
good artifact: it enumerated eight import paths, asked five questions of each,
and got the answers right, including flagging the one that failed this gate as
"Open, and the widest instance of this class." The gap is between *recording a
verdict* and *scheduling the work*. Three paths were marked Open; one of them is
K-1; none of the three has a task. §12.4 did the same thing with K-2 — measured
it, described it precisely, and filed it as discovered scope, where it sat
through a full remediation round.

So the practice §12.11 proposed needs one more clause, and it is the cheap half:
**a finding recorded as open must leave the recording session with a task
number, or it has not been recorded — it has been described.** Both of this
gate's blocking items were described. Both were accurate. Neither was scheduled.

**And one more instance, which is almost too neat to write down.** Task 10.66
adopted "fix the class, not the instance" as a standing acceptance criterion in
commit `58cb20d`. That same commit added `server/backup/backup.sh`'s
check-then-`CREATE ROLE`, which is the exact race task 10.69 then spent a whole
task removing from the Dart path three commits later — reproducing it 30/30 at
8-way concurrency to prove the fix did something. The class was named, adopted
as a rule, and re-instantiated in shell in the same round (K-9). It is a small
finding and I would not raise it except that it is the cleanest available
evidence for what §12.11's practice actually costs to follow: naming a class is
cheap and *searching for it* is the work, and nobody grepped for the second
spelling.

One in the gate's favour, again: reading the detail lines rather than the
verdicts has now caught something at six consecutive gates. This time it was two
of this document's own sentences — §4.19.1's "a file the user chose" and
`splash_screen.dart`'s "non-skippable gate" — each of which was contradicted by
something else already in the repository, and each of which had been read past.
