A removed member's pull, push and directory listing all close from the next request. A refused `Tags` row and a refused `Project_Tags` link each failed to vouch for a later row in the same push, while the legitimate three-row batch (new tag, link, observation) worked. |

### 18.3 N-1 — a contributor may put a teammate's name on a record they never made

> **Closed by task 11.24 on 2026-08-22 — see §19.** The analysis below stands
> as written and is the evidence; two things in it turned out to be narrower
> than the truth, and both are corrected in §19. It names two tables and there
> were three. It treats the fix as an insert-only question and the audit column
> made it an update question too.

**Reproduced live.** A contributor in a project pushes an `Observations` row
whose `user_id` is the project **owner's**. The server answers `inserted`, and
the owner's next pull delivers it: a bearing they never took, in their project,
under their name. The same works for an `Observation_Exclusions` row — a mark
that retires somebody's bearing from the analysis, attributed to a colleague who
did not make that judgement.

**The mechanism is §4.17's clause 2, doing exactly what it says.** The
row-naming invariant permits naming *someone this project already reaches*, on
the reasoning that a person the caller can already pull discloses nothing by
being named again. That reasoning is about **disclosure**, and it is still
correct. §4.17 names a second harm in the same breath — **attribution**,
"fabrication of the primary scientific record" — and says of the *third* clause
that this harm "alone settles which branch survives". Clause 2 was never
measured against it, because in Phase 10 clause 2 had **no reachable
instance**: a project's reach was one person's own devices. §4.17 says so, and
says what would change that: *"task 11.2's invitation record is the provenance
that reopens it."*

**What actually reopened it is not an invitation record.** It is
`Project_Memberships.user_id` landing inside `ProjectReachability`, which puts
every teammate into the vouching set as a side effect of being a teammate. The
provenance §4.17 planned for — *this person was invited to this project, so
their rows may arrive* — is a strictly narrower statement than the one now in
force, and nothing was written down when the wider one took effect.

**Why it does not meet §4's bar.** Read against §15.0's settled reading:

- **Not B3.** The actor must already be a contributor on the project — someone
  the owner deliberately invited and gave the right to record. They gain no
  right they did not have; a contributor can already push arbitrary bearings
  under their own name and move the position estimate exactly as far.
- **Not B2.** Nothing is disclosed. Clause 2's own precondition is that the
  project already reaches the person being named.
- **Not B1, and this is the closest call.** The fabricated row is *visible*:
  the Log and Team tabs show it with the named observer, which is what tasks
  11.4 and 11.5 built. Nothing is destroyed — the original rows are untouched
  (`Observations` stays `MutationRule.author`, and re-attributing a **stored**
  row is refused, verified this run). And it is recoverable: the named author
  can delete a row that names them, and an owner can take any observation out
  of the analysis with an `excluded` mark, which is the remedy task 11.7 built.
- **B4 in letter**, since `row_authorizer.dart`'s own doc says the exemption is
  "narrow enough to stop both" harms and it stops one. By §15.0, B4 blocks when
  what it leaves undefended is B1, B2 or B3. What it leaves undefended is
  attribution among people who are already trusted contributors on the project.

**Why it is nevertheless the one item here that should not simply be accepted.**
Phase 11 built two features whose entire purpose is provenance — the Team log's
"who recorded this" and observer provenance in position estimation — and this
is the one input that makes both of them say something false. The harm is not
theoretical for the people who use this app: field data behind a permit or a
publication is attributed evidence, and a bearing credited to the wrong observer
is a record nobody can defend. **Recorded as scheduled, with the task number to
be assigned by the planning session** (the ask is written out in
`DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md`'s Phase 11 Discovered Scope), rather than as accepted.

**The shape a fix would take, so the decision has something concrete in front
of it.** Clause 2 currently asks *"does this project reach the named person?"*
The narrower question §4.17 originally planned is *"is there an invitation or
membership record showing this person authored data that arrived with this
caller?"* — which is a different query, not a tightening of this one. A blunter
option that costs nothing today: keep clause 2 for `anyUser` rows and drop it
for `author`/`authorOrOwner` rows, so shared project vocabulary still
replicates but **a record that names an author must name the caller**. That
would refuse a legitimate first publish of a colleague's imported observations
— which is exactly the trade §4.17 already accepted for Phase 10 and which
`SyncHeldRowStore` already makes payable — so the cost is known and bounded.
**This is a design decision, not a patch, which is why it is not made here.**

### 18.4 New findings — the register

Every one of these is below §4's bar. They are disposed of here under §5's
rules — triaged once, blocking nothing, with the reason written down.

#### Registered — scheduled

Scheduled is the exception, and there is exactly one.

| ID | Finding | Task | Why scheduled rather than accepted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **N-1** | A contributor can insert an observation, or an exclusion mark, attributed to any teammate — §18.3 | **Task 11.24 — closed 2026-08-22, §19.** Wider than recorded here: the same defect was live on a third table (`Non_Detections`) and through the update path on the audit column | It is not a patch: §4.17's clause 2 has to be either narrowed to a real provenance record or split by rule, and both change what a legitimate first publish may carry. Phase 11 shipped two features whose whole purpose is provenance, and this is the one input that makes both of them say something false. Accepting it would be accepting that the Team log can lie about who took a bearing. |

#### Registered — accepted

| ID | Finding | Reason accepted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **N-2** | An `Observation_Exclusions` row may name an observation in another project, or one that exists nowhere. Measured `inserted` in both cases. | **The reads are project-scoped, so a foreign reference is inert.** Measured both ways, on the wire and in the client, with sabotage-verified tests — see §4.22, which also states the condition the acceptance rests on and names what would void it. The write is *not* constrained and the acceptance does not pretend otherwise. |
| **N-3** | Invitation issuance is unbounded and nothing prunes expired or redeemed invitations. Measured: sixty issued back to back, sixty accepted, sixty stored. | **Storage growth in your own project, by you.** Issuing requires ownership of that project, the stored code is a hash, and the only other content is an address the issuer typed. No disclosure and no loss — §5.6's device/host resource non-goal, on a server that is a laptop in a lab. Redemption, which is the half a stranger reaches, **is** rate limited (measured: 429 after eight attempts). If a cleanup job is ever wanted it is housekeeping, not security. |
| **N-4** | `RowAuthorizer._mayReplicate`'s doc comment says it "requires write access to the project"; the code returns `access.permitsSync`, which is **true for a viewer**. | **Unreachable, and only because of ordering.** `_authorizeRole` refuses a viewer on every project-scoped table before the replication exemption is consulted — measured this run, seven tables plus `Tags`, all refused. Registered rather than fixed silently because the safety is positional: moving or short-circuiting `_authorizeRole` would make the doc comment's claim the live behavior. The comment is wrong; the control is not. Same shape as M-14. |
| **N-5** | The client's role-gated controls default inconsistently while the role is still resolving — `?? true` (permit) in position estimation and observation sharing, `?? false` (refuse) in the map and log screens. | **The advisory layer, per §4.23.** What a permissive default produces is a control that renders enabled and then fails at the tap; the server refuses the write either way. That is task 11.12's usability subject, not a boundary. |
| **N-6** | The client's cached role providers are invalidated only by membership changes made **on this device** (`_afterMembershipChange`), so a role change pushed by another member does not refresh them until something else rebuilds. | **Same reason as N-5**, one step further: the stale answer is the *app's* answer, and the server's is resolved fresh on every request (`ProjectAuthorizer.resolve` has no cross-request cache — verified). A demoted contributor whose screen still offers a control gets a refusal from the server. |
| **N-7** | `Observation_Exclusions` added three unbounded columns in schema v7 — `observation_id`, `superseded_by_observation_id` and `reason` — and **L-7's scheduled fix (task 10.97) enumerates seven columns by name, none of them on this table.** Measured: a 1 MB `observation_id` is `inserted` and delivered to every member. | Accepted **as a finding**; the class is already scheduled. This is not a new defect — it is L-7 exactly, on a table that did not exist when L-7's column list was written, and it is the reason a hand-written column list is the wrong shape. **The action is a scheduling correction, not a task:** ask the planning session to widen 10.97 from a list of columns to a rule derived from `tableSpecs`, so schema v8's table inherits the bound instead of needing someone to remember. Written out in the plan's Discovered Scope. |
| **N-8** | The final last-write-wins tiebreak, when two edits share the same revision and timestamp, is `origin_device_id` compared lexically (`merge_resolver.dart:12-15,42`) — a value a device chooses for itself and stores in plain text, so a device configured to hold a high one wins every tie it is ever party to. Recorded as "probably acceptable" since Phase 10 (§4.12, discovered-scope item 6) with no task number and no named reason — exactly the shape task 10.72 exists to prevent. | **Michael decided 2026-08-22: status quo, accepted, with the reason written down rather than implied.** Winning a tie this way requires already being a trusted contributor on the project — the tiebreak is reached only after both edits pass ordinary authorization, so it is not a privilege escalation, only a preference between two authorized writes. The losing edit is not destroyed: it is captured to the local conflict store before being replaced (`sync_engine.dart:455`, `_recordConflicts`), so the record of what the loser said survives for provenance even though it stops being the live value. And no coordinate or observation content is disclosed by winning or losing a tie — the tiebreak decides which already-authorized value the project sees next, not who may see anything. Task 11.27 (§4.24) gave this its number; nothing about the mechanism changed. |

#### Found and fixed in this task

| ID | Finding | What was done |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **N-8** | **`GATE_SMOKE_SELFTEST=1` left the gate stack running and holding `127.0.0.1:8080`** — which is finding M-12 exactly, in the one branch task 10.108's fix did not reach. Bash keeps a **single** EXIT trap, so the self-test's `trap 'git checkout -- scripts/gate_wire.py' EXIT` silently replaced the `trap _teardown EXIT` installed eighty lines earlier, and no teardown ran at all. Measured, not inferred: after the self-test the containers were still up, `compose-teardown.log` did not exist for that run, and the next stack to want port 8080 failed to bind. | **Fixed here, as the class rather than the instance** (task 10.66's standing rule, which is what M-12's re-appearance is a violation of). There is now **one** EXIT handler, `_cleanup`, which restores `gate_wire.py` when a flag says to and then tears the stack down; the self-test sets the flag instead of installing a second trap, and the comment on `_cleanup` says why a future cleanup is a line inside it rather than another `trap`. No data was ever at risk — this is measurement hygiene — but it is the defect that makes the *next* run's result untrustworthy, which is what M-12 cost the eighth gate. **Verified by re-running the self-test on the fix**: it printed `Tearing down: …`, no container survived, and `gate_wire.py` came back clean, where the run before the fix left two containers up and produced no teardown log at all. The bash semantics behind it are one line: `trap f EXIT; trap 'echo restore' EXIT` runs only `restore`. |

#### Chased and not reproduced

- **A non-string reference crashing a reader.** `observation_id` accepts a JSON
  integer and even a nested object, both answered `inserted` — but nothing
  breaks downstream, and the reason is the same on both sides: Postgres binds
  the parameter into a `TEXT` column and SQLite's TEXT column affinity converts
  a numeric value to text on insert, so the value read back is always a string.
  `ObservationExclusion.fromRow`'s cast holds. Traced and measured rather than
  assumed. A control character in the same column **is** refused
  (`RowValidator`'s primary-key/identity shape rules do not cover it, but the
  database does) — reported as `invalid`, not as a `500`.
- **A refused row vouching for a later one in the same push.** §4.21.3's class,
  re-attacked in both spellings — a refused foreign `Tags` row and a refused
  `Project_Tags` link, each followed in the same batch by an observation naming
  that tag. Both refused, and the tag was still not delivered. The legitimate
  three-row batch works, which is the control. **The tag half of this stopped
  being reachable in task 11.219**: a tag is project-scoped, so nothing has to
  vouch for one and `_establishedThisPush` is deleted. The membership sets
  below are the whole of the within-push bookkeeping now.
- **`_membershipsGrantedThisPush` and `_ownershipsRemovedThisPush`.** Both
  re-derived and both attacked: two membership rows for one person in one
  publish drew `inserted` + `unauthorized`; one push ending **both** owner
  memberships drew `updated` + `unauthorized` and left the project with exactly
  one owner. The plan's note that the first set's safety "is not structural"
  still holds, and the direction is still the safe one — an extra refusal, never
  an extra grant.
- **Any other per-push state an earlier row could set.** `RowAuthorizer` holds
  six pieces: `_reachable`, `_accountEmails`, `_ownershipByProject`,
  `_establishedThisPush`, `_ownershipsRemovedThisPush`,
  `_membershipsGrantedThisPush`, plus the constant `access`. (Five since task
  11.219, which deleted `_establishedThisPush` with the tag reachability it
  existed for.) The first three are
  read-through snapshots that a push cannot widen — the only rows that would
  widen `_reachable`'s user set are membership rows and rows naming a stranger,
  and both are refused — so their staleness is strictly in the **refusing**
  direction. The one direction they are stale permissively is an owner who,
  inside one push, resigns and also does owner things; they were an owner when
  the push began, so that is not an escalation.
- **The diagnostics console's conditional verdict (§4.21.2).** Confirmed still
  conditional and still satisfied: both project routes sit behind one pipeline
  that requires a real loopback TCP peer **and** the operator token compared in
  constant time, and there is no per-user session anywhere in that router, so
  there is still no user identity to isolate one project *for*. The day it
  grows one, this is a live cross-project gap.
- **§5.10's accepted residual** — a viewer who clears the app and restores an
  archive of a project they may only read. Attacked rather than rediscovered,
  and it holds exactly as written: the client abstains (no membership rows, so
  clause 6 permits) and every one of that viewer's project rows is refused at
  the server, one table at a time, measured this run. The divergence stays on
  their own device.
- **§5.9(a)'s orphan-tag residual**, re-measured at the time: an outsider who
  knows an unlinked tag's id cannot overwrite it (the stored author stamp
  refuses them) but **can** link it into a project of their own, and did.
  **Closed by task 11.219 on 2026-09-10** — there is no orphan `Tags` row to
  reach: `project_id` is `NOT NULL` and half the primary key, so a tag row
  cannot exist without a project, and adding a tag to a project copies it
  rather than linking a shared one. See §5.9(a) for what that deleted.
- **§5.9(b)'s id-list columns**, re-measured against a real second project: an
  estimate citing another project's observation, project and user ids, and a
  non-detection listing another project's tag id, are both stored — and neither
  delivers one row of that project. The condition the acceptance rests on holds,
  and `assertSealedColumnsFeedNoReachability` (named
  `assertUnvalidatedIdListColumnsFeedNoReachability` until task 11.219) is the
  tripwire on it.

### 18.5 What holds, re-verified rather than assumed

Every entry on §3's existing inventory that the team surface touches was
re-attacked rather than carried:

- **§4.17, the row-naming invariant** — six fresh refusals across four tables:
  rewriting a teammate's name on their own `Users` row; writing address history
  for them; naming a stranger the project cannot reach on an `Observations`
  row; re-attributing a **stored** observation; a contributor adding an
  outsider to the project; and the project's own **owner** pushing a membership
  row for somebody else — the last two being the authorization-state half,
  which gets no exemption at all. **Two successes, which are N-1**, and both are
  inserts of a *new* field-data row under the clause-2 exemption.
- **§4.18, the email-claim invariant** — two fresh refusals: pointing a
  teammate's `Users` row at the attacker's own address, and claiming a
  teammate's address as the attacker's own prior one, which is the shape that
  would make the client merger fuse two people into one.
- **§4.13, uniform errors** — a fictional project and a forbidden one answered
  byte-identical `403`s on the new invitation routes.
- **§4.11, scope comes from the session** — one project's owner naming another
  project's invitation id on the revoke route changed nothing, and the target
  invitation was still pending afterwards (checked, not assumed).
- **§4.21, the role gradient** — measured on the wire across every
  project-scoped table, in both directions.

### 18.6 The instruments

`scripts/gate_smoke_test.sh` ran the whole stack of them against a live server:
**14/14 PASS**, the new one included. Two results are worth pulling out because
they are what stops this run being self-referential.

- **The adversarial pass matched its committed baseline exactly** — 36 held, 4
  failed, and the four are `Ce2`, `Dc`, `Dh` and `Eb`, the same four as at §16.
  No new failure, and none of the four has started passing. That is the check
  that would have caught this task breaking something elsewhere.
- **The new instrument is inside the harness, not beside it.** It is registered
  in `gate_smoke_test.sh`'s run list **and** in that file's `WIRE_INSTRUMENTS`,
  which is what makes the forced stale-`schema_major` self-test assert that it
  aborts — and which checks list membership in *both* directions, so deleting
  the `run_instrument` line for it would go red rather than quietly shrink the
  summary. Task 10.54 added an instrument to the list and not to the check, and
  §11.5 is what that cost; this one is in both from the first commit.

Verified two ways, because a claim about an instrument should not rest on the
instrument. By hand: bumping `SCHEMA_MAJOR` by 1000 makes
`verify_11_9_team_surface.py` exit on `PREFLIGHT ABORT` rather than run its
eighteen probes against a server it never reached. And through the harness:
`GATE_SMOKE_SELFTEST=1` reported **"all 8 wire-speaking instruments ran and
caught the forced-stale constant"** — eight, where every previous run of that
sentence said seven.

### 18.6.1 A note on what an instrument is worth here

Two of this run's positive controls caught **the instrument** rather than the
server, during development: a wrong enum value in the observation fixture and
three wrong column names in three table fixtures each produced a `BLIND`
control. Under the pre-control design every one of those would have printed
`refused` — a probe pushing a row the server rejected as malformed, reported as
the authorization control holding. That is precisely the failure §16 found three
of, and it is why "every instrument needs a positive control firing in the same
run" is a rule rather than a suggestion.

### 18.7 On the process

The stopping rule worked, and this is the first run where that can be said
without qualification. Eighteen probes produced one open finding, six accepted
register entries and seven chased-and-refuted claims — and **the run reached a
verdict**, because a below-bar finding is now written down rather than argued
about. Two of the six accepted entries (N-5, N-6) would have been findings under
the pre-§4 regime and cost a round each; §4.23 now answers both by naming the
property once instead of per feature, which is what task 11.11 asked for.

The one thing worth flagging about the method: **N-1 was not found by attacking
the inventory.** It was found by reading §4.17's own account of why its third
clause was removed, noticing that the argument applied to the surviving clause
under a condition Phase 11 had just created, and then going to look. The
inventory tells you where to point the instrument; the document's own reasoning
is what tells you which of its claims has quietly stopped being true.

## 19. Task 11.24 — N-1 closed, and the owner-only rules the server was never told (2026-08-22)

Two questions, one task, because they share every fixture and the same
judgement: **what does the server actually enforce, as against what somebody
has claimed it does?** Task 11.26 was merged into this one for that reason.

Everything below was measured against a running stack over raw HTTP before it
was changed, and again after. The instrument is
`scripts/verify_11_24_attribution.py`; it derives the affected table set from
`tableMutationRules` rather than carrying a list, and **aborts rather than
running** if a table names an author and has no probe.

### 19.1 The decision, and why the plan's lean survived contact with the code

`DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md`'s entry offered two shapes and leaned to (b) — *a record
that names an author must name the caller* — while instructing that the lean be
**measured, not adopted**, and reversed if the legitimate traffic it refuses
turned out to be large.

**It was measured. (b) is taken.** The measurement is what settles it, and the
number that matters is not the one the entry anticipated:

| What writes a record naming an author | Author is | Rows | How often | Refused now? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Recording a bearing | the signed-in user | 1 | constantly | no |
| Recording a non-detection | the signed-in user | 1 | constantly | no |
| Superseding or excluding | the signed-in user | 1 | occasionally | no |
| Editing your own record | the signed-in user | 1 | occasionally | no |
| Receiving teammates' rows through sync | — | page | continuously | no (receipts stop a re-offer) |
| Pasting a shared observation | the sender | 1 | several a day while triangulating | **yes** |
| Importing a project archive, or restoring one | the file | 10²–10⁴ | rare | **yes** |
| First publish of a project that absorbed either | mixed | whole project | once | **yes** |
| A loaner device after a second person signs in | the previous holder | their history | plausible | **yes** |

**Ordinary field work sends nothing to the held store.** There is no "recorded
by" picker anywhere in this app; every construction site sets the author to the
current user. What (b) refuses is a device **relaying** somebody else's
records — and in three of those four cases the author is a project member whose
own device pushes the same record, with the same identity, so the relayed copy
resolves to a no-op when it does.

So the plan's lean was right, but **not for the reason it gave.** It expected
the cost to be "the first publish of a colleague's imported observations", a
trade §4.17 had already accepted. The real shape is that the cost is **zero on
the path that runs every day** and bursty on four paths that are all relays.
That is a stronger argument for (b) than the one written down, and it is only
visible from the code.

**Option (a) — narrow clause 2 to a real provenance record — is rejected, and
the reason is the one the plan gave:** it is a new query and a new mechanism,
and nine rounds of evidence on this project say new mechanisms are where
findings come from. (b) reuses a trade §4.17 already accepted and a hold path
task 10.28 already built.

**A server-stamped "delivered by" value was considered as a companion and is
not being built.** It would make a legitimate cross-author row honest, but
§18.3's own caution is the deciding one: task 11.9 confirmed the fabricated row
is *delivered* with the victim's name on it and explicitly did **not** confirm
that anybody would notice it among a season's observations. A column nothing
renders is not visibility, and a fix whose load-bearing part is "somebody will
see it" is the weakest link in this finding's argument, not the strongest. It
stays available if a case for it ever needs one; it is not a substitute for the
refusal.

### 19.2 The update path is covered, and that was the time-sensitive half

Task 11.23 warned that the preferred shape, applied on insert only, would leave
task 11.18's *"…then withdrawn by *name*"* sentence forgeable — the audit
column is reachable through the **update** path, which permits a name that
merely matches what is already stored.

**The fix covers updates.** `last_modified_by` must name the caller on any
update that changes the stored row. Nothing legitimate is refused: a push that
reaches this check has already been established to change the row, so it is an
act, and the actor is the caller. It costs one thing and gains three:

- It closes 11.18's sentence at its root rather than at one table.
- It closes the audit column on **every** table at once, including
  `Tags.last_modified_by` — which task 11.23 found is read back as an
  *authorization input* (it decides who may maintain an unclaimed tag), and
  which is described in the code as "provenance that references nothing".
- It is not a new judgement. §4.19 rule 2 already decided this on the client's
  own untrusted-import path, in `ProjectMerger._patchFor`, with the reason *"a
  forgeable audit column is the worse trade."*

The one thing it costs: an instrument and two suites had rows that withdrew a
mark while leaving the author's name on the withdrawal. Each was corrected to
stamp its pusher, which is what a real device does.

### 19.3 Task 11.26's class — reproduced, judged, and swept

**The known instance, reproduced live before anything was fixed.** A
contributor pushed a `Project_Tags` row with `status` set to `inactive` and the
server answered `updated`. The tag was gone for the whole team. The same
contributor pushed a **tombstone** on that link and the server answered
`updated` again — a route the app has no button for at all, so the server was
accepting something strictly worse than the operation the app gates.

#### The bar judgement, stated out loud

**It meets §4's bar: B4 → B3.** This is the first finding since the eighth run
to do so. It changes no decision — Gate C is already shut on the NAU review
(§14.13) — and it is recorded as blocking anyway, because a finding that meets
the bar and gets filed as "the clearest thing to fix" is how the register
becomes a lie.

The reasoning, against §15.0's settled reading:

- **B4 in letter.** §4.21 states the role gradient as a security decision, and
  task 11.12 put deactivating a project's tag link on the owner rung with a
  stated reason (subtractive; it edits shared configuration every member sees).
  §4.23 states that the app's checks are advisory and the server is the
  boundary. A rule that exists only on the device is, by §4.23's own words, not
  enforced. So a control this model asserts did not fire.
- **B4 blocks when what it leaves undefended is B1, B2 or B3.** What it leaves
  undefended is a contributor performing an owner-only, team-visible,
  subtractive write at the server — **privilege escalation**, which is B3's
  territory. Same shape as L-1 (B4→B3), which is §15.0's own worked example.
- **Not B1.** Nothing irreplaceable is destroyed and nothing is silent: the
  observations referencing the tag are untouched, the link is reversible by
  re-adding it (a contributor-level act), and a tag vanishing from every
  member's picker is the opposite of unnoticed.
- **Not B2.** Removing a link narrows what a project reaches; it discloses
  nothing.

**Why this is B3 where N-1 is not**, since the two look alike and §18.3 argued
the other way: with N-1 the contributor gains **no right they did not have** —
they could already push arbitrary bearings under their own name and move the
estimate exactly as far. Here they gain a right the project deliberately
reserved to owners. That difference is the whole of it.

#### The sweep — every owner-only rule the app claims

Derived from the permissions matrix and from every `throw UnauthorizedMutation`
site in the app, then checked against the server one at a time. Nine of the
twelve owner-only claims already had a server twin and were re-measured rather
than assumed. Three did not:

| Claim | Server before | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Only an owner may take a tag out of a project | **not enforced** | `RowAuthorizer._authorizeProjectTagRemoval`, both the status change and the tombstone |
| Only an owner may withdraw an `excluded` mark | **enforced against the wrong value** | see below |
| Only an owner may publish a project | **not enforceable** | see §19.4 |

**The second one is a check that could be made not to fire, which §4's B4
names explicitly.** `_authorizeExclusionKind` read `incoming['kind']` — a value
the caller chose — where the client reads the stored row. Reproduced live: a
demoted owner's honest withdrawal of their own `excluded` mark answered
`unauthorized`, and the *same* withdrawal with `kind` flipped to `superseded`
in the same row answered `updated`. One row that both escaped the owner rung
and rewrote what the mark said it was. It now judges the stored kind and the
incoming one, and refuses if either is `excluded`.

The client never had this defect, which is §4.23's asymmetry running in the
unusual direction: **the boundary was the looser of the two.** Worth recording,
because §4.23 is written as though the risk only ever runs the other way.

### 19.4 Publishing a project is not a server-enforceable rule, and the record should say so

The app gates the Publish button on ownership. The server's only condition is
that the project id is not taken and that the `Projects` row names the caller
as owner — which the matrix already documents (row P1).

**Reproduced live**: a contributor holding a copy of somebody else's
unpublished project (which is what an archive import or a share leaves behind)
published it under their own name, and the genuine owner's next attempt on the
same project id drew `403 forbidden` — permanently, since a project id is the
primary key of every row that belongs to it and this app has no re-keying
operation.

**There is no server-side fix, and that is the finding.** For a project the
server has never seen there is no evidence that distinguishes its real owner
from somebody holding a copy: every row in the batch, memberships included, is
self-asserted. The server cannot answer the question, so a check here would be
a control that cannot fail — the shape §4's B4 warns about — rather than a
control.

**Recorded as an accepted risk rather than scheduled**, with the reason above,
and flagged to the planning session because the acceptance is Michael's to
make, not this task's. It is bounded by needing to already hold the project:
project ids are v4 UUIDs and are not guessable.

### 19.5 What is now asserted, and where

- `scripts/verify_11_24_attribution.py` — live, over raw HTTP. Derives its
  table set from the rule definitions; aborts if an author-naming table has no
  probe; every attack paired with a positive control that must be accepted.
- `scripts/verify_11_9_team_surface.py` — **its baseline is now empty.** It
  held N-1's two entries; both are refused, so both were removed rather than
  left as "known". That script fails a run in which either starts being
  admitted *and* fails a run in which a baselined item starts being refused, so
  the register and the build cannot silently disagree in either direction.
- `server/test/authz/authorization_test.dart` — the derived-coverage assertion
  (`every author-naming table has a case here`), which has been **watched to
  fail**: removing one table's case turns it red and names the table.
- `server/test/integration/membership_and_joining_test.dart` — the §4.17
  before/after pin, corrected. An invitation still opens naming for shared
  project vocabulary and now explicitly does **not** for a record that names an
  author.

### 19.6 What this leaves open

- **The held-row list has no cap.** `SyncHeldRowStore.held()` has no limit and
  the sync status screen renders one card per row. Refusals were rare; an
  archive import can now produce thousands, and a screen that is truthful and
  unreadable is the shape already recorded for the consent dialog and the
  conflict queue (task 10.87). This is its third instance and 10.87's brief
  does not cover it.
- **The publish-seizure acceptance in §19.4** needs Michael's decision, not a
  task.
- **A forged `last_modified_by` on an *insert* into a shared table** is still
  permitted, deliberately: refusing it would break the first publish of a
  project whose tags a colleague created, and a held `Tags` row cascades into
  every observation that references it. `Tags.last_modified_by` is therefore
  still forgeable at creation time, which hands maintenance of an *unclaimed*
  tag to the named person — a nuisance and a self-inflicted lockout, not
  attribution of a scientific record. Recorded rather than fixed.

## 20. Task 11.49 — the server's two reads, attacked (2026-08-29)

**What this is.** Inventory entries **27** (`GET /auth/sessions`) and **28**
(the closed-membership disclosure on `POST /sync/pull`) both carried an `Open`
verdict, because both were added to `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §3 *before*
anything attacked them — the right discipline, and the reason Gate C's
criterion 1 could not be met even with the NAU letter in hand. This is the
attack. **Both are now Hardened.**

**Why they needed a pass of their own.** Every attack the server inventory
records was aimed at a **mutation** — can this caller write a row they should
not. These two are **reads**, and a read fails differently: it corrupts
nothing, it *tells somebody something*. So every probe below is
disclosure-shaped. It asks what crossed and to whom.

### 20.1 What was run

| | Result |
| --- | --- |
| **`scripts/verify_11_49_server_reads.py`** (new) | **115 checks against a live stack: every attack refused, every positive control fired, every discriminator proved it could see a difference.** Clean on every run against the unmodified server, including the three consecutive repetitions used to confirm the timing probe is not flaky and two runs inside `gate_smoke_test.sh`. **Every one of those runs was on a Mac** — the same probe on a clean Linux runner found a real difference the next day (§20.3's overturn, task 11.72) |
| **`scripts/verify_11_49_broken_control.py`** (new) | **27 of 27 required attacks flipped to ADMITTED** against three deliberately broken servers, and the same instrument came back clean against the real one in the same run |
| `flutter test` | **1519 passed, 12 skipped, exit 0** — 1 m 12 s |
| Server suite, against real Postgres (`run_server_tests_docker.sh`) | **722 passed, zero failures, zero skips** — 1 m 02 s |
| `scripts/gate_smoke_test.sh` | **16/16 instruments PASS** — two of them added by this task, and the run was red before it on a defect nobody had noticed (P-6). 3 m 21 s |
| `GATE_SMOKE_SELFTEST=1 scripts/gate_smoke_test.sh` | **all 10 wire-speaking instruments aborted on `PREFLIGHT ABORT`** with a forced stale `schema_major` — ten rather than eight, because the set is now derived from the filesystem (P-3). `gate_wire.py` restored from the committed blob on exit, verified with `git status` |
| `flutter test test/e2e --tags e2e --run-skipped` | **60 passed** — 29 s |

**This was not a gate run and does not claim to be one.** It did not run
`scripts/run_offline_suite.sh`, did not re-audit task statuses, and did not
re-attack entries 14–20 or 23–26. What it did is give the two entries that had
no verdict one, and price what a real run now costs
(`SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §6.1).

### 20.2 Entry 27 — `GET /auth/sessions`

**Hardened, 2026-08-29.** Probes 1–6 of the instrument: **58 attacks, every one
attempted against a live server over raw HTTP and every one refused**, alongside
16 positive controls and 4 discriminators.

| Probe | Attacks that failed |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — make it answer for somebody else** | A victim's `user_id` in the query string; in the query string beside a `device_id`; in a `GET` body; in `X-User-Id`, `X-Forwarded-User`, a bare `user-id`, `On-Behalf-Of` and `X-Impersonate`; in a cookie; repeated twice in case only the first is read; array-shaped (`user_id[]`); the same id via `POST`; as a path segment (`404`, and no listing in the body); behind a `../` traversal. **Two session tokens presented at once** — sent as genuinely duplicated `Authorization` headers, which is why this instrument speaks `http.client` rather than `urllib`: `urllib` silently collapses them and would have scored the attack against whichever credential survived. A forged `device_id` trying to move `is_current_device` onto another row. A bit-flipped, truncated, extended, invented and wrong-kind token; no header, an empty bearer, a bare token, `Basic`, a lower-cased scheme. **Twelve of these are proven non-vacuous** — see §20.4 |
| **2 — what a row carries** | A field beyond the five the design names; the caller's session token, a second device's token, the SHA-256 the server actually stores, the first twenty characters of a token, the caller's email, the caller's `user_id`, a server-side `session_id` (compared against the real ones read out of Postgres), anything shaped like an IPv4 or IPv6 address. **The no-source-address decision is attacked rather than read**: the server *does* hold an address for the same caller in `auth_audit_log`, so the route's silence is a decision and not an absence of data. **Another person's existence:** a real `user_id` and a fictional one draw the same answer; and a second account signing in on a device id spelled identically to the caller's, once before and once after, moves neither `min(created_at)` nor `max(expires_at)` on the caller's row. `cache-control: no-store` present |
| **3 — the bound** | 150 further live sessions seeded for one account (**fixture, written straight into Postgres** — the front door caps one address at three magic links per fifteen minutes and ten per day, so this state is unreachable through it in one run). The listing came back with exactly **100** rows for 151 live sessions. A `limit` in the query string, in the body, and a negative one each failed to raise it. **The truncation does not hide the caller's own device**, which would leave somebody unable to tell which row to keep |
| **4 — the per-user rate limit** | 65 reads from one signed-in caller: **60 accepted, then `429`**, the refusal carrying no listing, and an audit row written. A second signed-in caller was unaffected. **An unauthenticated flood of 65 bad tokens did not spend a named user's bucket** — which is what checking the limit *after* authentication buys |
| **5 — revocation** | The revoked device left the list **on the very next request**, and its token stopped working on the very next request — not on a timer. Its row is still in Postgres, so the absence is the query filtering rather than the row being gone. Revoking a `device_id` belonging to **somebody else** revoked nothing (`sessions_revoked: 0`) and left that person's session working, which is the §4.11 claim that `device_id` is a selector inside an already-authorized scope. `revoke-all` then closed the caller's own listing |
| **6 — rows that outlive their session** | An expired session and one idle past `sessionIdleLifetime` are both absent from the listing and both refused as credentials, while all three rows are present in the database |

**The bound and the limit are read from the Dart source, not typed into the
instrument** — `maxListedSessions` and `RateLimitPolicy.sessionListPerUser` are
parsed out of `auth_service.dart` and `rate_limiter.dart`, so a probe cannot go
on passing against a server that changed them. Same premise as `gate_wire.py`.

### 20.3 Entry 28 — the closed-membership disclosure

**Hardened, 2026-08-29.** Probes 7–11: **31 attacks, all refused**, alongside 3
positive controls and 3 discriminators.

| Probe | Attacks that failed |
| --- | --- |
| **7 — the exemption as an existence oracle** | §4.27's property, measured rather than read. The prober is somebody who **can** reach the disclosure (they hold a closed stint on one project) asking about ids they hold no row for: a fictional project and a real one belonging to a stranger returned **byte-identical** answers — status, stable headers and body bytes. So did a caller who can never reach the branch at all, and the two kinds of caller got the same refusal as each other. Each compared response carries its own `x-trace-id`, which is how the run knows it compared two round trips and not one cached answer |
| **8 — manufacturing the key** | §4.27 claim 1 is that the exemption fires on a row only the server can produce. A removed member writing themselves a closed membership on a stranger's real project, and on a fictional one; a member of another project doing the same; both refused, and neither changed what either id answers afterwards. **An owner planting a `role` string this build cannot interpret** — the fail-closed leftover task 11.60 recorded — draws a per-row `invalid` outcome, so that state is **not reachable from this side of the wire** (§20.5) |
| **9 — what crosses** | One table and no other; only the caller's own rows; no open stint; `remaining: 0`; the cursor handed straight back; `server_seq`, `received_at` and `clock_skew_flag` all stripped; no `Users` row for the account that ended the stint; no `Projects` row, so not the project's name. A huge `batch_size`, a cursor past the end, a negative cursor and a cursor of one all returned the same one page. A `user_id` and a foreign `device_id` in the pull body were both ignored |
| **10 — still a refusal** | A removed member cannot push to the project, cannot acknowledge the page they were handed, does not see the project in `/projects/mine`, and cannot read its invitations. The disclosure is audited as its own kind of denial (`pull_membership_closed`) rather than blending into the flat refusals |
| **11 — how large the page can be made** | The disclosure query carries no `LIMIT`. An owner pushing twenty further closed stints for the same person had **all twenty refused `unauthorized`**, so what bounds this page is what may be written, not what may be read. Recorded as **P-4**, accepted |

#### The timing claim task 11.60 left unmeasured — now measured

Task 11.60 equalised the *query count* between "this project does not exist"
and "this project is not yours" and **said plainly that it never measured
whether the difference had been detectable.** Two gates had walked past the
underlying gap. It is measured now, on loopback — the most favourable ground an
attacker will ever get, and `/sync/pull` carries no per-user rate limit, so
nothing bounds how many samples they may take.

**A threshold on two medians is not the measurement, and the first version of
this probe proved it**: comparing `|median(absent) − median(forbidden)|`
against a fraction of the median went red on a clean server roughly one run in
three. The machine's own drift over a few seconds is larger than any effect
here, so that test was measuring the laptop. What separates a real difference
from drift is whether it has a **stable sign**: a branch that genuinely costs
more is slower in nearly every trial, and drift is slower in about half.

So: nine independent trials, a hundred interleaved rounds each, with the three
ids **rotated within every round** so none is systematically last. Two of the
three are fictional, which makes that pair a null whose true difference is
exactly zero — and that null is the discriminator: if its sign were unanimous
too, the run would be drift-dominated and would have measured nothing.

**Three consecutive runs on this host:**

| | forbidden − fictional | fictional − fictional (true zero) | per-request spread |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| run 1 | **+0.048 ms**, positive in 5/9 trials | −0.025 ms, positive in 4/9 | 8.13 ms |
| run 2 | **−0.000 ms**, positive in 5/9 | −0.021 ms, positive in 3/9 | 23.97 ms |
| run 3 | **+0.009 ms**, positive in 4/9 | +0.009 ms, positive in 5/9 | 18.25 ms |

**Verdict: this is no longer an unmeasured claim, and it is an acceptable
one.** The difference between the two answers is of the same size as the
difference between two measurements of the *same* answer — hundredths of a
millisecond — its sign is not stable, and a single request carries hundreds of
times more noise than the whole effect. Over a network, which is the only place
a real attacker stands, every one of those numbers gets worse for them.

**What this does not claim.** It is a measurement of this host, not a proof
about the algorithm; and the probe would report a *stable* sign if one appeared,
which is the thing to watch. It did exactly that against the deliberately broken
build in §20.4, where the refusal branch really does run one more query — so the
test is not vacuous.

> **Overturned, 2026-08-30, by the same probe on a different machine (task
> 11.72).** The verdict above — "the sign is not stable, and this is
> acceptable" — was produced on a developer's Mac, and its own last paragraph
> named the escape hatch it went through: *a measurement of this host.* Run on
> a clean Linux runner the identical probe reported **+0.052, +0.061 and
> +0.049 ms with the sign positive in 9 of 9 trials on each of three runs**,
> while the null pair flipped sign every time. The three tables above are the
> right method applied to a host that could not resolve the effect. **The
> conclusion to carry forward is not about timing: it is that "measured" is a
> claim about a machine, and this project has now made the wrong-machine
> mistake four times in three days.** The cause, the fix and the far more
> sensitive instrument that replaced this one are written up in §4.13 under
> "The clock is a channel too."

### 20.4 Watched to fail — task 10.66's standing criterion

**A check that cannot distinguish success from its own failure is not a check**,
and a run in which every attack is refused is exactly what a blind instrument
produces. This project has shipped three of those.

`scripts/verify_11_49_broken_control.py` builds a throwaway git worktree, patches
the **server** in three different places, brings each variant up as its own
compose project, and requires named attacks to flip from `refused` to
`ADMITTED`. The working tree is never touched. **The pairing is what makes it
evidence:** the same instrument, in the same run, is also required to come back
clean against the unmodified server — a clean run alone could be blindness, and
a red run alone could be a broken probe.

| Variant | What was removed | Required to flip | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **scope** | `GET /auth/sessions` stops scoping its query to the caller | 12 | **12 flipped**, plus 2 more. Every one of the redirect probes went `ADMITTED`, so all eleven of them can see a cross-user leak |
| **shape** | The row grows a `user_id` and a `source_address`; the 100-row bound and the per-user rate limit stop refusing; revoked and expired sessions stop being filtered | 9 | **9 flipped**, plus 4 more |
| **disclosure** | The refusal becomes a `404`-versus-`403` existence oracle; the disclosure stops being scoped to the caller and to ended stints; it stops stripping the server's own bookkeeping | 6 | **6 flipped**, plus 4 more, including the timing probe — which is direct evidence that the sign test in §20.3 is not vacuous |

**Two of the variants had to be written twice, and the corrections are the
useful part.** A first attempt deleted SQL predicates outright, leaving bare
`$2 IS NOT NULL` clauses Postgres cannot type — so the route answered `500` to
everything and the variant broke *itself* rather than the control it named. A
second left `received_at` (a `TIMESTAMPTZ`) in the response, which cannot be
JSON-encoded, with the same result. **A deliberately broken control that breaks
in the wrong place proves nothing**, and both were caught only because the
harness demands specific probes flip rather than accepting "it went red".

The third correction is the one worth remembering: the oracle variant is wired
the **unnatural way round** — `404` for a project that exists, `403` for one
that does not. The natural direction makes `gate_wire.preflight`, which pulls a
random and therefore fictional project id before anything else, abort the
instrument before a single probe is scored. A variant that never runs measures
nothing.

### 20.5 The fail-closed leftover — a verdict, as task 11.60 asked

**Accepted.** If a `Project_Memberships` row carries a `role` string this build
cannot interpret, the person holding it has an *open* stint, no access, and no
disclosure — they see "the server is refusing access" rather than "you were
removed".

- **It is not reachable from this side of the wire**, and that is measured
  rather than assumed: an owner pushing a row with `role: "supervisor"` gets a
  per-row `invalid` outcome. Reaching this state needs a server running a build
  that knows a role this client does not.
- **It fails closed.** Nobody gains access; the cost is a less specific error
  message, in a version-skewed deployment.
- It meets no clause of §4's bar: nothing is lost (their local copy is intact),
  nothing is disclosed, nothing is escalated. As B4-via-B1–B3 it leaves
  undefended only the *specificity of a message*.
- **What would change this:** the release that first adds a role must ship the
  client-side handling in the same release. That is a release-discipline note,
  not a task.

### 20.6 What the app shows when it cannot name the account that removed somebody

The planning session asked this on 2026-08-29, on the reasoning that **a bare
internal identifier shown to a person is not an acceptable answer** — it is a raw
value on a screen, and it confirms that an account exists without naming it.

**Read out of the code: the app never shows that account at all.**
`sync_status_screen.dart`'s `membershipEnded` copy says *"You're no longer a
member of this project… That is expected if you left it, or if an owner removed
you"* — it names neither the account nor the date. The `last_modified_by` value
arrives, is merged into the local row, and is not rendered on this path. So the
unresolvable-name case cannot produce a bare identifier here, because there is no
place on this screen where a name would go.

**Stated as a limit rather than a clean bill:** this is a reading of the one
screen the disclosure drives, not a sweep of every surface that renders an
edited-by name. If a later task puts "removed by <name>" on that screen, the
unresolvable case becomes real and this paragraph is where to start.

### 20.7 Findings — six, and none meets the bar

**Lettered `P-`, skipping `O-`**, because `O-1` and `0-1` are the same shape on
a screen and this document is read under pressure. `L-`, `M-` and `N-` are the
three preceding rounds.

| ID | Finding | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **P-1** | **`GET /projects/mine` has been attacked as a route and never as a read.** It has been asked whether it is session-scoped, whether a revoked session reaches it and whether a removed member still sees a project (round 8; task 11.9 probe 10). It has never been asked the questions §3 says a read must answer: nothing measures that a caller-supplied `user_id` is ignored, nothing states which fields a row may carry (it returns `owner_user_id`, another person's identifier), the query carries **no `LIMIT`**, there is **no per-user rate limit** on it — unlike `/auth/sessions`, which got one under task 10.56's standard treatment — and it does not set `cache-control: no-store`, which the sessions listing does | **Scheduled — needs a task number from the planning session.** Below the bar: it is an authenticated route, the scope check is the one thing that *has* been measured, and the harm on the unbounded half is resource use rather than disclosure. **Not attacked here, deliberately** — `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §6's stopping rule says to record it and stop, and eight gates went the other way |
| **P-2** | **Three documents and one source comment cited `server/test/security/existence_oracle_test.dart`, which has never existed.** The test is real and thorough; its file is `closed_membership_disclosure_test.dart` | **Fixed by this task.** A citation to a file nobody can open is a claim nobody can check, which is the same shape as a comment describing a mechanism the code does not have |
| **P-3** | **`scripts/verify_11_24_attribution.py` was in neither of `gate_smoke_test.sh`'s lists**, from the day it landed (2026-08-22) until today. It speaks the sync wire, so between gates nothing ran it and nothing would have noticed a stale envelope in it — **N-1's closure had no automated re-run at all.** It is the third instrument this has happened to; the file's own comments already record the first two, and task 10.65's fix could not catch it because that check is built out of the same hand-written lists | **Fixed by this task, at the class rather than the instance** (task 10.66). `gate_smoke_test.sh` now **derives** the wire-speaking set from the filesystem — a `scripts/*.py` that imports `gate_wire` and calls `preflight` *is* one — and fails the run if any such file never ran. It runs on every invocation, not only under `GATE_SMOKE_SELFTEST`, because a coverage gap visible only in a mode nobody runs between gates is the gap itself |
| **P-4** | **The closed-membership disclosure query carries no `LIMIT`.** Task 10.56 made bounding every route the standing rule rather than bounding the ones somebody thought were risky | **Accepted.** Measured, not assumed: an owner's attempt to push twenty further closed stints for the same person was refused twenty times over, so the page is bounded by what may be *written*, and every row on it is the caller's own. If a future task ever makes multiple closed stints writable, this becomes a real bound to add |
| **P-5** | **The adversarial pass's own timing check `Cg` measured the machine, not the server — and failed a live gate run doing it.** It compared the median of twelve consecutive requests to a real project against twelve to a fictional one and failed on a 50% difference: no interleaving, twelve samples, no null. Run under `gate_smoke_test.sh` on 2026-08-29 it reported `real 46.3ms vs fictional 4.3ms` and stopped the gate as an **unbaselined finding**, while a rotated, interleaved measurement of the same two answers put the difference at hundredths of a millisecond with no stable sign. Repeated ten times by hand it failed once more — in the run where the *fictional* id was measured first, which is the opposite of a real effect | **Fixed by this task**, to the shape §20.3 describes: rotated ids, a fictional-versus-fictional null, pass/fail on sign stability, and `INCONCLUSIVE` rather than `HELD` when the null's own sign is unanimous. **A check that cannot fail honestly is the same class as one that cannot fail at all**, and this one would have blocked the next gate at random while proving nothing |
| **P-6** | **`gate_smoke_test.sh` has been red since 2026-08-28 and nobody ran it.** `verify_instrument_unchecked_returns` — the linter task 10.65 added for exactly this class — flags `scripts/dev_magic_link.sh:78`, where a `grep` failure and "no match" are collapsed into one empty result. Task 11.37 introduced it the previous day | **Fixed by this task.** The site is genuinely safe (the input is already checked non-empty, the pattern is constant, and the branch *reports* rather than passing), so it carries a `# swallow-reviewed:` tag with that reasoning rather than a rewrite. **The finding is not the tag — it is the day between a gate instrument going red and anybody noticing**, which is P-3's point from the other direction |

**This is the first Gate C round run from committed instruments rather than
from somebody's memory of the last one.** Round 8 attacked entries 14, 15, 17
and 20 with about seventy checks written by hand during that run and never
saved, so every round since has either re-written them or gone without them.
§6.1 priced re-writing them at half a day of Opus time, every round, forever.
Task 11.64 spent that half day once. **The whole of this round's automated
half is now one command that takes three minutes and forty-five seconds.**

  The comprehensive `find` for an escaped `.link` file could not fail:
  round 8's five traversal addresses cannot put a file anywhere it
  looks, so it had reported nothing for two rounds. Found by the
  broken-control harness on its first real run — the check was required

  the five that a control inside the instrument could not have caught,
  which is the argument for the harness sitting outside it.

Task 11.71 added the sixth address and a control that plants a `.link` outside the directory and requires the search to see it; **the check has since been watched going red** against a server with the sanitiser deleted. The result above stands — it is now evidence rather than an assumption |
| 23–26 | `verify_11_9_team_surface.py` (**105 checks**) and `verify_11_24_attribution.py` | Both **PASS** — invitations, redemption, membership and role mutation on the push path, and the role gradient across every Phase 11 endpoint |
| 27, 28 | `verify_11_49_server_reads.py` (**146 checks**) | **PASS** — the two reads, re-attacked in full |

### 21.3 Finding P-1, closed — and why 10.56's sweep could not have found it

`GET /projects/mine` had been attacked as a *route* at four gates and never as
a **read**. Task 11.49 recorded that on 2026-08-29 and deliberately stopped,
under §6's stopping rule. What it lacked, all now closed:

- **Nothing measured that a caller-supplied `user_id` is ignored.** Eleven
  places a caller could put one — query string, `GET` body, three headers, a
  cookie, an `On-Behalf-Of`, a repeat, an array shape, a `project_id` — now do,
  live, and a second live caller with a real second project proves the check
  can see a difference.
- **No document said which fields a row may carry.** §4.28 does now, including
  the reasoning for keeping `owner_user_id` (every caller of this route already
  holds it, through the `Projects` row the same session may pull) and an
  explicit list of what may never appear. Two checks keep it true: a doc-code
  mirror in plain `flutter test`, and a live assertion on a real response.
- **No `LIMIT`.** `maxListedProjects` (200), with a deterministic `ORDER BY` so
  a truncated page is not a different page each time. Watched refusing at 250
  seeded memberships.
- **No per-user rate limit**, while `/auth/sessions` got one under 10.56.
  `projectListPerUser`, 60 per 15 minutes, watched refusing on the 61st read,
  with a second signed-in caller proving they are not locked out by the first.
- **No `cache-control: no-store`**, which the sessions listing has sent since
  task 11.35.

**Why 10.56 missed all three bounds, and this is the part worth carrying
forward.** That task bounded *every field on every route*. `/projects/mine` has
no fields — no body, no query, no path segment. A sweep keyed on "what does
this route read from the caller" cannot see a route that reads nothing, and the
thing 10.56 was actually defending against — an unbounded read available to
anyone with a session — was present here the whole time. **The question to ask
of a route is "what does answering it cost, and who may ask", not only "what
does it parse".**

### 21.4 New findings — two, and neither meets the bar

**Lettered `Q-`.** `L-`, `M-`, `N-` and `P-` are the four preceding rounds. **Q-2 came out of the gate's own measurement rather than the server**, which is where five of the last nine rounds' most useful findings came from.

| ID | Finding | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Q-2** | **The server suite raced itself at startup and went red in the middle of this gate.** `closed_membership_disclosure_test.dart` failed with `23505 duplicate key value violates unique constraint "pg_default_acl_role_nsp_obj_index"` on a run that followed a green one with no source change between them. Two parallel test files both **insert** that `pg_default_acl` row on a fresh database; `_retryOnConcurrentCatalogUpdate` covered the *update* arm of exactly this race (`XX000 tuple concurrently updated`, and its comment even names `pg_default_acl`) and not the insert arm | **Fixed by this task, and registered because the fix is not the finding.** Criterion 4 is *"four suites green in one pass"*, and an intermittently red suite turns that into "green in the pass we happened to look at" — which is the same defect as a check that cannot fail, with the sign reversed. Task 10.69 fixed one instance of this class (a concurrent `CREATE ROLE` race in the same machinery); this is the class recurring on a different catalog with a different SQLSTATE. The retry is narrowed to `pg_default_acl` so it cannot silently re-run an application-level unique violation twenty times. **Re-verified by three consecutive green runs**, 724 passed, zero skips |
| **Q-1** | **The project router writes no audit rows at all.** The auth routes record a `rate_limit_tripped` event when `/auth/sessions`'s per-user limit fires; `project_routes.dart` has no audit hook, so **both** of its rate-limit refusals — `/projects/mine`'s, added this round, and invite redemption's, which predates it — are invisible to an operator. A flood is refused correctly and leaves no trace anybody can look at | **Accepted.** Below §4's bar: what it leaves undefended is an operator's *view* of a flood, not B1, B2 or B3 — the limit itself fires, the caller is told, and nobody else's access is affected. §15.0's reading of B4 is what settles it. **Measured every run** by probe 12, which prints the audit-row count rather than asserting it, so the day somebody wires the hook up the number changes in the output |
