## 22. Verdicts — round 9, the join surface (task 11.85, 2026-08-31)

### 22.0 Why there was a round 9 at all

**On 2026-08-30 this document said the NAU letter was the only thing left, and
that was true when it was written.** Task 11.81 then replaced the per-address
invitation routes with one shared join code and an owner's approval, and
inventory entries 23 and 24 went from `Hardened` back to `Unexamined` —
**not a bookkeeping regression, the correct entry.** The verdict was earned
against routes that no longer exist, and *a verdict does not transfer to a
replacement because it kept the row number.* Entry 29 was new and had never
been attacked. So the server surface was genuinely less attacked on 2026-08-31
than it had been the week before, and §6's criterion 1 said so — after its
wording was corrected, because as written it counted `Unexamined` as "has a
verdict" and would have reported **Met** over the newest routes on this server,
the ones that grant membership.

### 22.1 The half nobody costed: four instruments speaking a dead protocol

The first push after task 11.83 turned the gate-instruments workflow red, and
every failure read the same — `404` on `POST /projects/<id>/invites`.
`verify_c2_existence_oracle`, `verify_11_9_team_surface`,
`verify_11_24_attribution` and `verify_11_49_server_reads` **all built their
fixtures by inviting somebody.**

**None of the four was a finding.** They are the class named *the attack corpus
cannot reach the check*: an instrument that can no longer get to the thing it
tests, which is not the same as a broken check and not the same as a finding.
Task 11.81's estimate counted twenty *test files* and got that right; the gate
instruments are Python under `scripts/` and were not in the count.

**The repair put the flow in one place instead of four.** `gate_wire.py` now
carries `enable_joining`, `request_to_join` and `join_by_code`, and each of the
four calls them. Four copies of "invite, redeem" is what made this a four-file
repair rather than a one-file one — task 10.66's standing rule, applied to the
instruments themselves.

**What it cost, measured rather than guessed.** The invitation flow was two
round trips per member (issue, redeem). The join-code flow is also two
(request, approve) plus **one per project** to switch joining on, which mints
and returns the code in the same response — so the fixture is one call per
project longer and **no** calls per member longer. `verify_11_9_team_surface.py`
runs 230 scored checks in **2.5 seconds** against a warm stack. What is
genuinely more expensive is on the server: approval writes a membership row and
mints the new member's `Users` row in one transaction, where redemption only
consumed a code.

**The one real constraint the new flow puts on an instrument** is the per-user
rate limit measured below: an account may create ten join requests per fifteen
minutes, so a probe that needs more than that needs more accounts, and one
probe in this file had to be re-pointed at a different fixture person for
exactly that reason. That is written into the file where it bites.

### 22.2 What was run

| Instrument | Checks | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `verify_11_9_team_surface.py` — entries 21–26, with 23 and 24 rewritten wholesale | 230 | clean; 2 admitted, both registered (R-1) |
| `verify_11_49_server_reads.py` — entries 27–28, plus new probe 13 for entry 29 | 180 | clean; 1 admitted, registered (R-2) |
| `verify_c2_existence_oracle.py` | — | clean (fixture repair only) |
| `verify_11_24_attribution.py` | — | clean (fixture repair only) |
| `test/features/more/join_request_name_rendering_test.dart` | 9 | green |
| `verify_11_85_broken_control.py` — three deliberately broken servers | 35 required flips | all flipped |

### 22.3 Watched to fail — task 10.66's standing criterion

`scripts/verify_11_85_broken_control.py` builds three servers from a throwaway
git worktree, each with a named control removed, and requires the round-9
probes to notice. **35 of 35 required attacks flipped from `refused` to
`ADMITTED`**, and the same instruments came back clean against the real server
in the same run.

| Variant | What was removed | Required flips |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `owner` | `_requireOwner` stops requiring ownership | 17 of 17 |
| `grant` | the owner's role choice is ignored, the deciding `UPDATE` stops requiring the request to be undecided, `idx_memberships_one_open` stops being unique, and the person-name validator stops refusing bidirectional overrides | 12 of 12 |
| `mine` | `myRequests` stops scoping to the caller and returns `project_id` on every decision | 6 of 6 |

**Two things the harness found that the probes would not have.**

1. **The `decided_at IS NULL` clause is not what refuses a second approval.**
   With only that clause removed, approving an already-approved request was
   still refused — by `idx_memberships_one_open`, which will not admit a second
   open membership for the same person. The clause is belt-and-braces and the
   database constraint is load-bearing. Both are in the variant now, and
   knowing which one holds is worth more than the flip.

2. **Three of entry 29's ten redirection probes were blind, and this caught
   them.** They took their reference from `mine_of(prober)` with no injection
   and compared each injected read against it — so against a server whose query
   is `WHERE (user_id = $1 OR TRUE)` the *baseline* is also everybody's rows,
   the comparison holds, and all ten report `refused` against a route with no
   scoping at all. **A check whose reference comes from the thing under test is
   not a check.** The reference is now the request id the fixture created.

**And one in the widget test, caught the same way.** The first draft of
`join_request_name_rendering_test.dart` asserted "the claim renders as two
lines". It stayed green against a build with `U+2028` stripped out of the tile,
because the attack string was long enough to wrap onto two lines by itself. It
now measures the **offset** the break falls at, from the tile's own render
object, with an in-test control — the same name written with a space, which
must not break. Three cases go red when the separator is stripped; the two
controls stay green.

### 22.4 New findings — two, and neither meets the bar

**R-1 is closed** (task 11.89, 2026-09-01); R-2 remains open and is registered.

**Lettered `R-`.** `L-` through `Q-` are the six preceding rounds.

| ID | Finding | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **R-1** | **A claimed name on a join request may carry a hard line break.** `RowValidator.isWellFormedPersonName` refuses two character classes — C0/C1 controls, and the bidirectional overrides, marks and isolates — and neither contains `U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR` or `U+2029 PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR`, which the text engine treats as hard breaks. So a stranger asking to join chooses what the **second line** of the owner's pending tile says, and can put an address-shaped string there. Measured live (16 name attacks, 14 refused, these 2 accepted) and measured on screen: the break lands exactly where the requester put it | **CLOSED 2026-09-01 by task 11.89** (commit `ceca8c7`). Not by adding two characters — **the rule is now an allowlist.** `isWellFormedPersonName` states what a name may *contain*: letters, combining marks, decimal digits, dash punctuation and space separators (`\p{L}\p{M}\p{Nd}\p{Pd}\p{Zs}`), plus `.` `,` the two apostrophes, the two middle dots, and `U+200C`/`U+200D`, which several Persian and Indic names need. **The cut that closes this finding is Unicode's own:** a space is `Zs`, and a line or paragraph separator is `Zl`/`Zp` — so `U+2028` and `U+2029` are refused as a class rather than as two instances, along with every other character nobody had thought of. The finding's own lesson is why: the denylist it defeated was written three days earlier, deliberately, by somebody thinking about exactly this attack. **Verified live against the real server** — probe 9's name attacks now stand at 24 of 24 refused, the two baseline entries are deleted, and eleven positive controls (Hebrew, Arabic, a Japanese name with `U+3000`, a katakana middle dot, a pasted no-break space, a Persian `U+200C`, Vietnamese combining marks) are accepted and stored byte-exact. **Verified on screen**: `join_request_name_rendering_test.dart` no longer asserts the defect — it asserts the property, that no name the validator accepts can put a line break on the approval tile, measured from the render object and with an in-test control proving the measurement can still see one. **The tile's layout was not touched**, deliberately: the layout is why this stayed below the bar, and making it the fix would let the next layout change reopen the finding silently. **What it costs, stated rather than discovered:** this rule governs the synced columns `Users.first_name`/`last_name`, so a row that was legal when written can now be refused. Measured in both directions by `test/data/sync/name_rule_widened_existing_rows_test.dart` — your own row is held, reported and fixable by you; a colleague's is dropped, recorded, reported, and not fixable by you until they correct it, at which point it arrives on its own |
| **R-2** | **A refused requester keeps a live read on the project's current name, indefinitely.** `JoinService.myRequests` joins the **live** `Projects` row for its `project_name`, and nothing prunes a decided request — so somebody the owner rejected, or whose request a rotation cleared, goes on reading whatever the project is called from then on. Watched changing from one name to another after a rename | **Registered — below §4's bar.** B2 is *"disclosure of animal coordinates or observer identity"*; a project's name is neither, and the requester already learned the name at the moment they asked, which entry 24 records as inherent to the design. What is not inherent is that the read stays *live* and the row never goes. **Two halves, and they have different owners.** The durability half is N-3's shape and belongs to **task 11.79**, which builds the retention bound — *that task's scope needs to include `project_join_requests`, and today it does not say so.* The live-join half is a design choice (snapshot the name at request time, or prune) and needs Michael's decision. A deleted project **does** drop out, which is the one place this route closes behind itself |

### 22.4.1 R-3 — the adversarial pass reported a blocking finding that three re-runs could not reproduce

**This one is about an instrument, not about the server, and it is the reason
the round did not end when the gate run went red.**

`gate_c_adversarial_pass.py`'s check `Cg` — a real foreign project and a
fictional one are not distinguishable by timing — **failed inside the full
`gate_smoke_test.sh` run** on 2026-08-31, reporting `real-minus-fictional
+0.125 ms, positive in 7/7 trials`. An unbaselined adversarial failure is a
Gate C blocker under criterion 4, so it had to be resolved rather than
re-run-until-green.

**Three consecutive runs of the same instrument, on the same host, with
nothing else running, all HELD**: `+0.030 ms` positive in 4/7, `-0.036 ms`
positive in 2/7, `+0.028 ms` positive in 5/7. The sign flips and the magnitude
is the noise floor. **The failing run was concurrent with the gate stack's own
seventeen other instruments on a laptop**; task 11.72 measured the real
residual at **+5.0 µs** on a quiet Linux runner, and 125 µs is twenty-five
times that.

**So the finding is against the check, not the server.** `Cg` already carries a
drift guard — if the fictional-versus-fictional null has a *stable* sign (0/7
or 7/7) it declares the run INCONCLUSIVE rather than passing or failing,
because a host whose drift dominates cannot resolve the effect. On the failing
run the null landed at 5/7, so the guard did not fire, and a load-driven bias
that pushed *both* comparisons positive was scored as a real one-sided effect.
**The guard tests the null's sign and not its magnitude**, and a bias smaller
than "always positive" but far larger than the effect passes straight through
it.

**Disposition: scheduled, and it needs a task number.** It is below §4's bar —
it produces a false *blocker*, not a missed one, so nothing is left undefended.
But criterion 4 is *"the adversarial pass matches its recorded baseline
exactly"*, and a check that reports a blocking finding when the machine is busy
makes that criterion mean "on a quiet machine", which nobody wrote down. The
obvious repair is to compare the between-pair difference against the **measured
null distribution** rather than against zero — the null is already collected
every run and is currently used only for its sign. Recorded in Phase 11's
Discovered Scope.

**CLOSED 2026-09-06 by task 11.90.** The rule now compares the effect against
**the resolution the run itself demonstrated**, which is `max(|null|)` — the
largest gap that run opened between two ids that are identical in truth. `Cg`
fails only when the between-pair sign is unanimous **and** the effect is larger
than that; a stable sign at a magnitude the run cannot resolve is now
INCONCLUSIVE, which is what R-3's own numbers produce. The old guard's case (a
null whose sign never changes) is kept rather than replaced — it is a second,
independent symptom of a drift-dominated host.

**It is not a wider tolerance, and that is the claim most worth attacking.**
The threshold is not a constant anybody chose; it is a measurement the run
makes at the same moment, on the same host, through the same socket, with the
same code. Load inflates the null, so it inflates the bar — but it inflates the
effect too, and a real oracle is compared against the null rather than against
zero, so it stays red however loaded the machine. That case is measured rather
than argued: self-test case 2 holds a 40 ms one-sided effect FAILED against a
null five hundred times larger than the quiet one.

**Where the rule lives, and why it is not in the instrument.** The whole
decision is `scripts/gate_timing_guard.py`, which takes two lists of numbers and
returns a verdict, so it can be broken on purpose in about a second instead of
needing a live stack, three project ids and a minute of requests.
`python3 scripts/gate_timing_guard.py --selftest` runs six cases including R-3's
own shape, and asserts in the same breath that **the rule it replaces called
that shape a finding** — if that assertion ever stops holding, the self-test has
stopped demonstrating the defect it was written for. `gate_smoke_test.sh` runs
it on every gate, beside the other static checks. **A guard nobody can afford to
break is a guard nobody has broken**, which is task 11.172's rule and the reason
this is a separate file rather than eight lines inside the pass.

**Watched firing on a live loaded stack, 2026-09-06, through all three of its
doors** — not only in the self-test. The machine was loaded deliberately: 24 to
48 CPU spinners on a 14-core laptop, load average above 200, and up to eight
copies of the adversarial pass sharing one stack, which is R-3's own condition.

- *The door the repair adds*, watched on real measurements: **effect 2.439 ms
  with the sign the same in every trial, against a resolution of 4.548 ms** →
  *"the effect has a stable sign but is no larger than the gap this run opened
  between two identical ids."* **The rule this task replaced would have reported
  that run as a Gate C blocker** — its null's sign was 1 of 3, not unanimous, so
  the old guard would have stayed quiet exactly as it did on 2026-08-31.
- *The old guard's door, kept*: null positive in 0 of 7, resolution 8.501 ms →
  *"the null's own sign never changed."*
- *The third door*: effect 0.062 ms against a 0.060 ms resolution with the signs
  disagreeing → *"nothing here is a measurement."*

Every INCONCLUSIVE run exited 0 with its baseline intact: a skipped `Cg` counts
in the check total, so an inconclusive run is not silently a lost check.

**Two things about that evidence, stated rather than smoothed over.** The
magnitude door needs the effect's sign to be unanimous, which at the shipped
seven trials is 1 in 64 — **it did not occur once in 46 loaded runs**, where the
signs ran 1/7 to 6/7 centered near 4. It was reached by running the same
instrument against the same live stack from a throwaway copy with the trial
count cut to three, so unanimity is 1 in 4 instead. **The measurements are real
and the load is real; only the number of trials was changed, and the copy was
deleted.** And the aside is worth keeping: across those 46 runs a unanimous sign
turned up *less* often than independent coin flips would give, which is why three
quiet re-runs could not reproduce R-3 and why its 7-of-7 was such an outlier.

**And the question task 11.88 left open is answered: `Cg` gets no baseline
entry.** A baseline has exactly two modes — still admitted, or now refused and
therefore a regression — and `Cg`'s signal is stably true in neither, which is
the standing rule 11.88 wrote after making the opposite mistake. With the guard
sound, the pressure that would have argued for one is gone: the load case that
produced R-3 is now INCONCLUSIVE rather than a failure. A `Cg` failure from here
means a one-sided effect **larger than the run's own resolution**, which at a
socket is milliseconds — three orders of magnitude above §4.13's accepted 5 µs
residual — and that is a finding to read rather than to pre-accept. The
magnitude enforcement for the residual itself stays where it can actually be
bounded: `server/test/security/authorization_timing_test.dart`, which times the
function directly, holds it under 25 µs, and runs on every commit.

### 22.5 What was measured rather than found

Neither of these is a finding. Both were assumptions until this round.

- **The join-request rate limit is 10 per account per 15 minutes**, watched
  refusing on the eleventh attempt — **in 39 milliseconds of wall time.** It
  bounds the *count* per account, not the rate: there is no delay between
  attempts and no backoff, so an attacker's cost is one account per ten
  guesses. Against 40 bits of code entropy that is a comfortable bound on
  guessing; it is a weak one on nuisance, and both halves are now numbers
  rather than adjectives. The bucket is the caller's own — an exhausted account
  did not lock out a fresh one, and could not slip a *real* code past its own
  limit.
- **Nothing prunes decided join requests.** Six rejections on a fresh project
  left six rows. The only bound anywhere is the 200-row cap on what the two
  list routes *return*, which bounds the response and not the table.
- **Q-1 is narrower than when it was written, and the instrument said so
  rather than repeating it.** The note in probe 12 used to say the project
  router *"has no audit hook at all"*. Task 11.81 gave it one — it records
  seven join events. What is still true is that **no route in that router
  audits a rate-limit refusal**, so a flood is still invisible to an operator.
  The instrument's own text is corrected, because a check that reports a
  false reason is a check nobody can act on.

### 22.6 What holds, re-verified rather than assumed

- **Entry 29's `project_id` argument survives the attempt to break it.** On
  all four decision states the field set is exactly the six the design names;
  `project_id` appears on the approved request and on none of the others; and
  that requester reads the same id from `GET /projects/mine`, while the
  rejected one's directory names nothing. The planning session's argument was
  attacked, not inherited.
- **There is no such thing as a leaked owner code.** A join request carrying
  `role`, `project_id` and `user_id` was accepted and none of them reached
  anything: the owner's chosen role is the role that landed.
- **A fabricated project id and a forbidden real one answer byte-identically**
  on all seven owner-only routes, and every unusable code draws one refusal.
- **The owner-only route set is derived from the router source and its count
  asserted**, so a route added later is attacked or the instrument goes red.
  That is the specific defect that let entry 23 keep a verdict earned against
  routes which had been deleted.

### 22.7 The NAU review — the item ten gates have not closed

`CLAUDE_DOCS/NAU_infosec_review_request.md` is written, current, and marked
cleared to send. The recipient address is still blank. With criterion 1
re-established, **it is once again the only thing between this project and a
deployed server** — and the round that had to be run to say that is the reason
the sentence should be read with the date attached.
